The only human genetic study of URAD (PMID: 37670727) links a missense variant (rs9579139) to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma risk, not to cardiac phenotypes. PMID: 38936684 discusses URAD transcripts within the purine catabolism pathway and notes that hyperuricemia is associated with cardiovascular disease, providing only a speculative, indirect biological rationale rather than variant-level evidence. The remaining papers concern bacterial uric acid degradation (PMID: 38814072) and Arabidopsis Urad domain enzymology (PMID: 20511299), which are non-human and irrelevant to heart failure. Therefore the relationship is best characterized as Novel, with some weight to Hypothesized given the tenuous urate–cardiovascular pathway link.

None of the provided articles address rheumatic heart disease, which is an autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal infection; no human genetic association or clinical study links DHTKD1 variants to rheumatic valvular disease. DHTKD1 evidence overwhelmingly concerns 2-aminoadipic/2-oxoadipic aciduria, Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2Q, ALS-like phenotypes, and eosinophilic esophagitis (PMIDs 23141293, 23141294, 26141459, 35052424, 29669943). The only cardiac-adjacent items are a mouse transgenic CryAB(R120G) cardiomyopathy transcriptomic screen listing DHTKD1 as a hub gene (PMID 40885924) and a knockout cell study proposing DHTKD1-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction in cardiometabolic disease (PMID 34484123); both are non-human/in vitro and unrelated to rheumatic pathology. These give only a very weak, indirect biological rationale, so a small share of probability goes to Hypothesized, with the bulk to Novel.

None of the provided articles addresses atrial fibrillation or any cardiac electrophysiological phenotype. The DGKH literature here concerns bipolar disorder genetics (GWAS and replication attempts), lithium response, ADHD, pheochromocytoma and oral cancer expression, lung cancer biology, and enzymology/splice variants of diacylglycerol kinase eta. No human variant study, animal model, or mechanistic pathway link to atrial arrhythmia is presented. There is therefore no evidentiary basis—genetic, functional, or biological—connecting DGKH to atrial fibrillation, making "Novel" the appropriate designation.

phenotype: Benign and in situ cervical and uterine neoplasms
literature_justification: None of the provided articles addresses benign or in situ cervical/uterine neoplasms in any way. The vast majority describe ARP6/ACTR6 as a SWR1/SRCAP chromatin-remodeling subunit mediating H2A.Z deposition in yeast, Arabidopsis, rice, chicken and Drosophila, with phenotypes in flowering, root growth, meiosis, neurogenesis and transposon control—none human disease. The only human genetic study (PMID 42472903) reports a rare ACTR6 variant associated with metabolic syndrome, an unrelated cardiometabolic phenotype, not a recognized precursor of uterine or cervical neoplasia. A generic biological plausibility exists because chromatin remodeling and H2A.Z deposition influence proliferation, nucleolar/rDNA transcription and genome stability (PMIDs 26164235, 22573822), which gives a small residual weight to "Hypothesized," but there is no direct link to the phenotype. Accordingly, the relationship is best classified as Novel.

None of the provided articles report any association between JPH4 variants or expression and triglyceride levels or lipid traits. The available literature covers JPH4 in cirrhosis susceptibility (TWAS), plasma proteome Mendelian randomization for urticaria, junctophilin biology in excitable cells (muscle/neurons, Drosophila models), and neurodegenerative/cardiomyopathy phenotypes — none of which measure or mechanistically implicate triglyceride metabolism. The liver-related cirrhosis TWAS (PMID 35646080) is the only tangential hepatic link, which could weakly motivate a hypothesized metabolic connection, but it does not address lipids and provides no logical basis for triglyceride regulation. No human genetic variant evidence for triglycerides exists here, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded.

None of the provided articles addresses red cell distribution width, erythropoiesis, anemia, or any hematological trait. UBR2 literature here concerns N-end rule ubiquitin ligase biology, cancer-induced muscle wasting, spermatogenesis/azoospermia, primary ovarian insufficiency, yeast proteostasis, and one exome-based gene-burden analysis for coronary artery disease (PMID 34385509) — none of which is a recognized precursor or mechanism for RDW. Human genetic studies exist for UBR2 (male infertility, POI, CAD), but they involve entirely unrelated phenotypes, so they do not support Existing status for RDW. A small residual probability is left for Hypothesized given UBR2's broad role in ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated protein quality control, which could conceivably touch erythrocyte homeostasis, but no such link is documented in these papers.

None of the provided articles addresses chronic lymphocytic (lymphoid) leukemia at all. The MAPK8IP1/IB1/JIP-1 literature here concerns type 2 diabetes and β-cell physiology, Alzheimer's disease and APP/LRP8 interactions, Parkinson's disease models, excitotoxicity, keratoconus, seasonality, and glioma prognostic signatures. The only tangential cancer-relevant biology is JIP-1 scaffolding of the JNK pathway with Bcl-2/Bcl-XL phosphorylation in apoptosis (PMID 10913135) and an autophagy-related glioma signature (PMID 33194668), neither of which involves CLL or any lymphoid malignancy. There are no human genetic variant studies linking MAPK8IP1 to CLL or to a recognized CLL precursor (e.g., MBL). Therefore the relationship is essentially novel, with only a weak generic apoptosis-pathway rationale supporting a small hypothesized allocation.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: All provided articles concern MAX (MYC-associated factor X) in the context of tumor predisposition—pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma, pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, MEN5—or biophysical/structural studies of the MYC-MAX heterodimer and DNA binding. None report any anthropometric, adiposity, or fat-distribution phenotype, and no GWAS or association study of waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI is present. The only tenuous biological link is that the MYC/MAX network regulates metabolism and proliferation in neoplastic cells (PMID 40279415), which is a mouse/cell-line result and only remotely relevant to body fat distribution. Therefore the evidence supports "Novel," with a small allocation to "Hypothesized" for the generic metabolic role of the MYC network.

No articles were provided, so there is no literature evidence of any kind linking SLC25A52 variants to female infertility. SLC25A52 (MCART2) is an orphan mitochondrial carrier family member with little characterized function, and no human genetic studies, probands, or families are cited. A small allowance is retained for "Hypothesized" because mitochondrial carrier proteins are broadly relevant to oocyte energy metabolism and some SLC25 members are germline-enriched, which could provide a biological rationale in unseen literature. With no supporting citations at all, "Novel" is the most appropriate classification.

Neither article addresses asthma. One reports a ZNF782 variant (p.Arg321His) segregating in a family with intracranial aneurysms, a phenotype unrelated to asthma, and the variant showed no association in a larger cohort. The other is a C. elegans study of praziquantel susceptibility implicating znf-782 among candidate genes, which is non-human and unrelated to asthma. There is no expression, pathway, or mechanistic evidence linking ZNF782 to airway inflammation or asthma. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

None of the provided articles mention varicose veins or any venous/vascular phenotype. ZIC4 literature is dominated by cerebellar development, Dandy-Walker malformation (via contiguous ZIC1;ZIC4 deletions), craniosynostosis (ZIC1), paraneoplastic cerebellar antibodies, gliomas/meningiomas, and neuroimaging genomics. Some peripheral cardiovascular-adjacent findings exist (a SNP near ZIC4 associated with VO2max training response), but this concerns cardiorespiratory fitness, not varicose veins, and provides no mechanistic link to venous valve or vein wall biology. There is therefore no direct or indirect evidence connecting ZIC4 variation or biology to varicose veins.

None of the provided articles measure C-reactive protein or report any human genetic variant in MICU2 associated with CRP levels or inflammation biomarkers. The literature is entirely focused on MICU2 as a regulatory subunit of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter, with human variant evidence linked only to a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID 29053821) and mouse work linking Micu2 loss to cardiovascular pathology. The only tangential biological link is the Micu2-/- mouse aorta showing increased expression of reactive oxygen species and inflammation-related genes (PMID 29073106), which offers a weak, indirect mechanistic rationale for an inflammatory readout such as CRP, and this is animal rather than human evidence. Therefore the relationship is best judged as Novel, with some weight given to Hypothesized on the basis of mitochondrial calcium–driven inflammatory signaling.

None of the provided articles addresses rheumatic heart disease in any form. The retrieved literature concerns ARHGEF28/RGNEF in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, age-related hearing loss (note the acronym "ARHL"/"ARHI", which is a homonym-like confusion with rheumatic heart disease abbreviations), cancers (thyroid, ovarian, rectal, canine oral), synucleinopathies, pig fetal mummification, and focal adhesion/RhoA signaling biology. There is no human genetic association, expression, or mechanistic evidence linking ARHGEF28 to rheumatic heart disease, valvular carditis, or group A streptococcal autoimmunity. The gene's known roles in Rho GTPase signaling and cytoskeletal regulation are generic and do not provide a specific biological rationale for rheumatic heart disease, so only minimal weight is given to "Hypothesized".

None of the provided articles addresses chronic obstructive pulmonary disease at all. UBR3 associations reported here concern cardiometabolic traits/BMI and type 2 diabetes (PMIDs 39210047, 41073786, 41651857), IgA nephropathy (37958966), intracranial aneurysm (30121816), gut microbiome (27694960), neurodevelopmental phenotypes (33994118, 32344861), intervertebral disc degeneration (35332432), and auditory myosin biology in Drosophila/mammals (27331610). No genetic variant, expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence connects UBR3 to airway obstruction, emphysema, or lung function. There is not even a plausible mechanistic bridge stated in these abstracts, so a Novel classification is strongly favored, with a small allowance for indirect inflammation-related biology (DUSP1/p38) that could be argued as loosely relevant.

None of the provided articles measure or mention mean corpuscular volume or any erythrocyte index. The human genetic studies involving EXOC1 concern cervical cancer susceptibility (rs13117307), Tourette syndrome de novo variants, and type 2 diabetes interaction loci—none of which are precursors or mechanisms of MCV. The only hematologic link is a whole-exome pilot study of primary platelet secretion defects that listed EXOC1 among candidate genes (PMID 30819905), which concerns platelet granule secretion rather than red cell volume, providing at best weak, indirect biological plausibility via exocyst-mediated vesicle trafficking (also supported by yeast/mouse exocyst function studies). Therefore the evidence base here supports "Novel" with a modest allowance for a hypothesized biological rationale, and no basis for Established.

None of the provided articles report any human genetic variant in USO1 associated with stature. The USO1 literature here is entirely cell-biological — ER-to-Golgi vesicle tethering in yeast, Aspergillus, Toxoplasma and mammalian cells, plus roles in liver cancer, B-ALL and MDS (PMIDs 34293111, 34162911, 34058203, 8603910, 37249218). The "height" papers are unrelated: plant/algal phytoremediation studies measuring plant height, a school-children drinking-water nutrition study, and a rodent overfeeding study, with no USO1 involvement. There are thus only incidental co-mentions arising from the word "height," giving no logical or mechanistic basis for a USO1–human height association. A small residual probability is assigned to Hypothesized since secretory-pathway/Golgi trafficking genes could conceivably influence growth, but no such evidence is presented.

None of the provided articles report any association between ANKRD12 variants and migraine or headache phenotypes. The ANKRD12 findings concern rare coding variant associations with sleep-related traits, cognitive function, neuroticism, depressive symptoms, alcohol consumption, and inflammatory airway disease (asthma/COPD), none of which is an established migraine precursor or subtype. There is only weak indirect plausibility from ANKRD12's expression in central nervous system neurons and its links to neuropsychiatric traits, which could support a speculative biological hypothesis but not a genetic association. No probands or families with migraine carrying ANKRD12 variants are described, so Established is excluded, and Existing is essentially unsupported.

None of the provided articles measure or discuss serum/plasma albumin concentration. The HNRNPA1 literature here concerns neuromuscular and neurodegenerative phenotypes (ALS, distal myopathy, multisystem proteinopathy, inclusion body myopathy, multiple sclerosis), RNA-binding/stress granule biology, cancer, and one mouse model of congenital heart defects. There is no genetic association study, GWAS, or quantitative biochemical trait analysis linking HNRNPA1 variants to albumin levels, and no plausible direct hepatic/albumin-synthesis mechanism is articulated in these abstracts. A small residual probability is assigned to "Hypothesized" because hnRNPA1 is a ubiquitous regulator of mRNA splicing/stability that could conceivably affect hepatic gene expression, but this is speculative and not supported by any cited work.

No articles were provided linking ENSG00000144785 to Height, so there is no citable human genetic evidence (no variants in probands, families, or cohorts) and no functional or animal-model data supporting a biological role in skeletal growth or stature. Without at least one credible human study, the "Established" and "Existing" categories cannot be supported. A small probability is retained for "Existing"/"Hypothesized" because height is extremely polygenic and large GWAS meta-analyses implicate thousands of loci, so an association could exist in literature not retrieved here. On the available evidence, the relationship is best described as Novel.

None of the provided articles address rheumatic heart disease, which is an acquired, post-streptococcal autoimmune valvular disease rather than a sarcomeric genetic disorder. All papers concern TTN truncating/missense variants in dilated cardiomyopathy, peripartum and chemotherapy-related cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, and skeletal titinopathies. There is no study reporting TTN variants in rheumatic fever/rheumatic valve disease cohorts, and no precursor or mechanistic link (e.g., streptococcal immunity, valve development) is described. A small residual probability for "hypothesized" reflects only the generic relevance of titin to myocardial remodeling and heart failure that can complicate rheumatic valve disease, which is incidental rather than causal.

Most retrieved articles use "APC" as the homonym for activated protein C (a plasma serine protease in sepsis/pancreatitis therapy: PMIDs 15987389, 18008033, 17127435, 16943720, 16520928, 16420659, 10230242) and must be dismissed as irrelevant to the adenomatous polyposis coli gene. The genuine APC-gene papers concern familial adenomatous polyposis and pancreatic adenocarcinoma (8950667, 9364657, 19150414, 8111410), where pancreatitis is mentioned only as a separate risk factor or differential diagnosis, not as an APC-variant phenotype; the FAP/ERCP case report (38826909) describes procedure-related pancreatitis prophylaxis, not a genetic cause. The strongest mechanistic link is the mouse pancreas-specific β-catenin (Wnt/APC pathway) deletion causing perinatal edematous pancreatitis (16169491), which is animal data and thus supports "Hypothesized" only. The phenome-wide hereditary cancer gene study (35446370) could conceivably report non-cancer disease associations in humans, leaving some probability for "Existing," but no cited result specifically links APC variants to pancreatitis in independent probands, so "Established" is essentially excluded.

None of the provided articles report valvular phenotypes (mitral/aortic valve prolapse, regurgitation, stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve) in association with TTN variants. The evidence base here is uniformly about dilated cardiomyopathy (PMIDs 22335739, 25589632, 27869827, 33996946), heart failure (40195560), atrial fibrillation (30535219, 39453294), and skeletal titinopathies (32778822, 33458580, 39198997). At best, one could argue biological plausibility because titin truncations cause ventricular dilation and annular remodeling that may produce secondary functional mitral regurgitation, which supports a modest Hypothesized weight, but no article measures or reports valvular disease. No human study in this set identifies TTN variants in probands or families with non-rheumatic valvular heart disease, so Established is effectively excluded and Existing is unsupported.

All FBN1 articles concern Marfan syndrome and related fibrillinopathies (ectopia lentis, acromelic dysplasias, Weill-Marchesani-like syndrome, familial pneumothorax, aortic dissection), with no genetic study linking FBN1 variants to rheumatic heart disease. The rheumatic heart disease papers (screening, epidemiology, acute rheumatic fever management) do not mention FBN1 at all, making the co-mention incidental. The only bridging article is a single case report of a Marfan patient who coincidentally had rheumatic mitral stenosis (PMID 24653594), explicitly noted as unique and post-streptococcal in origin, which is coincidence rather than evidence of causality. A weak hypothetical link could be argued because FBN1 affects mitral valve structure (prolapse, regurgitation), which is a valvular phenotype but mechanistically distinct from autoimmune rheumatic valvulopathy. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for a hypothesized valvular-connective-tissue rationale.

None of the provided articles report serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) measurements in relation to PKD1 genotype; all human genetic studies focus on renal outcomes (eGFR, kidney volume, ESRD age) in ADPKD cohorts (PMIDs 23431072, 26453610, 31740684, 24611717, 32457805). A biological rationale exists because PKD1 mutations cause polycystic liver disease and hepatic cystic involvement, which can perturb liver biochemistry (PMIDs 15701294, 15382167), and a humanized Pkd1RC/RC mouse base-editing study reported "improved liver function" — but this is animal, not human, evidence (PMID 41381416). Therefore the strongest defensible category is Hypothesized, with some probability for Existing given the well-recognized hepatic phenotype in human PKD1 carriers, and a residual chance the co-mention is purely incidental. No two human studies demonstrate PKD1 variants associated with AST levels, so Established is essentially excluded.

No human genetic study in the list links POLB variants to height or stature; human POLB work concerns cancer, lupus, bladder cancer risk, and Alzheimer's disease. The strongest relevant evidence is animal-based: the knock-in PolbL301R/V303R mouse is viable and fertile "yet small in stature" (PMID 38619421), suggesting a plausible organismal role for Pol β in body size/growth. Zebrafish work shows polb transcript changes accompanying reduced body length after nanoplastic exposure (PMID 36119974), but this is a nonspecific toxicological effect rather than variant-driven evidence. Because the supporting data are murine/zebrafish and mechanistic rather than human genetic, Hypothesized is the most appropriate category, with residual probability on Novel given the weak and indirect nature of the growth phenotype.

Nearly all retrieved articles concern the plant transcription factor ICE1 (INDUCER OF CBF EXPRESSION 1) in Arabidopsis, tomato, bamboo, and conifers, which is a homonymous acronym unrelated to the human ICE1 (interactor of little elongation complex ELL subunit 1) gene; the only "height" mention is incidental (Cryptomeria fortunei tree height, PMID 33744519). The two genuinely human studies involving ICE1 concern heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (PMID 29934777) and parent-of-origin × environment effects in cleft palate (PMID 28898263), neither of which addresses stature or any recognized precursor of human height. No human variant association, expression, or animal-model evidence linking ICE1 to skeletal growth or body height is present in this literature set. Therefore the relationship is best characterized as Novel, with only a small allowance for indirect biological plausibility.

No human study in this set reports APOB variants associated with height; height appears only as an anthropometric covariate or matching variable in lipid/hypercholesterolemia studies (e.g., PMIDs 7749818, 7918304, 8449482, 37105291). The large human sequencing studies (PMIDs 37072623, 38160284) report APOB associations with LDL/apoB levels and separately report height loci in other genes (ADAMTS17, ACAN, NPR2, PCSK5), providing no APOB–height link. The polygenic expressivity paper (PMID 31653860) uses height PGS for sex-chromosome aneuploidies and cholesterol PGS for APOB-related FH/FHBL, again keeping the two phenotypes separate. The only supportive evidence is a caprine GWAS (PMID 36292658) in which APOB fell within regions associated with withers height, rump height, and body length — animal, not human, evidence, which caps the assessment at Hypothesized. Remaining probability reflects the small chance that unlisted human data support a weak association.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: None of the provided articles report human genetic association studies of MIB1 variants with waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI or any adiposity/fat-distribution trait. The literature set is dominated by MIB1's role as a Notch-pathway E3 ubiquitin ligase in cardiac development (PMID 36325906), aortic disease (PMID 35052463), cancer biology (PMIDs 38252226, 40513658, 37546549, 30044990), and developmental models in zebrafish, Drosophila, and mouse (PMIDs 19005681, 37974242, 30093553) — none measure body-fat distribution. The only tangential adiposity-adjacent item is a duck genome selection-signal study in which MIB1 appears among growth/development loci in a breed noted for low subcutaneous fat (PMID 37121157); this is non-human, indirect, and gene-list based, so it supports at most a weak "Hypothesized" rationale via Notch signaling in adipogenesis/mesoderm development. No human proband, family, or cohort evidence exists here, precluding Existing or Established.

No article reports human genetic variants in NDUFB8 associated with aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels. The only abstract mentioning AST (PMID 33899910) is a baboon maternal nutrient reduction study where elevated maternal plasma AST and increased fetal cardiac NDUFB8 transcripts are co-reported incidentally, with no genetic variant analysis and in a non-human primate. PMID 29429571 establishes biallelic NDUFB8 variants as causing Leigh-like complex I deficiency in two probands, a mitochondrial disease that can plausibly involve hepatic/multisystem dysfunction and transaminase elevation, but AST is not measured or reported as an outcome. Other papers (35220898, 32669663, 41354732) address NDUFB8 as a generic OXPHOS marker in mouse or cell models, providing only indirect biological plausibility. Therefore the evidence sits between an incidental co-mention (Novel) and a weak mechanistic/biological rationale (Hypothesized), with insufficient support for Existing or Established.

None of the provided articles report APC variants in patients with peptic ulcer disease; the human APC literature here is entirely about familial adenomatous polyposis, colorectal adenomas/cancer, hepatoblastoma, ovarian cancer and supernumerary teeth (PMIDs 37800450, 41801175, 33664379, 31383941, 36901686). The only mention of "peptic ulcer" comes from an SGK1 review (PMID 20541034) where peptic ulcer is listed among SGK1-related pathologies and APC appears only in a separate mouse intestinal tumour context — an incidental co-mention, not evidence. The strongest biologically adjacent data are murine: Apc(Min/+) mice develop gastritis, gastric atrophy, intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia (PMID 31810128), which touches gastric mucosal injury but is animal-based and concerns precancerous lesions rather than peptic ulceration, so it can only support "Hypothesized" at most. Human FAP upper-GI involvement is described as polyps, not ulcers (PMID 8538033). Therefore the relationship is best judged Novel, with some weight on Hypothesized given the mouse gastric mucosal phenotype.

All retrieved articles concern CBL as an E3 ubiquitin ligase in RAS pathway signaling, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, CMML, myeloproliferative neoplasms, CBL syndrome, and immune dysregulation; none measure lipid traits or HDL cholesterol. No human genetic association study linking CBL variants to HDL levels or dyslipidemia appears in the list, and no cited phenotype (JMML, CMML, autoinflammation, ocular findings) is a recognized precursor or subtype of altered HDL cholesterol. A small residual probability is allotted to "Hypothesized" because CBL participates in insulin/metabolic signaling pathways that could conceivably intersect with lipid metabolism, but no article here provides such evidence. The co-mentions are therefore incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

No article in this set reports AXL variants associated with human stature; the mentions of "height" are either incidental (intervertebral disc height index in the kaempferol/IVDD paper, PMID 42525295), in dogs (PMID 41284863, where height associations concern breed-differentiating loci, not AXL), or generic background about RTKs and short stature (PMID 30255986). The only human variant study is AXL sequence variants in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (PMID 24476074), a reproductive/GnRH-neuron phenotype in which pubertal timing can indirectly influence growth—this offers weak, indirect support for an "Existing" classification at best. Broader AXL biology (TAM receptor signaling, developmental GnRH neuron migration, growth-related RTK pathways) provides a plausible but untested biological rationale, supporting "Hypothesized." Given that most cited work is cancer, viral entry, or macrophage biology with no relevance to stature, substantial probability also remains for "Novel."

None of the provided articles report any association between BLTP1 (KIAA1109) variants and body mass index, adiposity, or obesity in humans; the human genetic literature here concerns biallelic loss-of-function variants causing Alkuraya-Kučinskas syndrome, a lethal/severe developmental disorder with brain malformations and arthrogryposis (PMIDs 39228063, 42381180, 30485398, 25558065, 38278647). There is thus no evidence supporting "Established" or "Existing" for BMI. Some weight goes to "Hypothesized" because BLTP1 functions as a bridge-like bulk lipid transfer protein controlling phospholipid trafficking and membrane lipid composition, with animal/model data showing lipid desaturation defects, cold resilience, growth impairment and rescue by lecithin (PMIDs 36357390, 40973493, 37455813, 41299140) — biology plausibly relevant to lipid metabolism and body composition, though never tested against BMI. The remainder is assigned to "Novel" since the co-mention of BMI is essentially incidental in this literature.

None of the provided articles addresses rheumatoid arthritis in any form; the literature on CPXM2 concerns retinal pigment epithelium in age-related macular degeneration, cardiac aging in mice, hepatocellular carcinoma, osteosarcoma, osteogenic DNA methylation, pilocytic astrocytoma CSF proteomics, late-onset Alzheimer's disease SNPs, placental transcriptomics in sickle cell disease, Apert syndrome fibroblasts, and mouse inner ear development. No genetic association, variant, expression, or pathway evidence links CPXM2 to rheumatoid arthritis or to a recognized RA precursor or mechanism. The only inflammation-adjacent mentions (placental inflammation, ECM organization) are incidental and provide no logical basis for an RA link. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small residual allowance for tenuous biological plausibility via ECM/inflammatory gene co-expression.

None of the provided articles report an association between ADCY6 variants and stature/height. Human genetic studies of ADCY6 concern hemolysis in sickle cell anemia (PMID 27067484, 18324973), blood pressure and hemodynamics (PMID 20732959, 17916776), and lethal congenital contracture syndrome 8/arthrogryposis (PMID 24319099, 31846058); the latter involves fetal akinesia and skeletal contractures, which could indirectly touch on body proportions but is not a height association, and no anthropometric height data are given. PMID 20732959 mentions "anthropometric parameters" in healthy subjects but reports only blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes. Remaining papers are animal/in vitro (cilia/Hedgehog signaling, PMID 26092933) — Hedgehog and cAMP/PKA signaling in growth plate biology gives a thin biological rationale supporting a "hypothesized" reading, but nothing measured height. Overall the evidence base here is essentially absent for height, so Novel is most probable with some weight to Hypothesized.

The SETD1A literature provided is dominated by schizophrenia, neurodevelopmental disorders, speech delay, and hematopoiesis/leukemia biology; no study reports SETD1A variants in patients with type 2 diabetes or any diabetes-related metabolic trait. The only T2D co-mentions are (i) a broad review of SETD-family enzymes in inflammatory diseases that lists atherosclerosis and type 2 diabetes among conditions influenced by the family generally, and (ii) a mechanistic vascular-regeneration study in diabetic endothelial cells/mice where SETD1A is named as one of several H3K4me3 writers recruited by YY1 to the MAML1 promoter. These give a tenuous, non-genetic biological link (chromatin/H3K4me3 regulation in diabetic vascular and immune contexts), largely in mouse and cell models, which supports at most a weak "Hypothesized" rating rather than "Existing." No human genetic association, precursor phenotype, or replicated proband evidence exists, so Established is effectively excluded.

Every retrieved article concerns NUP98 rearrangements in acute leukemias (AML, T-ALL, AMKL), menin-KMT2A inhibition, and HOXA dysregulation; none measures stature or reports height-associated NUP98 variants in humans. The only tangential link is the NSD1 review (PMID 34575025), which notes that NSD1 loss-of-function causes Sotos overgrowth syndrome and that NUP98::NSD1 fusions occur in leukemia — but that growth phenotype is attributable to NSD1, not NUP98, and the fusion is a somatic leukemogenic event, not a germline determinant of height. No proband, family, or cohort study connects NUP98 variation to height, so Established and Existing are effectively unsupported. A small amount of probability is given to Hypothesized because NUP98 fusion partners (NSD1, KDM5A) are chromatin regulators implicated in growth/developmental syndromes, providing a thin biological rationale.

The most directly relevant article (PMID 30811992) shows that Pum1 and Pum2 knockout mice exhibit gene dosage–dependent reductions in body and organ size via translational repression of Cdkn1b, providing strong biological/mechanistic support for a role of PUM2 in growth and body size — but this is a mouse model, not human genetic evidence. The only human variant study of PUM2 (PMID 17154300) examined male infertility and found essentially no functionally relevant variation, and reported nothing about stature. Other listed papers concern cardiomyocyte apoptosis, colitis, lupus, osteoarthritis, epilepsy, pulmonary hypertension, and neural development, and contribute only general functional context (e.g., PUM2 targets regulating proliferation and cell cycle). Since no human study reports PUM2 variants associated with height, the evidence supports "Hypothesized" based on animal models and pathway biology rather than "Existing" or "Established."

Nearly all retrieved articles concern PKD1 in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (genotype–phenotype correlations, mutation screening, structural biology), with no human study reporting association between PKD1 variants and LDL cholesterol or lipid traits. The only lipid-relevant item is PMID 38901424, which reports somatic PKD1 mutant clones in human cirrhotic liver and shows in mouse and cell models that Pkd1 loss protects against hepatic steatosis and glucose intolerance via mTOR signaling without SREBP-1c activation—an indirect, largely non-human mechanistic link to lipid metabolism. This supports a biological hypothesis (SREBP/mTOR lipogenic pathway, hepatic lipid handling) but not a variant-level human association with LDL cholesterol. No two independent human studies with PKD1 variants and LDL levels exist here, so Established is excluded and Existing is minimal. The balance therefore sits between Hypothesized (given the plausible hepatic lipid-metabolism biology) and Novel (given purely incidental co-mention in the remaining ADPKD literature).

The only provided article concerns splice-site mutation detection in myeloproliferative diseases, where KLHDC1 appears merely as one of several genes with a candidate splicing variant in leukemia patients. There is no mention of height, growth, stature, or any anthropometric phenotype anywhere in the provided literature. No human genetic association study linking KLHDC1 variants to height is present, nor any biological/functional rationale connecting KLHDC1 to skeletal growth. Therefore the co-mention is incidental and the relationship should be classified as Novel.

No article reports a direct genetic association between UBR3 variants and hypertension; the Kazakh intracranial aneurysm study (PMID 30121816) only adjusts for hypertension as a confounder, and other papers concern deafness, disc degeneration, IgA nephropathy, neurodevelopmental disorders, or microbiome. However, large human sequencing studies report UBR3 protein-truncating variants associated with "cardiometabolic disease" (PMID 39210047) and with substantially increased BMI and type 2 diabetes risk (PMIDs 41073786, 41651857), phenotypes that are well-recognized risk factors strongly linked to hypertension, which supports the "Existing" category under the stated rules. Because the link to hypertension itself is inferential rather than directly measured, substantial probability remains for "Novel," and biological/functional-only support (E3 ligase biology, adipogenesis regulation, PMID 41325391) justifies some weight on "Hypothesized." There are no independent human probands or families demonstrating UBR3 variants causing hypertension, so "Established" is effectively excluded.

No article in this set reports an association between PPM1D variants and HDL cholesterol specifically. The closest human evidence is PMID 40399534, in which whole-genome sequencing of 10,241 ischemic stroke patients identified eight carriers of gain-of-function PPM1D coding mutations who showed lower LDL and total cholesterol, fibrinogen and inflammation — a lipid phenotype, but not HDL, and based on only eight carriers without replication. Mouse Sec24a knockouts are viable and show only hypocholesterolemia via reduced PCSK9 secretion, with no reported growth/skeletal phenotype (PMIDs 23580231, 24876386). Thus a plausible collagen-secretion/skeletal-growth mechanism exists (hypothesized), but the remaining papers are about ER/COPII trafficking, viral hijacking, and plant/bacterial biology with no height relevance, leaving substantial probability that the association is novel.

The soybean study (PMID 37204820) shows an SNW/SKIP-family ortholog (GmGBP1) modulating plant height via gibberellin/SAUR signaling, which is plant, not human, biology, and the INPP5K "SKIP" short-stature paper (PMID 28190459) is a homonym acronym and must be dismissed. Other papers concern cancer, splicing, telomeres, or ALS and are unrelated to stature. Every provided article links MYBPC3 to hypertrophic (or dilated) cardiomyopathy, a sarcomeric genetic disease, with no mention of rheumatic heart disease, rheumatic fever, streptococcal infection, or valvular rheumatic pathology. None of the studies report probands, families, or cohorts with rheumatic heart disease carrying MYBPC3 variants, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. There is also no biological or pathway rationale presented connecting cardiac myosin-binding protein-C to the autoimmune/post-infectious mechanisms of rheumatic heart disease, leaving only minimal weight for Hypothesized (nonspecific shared downstream heart failure/hypertrophy remodeling). No article reports human sequence variants in UBR2 associated with body weight, BMI, or weight loss; the human genetic studies listed link UBR2 variants to oligospermia, azoospermia, primary ovarian insufficiency, coronary artery disease, and multiple sclerosis, none of which are weight phenotypes. However, the biological evidence connecting UBR2 to weight-relevant processes is strong: UBR2 is an E3 ligase upregulated in cancer cachexia and muscle atrophy, selectively degrading MHC-IIb/IIx and driving fast-twitch muscle loss in mice, with elevated UBR2 expression (not variants) in muscle of cachectic cancer patients (PMID 36252004, 34950660, 30705122, 40511880, 26913136). Additionally, constitutively active UBR2 expression ameliorates obesity- and high-fat-diet-induced hepatic steatosis in mice (PMID 35245436), further tying the gene to body-composition/metabolic regulation, but in animal/in vitro models. This pattern—mechanistic and expression-level relevance to muscle mass and adiposity without human variant-based association—fits Hypothesized.

Supporting biology is strong: PKD1/PC-1 is a mechanosensor expressed in arterial smooth muscle and endothelial cells, with altered function in vasculature during ADPKD and hypertension (PMID 37823335), and ADPKD is known to carry vascular complications—this is classic "Hypothesized" pathway/expression evidence. All remaining papers concern ADPKD genotype–phenotype (renal) relationships, structural biology, or unrelated tumors, and contain no PAD probands or families with PKD1 variants (e.g., PMIDs 23431072, 33602752, 31740684). The strongest mechanistic link is experimental and murine: ASXL1-mutant hematopoietic cells accelerate atherosclerosis in Ldlr-/- mice through IRAK1-TAK1/NF-κB-driven inflammation (PMID 39653824, 39663508), which affects plaque biology rather than circulating LDL levels. Other hypertension papers (PVAT/H2S exercise, spontaneously hypertensive rats/ACE2) do not involve TCF12 at all. A plausible biological rationale exists indirectly: PKD1 mutations cause progressive cystic kidney disease and ESRD, which alters erythropoietin production and thus hematocrit (cyst-derived EPO can preserve or raise hematocrit, while renal failure causes anemia), supporting "Hypothesized" (PMIDs 23064367, 31740684, 37509056). Because the connection is inferential and none of the listed papers make it explicitly, a substantial share also remains on "Novel."

A plausible indirect mechanism exists—PKD1-driven kidney cyst disease alters erythropoietin production, causing anemia or occasionally erythrocytosis—supporting a hypothesized biological link rather than demonstrated genetic association. The UK Biobank rare-variant study (PMID 35177841) analyzed cardiometabolic traits and confirmed PKD1 for kidney disease, not for erythrocyte counts. Therefore the weight falls mainly on Hypothesized, with some residual probability for Existing (via kidney-function-mediated erythropoiesis) and Novel.

However, the biology is directly relevant: TET2 loss in human HSCs alters neutrophil development, NET formation, and exacerbates inflammatory responses (PMID 37267914), and TET2-mutant clones drive IL-1β/NLRP3 inflammasome activation and heightened myeloid inflammation (PMIDs 28104796, 29471939, 37781816, 41342736), mechanisms central to sepsis and SIRS pathophysiology. Statements that CH carriers have increased risk of "severe infections" or worse outcomes during infection appear only as background context (PMIDs 37267914, 41342736), which is citation rather than primary evidence, so Established is not supportable and Existing is only weakly supported. The bulk of causal evidence rests on mouse models, human cell engineering, and in vitro macrophage/neutrophil studies, placing the relationship best in the Hypothesized category.

The only allergy-adjacent mentions are a case report of an autoinflammatory syndrome with a coincidental SETD1A variant alongside NLRP12 (PMID 42157874) and a review noting SETD1A in psoriasis–Parkinson pleiotropy and atopic dermatitis pathways (PMID 41465136); neither reports asthma phenotypes or genetic association with asthma. There is, however, plausible mechanistic biology: TET2 loss drives NLRP3/IL-1β inflammasome hyperactivation, type I interferon signaling via mitochondrial DNA, altered neutrophil/NET biology, and macrophage inflammatory skewing (PMIDs 28104796, 37781816, 35931086, 37267914), pathways relevant to granulomatous and fibrotic lung disease. This supports some weight for "Hypothesized," but no direct human genetic association with the stated phenotype is present, so "Novel" remains the most likely descriptor based on this evidence set.

The only tangential renal signal is the report that individuals with dominant KDM5B missense variants more frequently present with renal and skin anomalies (PMID 39202393), which could plausibly influence creatinine, but this is a single case-series observation without any biochemical measurement, so it supports at most a weak "Existing"/"Hypothesized" claim. No replicated human genetic evidence for creatinine exists in this set, so Established is effectively excluded, and the balance favors Novel with some weight for the indirect renal/biological plausibility.
