Direct human genetic evidence for a POR–height relationship comes from the UK Biobank exome-imputation study (PMID 35649421), where a POR missense variant implicated in Antley-Bixler syndrome was significantly associated with a 1.76 cm (SE 0.27) increase in adult height in heterozygous carriers — a quantitative, variant-level association in a large cohort. A second, independent human report (PMID 15483095) describes 10 Japanese patients from eight families with biallelic POR mutations showing "relatively large height gain and delayed bone age from the pubertal period," a clinically observed growth/height phenotype tied to specific variants. Additional PORD literature (PMIDs 16467261, 21164260, 17960482, 19500762) consistently documents skeletal malformations and bone/growth abnormalities as a distinguishing feature of POR deficiency, supporting biological plausibility, and one epigenetic study links steroidogenesis-gene methylation, including POR pathway genes, to stunted height growth (PMID 37468957). Because the two variant-level human reports differ in strength (one large cohort association, one descriptive case series) and formal replication of the height association is limited, probability is split between Established and Existing, with the balance slightly toward Existing.

Neither provided article examines height or any anthropometric trait in relation to ZNF367. The hepatocellular carcinoma GWAS (PMID: 42357869) mentions ZNF367 only as a gene within a chromatin-accessible region identified by regulome-wide analysis, and its BMI-related comment concerns polygenic BMI risk rather than ZNF367 or height. The pan-cancer analysis (PMID: 41212452) is about diagnostic/prognostic value of ZNF367 in cancers, with no growth or skeletal phenotype. There is no human genetic variant evidence linking ZNF367 to height, and no plausible mechanistic/biological argument presented in these abstracts, though ZNF367's role as a cell-cycle/proliferation transcription factor gives a very weak hypothetical basis.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in KEAP1 associated with waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI, nor any anthropometric or body-fat-distribution phenotype, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported (no GWAS, family, or cohort study is cited). The literature is dominated by mechanistic KEAP1-NRF2 biology in oxidative stress, cancer, vascular aging, kidney and lung disease. The only tangential metabolic relevance comes from the hepatic lipotoxicity/NAFLD work (PMID 31913745) and general statements that the KEAP1-NRF2 axis is a regulatory node in non-communicable disease (PMIDs 32284348, 37146513), which provides a plausible but indirect biological rationale (oxidative stress and lipid handling in adipose/liver tissue) for a relationship with fat distribution. This supports a "Hypothesized" classification, with substantial residual probability for "Novel" since the co-mentions are essentially incidental to WHRadjBMI.

None of the provided articles report any human genetic association between CHAD variants and height or any anthropometric/stature trait. The human genetic studies cited involve entirely different phenotypes: CHAD p.Ala342Asp in prostate cancer risk (PMID 27902461), CHAD expression in leiomyosarcoma (PMID 36860591) and head and neck cancer prognosis (PMID 36081907), and one paper concerns a bacterial CHAD domain, a homonym unrelated to chondroadherin (PMID 35299638). The only skeletally relevant work is a mouse study of the paralogous gene Chadl, showing intervertebral disc degeneration, altered disc height index, and vertebral trabecular/cortical bone changes (PMID 42282628) — this is an animal model of a different gene, so it supports at most a hypothesized, biologically plausible link via cartilage extracellular matrix and growth-plate/skeletal biology. Because chondroadherin is a cartilage matrix leucine-rich protein regulating chondrocyte behavior, a mechanistic rationale for stature exists, but no human variant evidence for height is present here, so the weight falls between Hypothesized and Novel.

None of the provided articles report any association between MYO1D variants and human height or stature. The human genetic literature on MYO1D concerns laterality defects/heterotaxy with congenital heart disease and sperm abnormalities (PMIDs 38684630, 34589502, 40467998), multiple sclerosis fine mapping (40884622), and autism linkage (17376794) — none of which involve anthropometric height. The only tangentially relevant biology is MYO1D's upregulation in a goose skeletal-muscle transcriptome study following FST overexpression (41153936) and its general cytoskeletal/motor roles, which at best offers a very weak, non-human, indirect rationale for a growth/musculoskeletal link. Therefore the relationship is essentially incidental co-mention, favoring "Novel," with a modest allowance for "Hypothesized" based on muscle-development expression data.

Most PRPH2 literature concerns inherited macular/pattern dystrophies (CACD, AOFVD, butterfly dystrophy) that phenocopy and are frequently misdiagnosed as AMD (PMIDs 30215852, 19243827, 39515456, 32717343), which supports a phenotypic overlap rather than a causal role in true AMD. There is at least one credible human genetic study reporting a novel PRPH2 SNP (c.582-67T>A) associated with increased AMD risk (PMID 33354892), with the same variant subsequently examined in an AMD progression cohort (PMID 36902750), and an autosomal dominant late-onset macular dystrophy with AMD-like features attributed to an RDS/PRPH2 mutation (PMID 12882809). However, candidate-gene analyses of RDS/peripherin in AMD families were negative (PMIDs 10202289, 17362467), and no two independent studies demonstrate PRPH2 variants causing bona fide AMD in their own patient results, so Established cannot be supported. The weight of evidence therefore fits "Existing": limited, non-definitive human association plus strong links to AMD-mimicking macular dystrophy phenotypes.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: The UK Biobank exome-sequencing study (PMID 40912257) provides direct human genetic evidence, identifying COL5A3 among genes with rare putatively damaging variation associated with adiposity/fat-distribution traits including waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI, reinforced by CRISPR knockdown in human white adipose cells that increased lipid accumulation. However, this is a single cohort/study without independent replication in separate probands or cohorts, so the "Established" criterion (≥2 independent human genetic studies) is not met. Supporting but non-genetic/non-human biology includes COL5A3 as a hub gene in porcine intramuscular fat deposition networks (PMID 36078046) and hepatic expression differences in diet-induced glucose intolerance in mice (PMID 31650267), which bolster biological plausibility. Other papers concern collagen V in Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, osteoblast differentiation, autism mosaic mutations, and developmental expression, and are not relevant to WHRadjBMI. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the single study's gene-level association is considered suggestive.

No article in this set reports a human genetic association between NR1H3 variants and aspartate aminotransferase levels; human NR1H3 variant studies concern HDL/lipids (PMID 27135400, 19060910, 34995504), multiple sclerosis (PMID 27253448, 27764667, 27764668), blood pressure response (PMID 36950018), and insulin resistance (PMID 41249132), none of which report AST as an outcome. Several papers mentioning "AST" are homonyms or incidental abbreviations: the astaxanthin study (PMID 37893992) uses AST for astaxanthin, and the SCAP degrader work (PMID 32432943) lists GOT1/AST only in an abbreviation glossary, both in animals. Biological plausibility is nevertheless strong, since NR1H3/LXRα drives hepatic lipogenesis and steatosis, and LXRα knockdown improved post-transplant liver function (transaminases) in rat fatty liver (PMID 26256083) — animal/mechanistic evidence supporting a Hypothesized rating. A small allowance for "Existing" reflects indirect human links via insulin resistance/NAFLD-related lipid traits, which are recognized risk factors for transaminase elevation, but this is not direct evidence.

The strongest human genetic evidence is the exome-wide association study of plasma lipids in >300,000 individuals with replication in >280,000 (PMID 29083408), which explicitly names JAK2 as one of two loci where the human lipid signal (TC/LDL-C/HDL-C/TG) was corroborated by experimental mouse work — this provides discovery plus replication cohorts for a coding-variant signal at JAK2. A candidate-gene tagging-SNP study in 2,760 women (PMID 18239666) reported nominal associations of rs3780378 with total and LDL cholesterol, but these did not survive multiple-testing correction, so it supports rather than independently establishes the link. Remaining articles are mechanistic or model-based: Jak2V617F mouse atherosclerosis/LDL-lowering studies (PMIDs 40766664, 41720401, 40825505), JAK-mediated PCSK9/LDLR regulation in hepatocytes (PMID 21196532), and pharmacologic JAK1/2 inhibition (baricitinib) raising LDL-C in RA patients (PMIDs 29687421, 30777075) — the latter is drug-level, not variant-level, evidence but strongly reinforces biological plausibility. Because essentially one primary human genetic study carries the association, with a second only nominally supportive, points are split between Established and Existing, favoring Existing slightly.

No human genetic study in this set reports an association between AMD1 variants and human height. The human variant papers concern childhood/juvenile obesity and BMI (PMID 22496743, 26558825, 30262717 — with the Danish cohort failing to replicate), cancer survival (30650190), and intellectual disability 3'UTR variants (30097719); none measured or associated stature. The only "height" findings come from plants, where the AMD1 ortholog SAMDC modulates polyamine levels and alters plant height in tobacco, maize, rice and bermudagrass (27064210, 32879344, 29465802, 35819059), providing biological plausibility that polyamine biosynthesis influences growth, but this is non-human and the phenotype is only nominally the same. This supports at most a Hypothesized relationship, with substantial probability that the co-mentions are incidental homonym/plant-phenotype artifacts (Novel).

Nearly all of the provided articles report LDLR variants in the context of familial hypercholesterolemia and premature coronary/atherosclerotic disease, not valvular pathology per se; none present a cohort or family series in which LDLR variants are shown to cause non-rheumatic valvular heart disease as the primary outcome. Only two papers make incidental valve-related observations: a Tunisian family study in which a patient carrying an LDLR splice-site variant/LDLRAP1 variant had a quadricuspid aortic valve (PMID 41492187, and the valve finding is attributed to the recessive LDLRAP1 case), and a heart-transplant screening cohort in which one patient with valvular disease carried a controversial LDLR variant (PMID 36769882) — both anecdotal and not replicated. However, LDLR pathogenic variants unequivocally cause FH with markedly elevated LDL-C, which is a well-recognized causal risk factor/precursor mechanism for calcific aortic valve disease and supravalvular/valvular aortic stenosis in human patients, satisfying the "Existing" definition. Established cannot be supported because I cannot cite two independent human studies whose own results demonstrate LDLR variants causing valvular disease in probands or families.

Only one article in this list provides direct human genetic evidence linking G6PC1 (G6PC) variation to serum C-reactive protein: PMID 37493001, which reports that rare protein-altering/loss-of-function variant burden in CRP and G6PC modifies the obesity–serum CRP relationship in a white British cohort. This is a credible, large human study, but it is a single report without independent replication in the provided literature, so "Established" cannot be supported (I cannot name two independent human studies demonstrating the association in their own results). The remaining papers concern glycogen storage disease type I/Ib caused by G6PC1 or SLC37A4 variants, with inflammatory phenotypes (IBD, neutrophil dysfunction, infections) that provide biological plausibility for inflammation-related CRP effects but not direct CRP genetic association. Hence the bulk of the probability sits with "Existing," with a modest allocation to "Hypothesized" for the mechanistic/inflammatory link and a small residual to "Established."

Multiple independent human population studies report association of HECTD4 (C12orf51) variants (rs2074356, rs11066280, rs77768175) with type 2 diabetes risk and closely related glycemic traits: a prospective Korean cohort showing reduced T2D hazard for minor allele homozygotes (PMID 26891264), a GWAS of KoGES cohorts linking HECTD4 SNPs to fasting glucose, triglycerides and T2D prevalence (PMID 35713687), a meta-analysis identifying C12orf51 for 1-h plasma glucose as a T2D predisposing trait (PMID 23575436), and Korean GWAS of T2DM/glycemic traits and thoracic-to-hip ratio with protective effects on T2D (PMIDs 25349825, 26675016). Additional supportive human data link the locus to metabolic syndrome pleiotropy, obesity, and blood pressure (PMIDs 24981077, 39521882, 24142389). However, this is a well-known 12q24 (ALDH2/ACAD10/BRAP) LD region where the causal gene is difficult to isolate, and no family/proband studies demonstrate causation, so Established is not warranted. Mechanistic cell and mouse work (ethanol-induced HECTD4 expression, CYP2E1/lipogenic genes) supports biological plausibility but is non-human and thus adds to Hypothesized rather than Existing.

None of the provided articles examine stature/height or any growth-related anthropometric trait in relation to SOCS5. The literature covers SOCS5 in allergic disease and Th1/Th2 balance (PMIDs 12242343, 16210657, 17456221), cancer prognosis (33758600, 31406106), inflammatory/infectious models (39415256, 41923629, 16318583), and nephrotic syndrome (22252769). The only human genetic association study of a quantitative trait involving the SOCS5 region concerns blood pressure (CRIPT-SOCS5 locus, PMID 24376456), which is unrelated to height. Some weak biological plausibility exists via JAK/STAT and growth-factor (EGFR, growth hormone-like cytokine) signaling, warranting a small "Hypothesized" allocation, but there is no direct evidence linking SOCS5 variants or function to height.

The strongest primary human evidence here is PMID 38952118, which reports 9 patients with heterozygous IGF1 variants (haploinsufficiency), their short-stature phenotype and growth response to rhGH — a genuine multi-proband human genetic study. Several other items (PMIDs 23428682, 23182818, 29249625, 30864634) are reviews summarizing homozygous and heterozygous IGF1 mutations causing pre- and postnatal growth failure, plus association studies of IGF1 polymorphisms with height/head circumference; these restate the association rather than provide new primary results, so they count as citations, not replication. One primary human genetic study (PMID 2394448) actually reported no association of IGF1 RFLPs with stature in African Pygmies, and PMID 40770099 examines parent-of-origin effects on IGF1 levels and height at the population level. Because only one clearly primary, variant-level human report of IGF1 itself is present in this list, Established cannot be fully secured, though the underlying literature is widely regarded as definitive, so probability is split between Established and Existing. Animal/in vitro data (Igf1 knockout mice, CTCF regulation of IGF1) support biological plausibility but only underpin the Hypothesized tier.

Biallelic G6PC1 variants cause glycogen storage disease type Ia, whose defining biochemical phenotype includes hyperlipidemia (hypertriglyceridemia and elevated cholesterol), a well-recognized dyslipidemia state directly relevant to total cholesterol. Human evidence comes from genotyped cohorts and probands: the Korean cohort with the c.648G>T G6PC variant reporting dyslipidemia (PMID 32046761), a homozygous R83C proband with explicitly reported total cholesterol values (PMID 23312056), the Saudi hepatic GSD cohort with genotype–phenotype correlations (PMID 40743267), and the Dutch GSDIa cohort relating G6PC1 genotype to serum triglycerides (PMID 35811762); reviews reinforce the lipid phenotype (PMID 21599942). However, most reports emphasize triglycerides rather than total cholesterol as a specific, replicated quantitative endpoint, and no population-level association study of G6PC1 variants with total cholesterol is present, so the evidence is credible but not definitive for this exact trait. Supporting mechanistic and non-human data (liver-specific G6pc knockout, proteomics of cholesterol-related proteins) provide additional biological plausibility but count toward Hypothesized.

The human evidence linking RTL1 to growth/height comes from Temple syndrome and Kagami-Ogata syndrome (PMIDs 41926606, 39446997, 32592473, 37842090), imprinting disorders of the 14q32 cluster that feature pre-/postnatal growth restriction and short stature; however, these arise from UPD, epimutations, or multigenic deletions that cannot isolate RTL1 from neighbouring DLK1, MEG3, or DIO3, so no article reports RTL1-specific variants in independent human probands or cohorts. The mechanistic support for RTL1 in growth is largely non-human: mouse over-/under-expression models (33484574, 41645234), equine placental angiogenesis and IUGR (33693478), and ovine callipyge muscle hypertrophy where PEG11/RTL1 overexpression drives growth phenotypes (26474044, 20072617, 15298706, 17121598). This combination places most weight between Existing (human imprinting-disorder short stature attributed in part to RTL1 dosage) and Hypothesized (strong but animal/functional evidence). Established is untenable because no two human studies demonstrate gene-specific variants affecting height, and Novel is excluded given clear biological relevance to fetal/muscle growth.

No human study in this set reports variants in SMURF2 associated with stature or height; the only height-adjacent genetic finding is an ovine GWAS in Hulun Buir sheep where SMURF2 emerged near loci for tail fat traits (body size genes cited there were SMARCA5 and GAB1), which is animal, not human, evidence (PMID 31045295). Other human genetic reports involve telomere length (PMID 24478790), Alzheimer's rare variants (PMID 41960309), and autoimmune fibrosis (PMID 41687842) — unrelated to height. However, SMURF2 biology is plausibly relevant to skeletal growth: it is a HECT E3 ligase controlling TGF-β/BMP–SMAD signaling and mediates RUNX2 ubiquitination and osteogenic differentiation (PMIDs 38810422, 40825401, 37490283), pathways central to chondrocyte/osteoblast function and longitudinal bone growth. This supports a Hypothesized relationship, with residual probability for Novel since the co-mentions are largely incidental and no direct growth-plate or stature phenotype is documented.

PKD1 mutations cause ADPKD, and cardiac valvular abnormalities (notably mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation) are repeatedly described as an extrarenal manifestation of the disease in human reviews (PMIDs 40980664, 28682033, 11245774, 10412869), with a bimodal age distribution attributed partly to genetic factors. However, every article in this list that mentions valvular involvement is a narrative review restating known background; none report their own cohort of probands or families in which PKD1 variants were identified together with valvular phenotypes. The primary genetic studies here (23431072, 26453610, 31740684, 26139440) focus exclusively on renal outcomes, and mechanistic work (30093605, 37823335, 23064367) is structural/vascular or murine. Therefore replication criteria for "Established" are not met from this evidence set, and "Existing" is the best fit, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given that much of the direct support is biological/review-level rather than variant–phenotype data.

No human study in this set links PTPRK variants to stature; human genetic reports concern Alzheimer's disease, coeliac disease, type 1 diabetes, sprint performance, and cancer, none of which are height phenotypes. The only body-size evidence is a caprine GWAS in Karachai goats where PTPRK was a candidate near SNPs associated with withers height, rump height, and body length (PMID 36292658), which is animal, not human, evidence and therefore supports at most "Hypothesized". Other papers describe PTPRK biology in adhesion, EGFR/β-catenin/STAT3 signaling, metabolism, and growth-related pathways, giving plausible but indirect mechanistic relevance to growth. Remaining articles are cancer, immunity, or homonym-adjacent co-mentions with no bearing on height, supporting a substantial probability of "Novel".

The clearest human evidence is the Amish cohort with a homozygous SAMHD1 splice mutation (c.1411-2A>G) in 14 individuals, where intrauterine growth restriction, failure to thrive and short stature were explicit early features (PMID 21402907) — this is a single, though sizeable, family-based report linking SAMHD1 variants to a height-related phenotype. Large phenotype series of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome caused by SAMHD1 and related genes (PMIDs 25604658, 40302656) document neurological, cutaneous, and systemic features but do not independently establish growth/height effects, so they function largely as background rather than replication. No GWAS or rare-variant association study of adult height implicating SAMHD1 is present; the UK Biobank exome study concerns ovarian ageing and cancer, not stature (PMID 39261734). Remaining papers address antiviral dNTPase biology, interferon signalling, cancer, and inflammasome activation, which offer at most a mechanistic (hypothesized) rationale for growth impairment via chronic type I interferon-driven inflammation. Therefore "Existing" is most probable, with Established unsupported for lack of at least two independent human reports of variants affecting height.

Two large human sequencing studies directly implicate UBR3 rare protein-truncating variants in cardiometabolic phenotypes: a WGS gene-based analysis of ~709,000 UK Biobank and All of Us participants reports that UBR3 PTVs independently increase BMI and type 2 diabetes risk (PMID 41073786), and a pan-ancestry rare coding variant analysis across three biobanks highlights UBR3 for cardiometabolic disease (PMID 39210047). A further WGS anthropometric analysis confirms UBR3 PTVs raise BMI by ~2.7 kg/m2 (PMID 41651857), a well-recognized risk factor strongly linked to T2D. These are human burden-test association signals in partially overlapping cohorts rather than causal demonstrations in independent probands or families, so the criteria for "Established" (at least two studies reporting causal variants in distinct patients/families) are not met. Other listed papers concern hearing, disc degeneration, IgA nephropathy, neurodevelopmental disorders, or adipogenesis biology and provide only supportive or unrelated context.

None of the provided articles examine stature or growth phenotypes in relation to HMG20B. The literature focuses on HMG20B (BRAF35) as a component of the LSD1–CoREST repressor complex in leukemia, Merkel cell carcinoma, erythroid and neuronal differentiation, cytokinesis with BRCA2, and EMT. The only human genetic-variant study (PMID 38200130) implicates HMG20B regulatory variants in skin pigmentation, not height, and pigmentation is not a precursor or mechanism for stature. There is no expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking HMG20B to skeletal growth, so co-mentions are incidental and the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for a general chromatin/differentiation biology rationale.

The strongest evidence connecting TRPM7 to skeletal growth is mechanistic and non-human: TRPM7-mediated Ca2+ influx downstream of CNP in growth plate chondrocytes drives extracellular matrix synthesis and long bone outgrowth (PMID 40456620), and mouse/zebrafish studies implicate TRPM6/7 in skeletogenesis and embryonic development (PMIDs 20932259, 38631163). Human genetic reports of TRPM7 variants exist (heterozygous variants with hypomagnesemia and developmental delay, PMID 39099563; a newly described hypomagnesemic tubulopathy from reduced TRPM7 activity, PMID 38350738; stillbirth-associated variants, PMID 31423533), but none of these present height or growth measurements as a demonstrated variant-associated phenotype, so I cannot cite two independent human cohorts/families establishing a height association. The growth-retardation phenotype in Kenny-Caffey syndrome belongs to FAM111A, not TRPM7 (PMID 35715480). Therefore the relationship is best described as biologically plausible/hypothesized, with modest probability that a limited human report supports an association.

PMID 38982111 provides direct human evidence: a whole-exome sequencing analysis of 304,119 UK Biobank participants identifying ANKRD12 (alongside GIGYF1) as a novel gene associated with alcohol consumption via rare coding variants. PMID 39031522 also examines rare and common variants for alcohol consumption and was retrieved for this gene, but its abstract does not explicitly name ANKRD12 and it likely draws on overlapping UK Biobank data, so independent replication cannot be confirmed. Other papers (PMIDs 38177695, 37231097, 39472661, 39511343, 42238450) show ANKRD12 rare coding variants affect cognition, neuroticism, depressive symptoms, sleep and inflammatory traits—supportive of neurobehavioral pleiotropy relevant to drinking behavior but not direct evidence for alcohol consumption. The pig alternative-splicing paper (38474122) is incidental. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing" (at least one credible human genetic study) with some chance of "Established" if the second alcohol-consumption paper independently implicates the gene.

None of the provided articles examine height, growth, stature, or any anthropometric trait. The literature concerns YEATS2's role as a YEATS-domain chromatin reader in the ATAC complex in lung, liver, and pancreatic cancer (PMIDs 40541806, 38619971, 40216980), post-translational regulation (PMID 40449592), noncoding pentanucleotide repeat expansions causing familial adult myoclonus epilepsy (PMIDs 37021642, 40571639), immune biomarker prediction in HFMD (PMID 36791943), and amplification in liposarcoma (PMID 29610390). While YEATS2 regulates ribosomal gene transcription and cell proliferation, which is only very loosely relevant to growth/body size, no human genetic or phenotypic evidence links YEATS2 variants to height. Therefore the relationship is essentially Novel, with a small allowance for a generic proliferation/growth biology rationale under Hypothesized.

Multiple independent human reports describe biallelic SEC24D variants causing Cole-Carpenter syndrome 2 / recessive osteogenesis imperfecta with prominent short stature and limb/trunk shortening: PMID 25683121 (compound heterozygous alleles in a 7-year-old boy with short stature and craniofacial malformations, plus two affected fetuses), PMID 30462379 (Japanese boy with short-trunk short stature, p.Arg484*/p.Arg313His), PMID 41188448 (homozygous synonymous splice-disrupting variant with limb shortening and severe skeletal deformity), PMID 39780448 (fetus with severe growth restriction and foreshortened long bones), and PMID 41495099 (family with severe OI including short stature). These are single-gene point variants in independent probands/families with functional support, satisfying replication for a stature-related phenotype. However, the evidence concerns syndromic short stature rather than common variation influencing population height, so some probability remains for "Existing" (short stature as a subtype/extreme of the height phenotype). Animal/in vitro data (zebrafish feelgood, MSC differentiation studies) add mechanistic plausibility but are not counted toward human evidence.

The only provided article (PMID: 21131782) characterizes Zbtb45 as a BTB/POZ zinc finger factor regulating glial differentiation of neural stem cells and oligodendrocyte precursors in mouse embryonic tissue and cell culture — no human genetic variants and no anthropometric or skeletal growth phenotypes are examined. There is no study here reporting association of ZBTB45 variants with height in any human cohort, family, or proband, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. The described biology (CNS glial differentiation, Mediator subunit interaction) has no clear mechanistic link to skeletal growth or stature, so even a hypothesized relationship is weakly supported. Accordingly, the evidence base is best described as Novel, with a small allowance for a speculative biological pathway argument.

None of the provided articles report any measurement of stature/height or association of FBLN5 variants with height. The literature consistently links FBLN5 to elastic-fiber disorders (autosomal recessive/dominant cutis laxa), demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy (CMT1H), age-related macular degeneration, pseudoexfoliation, and as a candidate in thoracic aortic aneurysm — none of which is a recognized precursor or determinant of adult height. Some cutis laxa syndromes can include growth issues, but no abstract here reports short stature or growth parameters attributable to FBLN5, so any connection is speculative at best (extracellular matrix/connective tissue biology could conceivably influence skeletal growth, giving minimal weight to "Hypothesized"). No human study with variants and height phenotypes can be cited, so Established is excluded.

All of the provided articles concern RFC1 intronic repeat expansions and their role in CANVAS, late-onset cerebellar ataxia, sensory neuropathy, and vestibular areflexia, plus diagnostic sequencing methodology. None reports any anthropometric measure, growth phenotype, or height association for RFC1. The closest tangential mention is a related-gene paper on RFC4 deficiency describing a multisystemic disorder with decreased body weight (PMID 39106866), but this concerns a different gene and does not report height as an RFC1-linked trait. There is also no functional or pathway evidence linking RFC1 biology to skeletal growth in these papers. Therefore the gene–phenotype pairing appears incidental and is best classified as Novel.

Only one article in this set directly addresses the gene–phenotype pair: "Is polycystin 1 (PKD1) a novel risk locus for venous thromboembolism?" (PMID 41352608), whose interrogative framing suggests a single, preliminary human genetic association report rather than replicated causal evidence. No second independent study with VTE-affected probands or families carrying PKD1 variants is present, so Established cannot be supported. The remaining literature concerns ADPKD pathogenesis, PKD1–PKD2 channel structure/signaling, cystogenesis models, and oncology, which are incidental to VTE; the familial stroke exome study (PMID 36580209) attributes cerebral venous sinus thrombosis to F2, not PKD1. Vascular polycystin biology (PMID 37823335) offers only indirect mechanistic plausibility, supporting a modest Hypothesized weight, with a small residual probability that the single title reflects a negative or purely speculative finding (Novel).

The only human genetic evidence linking FASN to height is a single case report of a de novo missense variant (p.Ala2132Val) in a patient with severe short stature (-6.98 SDS), hypopituitarism, and multisystem features, with supporting functional data showing reduced de novo palmitate synthesis and FASN expression in developing hypothalamus/Rathke's pouch (PMID 40185395). This is credible but represents one proband, so replication in independent human probands/cohorts is lacking, precluding "Established." Additional height-relevant associations come from livestock: FASN SNPs associated with wither height in Guizhou white goats (PMID 38927592) and yearling height in Nellore cattle (PMID 22941250), which support biological plausibility but are non-human, contributing to "Hypothesized." Other human GWAS papers (acne, Parkinson's, HGF levels, erythrocyte fatty acids) mention FASN but the height association in PMID 27341449 belongs to CPT1A, not FASN, and thus does not count.

Direct human genetic evidence exists: a whole-exome collapsing analysis found a significant excess of rare damaging STAB2 variants in unprovoked VTE cases versus controls with supporting functional (surface expression, VWF level) data (PMID 32457982), and a large multipopulation GWAS prioritized STAB2 among VTE loci with suggestive zebrafish functional support (PMID 40554366). Additional human reports describe rare STAB2 variants in unexplained/severe VTE (PMID 41831330), CTEPH (PMID 40726512), and thrombotic storm (PMIDs 29178990, 33560088), and mechanistic work shows stabilin-2 clears VWF-FVIII, a strongly linked VTE risk mechanism (PMIDs 30124466, 39970990, 37085036). Mouse knockout data (PMID 34152080) support causality but are non-human and count toward hypothesized. Because the strongest case–control evidence rests largely on one collapsing analysis, with subsequent studies being small, phenotype-adjacent, or largely citing the original association, replication in independent probands is suggestive rather than definitive, favoring Existing over Established.

The strongest evidence linking NR1I2 (PXR) to HDL cholesterol comes from rodent and pharmacological studies: PXR agonists raise apoA1/HDL-C in wild-type but not PXR-knockout mice (PMID 15225665), PXR agonism lowers HDL in humanized CETP mice (PMID 19150509), CAR/PXR knockouts alter HDL after bile duct ligation (PMID 15684063), and PPARα/PXR agonist synergy elevates murine HDL-C (PMID 20036888). Reviews add human pharmacological/mechanistic context (4β-hydroxycholesterol and reverse HDL cholesterol transport, PMID 33182477) but not genetic association data. All human NR1I2 variant studies listed concern drug-induced hepatotoxicity, IBD susceptibility, warfarin dosing, epilepsy response, tacrolimus and voriconazole levels—none report HDL cholesterol as an outcome. Because no human study of NR1I2 variants with HDL levels is present, the relationship is best classified as Hypothesized, with a small allowance for unlisted human genetic evidence.

Multiple independent human reports describe LCAT mutation carriers with elevated plasma triglycerides as part of the dyslipidemic phenotype: a compound heterozygote (tyr83stop/tyr156asn) with elevated TG (PMID 8445342), a G71R/R140H compound heterozygote with elevated TG (PMID 16216249), a fish-eye disease proband with novel Thr123Ile/Tyr144Cys mutations and elevated TG (PMID 8820100), an Oklahoma FED kindred with elevated TG and LCAT exon-1 mutations (PMID 24636183), and FLD patients with novel homozygous missense variants showing TG-rich VLDL particles (PMID 31684177). These constitute independent probands/families with variant-level evidence in humans, supporting an Established call, though the primary genetic signal for LCAT in GWAS is HDL-C rather than TG (PMID 19060906), and some TG changes are secondary/variable, which keeps meaningful weight on Existing. Non-genetic human data (LCAT activity/levels correlating with TG; PMIDs 19671930, 218270) add supportive but non-variant evidence.

The BRaVa consortium meta-analysis (PMID 42238450) explicitly reports that damaging rare coding variation in ANKRD12 is associated with asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a large human multi-biobank study, providing direct human genetic evidence at gene level. This is a single (albeit large and cross-ancestry) association report rather than replicated clinical demonstration in independent probands/families, so it falls short of Established; no article demonstrates a causal ANKRD12 variant in COPD patients across two independent studies. The other papers implicate ANKRD12 in cognition, sleep, alcohol consumption, neuroticism and depressive symptoms (PMIDs 38177695, 37231097, 38982111, 39472661, 39511343), and note inflammatory trait associations, which offer weak supportive biological plausibility for inflammatory transcriptional dysregulation but not COPD-specific evidence. Accordingly, the evidence best fits "Existing," with small residual weight for "Hypothesized" if the gene-based signal is considered only suggestive.

None of the provided articles examine stature or height as a phenotype. The TRANK1 literature here is dominated by psychiatric genetics (bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, Kleine-Levin syndrome) plus incidental candidate-gene mentions in keratoconus and bladder exstrophy exome/genome studies, and a cell-biology paper where TRANK1 appears as a mitochondrial motor adaptor in Alzheimer models. No human genetic association, family, or cohort study links TRANK1 variants to height, and no biological mechanism connecting TRANK1 to skeletal growth is described. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a small allowance for hypothesized biology given TRANK1's broad expression and trafficking roles.

None of the provided articles examine height. The human genetic study (PMID 36450729) associates rare BOD1L1 variants with intraocular pressure/glaucoma, not stature or any recognized precursor of height. The mechanistic papers (PMIDs 38989615, 35439434) describe BOD1L's role in SETD1A chromatin binding and RIF1-dependent NHEJ in cell lines, which is generic chromatin/DNA-repair biology without a specific link to skeletal growth or body size. The anuran study (PMID 41008613) mentions Bod1l only as a candidate sex-determining gene in frogs, an incidental non-human co-mention. Thus there is no evidence, and only a very weak speculative chromatin-regulation rationale, supporting a BOD1L1–height relationship.

Two large-scale human rare-variant association studies report KDM5B burden associations with atrial fibrillation in their own results: PMID 40050430 (meta-analysis of 52,416 AF cases and 277,762 controls, with broad replication in MyCode, deCODE and UK Biobank) and PMID 42147184 (a massive RVAS with ~130,000 AF cases identifying KDM5B among 15 genome-wide significant genes not nominated by GWAS). PMID 38922602 and PMID 38390584 further support rare-variant contributions to AF/arrhythmia from exome collapsing analyses. Mechanistic support comes from CRISPR knockout of KDM5B in stem-cell-derived atrial cardiomyocytes shortening action potential duration, though this is in vitro and supports rather than establishes causality. The main caveat is potential cohort overlap between the two burden studies and the absence of classical family/proband segregation evidence, which keeps substantial weight on "Existing"; the remaining articles concern neurodevelopmental, cognitive, oncologic or bone phenotypes and are not relevant to AF.

The central paper (PMID 37556547) explicitly describes TNIK as an obesity- and T2D-associated gene and reports human genetic associations of TNIK variants with blood glucose, HbA1c, BMI, body fat percentage, and feeding behaviour using the T2D Knowledge Portal and UK Biobank, supplementing this with Drosophila and Tnik knockout mouse data showing protection from insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis. This constitutes credible but non-definitive human association evidence (GWAS/biobank-level, plus T2D-precursor traits such as glycaemia and adiposity), which fits "Existing" rather than "Established," since no independent probands or families with causal TNIK variants are reported. Other TNIK papers concern colorectal cancer Wnt signalling, neuropsychiatric/antipsychotic pharmacogenomics, vitamin D/BMD in a T2D cohort (incidental), and methylation studies, providing only background or incidental co-mention. Residual weight is placed on "Hypothesized" because much of the mechanistic support is animal/in vitro, and a small amount on "Established" given the strength of the biobank replication.

The most direct evidence linking THOC1 to growth/height is a mouse allelic series in which hypomorphic Thoc1 alleles reduce protein levels and produce a dwarf phenotype detectable from mid-gestation (PMID 17211872) — an animal model, not human genetic evidence, so it supports "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing." The only human THOC1 variant evidence concerns late-onset non-syndromic hearing loss (PMID 32776944) and a multigene 18p11.32-p11.21 deletion associated with deafness (PMID 39058882), neither of which measures stature and the latter cannot isolate THOC1 from neighboring genes. Short stature and growth disturbance are reported for other TREX subunits (THOC6/BBIS, PMIDs 30238602, 30476144; THOC2, PMID 32116545), which provides pathway-level plausibility for THOC1 but not direct gene-phenotype evidence. Because no human study reports THOC1 variants associated with height, "Established" is untenable and "Existing" is only weakly supported; the strong murine growth phenotype and TREX developmental biology make "Hypothesized" the best fit.

None of the provided articles report any measurement of or association with HDL cholesterol or lipid traits. SMAD6 evidence is concentrated in craniosynostosis, radioulnar synostosis, congenital heart disease/bicuspid aortic valve, pulmonary arterial hypertension, conduction disease, and neurodevelopmental phenotypes (PMIDs 32499606, 36414630, 38290823, 40133303, 39747593, 40715143). While SMAD6 is a BMP-pathway inhibitor with roles in vascular biology and cardiovascular disease, cardiovascular malformation is not a recognized precursor or subtype of HDL cholesterol levels, and no metabolic or lipoprotein pathway link is described. A small allowance is given to "Hypothesized" because BMP/TGF-β signaling has indirect connections to vascular and metabolic biology, but no article here supports it. Overall the co-mentions appear incidental, supporting "Novel".

No article in this set reports human genetic variants in PCSK6 associated with HDL cholesterol; the only HDL mention (PMID 28456517) concerns PCSK9-targeting antibodies, a different gene/homonym-adjacent convertase. Human genetic studies of PCSK6 here concern IPF survival (36780644), premature myocardial infarction/coronary stenosis (39039525), prediabetes status change (35769078), and a CRP pathway analysis (24763700) — cardiometabolic but none measuring or attributing HDL-C to PCSK6 variants. Biologically, however, PACE4/PCSK6 is described as inactivating endothelial and lipoprotein lipases and as a convertase family member implicated in dyslipidemia and vascular disease (17351764, 36188622, 31893970), which provides a plausible mechanistic pathway to HDL metabolism without direct variant evidence. This supports "Hypothesized" as the most likely category, with residual weight on "Novel" since the HDL link is largely incidental/co-mentioned, and only minimal weight on "Existing" via loosely related cardiometabolic associations.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in GLIS2 associated with height or stature; the human literature is exclusively about nephronophthisis/cystic kidney disease and end-stage renal failure (PMIDs 17618285, 26374130, 34917135, 21068128). The only paper touching body size is a bovine FGF10 promoter study in Qinchuan cattle, where a SNP is predicted in silico to abolish a GLIS2 transcription-factor binding site associated with body measurement traits (PMID 35446746) — this is non-human, indirect, and does not constitute evidence of GLIS2 variants affecting human height. A weak biological rationale exists (GLIS2 is a Krüppel-like zinc finger repressor in hedgehog/Gli signaling, a pathway central to skeletal growth; PMIDs 21816948, 29779043), which supports a modest allocation to Hypothesized. Childhood-onset kidney failure from GLIS2 loss could secondarily impair growth, but no such phenotype data are reported. Overall the evidence best fits Novel, with some weight on Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in PPIG associated with height or stature. The papers concern alternative splicing in pigs (adipose deposition traits, not height), psoriasis-related splicing factors, atopic dermatitis network analysis, goat/sheep prolificacy, coronavirus–cyclophilin interactions, and colorectal cancer isoform analysis. The pig study (PMID 38474122) is non-human and relates to fat deposition/meat quality, so it cannot support Existing or Established. At best, PPIG's general role as a splicing regulator provides a weak, non-specific biological rationale, which does not directly implicate skeletal growth. Therefore the relationship is essentially Novel, with only a small allowance for a hypothesized pathway link.

Several human reports directly link NR1H4 variants to transaminase elevation: a homozygous loss-of-function NR1H4 variant presenting as idiopathic mildly elevated transaminases (PMID 40728263), a novel homozygous NR1H4 variant in PFIC5 with elevated transaminase activity (PMID 41146118), and ICP patients carrying an NR1H4 nonsense variant (Tyr149Ter) among mutation carriers with higher mean ALT/AST (PMID 36046230). Population-level support comes from UK Biobank analyses showing NR1H4 missense variants associating with serum liver function tests within an FXR/RXR enrichment framework (PMID 36098472), and a case–control study of NR1H4 polymorphisms in antituberculosis drug-induced liver injury, a transaminase-defined phenotype (PMID 39512799). These are independent human probands and cohorts, supporting Established, though AST is often a secondary readout of cholestatic/hepatocellular disease rather than the primary tested trait, leaving substantial weight on Existing. Purely descriptive reviews (PMIDs 33384548, 35070006, 31201556) count as background citation rather than primary evidence.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: No article in this set reports an association or linkage between INSR variants and waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI. The only study measuring WHR (18828733) found suggestive linkage for ABCC8, not INSR, and thus provides no support. However, multiple human studies document that INSR variants cause monogenic insulin resistance syndromes (type A insulin resistance, Rabson–Mendenhall, Donohue; PMIDs 29369573, 40094207, 33479580, 40064328) and INSR polymorphisms have been linked in humans to hyperinsulinemia, obesity-related intervention response, and PCOS/hyperandrogenism (7584931, 38973289, 40725495, 39950870) — traits that are recognized mechanistic correlates and risk factors for central fat distribution, supporting an "Existing" (indirect) classification. Because none of these directly measure body-fat distribution phenotypes, a substantial share of probability also belongs to "Hypothesized," where INSR's role in insulin signaling and adipose biology makes it a strong biological candidate. Established is not warranted, as no two independent human studies report variant-level associations with WHRadjBMI itself.

None of the provided articles examine stature or height as a phenotype. The PIK3C2B literature here concerns focal epilepsy (PMID 35786744), myotubular/X-linked myotubular myopathy in mouse and zebrafish models (PMIDs 27548528, 37975768, 41955018), cancer somatic mutations (PMIDs 22510280, 29088297, 29728604), prostate cancer SNPs (PMID 20197460), and Hirschsprung disease noncoding variants (PMID 32948616). At best, an indirect link could be argued through muscle development and growth-related PI3K/mTORC1 signaling, which supports only a weak hypothesized biological connection, not a height association. No human genetic study reports variants in PIK3C2B associated with height, so Novel is heavily favored.

Human studies of clonal hematopoiesis link somatic ASXL1 mutations to smoking and to COPD-related contexts: the UK Biobank analysis found ASXL1 loss-of-function mutations most strongly associated with current and past smoking (the dominant COPD risk factor), while COPD itself was associated with myeloid CH (PMID 32518416), and the LifeLines ≥80 cohort reported CH association with COPD and ASXL1/spliceosome variants with smoking/DNA-damaging exposures (PMID 33877299). Clinical cohorts of COPD patients show CHIP (which includes ASXL1 among its most common driver genes) associates with current smoking, exacerbation history and future exacerbation risk (PMIDs 38320547, 40551798), but these do not isolate ASXL1 causally. No study demonstrates germline ASXL1 variants causing COPD in independent probands or families, so Established is not supported. The remaining evidence base (ASXL1 inflammatory/innate-immune and senescence biology, mouse atherosclerosis models) supports a plausible mechanistic link, justifying residual weight on Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in NIM1K associated with height or any growth-related trait. Most hits (PMIDs 9599658, 7629122, 7937842, 1819510, 11408575) concern yeast/fungal cdr1/nim1 or NIMA-related kinases, which are homonymous acronyms rather than the human NIM1K gene. The only genuine NIM1K papers are a cell-biological study of PDE6D-dependent ciliary trafficking (PMID 36672247) and a bovine milk-yield GWAS (PMID 34828436), neither of which addresses stature in humans. Ciliary localization offers at most a very weak biological rationale (ciliopathies can affect skeletal growth), giving a small residual weight to Hypothesized, but overall the evidence base supports Novel.

The strongest relevant evidence is biological/animal: Angptl1 knock-in reporter mice show expression in paraxial mesoderm, perichondrium, joint capsules and intermuscular connective tissue, directly implicating it in cartilage/skeletal development (PMID 17676644), and mouse cell studies show effects on osteoblast/osteoclast phenotype (PMID 33910546), both of which are mechanistically pertinent to skeletal growth and stature. The only human genetic report is a de novo 1q24.3q31.1 interstitial deletion with multiple pituitary hormone deficiency in which ANGPTL1 is one of eight candidate genes (PMID 24311370); a multigene CNV cannot single out ANGPTL1 and the growth phenotype is more plausibly attributable to LHX4, so this does not establish or robustly support an ANGPTL1–height association. A caprine selection-signature study lists ANGPTL1 among many genes in regions associated with adaptation/growth (PMID 40723324), which is non-human and non-specific. No human cohort, family, or GWAS evidence linking ANGPTL1 variants to height is present, so Established is essentially excluded and Hypothesized is the best fit, with limited weight to Existing from the deletion case.

The only direct human genetic evidence linking SLC27A3 to height is the Japanese GWAS/gene-based analysis (PMID 31562340), which reported multiple height-increasing rare and low-frequency nonsynonymous variants in SLC27A3 passing exome-wide SKAT-O significance in 191,787 individuals. This is a single, credible study in one population without an independent replication cohort reported here, so the "Established" threshold (two or more independent probands/families/cohorts demonstrating the link in their own results) is not met. Other SLC27A3 papers concern asthma, COPD, autism, neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, glioblastoma, adipose methylation, or sheep milk fat content, and one is a multigene 1q21.3 microdeletion (PMID 31602190) that cannot isolate SLC27A3. The gene's role in fatty acid transport and growth-relevant metabolism provides plausible biology but does not add human height-specific variant evidence.

The single provided article concerns von Willebrand factor type C (VWC) domains of Chordin family proteins (Chordin, CHL2, CV-2) and their SD1 subdomain binding to BMP-2 and Tsg — it addresses a protein domain type, not the VWCE gene itself, and thus is largely a homonym/domain-level co-mention. No human genetic study, variant, family, or cohort linking VWCE to height is present, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. A modest weight is retained for Hypothesized because BMP signaling modulation via VWC domains is biologically relevant to skeletal growth and stature, offering a plausible but indirect mechanistic rationale; however, the work is in vitro (C2C12 cells) and not about VWCE. On this evidence base, Novel is the most appropriate classification.

The primary human evidence is a single large-scale exome sequencing study in UK Biobank (PMID 37601970) reporting that rare heterozygous loss-of-function variants in DIDO1 increase adult BMI in women with large effect sizes. This is a credible, well-powered human genetic finding, but it derives from one cohort/analysis without independent replication reported in the provided literature, so it falls short of "Established." Strong supporting biology comes from mouse models: DIDO N-terminal mutants show a lean, lipodystrophic phenotype and DIDO1 is required for adipocyte differentiation via C/EBPα and PPARγ (PMID 38194457), reinforcing biological plausibility but counting toward Hypothesized rather than human genetic evidence. Other DIDO1 papers concern stemness, splicing, mitotic checkpoint, and cancer, and the DIO1/DIO2 thyroid papers are homonym-adjacent and irrelevant.

None of the provided articles address hip circumference, body fat distribution, adiposity, or any anthropometric trait. The literature exclusively concerns CCNA2 as a cell-cycle cyclin in cancer biology (bladder, lung, colorectal, hepatocellular, therapy-related AML), estrogen/Wnt signaling, cohesin regulation, and SAMHD1 phosphorylation. No human genetic association study links CCNA2 variants to hip circumference; the only human GWAS/TWAS-type paper concerns prostate-specific antigen levels (PMID 37205487), which is unrelated to hip circumference. A small residual probability is given to "hypothesized" because CCNA2's role in cell proliferation and estrogen/endometrial responses (PMID 41321316) could be loosely argued to touch on tissue growth, but this is not a directly relevant biological basis for hip circumference. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

Direct human evidence linking FLNC variants to atrial fibrillation is limited to a small number of case/family reports: PMID 41117735 describes novel FLNC (and TGFB3) mutations in early-onset familial AF with diastolic dysfunction, and PMID 42148251 reports AF as the initial manifestation of an overlapping cardiomyopathy phenotype. A review (PMID 35159226) explicitly lists filamin C among cytoskeletal protein variants driving genetic AF, noting AF often precedes overt cardiomyopathy, but this is background synthesis rather than primary evidence. The bulk of the remaining literature (PMIDs 27908349, 32112656, 34535832, 39937464, 40195560) firmly establishes FLNC truncating variants as causes of arrhythmogenic/dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure—well-recognized substrates and risk factors for AF—which supports "Existing" rather than "Established." Because I cannot cite two independent primary studies with replicated FLNC-AF probands/families as their own principal result, Established is not warranted; some probability remains for Hypothesized given much support is mechanistic/indirect via cardiomyopathy.

The only human genetic-variant study directly addressing serum aspartate aminotransferase is the large GWAS meta-analysis of liver enzymes in UK Biobank and BioBank Japan (PMID 33547301), which reported ~190 AST-associated loci; if TNFRSF10B is among these, it provides credible but single-report (albeit two-cohort) evidence, supporting "Existing" rather than clearly replicated "Established" status. Other TNFRSF10B/DR5 variant studies (PMIDs 37752286, 16217763, 10582684, 15802890, 25587027) concern cancers and hematologic malignancies, not aminotransferase levels. Several papers show DR5/TRAIL pathway modulation altering serum AST/ALT, but these are mouse and in vitro models (PMIDs 37274104, 29033903), which support a "Hypothesized" biological link rather than human genetic evidence. Remaining articles mention AST only incidentally or as abbreviation lists (e.g., PMID 32432943), contributing no evidence. Hence the weight is concentrated on Existing with meaningful probability on Hypothesized and some on Established.

No articles were provided linking C4orf17 to height or to any related phenotype. Without any literature—genetic association studies, functional data, expression evidence, or animal models—there is no basis to support an established, existing, or even hypothesized relationship. C4orf17 is a poorly characterized open reading frame with no well-documented biology relevant to skeletal growth. A small probability is retained for categories above "Novel" to account for the possibility that relevant GWAS literature exists but was not retrieved in this search.

Direct human genetic evidence exists in multiple independent families/probands: Olson et al. (PMID 9563954) identified cosegregating ACTC1 missense mutations in two unrelated families with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, explicitly framed as a heritable form of heart failure; Olson et al. (PMID 10966831) reported de novo and familial ACTC1 mutations in HCM with congestive heart failure phenotypes; a large multigenerational family with ASD and late-onset DCM carried ACTC1 p.Gly247Asp (PMID 31430208); and additional independent probands include a de novo ACTC1 variant in fatal infantile DCM (PMID 39759977), pediatric acute heart failure cohorts with ACTC1 findings (PMID 41572441), a neonate with dilation/dysfunction (PMID 40425186), and LVNC/HCM cases progressing to heart failure (PMIDs 17611253, 37489518). These are human, variant-level, replicated across independent kindreds, with heart failure arising through the well-recognized DCM/HCM/LVNC route. Some uncertainty remains because "heart failure" is a downstream consequence rather than the directly mapped phenotype, and much mechanistic work (Actc1E99K mice, NRVCM SRF signaling) is non-human, which supports a substantial residual weight on Existing.

The strongest evidence is mechanistic/functional rather than genetic: agonistic anti-TRAIL-R2/DR5 antibody induced human hepatocyte apoptosis and elevated ALT in chimeric mice with humanized livers (PMID 30202993), bile duct ligation upregulated TRAIL-R2/DR5 and sensitized mouse liver to TRAIL-mediated injury with elevated serum ALT (PMID 12388624), and DR5 signaling mediates lipotoxic hepatocyte injury and inflammatory EV release in NASH models (PMIDs 26764184, 19226377). None of these involve human germline or somatic variants in TNFRSF10B tested against ALT levels; the cancer genetics papers (PMIDs 10582684, 16217763, 37752286) report TNFRSF10B/TNFRSF10A variants but for oncologic phenotypes, not transaminase levels. Proteomic studies list TNFRSF10B as a circulating biomarker of metabolic aging or PAH prognosis (PMIDs 41356597, 40451321), which is expression-level, not variant evidence. Therefore the relationship is biologically plausible and supported by pathway/animal data (Hypothesized), with only a small chance that a credible human variant–ALT association exists.

All retrieved articles link KIAA0586/TALPID3 to ciliopathies — Joubert syndrome, short-rib thoracic dysplasia/short-rib polydactyly, hydrolethalus syndrome, and craniosynostosis — with no abstract reporting weight, growth parameters, body mass, or obesity as an assessed phenotype (PMIDs 26096313, 26386044, 26166481, 26026149, 39063141). No paper presents human variant data associated with weight, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported; there are no two independent probands/cohorts demonstrating a KIAA0586–weight link. Some hypothesized-level plausibility remains because KIAA0586 is essential for primary ciliogenesis and Hedgehog signaling, and primary cilia dysfunction is mechanistically tied to energy homeostasis and obesity in other ciliopathies, while skeletal ciliopathy phenotypes (short ribs, short limbs) could indirectly influence body size. However, this remains inferential rather than documented, so the bulk of probability lies with Novel and secondarily Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles report any genetic association between SPSB1 and human height; the human genetic studies concern aortic aneurysm/aortic dimensions (PMID 40409638, 41251448), carpal tunnel syndrome (40382669), venous thromboembolism (31420334), anthrax vaccine antibody response (22658931), and keratoconus (18795334), with no height GWAS or anthropometric outcome. The only biologically suggestive link is that SPSB1 negatively regulates TGF-β type II receptor signaling (PMID 26032413), a pathway central to skeletal growth and connective tissue biology, and SPSB family members are implicated in growth/reproduction in invertebrates (PMID 39251721) — these support at most a weak, indirect hypothesis. Structural/biochemical papers (20561531, 19154741, 16369487) are purely mechanistic and unrelated to stature. No human variant evidence for height exists here, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded, with the remaining weight split between Novel and a modest Hypothesized allowance based on TGF-β pathway relevance.

Human evidence directly links PKP2 to AF: a large sequencing meta-analysis of >52,000 AF cases found a novel rare coding-variant burden association for PKP2 with replication in MyCode, deCODE and UK Biobank (PMID 40050430), and GWAS prioritized PKP2 among AF candidate genes (PMID 30061737). Additional supportive human data include rare pathogenic variant prevalence studies in AF cohorts (PMIDs 38922602, 36669898) and clinical observations of increased atrial arrhythmia/AF and atrial structural abnormalities in PKP2-genotyped ARVC patients (PMID 27572111, 30364518), though the latter familial report involves a large multigene deletion and cannot isolate PKP2. Mechanistic support comes from a murine PKP2 conditional knockout showing atrial cardiomyopathy and proarrhythmic calcium handling (PMID 39446303), which is animal data and supports only the hypothesized tier. Because the AF-specific human evidence is largely gene-burden association and secondary phenotype observations in ARVC rather than at least two independent proband/family studies demonstrating PKP2 point variants causing AF, "Existing" is the most appropriate primary category, with meaningful weight for "Established" given replication of the burden signal.

Every retrieved article concerns SRSF2 as a spliceosome gene mutated in clonal hematopoiesis and myeloid neoplasms (MDS, CMML, MPN, AML); none reports lipid measurements, HDL cholesterol levels, or lipid-trait GWAS associations. The only tangential link is that CHIP, which includes SRSF2 mutations, is a cardiovascular risk factor acting through inflammation independent of traditional lipid risk factors (PMIDs 34298011, 37197843) — this provides at most a weak, indirect biological rationale rather than any HDL-specific evidence. No human study here demonstrates SRSF2 variants associated with HDL cholesterol or a recognized HDL precursor phenotype, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The modest Hypothesized weight reflects the CHIP–atherosclerosis/inflammation biology that could conceivably intersect lipid metabolism, but the dominant conclusion from this literature set is that the gene–phenotype pairing is incidental.

Two human reports describe biallelic DPP9 rare variants causing a Mendelian disorder (DPP9 deficiency / Hatipoglu immunodeficiency syndrome) in which poor growth and failure to thrive are core features: PMID 36112693 reports three unrelated families with hypomorphic/knockout DPP9 alleles and poor growth, and PMID 41082409 reports twins with a biallelic DPP9 mutation and failure to thrive. These are independent human probands with single-gene (not CNV) variants, so growth/stature impairment is genuinely linked to DPP9, although "failure to thrive" is a composite growth phenotype rather than measured height per se, and no GWAS of height implicates DPP9 in this set. A separate human candidate-gene study links DPP9 to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (PMID 18940951), a skeletal/spinal phenotype loosely related to stature, adding weak supportive evidence. Most other papers concern COVID-19 severity, inflammasome biology, or kidney ferroptosis and are irrelevant to height. Hence the evidence best supports "Existing," with meaningful probability for "Established" given two independent Mendelian reports of growth failure.

No human study in this set reports FRYL variants associated with height or stature as a measured outcome. The only human variant-level evidence is the de novo FRYL neurodevelopmental disorder cohort (PMID 38479391), which describes developmental delay, intellectual disability, dysmorphic features and multi-system anomalies but does not explicitly establish a height/growth phenotype, so it cannot support "Established" and only weakly supports "Existing". Strong supporting biology comes from non-human work: Fryl-knockout mice show growth retardation and significantly lower body weight (PMID 29409347), and FRYL appears as a candidate gene for body weight in broiler chicken and duck GWAS (PMIDs 31235723, 38909509) — these are animal data and therefore map to "Hypothesized". Remaining articles (Salmonella screen, sGC/Notch hypertension, exosome circ-Fryl, WM lymphoma exome, GERD/COPD) are unrelated to height and contribute nothing.

The only direct evidence linking YLPM1 to BMI comes from a single cross-ancestry gene-based rare variant association study of BMI in 839,110 individuals (PMID 41168175), whose preprint version (PMID 39484254) reports the identical cohort and results; these therefore constitute one study rather than two independent replications. That study is human, large, and internally cross-ancestry with consistent effects and links to body-fat percentage and severe obesity, which is strong but not independently replicated evidence. Other listed papers involve YLPM1 in clonal hematopoiesis, GIST somatic mutations, or psychiatric traits (PMIDs 39210047, 38744975, 34568833, 39489749, 42372879), which are unrelated homonym-free but phenotype-irrelevant contexts, and one pig multi-omics study (PMID 41463911) that is non-human. Hence "Existing" is the most defensible category, with meaningful probability given to "Established" because the single study is exceptionally large and spans two biobanks and six ancestries.

Direct human evidence exists: biallelic NPR1 loss-of-function variants were identified in patients with early-onset/neonatal systemic hypertension (PMID 37080586), supporting a causal Mendelian role, and large exome-based meta-analyses show aggregation of rare/low-frequency missense NPR1 variants associated with blood pressure (PMID 27618448), with further UK Biobank rare-variant analyses implicating NPR1-related risk (PMIDs 34722352, 38090255). Common NPR1/NPRA polymorphisms have been repeatedly associated with hypertension, family history of hypertension, and left ventricular mass in multiple populations (PMIDs 12872042, 26782497, 19126660, 16875975), and functional work shows BP-associated NPR1 variants alter guanylate cyclase activity (PMID 31430210). A human genetic analysis of >700,000 individuals also links NPR1 coding variation to blood pressure, and NPR1 agonists lower BP in resistant hypertension trials (PMIDs 39261724, 41563174). However, only a single paper reports Mendelian probands/families with monogenic NPR1-caused hypertension, so full replication in independent families is not clearly documented, keeping substantial weight on Existing.

Human genetic evidence exists: the UK Biobank exome analyses of 200,000 and then 470,000 participants identified DNMT3A rare coding variants at exome-wide significance for hypertension (PMID 38090255), and separate human studies report germline and somatic DNMT3A variants in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PMIDs 38234783, 40878867). However, the UK Biobank findings are essentially one dataset expanded rather than truly independent replication, and the PAH work appears to come from a closely related group and addresses a distinct (pulmonary) hypertension phenotype; no familial segregation across multiple independent probands is demonstrated for systemic hypertension. Supporting mechanistic and animal work (hypothalamic Dnmt3a-Agtr1a methylation in salt-sensitive hypertension, PMIDs 30385711, 38160798) and CHIP-cardiovascular literature strengthen biological plausibility but are not human variant-based causal proof. Therefore "Existing" is the most probable category, with some weight on "Established" given the exome-wide significant human association, and a smaller share to "Hypothesized."

Most of the listed articles establish FBN1 as the cause of Marfan syndrome with aortic root dilatation/dissection (PMIDs 17701892, 32130918, 33174221, 37684520), which is aortopathy rather than primary valve disease, and several only restate this as background. Direct human evidence linking FBN1 variants to aortic valve disorders is thinner: a preliminary report of a new fibrillin mutation in patients with aortic valve disease and ascending aortic dilation (PMID 22477503) and a single case of genetically confirmed Marfan syndrome with unicommissural unicuspid aortic valve and severe stenosis (PMID 42553922); the large genotype–phenotype cohort mainly documents mitral valve abnormalities and aortic dilatation (PMID 17701892). The bicuspid aortic valve work (PMID 14502156) implicates fibrillin-1 protein deficiency and matrix metalloproteinase remodeling without identifying causal FBN1 variants, i.e., mechanistic/biological support, and one kindred with aortic valve incompetence actually excluded FBN1 linkage (PMID 8130364). Thus credible but limited human genetic evidence, plus strong precursor/mechanistic links (valve regurgitation secondary to root dilatation), best fits "Existing," with some probability that curated Marfan cohorts would be judged as established causal evidence for valvular manifestations.

No human genetic study in the list links CCNA2 variants to body weight or obesity. The strongest evidence is the Berlin Fat Mouse study (PMID 24772056), where unique promoter mutations in Ccna2 within a juvenile-obesity QTL region were associated with altered adipose expression and metabolite profiles—compelling but strictly murine. Animal genomic scans in mink (PMID 38389405) and goats (PMID 39187139) mention CCNA2 only for immune or reproductive traits, not weight, and other papers merely use Ccna2 as a proliferation marker in contexts where body weight is an incidental measurement (PMIDs 30740593, 32454116, 40495121, 38085574, 38023376, 17942131). This constitutes plausible biological/pathway and animal-model relevance without human variant evidence, so "Hypothesized" dominates, with residual probability for "Novel" since some co-mentions are purely incidental.

No article reports human genetic variants in UBR2 associated with body mass index or obesity; the human variant studies concern spermatogenic failure/azoospermia (PMID 26940145, 25739334), primary ovarian insufficiency (PMID 33095795, 34794894) and coronary artery disease gene-based analyses (PMID 34385509), none of which are BMI phenotypes. However, there is directly relevant biology: UBR2 (Ubr1 family) activation ameliorates diet- and obesity-induced hepatic steatosis in mice via amino acid-induced Plin2 ubiquitination (PMID 35245436), and UBR2 drives skeletal-muscle mass loss in cancer cachexia models (PMID 36252004, 30705122, 26913136), linking the gene to lipid storage and lean body mass regulation. These are animal/in vitro mechanistic data, which supports "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing" or "Established." A modest probability of "Novel" remains because the connection to BMI per se is indirect and no BMI measurements are reported.

The key human evidence is a single large-scale exome-sequencing study in UK Biobank (PMID 37601970) reporting that rare heterozygous loss-of-function variants in DIDO1 raise adult BMI in women with large effect sizes; this is credible but represents one cohort without independent replication, so "Established" cannot be supported. Strong supporting biological evidence comes from mouse work showing DIDO is required for adipogenesis and that N-terminal DIDO mutants are lean/lipodystrophic with reduced fat even on a high-nutrient diet (PMID 38194457), plus other Dido1 mouse/ESC studies (PMIDs 35672775, 28330622) that establish plausible mechanism but are non-human. Human DIDO1 variants have also been implicated as modifiers of age at onset in Machado-Joseph disease (PMID 34871736), which is unrelated to weight. Nearly all remaining papers concern DIO1 (iodothyronine deiodinase), a homonymous acronym, and were dismissed. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing" with a modest chance of "Established."

Only one article in this set directly examines lipid parameters in relation to HBB genotypes: PMID 22385543 correlates specific β-thalassemia mutation types with lipid profile alterations (including HDL cholesterol) in human patients from southern Iran, providing credible but single-study, non-replicated evidence. β-thalassemia itself is well recognized to be accompanied by hypocholesterolemia and reduced HDL, so a genotype–lipid link is biologically plausible and clinically supported, which supports "Existing" rather than merely "Hypothesized." All other listed papers are purely molecular/diagnostic descriptions of HBB variants (novel mutations, mutation spectra, unstable hemoglobins, sequencing methods) with no lipid phenotype, so they represent incidental co-mention and cannot support replication. Because at least two independent human studies demonstrating the HBB–HDL association in their own results cannot be cited, "Established" is not warranted.

The two MIC-1/GDF15 papers concern a homonymous acronym (macrophage inhibitory cytokine-1, i.e., GDF15) and are irrelevant to RMC1. No article in the list reports a direct human genetic association between RMC1 variants and BMI. The vegetarianism GWAS (PMID 37792698) implicates RMC1 in human dietary behavior at a chr18 locus shared with NPC1/TMEM241, and notes potential roles in lipid metabolism and brain function—suggestive, but the phenotype is diet choice, not BMI, and the signal cannot be resolved to RMC1 alone. The strength-athlete polygenic study (PMID 33278272) lists an RMC1 polymorphism among human strength markers, a body-composition-adjacent but not BMI phenotype. Remaining papers (HUWE1-RMC1 mitochondrial axis in zebrafish; gastric cancer TWAS) provide only mechanistic/unrelated context, supporting at most a hypothesized biological link.

The only direct human genetic evidence comes from the meta-GWAS of early growth (PMID 25281659), which reports in its own results that ZNFX1 was among 11 loci reaching genome-wide significance for infant length, and refers to ZNFX1 as one of the 180 previously known adult height loci — but that prior adult-height evidence is only restated as background, not independently reported here, so it counts as citation rather than replication. The other candidate human paper (PMID 21284329) involves a 4.7 Mb 20q13.13 duplication spanning eight genes in patients with isolated GH deficiency, which cannot implicate ZNFX1 specifically. All remaining articles concern ZNFX1 as an innate immune/dsRNA sensor in immunodeficiency, HLH, inflammasome regulation, mycobacterial infection, and cancer, with no relevance to stature. Thus a credible but single, non-definitive human association supports "Existing," with some weight to "Established" given the locus's inclusion in known adult-height GWAS catalogs.

None of the provided articles examine aspartate aminotransferase (AST/SGOT) levels in relation to NOTCH4 variation. The only paper mentioning SGOT (PMID 25049554) is a cattle nutrition study with no gene content and represents an incidental co-mention/homonym-type artifact. The NOTCH4 papers concern psoriasis (PMID 33134369), schizophrenia (PMID 27318676), asthma/Treg biology (PMID 32929274), atherosclerosis (PMID 36044575), tumors and podocyte injury—none of which is a recognized precursor, subtype, or mechanism for serum AST elevation. There is no human genetic or even plausible biological link to hepatocellular enzyme levels presented here, so the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for hypothesized organ-injury/inflammation biology.

Human evidence for CAPN15 biallelic variants is centered on oculogastrointestinal neurodevelopmental syndrome (eye anomalies, developmental delay, congenital malformations), but growth-related features are reported: PMID 32885237 describes five individuals from four independent families with predicted damaging biallelic CAPN15 variants, several of whom had growth deficits, with knockout mice also showing diminished growth; PMID 33410501 reports siblings with a homozygous intronic deletion presenting with failure to thrive and microcephaly. These are syndromic growth impairments in small numbers of probands rather than dedicated height association studies (e.g., GWAS of stature), so the evidence supports a limited/indirect link to Height rather than a definitive, replicated one. Animal model data (Capn15 knockout mice with reduced growth and brain volume changes) reinforce plausible biology but cannot count toward human evidence. Accordingly, most weight goes to Existing, with meaningful probability for Established (two human reports mentioning growth deficits) and Hypothesized (if growth features are considered incidental syndromic descriptors).

Multiple independent human cohort studies of germline mismatch repair mutation carriers report an increased risk of urothelial bladder cancer specifically in MSH2 carriers: the Dutch Lynch syndrome cohort (PMID 20591884), a US MMR-mutation carrier cohort (PMID 22883484), and the Finnish carrier cohort (PMID 22476430), plus hospital-based ascertainment of Lynch/MSH2-associated dMMR bladder cancer (PMID 34213665) and case reports of MSH2 carriers with bladder tumors (PMID 39552452, 17237705). These are independent probands/families with single-gene germline MSH2 variants, supporting a causal, penetrance-modifying role, which favors "Established." Counterweight exists: the Manchester cohort found no significant bladder cancer excess (PMID 23054215) and early-onset bladder cancer series showed low MMR deficiency (PMID 25319978), and several papers concern upper tract rather than bladder disease (PMID 36630951, 37914149), so a substantial share of probability remains on "Existing." Somatic expression/MSI studies (PMID 12712438, 11161395) are supportive but not variant-based.

Human evidence linking LRP4 variants to stature comes chiefly from Cenani-Lenz syndactyly reports: a Pakistani family with a novel LRP4 splice variant (c.316+1G>A) showing short stature and limb shortening (PMID 28559208), and three further consanguineous families with novel homozygous LRP4 missense variants causing limb-shortening CLS (PMID 34857885), plus LRP4-related sclerosteosis with skeletal overgrowth (PMID 40824295).
