There are no two independent human studies isolating HMGXB4 variants with height, so Established is untenable; the balance falls between Novel and a weak Hypothesized/Existing based on a developmental-disorder syndrome that could involve growth.

None of the listed articles report human genetic variants in COL8A1 associated with stature or height; the human studies concern glaucoma/corneal thickness, Fuchs dystrophy, AMD, lupus nephritis, atopic eczema and cancers. The strongest biologically relevant item is the zebrafish study (PMID 19035365), in which a col8a1 missense mutation disrupts notochord morphogenesis and the mutated residue is homologous to the COL10A1 residue causing Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, a short-stature skeletal dysplasia—this provides an indirect, animal-model-based rationale for a skeletal/growth role. Additional collagen/ECM biology (myopia scleral collagen, ECM remodeling in SHMS with craniofacial malformations, cattle puberty QTL) supports a general structural ECM function but not height specifically. Because the supporting evidence is non-human/functional rather than human variant-based, Hypothesized is most appropriate, with substantial residual probability for Novel.

Biallelic CTC1 variants cause Coats plus syndrome/CRMCC, in which pre- and postnatal growth retardation and short stature are cardinal features, and several independent human reports describe probands with molecularly confirmed CTC1 variants and growth failure (PMID 34706368: compound heterozygous truncating variants with prenatal/postnatal growth retardation; PMID 25843205: adolescent with heterozygous deleterious CTC1 mutations and intrauterine growth retardation with skeletal demineralization; PMID 30393977: Brazilian family with CTC1 variants, progeroid features and skeletal disease). These are independent probands/families with variant-level evidence in humans, supporting an Established call for short stature/growth as part of the phenotype. However, the evidence is from rare syndromic case reports rather than dedicated height studies or population cohorts, and one listed case with short stature lacked CTC1 mutations (PMID 23824919), so substantial probability remains for Existing. Reviews and other case reports mainly restate the syndromic association without new height-specific data.

No article reports human genetic variants in SNED1 associated with height, so Established and Existing are poorly supported. The strongest biological argument comes from the murine Sned1 knockout, which shows early neonatal lethality, growth impairment and craniofacial/skeletal malformations, indicating a plausible role in skeletal growth and body size (PMID 33012048), reinforced by the ECM/integrin adhesion work relevant to morphogenesis (PMID 39713860). A human epigenome-wide study found SNED1 methylation probes associated with BMI and fat-free mass in preschool children (PMID 29084944), which is body composition rather than stature and involves methylation rather than sequence variants, so it supports a hypothesized rather than variant-based association. Remaining papers (methylation in cognitive impairment, glioblastoma prognosis, maternal diet) are unrelated to height and are incidental co-mentions.

None of the provided articles report any association between SPRED2 variants and serum creatinine or kidney function; there are no renal-function GWAS or clinical nephrology studies in the list. Human genetic evidence for SPRED2 concerns recessive Noonan-like syndrome (34626534, 38254922, 36608738), rheumatoid arthritis susceptibility (20453842, 35633988), clonal hematopoiesis (38744975), and telomere length via proteomic MR (39284832) — none of which is a recognized precursor or direct determinant of serum creatinine levels. Some weak biological plausibility exists through RAS/MAPK signaling and metabolic/inflammatory phenotypes in Spred2-knockout mice (30723473, 15946934), and RASopathies can occasionally involve renal anomalies, but these are murine/indirect and not creatinine-specific. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a modest allowance for Hypothesized based on pathway/animal biology.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report THBD variation associated with VTE: a large Chinese case–control plus family study identified the functional 5'UTR variant c.-151G>T conferring ~2.8–3.4-fold risk (PMID 23332921); a GWAS in African Americans identified and replicated chromosome 20 eQTLs for THBD (rs2567617, rs1998081) with ~2.3-fold risk (PMID 26888256), later reproduced in a sickle cell cohort (PMID 32384541); and rare patient-derived variants (G250R, L433P, C175S) show loss of protein C/TAFI activation consistent with prothrombotic effect (PMIDs 35436795, 39841007), plus a pedigree with a heterozygous THBD mutation and DVT (PMID 41454398). However, the most-studied common variant c.1418C>T yields inconsistent results, with negative recurrence studies (PMIDs 26743062, 28049360) and a meta-analysis describing the association as controversial (PMID 36278273), so the causal role is supported but not definitively established across cohorts. This mixture of replicated association plus supportive functional data, tempered by contradictory findings, fits best between Existing and Established, with weight on Existing.

The strongest direct human genetic evidence is the large sequencing meta-analysis (PMID 40050430), which found a rare coding-variant burden association between MYBPC3 and atrial fibrillation in 52,416 cases and replicated it in independent MyCode, deCODE and UK Biobank samples — a single primary study, albeit with internal replication. Additional human support is indirect but strong: MYBPC3 is a principal cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (PMIDs 28912181, 32841044, 35583889), a well-recognized substrate/risk factor for AF, and AF substrate and ablation outcomes have been specifically studied in MYBPC3-mediated HCM (PMID 38819352); a case report with an MYBPC3 nonsense variant presented with AF (PMID 37271167). However, genotype-focused HCM cohort studies found that MYBPC3 was not an independent predictor of AF (PMID 26869393) and that MYH7, not MYBPC3, carried higher incident AF risk (PMID 30354366), tempering claims of an established causal MYBPC3–AF relationship. Because only one primary study directly demonstrates MYBPC3 variant burden causing/associating with AF in probands, "Existing" is the most defensible category, with substantial weight also given to "Established."

Multiple independent human cohorts of genetically defined NF1 patients report significantly reduced serum 25(OH)D compared with matched controls, with original results (not merely background citation): Lammert et al. (PMID 16571643; 55 NF1 vs 58 controls, inverse correlation with neurofibroma number), Armstrong et al. (PMID 21648285; 109 children with NF1 vs 218 matched controls), an Italian adult series (PMID 36837874; 31 NF1 vs 31 matched controls), Schnabel et al. histomorphometry/vitamin D study (PMID 19415373), Brunetti-Pierri-type metabolic bone studies (PMID 18289904, 22120694), and a VDR expression study correlating 25(OH)D and VDR mRNA with tumor burden (PMID 30299316). A systematic review/meta-analysis (PMID 38141750) supports replication across cohorts. Counter-evidence exists (PMID 26161090, Brazilian case–control found no difference; PMID 30421324 found no correlation of TBS with 25OHD), and none of the studies analyze specific NF1 allelic variants, tempering certainty, so substantial weight remains on "Existing." Because all supporting data are human cohorts with a monogenic NF1 disease phenotype, Hypothesized and Novel receive little weight.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: No article in this list reports an association between SLC5A3 variants and waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI specifically, so Established cannot be supported (no two independent human cohorts with WHRadjBMI results). However, the cross-ancestry rare-variant gene-based study (PMID 41168175) provides credible human genetic evidence that SLC5A3 is associated with BMI/severe obesity and related adiposity traits such as body-fat percentage, with expression in adipose tissue — a strongly related adiposity phenotype that could support "Existing" as a proxy, though WHRadjBMI is a distinct fat-distribution trait. Additional human data link SLC5A3 region variants to metabolic traits (2-hour postprandial glucose in prediabetes, PMID 35299963) and to coronary disease loci with adipose/aortic eQTLs (PMIDs 28458444, 25697262), supporting metabolic relevance but not body fat distribution per se. Mechanistic support comes from non-human/in vitro adipocyte work showing SMIT (Slc5a3) regulation in 3T3-L1 adipocytes by TNF-alpha and insulin-resistance signaling (PMID 9882452), which belongs under Hypothesized. Overall, evidence is split between an indirect human adiposity association and purely biological plausibility for WHRadjBMI.

The BRaVa consortium paper (PMID 42238450) is a large human rare-variant meta-analysis across ten biobanks that explicitly reports ultra-rare predicted loss-of-function variants in NAA15 associated with type 2 diabetes risk, linking N-terminal acetylation to T2D. This is a single credible human genetic association rather than replicated clinical evidence in independent probands or families, so it does not meet the bar for "Established" (no two independent proband/family-based causal reports exist). All other listed articles concern NAA15-related neurodevelopmental syndrome, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dystonia, and ophthalmic manifestations, which are unrelated to T2D and do not add evidence. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with a small residual probability for "Hypothesized" if one discounts the meta-analytic signal as preliminary.

Multiple human studies directly report red-cell indices, including MCHC, in carriers of α-globin (HBA2) variants. PMID 23696099 is an African-American GWAS with discovery and replication cohorts showing rs9924561 at HBA1/HBA2 explaining ~2.9% of MCHC variance, though it cannot fully resolve HBA2 from HBA1. Point-mutation evidence specific to HBA2 comes from PMID 37213176 (novel Hb Liangqing, HBA2:c.224A>G, with hematological characterization in Chinese families) and PMID 22593821 (HBA2 α2 IVS-I −5nt with markedly reduced MCHC), plus genotype–phenotype cohorts such as PMID 24551772 (722 carriers across ten α-thal genotypes with MCHC compared), PMID 29346671 (deletional vs. nondeletional, largely HBA2-based, HbH disease) and PMID 39991167. Because much of the strongest quantitative evidence rests on multi-gene α-globin deletions or the combined HBA1/HBA2 locus, some probability is retained for "Existing." Non-genetic or homonym-type papers (e.g., HbA2 fraction in diabetes, PMID 39574185) were discounted.

The strongest direct human genetic evidence is PMID 21194676, a gene-centric meta-analysis of 114,223 individuals across 47 studies in which an uncommon IL11 coding variant (rs4252548, R112H) was strongly associated with adult height (p < 3 × 10⁻¹¹), with consistent effect direction across ancestries. PMID 29237553 provides functional support, showing that the height-associated R112H substitution destabilizes IL-11 and impairs osteoclast progenitor support, but it is in vitro follow-up rather than an independent human cohort. PMID 28146470 (GIANT rare/low-frequency coding variants) implicates the receptor gene IL11RA rather than IL11 itself, and PMIDs 30374069 and 37199584 restate the height association as background while their own results concern osteoarthritis/bone biology. Thus a single large (though multi-cohort) primary association plus mechanistic validation supports at least "Existing," with substantial but not fully independent replication pushing toward "Established."

Multiple independent human reports document biallelic or heterozygous WNT1 variants in probands and families with osteogenesis imperfecta/early-onset osteoporosis in which short stature or progressive height loss is an explicit clinical feature: PMID 30896082 (10 new AR WNT1 patients with short stature), PMID 28665926 (consanguineous family with homozygous WNT1 splice variant, short stature), PMID 36873675 (novel WNT1 c.620G>A with small stature), PMID 32413570 (WNT1 homozygous variants with short stature among recessive OI families), and PMID 41128774 (heterozygous WNT1 variant causing rapid height loss in two adults). Large cohorts (PMID 40282376, 40650436) also list short stature among WNT1-related OI phenotypes. These are human genetic studies in independent probands/families, supporting replication, though the height effect is a component of a skeletal dysplasia phenotype rather than a direct quantitative-height association, leaving some probability for "Existing". Papers on WISP3 (Wnt1-inducible signaling pathway protein 3, PMIDs 34430442, 22791401) were dismissed as homonym/different gene.

Multiple human cohort studies report that somatic TET2 mutations (clonal hematopoiesis) are associated with incident heart failure, HFpEF, and worse prognosis/progression in HFrEF and chronic ischemic HF, with gene-specific and clone-size (VAF) analyses (PMIDs 33241418, 33832602, 34210413, 38270950, 37333361, 37681311). A Mendelian randomization study (PMID 41107060) attempts causal inference for clonal hematopoiesis with cardiac disease and remodelling, and murine Tet2 models provide mechanistic support (inflammasome/IL-1β/IL-6), but the mouse data alone cannot establish human causality. These are observational cohort associations with somatic variants rather than replicated causal proof in independent probands or families, so "Established" is not fully supported, though gene-specific human replication across several independent cohorts is notable. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with a meaningful chance a reviewer would consider the replicated, gene-resolved human data as "Established."

phenotype: Specific developmental disorders of scholastic skills
literature_justification: ANKRD11 intragenic loss-of-function variants are unequivocally causal for KBG syndrome, demonstrated with de novo and segregating variants in independent probands and families (PMID 21782149, PMID 36446582, PMID 33955014, PMID 40459271), with learning difficulties/intellectual disability being a core neurodevelopmental component and school-related learning problems repeatedly documented (PMID 23184435, PMID 22307766). These are human, variant-level studies with replication, satisfying the criteria for a causal gene–disease link at the level of neurodevelopmental/learning impairment. However, the specific ICD entity "specific developmental disorders of scholastic skills" (isolated dyslexia/dyscalculia-type disorders) is not the primary phenotype tested; in KBG the learning impairment occurs as part of a syndromic global developmental delay/intellectual disability, so the mapping is inferential rather than directly demonstrated. Points are therefore split between Established and Existing, with little support for a purely biological/hypothesized-only or novel classification given abundant human variant data.

No article in this set reports genetic variants in FURIN associated with human height or stature; the FURIN variant studies presented concern post-exercise blood pressure (PMID 30706700), schizophrenia eQTLs (PMID 31548722), aortic aneurysm (PMID 38636100), and heart failure regulatory loci (PMID 41073375), none of which is a height phenotype. The strongest relevant item is a human biomarker study measuring serum furin in children with growth hormone deficiency versus idiopathic short stature before and after GH therapy (PMID 40882555), which supports a biological/expression link to growth but not a variant-level association. Additional indirect biology comes from furin-dependent processing of growth-relevant substrates such as TGF-β/BMP pathway components and microfibril-related proteases (PMIDs 38636100, 22922164, 28176809), again mechanistic rather than genetic. Several papers mention "height" only as pulse height in flow cytometry (PMID 25702121), a homonym to be dismissed. Hence Hypothesized is most appropriate, with residual probability for Novel and a small allowance for undocumented Existing evidence.

No article in this set reports human genetic variants in GRK3 (ADRBK2) associated with HDL cholesterol or any lipid trait; the human genetic studies present concern bipolar disorder and schizophrenia (PMIDs 12808434, 15006433, 16359584), which are unrelated to HDL. The only paper that measures HDL-c at all is a rat berberine/diabetic nephropathy study (PMID 23196710), in which GRK3 renal protein expression and serum lipids change in parallel after drug treatment — an incidental, non-genetic, animal co-mention rather than evidence of a gene–phenotype link. Some metabolic plausibility exists via GRK modulation of GLP-1 receptor signaling and glucose metabolism (PMID 34054727) and cardiometabolic GPCR regulation (PMID 28328744, 40772312), which provides a thin biological rationale supporting a "Hypothesized" reading. Overall the evidence is essentially incidental co-mention, so Novel is most likely, with a substantial minority weight for Hypothesized based on indirect metabolic biology.

PKD2 pathogenic variants cause ADPKD, a human monogenic disease in which early hypertension and elevated systolic blood pressure are well-recognized features, making systolic BP a strongly linked downstream phenotype (PMID 38096797, 37823335). One human study genotyped patients carrying truncating PKD1 or PKD2 variants and reported significantly higher systolic blood pressure than controls (PMID 38892431), but it pooled the two genes and was small, so it does not isolate PKD2. The large mutation-screening cohorts (PMIDs 22508176, 23431072, 26453610, 24611717, 32457805) genotype PKD2 in many independent families but analyze renal survival/eGFR rather than blood pressure, so they are background rather than replicated BP evidence. Mechanistic work on polycystin-2 in vascular smooth muscle/endothelium and cAMP signaling supports biological plausibility (PMIDs 37823335, 41748625). Therefore Existing is most likely, with Established insufficiently supported by at least two primary human PKD2-specific BP studies.

Human genetic evidence directly linking SMAD6 to aortic valve disease is present: PMID 32748548 reports its own analysis of rare deleterious SMAD6 variants enriched in bicuspid aortic valve patients with early-onset complications, and PMID 40646242 screens SMAD6 as an accepted monogenic BAV gene in 740 sporadic BAV patients (finding rare variants in ~2%, though without significant enrichment). Additional human reports (PMID 36414630 review, PMID 38290823 biallelic variants with complex cardiovascular phenotype, PMID 36049609 nonsense variant with severe coarctation) largely restate the association as background or describe left-ventricular outflow tract phenotypes rather than providing independent BAV proband series. The Madh6 knockout mouse (PMID 10655064) shows cardiac valve hyperplasia and aortic ossification, giving strong supportive but non-human mechanistic evidence. Because I can confidently cite only one to two primary human studies with their own probands—and the seminal SMAD6/BAV cohort paper is not in this list—the evidence best fits "Existing," with meaningful probability that the full literature supports "Established."

Several human genetic reports implicate GDF11 in growth/skeletal phenotypes: a de novo nonsense variant (Tyr336*) in an Undiagnosed Diseases Network participant with growth delay and multisystem abnormalities (PMID 41414712), a series of heterozygous loss-of-function variants expanding GDF11-associated phenotypes including craniofacial/vertebral and growth features (PMID 34113007), and a family with a Furin-site GDF11 variant showing clefting with vertebral/rib segmentation defects (PMID 31215115). A population biobank GWAS of GDF11 reports pleiotropic health effects (PMID 39237910), which plausibly includes anthropometric/height traits, though the abstract does not explicitly state height. Because the direct evidence largely concerns growth delay and skeletal/vertebral patterning rather than explicitly measured height in independent height cohorts, points are split between Established and Existing, with some residual weight on Hypothesized given the substantial mouse and TGF-β pathway biology (e.g., PMID 42449098, 38235060).

Biallelic CLDN10 variants cause HELIX syndrome/salt-losing tubulopathy in humans, and several independent reports document impaired kidney function progressing toward renal insufficiency: PMID 28686597 describes two unrelated families homozygous for c.144C>G (p.N48K) with mild kidney failure, Mg2+ retention and secondary hyperparathyroidism; PMID 30482581 reports a proband with a homozygous claudin-10 mutation whose eGFR declined to 59 mL/min/1.73 m2 and notes progressive loss of kidney function in up to a third of reported cases; PMID 28674042 identified compound heterozygous CLDN10 variants in two unrelated patients with salt-losing nephropathy and impaired urinary concentration. Additional human population-scale support comes from the UK Biobank exome-imputation study (PMID 36890159), which linked a CLDN10 frameshift allele to kidney function traits with functional follow-up. The counterargument keeping some weight on Existing is that the core phenotype is a tubulopathy, with chronic renal failure a variable, secondary and not universally penetrant consequence rather than the primary reported outcome, so causality for CKD per se is somewhat less definitive than for the tubular phenotype.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in SEC23IP associated with height or stature; human genetic studies cited involve Parkinson's disease (PMIDs 37865667, 36511626, 33002040), adult ADHD exome chip findings (PMID 27754487), and carotid intima-media thickness (PMID 29206233), none of which relate to anthropometric growth. Indirect biological plausibility exists: Sec23IP recruits VPS13B to ER exit sites and its depletion delays procollagen ER export (PMID 39352497), and COPII-mediated collagen secretion defects are mechanistically linked to skeletal growth and short stature; O-GlcNAc regulation of Sec23IP further supports a secretory-pathway role (PMID 42486260). Additionally, rat Sec23ip expression correlated with femur strength (PMID 19482074), an animal-model bone phenotype rather than human height evidence. Thus the evidence supports a hypothesized biological link at best, with substantial probability that the co-mentions are incidental (Novel).

No article in this set reports a genetic variant in LARP1 associated with red cell distribution width or anisocytosis in a human cohort, family, or GWAS. The strongest biological link comes from the 5q− syndrome work (PMID 28673543), where LARP1 lies within the commonly deleted 5q region and its knockdown in human CD34+ bone marrow progenitors reduces 5'TOP mRNAs and induces p53, a mechanism directly implicated in macrocytic anemia and ineffective erythropoiesis — phenotypes tightly related to RDW. However, this is a multigene deletion plus in vitro knockdown, which cannot single out LARP1 as the causal gene and therefore does not qualify as human variant-level evidence. Other papers concern cancer, neurodevelopmental disorders (PMID 39182167), viral replication, and translational control, and are not relevant to erythrocyte indices. This profile best fits "Hypothesized," with some residual probability for "Existing" given the erythroid-progenitor human cell data.

No article in this set reports a human genetic variant in VCAM1 associated with neutrophil percentage or any blood-count trait; human variant studies concern stroke in sickle cell disease (PMID 12393616), open-angle glaucoma (PMID 33627673), stroke GWAS drug targets (PMID 36180795) and sVCAM-1 protein levels (PMID 38374343), none of which is a recognized precursor of neutrophil percentage. However, VCAM1 biology is directly relevant to the phenotype: it mediates leukocyte/neutrophil adhesion and recruitment to endothelium (PMID 37442359), and animal/in vitro work shows VCAM-1 upregulation accompanying increased circulating neutrophil percentage in mice (PMID 32574508) and enhanced neutrophil migration with Vcam1 upregulation in endothelial insulin-resistant mice (PMID 37448347). These are non-human or mechanistic data, so points concentrate in Hypothesized, with residual weight in Existing given the plausible pleiotropy of sVCAM-1-associated variants with leukocyte traits. Established is essentially excluded because no two independent human cohorts link VCAM1 variants to neutrophil percentage.

phenotype: Leukocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: LYST is the causative gene for Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, a human autosomal recessive disorder whose defining features include neutropenia/leukopenia and abnormal giant granules in leukocytes, making an effect on circulating white blood cell counts biologically and clinically direct rather than incidental. Human mutation-reporting studies in independent probands exist (PMID 8896560, 9215679, 8717042, 28183707), and LYST is listed among genes causing syndromic congenital neutropenia (PMID 20008220); a clinical case documents leukopenia with normalization on G-CSF in a CHS patient (PMID 10466444). However, these papers report a syndromic qualitative diagnosis rather than a quantitative association with automated leukocyte count as a measured trait, and no cohort/GWAS-type evidence for the specific laboratory phenotype is present in this list. Therefore evidence is credible and human-based but not definitive for the exact quantitative phenotype, favoring "Existing" with meaningful probability for "Established."

No article reports germline variants in KLF2 associated with neutrophil percentage or any blood-count trait in human cohorts; the genetic literature here concerns somatic KLF2 mutations in B-cell malignancies (splenic marginal zone lymphoma, hairy cell leukemia, DLBCL, MCL), which are tumor-driver events unrelated to neutrophil counts. However, there is directly relevant biology: KLF2 is described as an immune-regulatory Kruppel-like factor, and human neutrophil KLF2 expression is reduced in polycythemia vera/essential thrombocythemia with upregulation of prothrombotic genes, indicating KLF2 functions in neutrophils. KLF2 also appears among genes mutated in pediatric AML relapse, a myeloid context but without any neutrophil-percentage phenotype measurement. This supports a plausible mechanistic (Hypothesized) link rather than documented genetic association, so Established is effectively excluded and Existing is minimal.

None of the provided articles report any measurement of stature or height-associated variants in PTPN14. Human genetic findings concern lymphedema–choanal atresia (PMID 20826270), hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia modification (PMID 22233626), gingival fibromatosis with distinctive craniofacial features (PMID 33491997), and primary lymphedema classification (PMID 38896493) — craniofacial dysmorphism such as relative macrocephaly is not a stature phenotype. The mouse knockout work (PMID 40533389) describes corneal, uterine, cardiac and renal defects with partial lethality, and PTPN14 functions in the Hippo/YAP pathway, which broadly governs organ size and growth — this provides only a tenuous biological rationale for a growth/height link. Given that plausibility, a minority of weight is assigned to Hypothesized, but the dominant conclusion is that the gene–height relationship is Novel in this literature set.

The strongest evidence is a single large human exome-sequencing study (PMID 38575728) reporting that rare protein-truncating variants in BSN are associated with severe adult-onset obesity, type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease, which is a direct human genetic association with T2D. Additional human studies (PMIDs 36865254, 37865656, 39228706, 39910307) robustly replicate BSN loss-of-function association with obesity/BMI—a well-recognized major risk factor and mechanistic precursor of type 2 diabetes—strengthening the "Existing" category. However, no independent second cohort has been reported that specifically replicates the T2D endpoint itself; the All of Us PheWAS highlighted cardiopulmonary phenotypes rather than T2D, and other BSN literature concerns epilepsy, neurodevelopmental disorders, and tauopathy. Because I cannot cite two independent studies whose own results demonstrate BSN variants causing T2D in separate probands/cohorts, "Established" is not warranted, though the very large discovery study and consistent adiposity/metabolic phenotype leave some probability there.

The clearest human evidence linking XPC variants to a height-related phenotype is a single case report of a 12-year-old with a novel germline XPC mutation (c.547A>T) presenting with De Sanctis-Cacchione syndrome including short stature and microcephaly (PMID 28255305). Other XP literature associates growth deficiency/dwarfing chiefly with XPA, XPD, CSA/CSB rather than XPC (PMID 23622385), and classic XP-C patients are described without neurodevelopmental or growth abnormalities (PMID 7252263). Genotype–phenotype cohort studies of XP (PMIDs 25256075, 41483010, 33087273) may capture growth features but do not clearly report replicated XPC-specific short stature. Because only one proband-level report demonstrates the link, this meets "Existing" but falls short of the two independent probands/cohorts required for "Established"; remaining weight is split between hypothesized (biologically plausible via NER/DNA-damage-driven growth failure) and novel.

The strongest evidence linking CRBN to AST levels comes from functional models rather than human genetic variation: CRBN-knockout HepG2 cells show reduced CCl4-induced AST/ALT release (PMID 39139558), and Crbn-null mice display attenuated alcohol-induced elevations of serum AST via AMPK and CRBN–YY1–CYP2E1 signaling (PMIDs 26410577, 32053237). These are in vitro/animal data, which support a Hypothesized relationship with strong mechanistic plausibility for hepatocellular injury markers. No human study reports CRBN germline or somatic variants associated with AST levels; the only human variant work (PMID 31619706) examined CRBN SNVs in myeloma treatment outcomes and noted trends for hypoalbuminemia and hyperbilirubinemia grades, not AST, and was not confirmatory. Remaining papers concern CRBN mutations in myeloma drug resistance or molecular glue biology and are irrelevant to AST, so Established cannot be supported (no two human cohort/proband studies exist).

None of the provided articles mention mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration or any erythrocyte/hematologic trait. All papers concern CHEK2/CHK2 as a DNA damage checkpoint kinase and its variants in breast and other cancer predisposition, functional yeast complementation assays, minigene splicing analyses, and cell cycle arrest mechanisms in cancer cell lines. There is no human genetic association study of red blood cell indices here, and no biological argument linking CHK2 signaling to hemoglobin concentration in erythrocytes. A small amount of weight is retained for "Hypothesized" because DNA damage response genes are broadly relevant to hematopoietic stem cell function, but nothing in this literature set supports it directly.

Multiple human studies link somatic TET2 clonal hematopoiesis to inflammatory phenotypes with hs-CRP measurements: the Montreal Heart Institute Biobank study found CHIP (with TET2 as the second most common driver) associated with 21% higher hs-CRP (PMID 32492156), the PROSCIS-Berlin stroke cohort showed TET2/PPM1D clones accompanied by elevated hs-CRP and IL-6 (PMID 36441964), and the CANTOS exploratory analysis specifically examined TET2 carriers in a trial whose primary biomarker endpoint is hsCRP/IL-1β signaling (PMID 35385050). A germline SNP study in the Tromsø cohort explicitly tested epigenetic-regulator polymorphisms (including TET2) against hs-CRP levels (PMID 37382343), and large proteomic analyses report TET2-specific inflammatory protein perturbations with Mendelian randomization support (PMID 39554199). However, most CRP associations are reported for pooled CHIP rather than TET2 alone, and much mechanistic support (IL-1β/NLRP3, Tet2−/− mice) is murine (PMIDs 29471939, 36196576), so gene-specific replication for CRP is suggestive but not fully definitive, favoring "Existing" with substantial weight on "Established."

Nearly all provided articles concern LOXL1 variants and exfoliation syndrome/glaucoma (e.g., PMIDs 17690259, 28534485, 24938310, 29452408), with no measurement or genetic association with height or stature. The only tangential link is a case report of a novel fibrotic disorder in a patient with marfanoid stature where increased lysyl oxidase (LOX/LOXL) crosslinking activity was noted (PMID 20560960), but no LOXL1 variants were implicated and this is a single non-genetic observation; it provides at best a weak biological rationale (connective tissue/elastic fiber biology potentially relevant to skeletal growth), supporting a small Hypothesized weight. No human study reports LOXL1 variants associated with height, so Established is essentially excluded, and Existing is very unlikely. Consequently, the evidence base supports Novel as the most probable category, with residual probability for Hypothesized via extracellular matrix/elastogenesis biology.

No human study in this set reports APOB variants associated with hematocrit; the human papers (schizophrenia comorbidity clustering, androgen abuse, soccer biomarker monitoring, HTG-pancreatitis, pre-eclampsia, obesity rheology) merely co-measure ApoB protein and HCT as unrelated laboratory biomarkers, with no genetic analysis. The APOB genetic literature here concerns hypobetalipoproteinemia, familial defective apoB-100 and hypercholesterolemia (PMIDs 33983694, 34852964, 12639976, 15818469, 27919345, 15308601, 41549954), phenotypes unrelated to erythrocyte mass. The single genetic association with hematological traits including HCT comes from a yak GWAS (PMID 31212963), which is an animal study and therefore supports at most a "Hypothesized" biological link. Given a plausible but only non-human/indirect basis (lipoprotein–erythrocyte membrane/androgen-lipid interplay), Hypothesized is most appropriate, with residual weight to Novel since the co-mentions are largely incidental.

Multiple independent human studies report association of NPPA variants with blood pressure and hypertension: a large multi-cohort study of rs5068/rs198358 linked to circulating natriuretic peptides, lower BP and reduced odds of hypertension (PMID 19219041); a prospective cohort of 18,437 women showing rs5063/rs5065 associated with BP progression and incident hypertension (PMID 17984371); and a Chinese Han case-control study of NPPA tag-SNPs, serum ANP and hypertension (PMID 31341238). Mechanistic human work demonstrates that rs5068 alters miR-425 binding and ANP production, providing a plausible causal mechanism (PMID 23867623), and additional cohorts report NPPA variants with hypertension history and BP responses (PMIDs 21276798, 26224401). However, this evidence is from population-based association/GWAS designs rather than causal segregation in independent probands or families, so full "Established" criteria as strictly defined are not clearly met, leaving the weight split between Established and Existing. Animal data (Nppa knockout rats, SHR linkage) support but do not substitute for human causal evidence.

Neither article examines stature/height. PMID 25688259 reports a suggestive (not genome-wide significant) association of OLFML2B with systolic blood pressure in Zuni Indians, a phenotype unrelated to height. PMID 30915543 is an evolutionary/expression/in-silico SNP analysis of olfactomedin-domain genes, noting OLFML2B has many predicted damaging SNPs, but provides no link to skeletal growth or body height. There is thus no genetic or biological evidence connecting OLFML2B variation to height, only incidental co-mention, supporting a Novel classification with a small allowance for indirect biological plausibility.

Human evidence links somatic DNMT3A clonal hematopoiesis (CHIP) mutations to atrial fibrillation: the allogeneic transplant cohort found AF in hospital occurred more often in carriers of DNMT3A/TET2/ASXL1 mutations with the greatest effect for DNMT3A (PMID 35724849), and large genome-wide/Mendelian randomization analyses report that genetic predisposition to CH (with DNMT3A as the dominant subtype) increases AF risk (PMIDs 35835912, 41541724). However, several studies and reviews attribute the AF signal chiefly to TET2 and ASXL1 rather than DNMT3A (PMIDs 38598228, 40804878), so the DNMT3A-specific association is suggestive but not definitive, and no germline DNMT3A variants have been shown to cause AF in independent probands/families. Supporting mechanistic work (DNMT3A silencing RASSF1A in cardiac fibrosis, paracrine fibroblast activation, arrhythmias in Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome) is largely animal/in vitro or non-AF phenotypes and supports the Hypothesized weight (PMIDs 24945829, 38242884, 38845031). Overall this fits "Existing" — credible but limited human association evidence, largely via the CHIP risk-factor pathway.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in CCAR1 associated with height or any anthropometric trait; the literature is dominated by cancer biology (PDAC, prostate, colon, medulloblastoma), autoantibody/myositis studies, and RNA/splicing biology. The only tangentially relevant work is the KDM4B–CCAR1–MED1 axis in osteoclast differentiation and bone homeostasis (PMID 34031372), which is mouse/in vitro and concerns bone resorption and osteoporosis rather than skeletal growth or stature, giving at best a weak biological rationale for a skeletal phenotype. The C. elegans hemidesmosome/perlecan splicing work (PMID 29748380) also touches extracellular matrix biology relevant to tissue architecture, but is non-human and not height-related. With no human association data and only indirect bone-related biology, the evidence base supports Novel with a moderate allowance for Hypothesized.

The strongest thyroid-specific evidence is from rats: congenic KDP rats carrying the Cblb nonsense mutation develop autoimmune thyroiditis with alopecia as a clinical sign of hypothyroidism (PMID 21918539), supported by the positional cloning of Cblb as the rat T1D susceptibility gene with thyroid infiltration (PMIDs 12118252, 15897618). These are animal, not human, data, so they support "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing/Established." Human evidence links CBLB variants to autoimmunity generally—an exon 12 SNP associated with type 1 diabetes (PMID 15629882), homozygous loss-of-function mutations causing early-onset autoimmunity and urticaria (PMID 36006710), and a GWAS locus for urticaria (PMID 37430141)—but none report hypothyroidism or autoimmune thyroiditis as a measured phenotype in patients. Because autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is a well-recognized mechanism of hypothyroidism and CBLB is a validated negative regulator of T-cell autoreactivity, a modest share goes to "Existing," but no human proband-level thyroid phenotype is documented, so "Established" is essentially excluded.

None of the provided articles report any human genetic association between RRBP1 variants and stature/height; the human genetic studies concern lipids (PMID 35931049), COPD susceptibility (PMID 35513865), blood pressure/potassium (PMID 36803854) and Alzheimer's risk (PMID 31951107), so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The only indirectly relevant biology is RRBP1/p180's well-documented role in ER ribosome association and procollagen/collagen biosynthesis and secretion (PMIDs 20647306, 22156060, 31004060), which could plausibly touch on connective tissue and skeletal growth, and a comparative fox transcriptome study in which RRBP1 appeared under artificial selection in animals differing in body size (PMID 34646484) — animal/in vitro evidence at best, which maps to Hypothesized. However, these links are speculative and not framed around growth or stature, so a substantial probability remains that the gene–height relationship is entirely Novel. Points are therefore split roughly evenly between Hypothesized and Novel with minimal weight to human-evidence categories.

The strongest link between EZH1 and skeletal/linear growth comes from a mouse study showing that combined Ezh1/Ezh2 loss in chondrocytes severely impairs growth plate chondrogenesis and skeletal growth (PMID 27897169); this is animal/functional evidence, supporting "Hypothesized" rather than "Established." Human EZH1 variant reports (PMIDs 37433783, 37314226, 38814056) describe dominant and recessive neurodevelopmental disorders, and one family with biallelic loss-of-function shows central precocious puberty—a condition that affects growth trajectory and final height—but the authors explicitly note absence of overgrowth or Weaver-like features, so direct height association is weak and unreplicated. The height GWAS and Weaver syndrome findings cited in these papers pertain to EZH2, not EZH1, and cannot be transferred to the paralog. No two independent human studies report EZH1 variants specifically associated with height measurements, so "Established" is excluded; a modest allocation to "Existing" reflects the precocious puberty/growth-related human phenotype.

Two large human rare-variant sequencing studies implicate UBR3 in cardiometabolic disease (PMID 39210047) and specifically report that protein-truncating variants in UBR3 independently increase BMI and type 2 diabetes risk (PMID 41073786). Type 2 diabetes and adiposity are canonical determinants of HbA1c, so this qualifies as association with a well-recognized precursor/risk factor rather than direct evidence on HbA1c levels themselves. Neither study reports HbA1c as the primary tested trait, and the two analyses draw on overlapping biobanks (UK Biobank, All of Us), limiting true independent replication for this specific quantitative phenotype. Other listed papers concern deafness, disc degeneration, IgA nephropathy, aneurysm, and adipogenesis, with only the adipogenesis work (PMID 41325391) offering weak metabolic-biology support. Therefore "Existing" is most probable, with some weight on "Established."

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in DGKH associated with hypertension or blood pressure traits; the DGKH literature is dominated by bipolar disorder, panic disorder, nephrolithiasis, melanoma, and lipid-signaling biochemistry. The only hypertension link is a generic family-level statement in a DGK review (PMID 27583247) noting that "several DGK isozymes" may be drug targets for cardiac hypertrophy and hypertension, without implicating DGKη specifically. A tangential mention of possible "vascular disorders" appears in the NPY-autoantibody GWAS (PMID 35627254), but no blood-pressure phenotype is tested. Thus there is no credible human association evidence (excluding Established/Existing), and only a very weak pathway-level rationale (diacylglycerol/PKC signaling relevant to vascular tone) that provides marginal support for Hypothesized; most weight belongs to Novel.

Two human studies present their own primary genetic results linking NR1H4 variants to cholesterol traits: the Icelandic whole-genome sequencing/imputation study identified the rare missense variant NR1H4 R436H associating with lower total and non-HDL cholesterol in ~150,000 individuals with protection from coronary artery disease (PMID 30271901), and the meta-analysis/pathway study reported that missense variants in NR1H4 associate with serum LDL levels in UK Biobank, concluding that steatosis-protective NR1H4 variants raise LDL (PMID 36098472). These are independent cohorts of human participants with variant-level data, which supports an Established call. Additional supportive but non-genetic human evidence comes from pharmacological FXR agonism (obeticholic acid) reproducibly raising LDL-c and lowering HDL-c (PMIDs 33636214, 31197565), consistent with an on-target FXR effect on lipoproteins. The remaining articles concern PFIC5/cholestasis phenotypes and are largely irrelevant or only incidental to LDL, so some probability remains on Existing in case the LDL-specific replication is judged insufficient.

None of the provided articles address platelets or platelet counts/function in relation to TNFRSF10B. The literature set concerns TRAIL/DR5-mediated apoptosis in cancer (CLL, mesothelioma, gastric carcinoma), autoimmune models, kidney disease, hepatocyte lipotoxicity, and plasma proteomic aging/PAH biomarkers, with no platelet phenotype measured. There are no human genetic variant studies linking TNFRSF10B to platelet traits; del(8p) in CLL spans multiple genes and concerns leukemia prognosis, not platelets. At most, a weak biological plausibility exists via generic apoptosis/hematopoiesis pathways (e.g., TRAIL effects on marrow hemopoiesis in MDS), justifying a small allocation to Hypothesized, but the dominant conclusion is Novel.

The strongest evidence is a human multi-biobank meta-analysis (All of Us, BioVU, UK Biobank) showing that clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential increases risk of aortic valve stenosis, with elevated risk specifically among carriers of TET2 or ASXL1 somatic mutations (PMID 41252200); aortic valve stenosis is the archetypal non-rheumatic valvular heart disease. Additional human evidence links ASXL1-mutant CHIP to inflammatory cardiovascular phenotypes and to prognosis in aortic stenosis (PMIDs 34298011, 40773119, 38598228), supporting an association rather than definitive causation. Mechanistic support comes largely from mouse and in vitro work (ASXL1-mutant myeloid cells driving inflammation and atherosclerosis; Tet2-/- bone marrow promoting valve calcification; PMIDs 39653824, 39663508), which underpins the Hypothesized share. No study reports germline ASXL1 variants segregating in independent probands or families causing valvular disease, so Established cannot be supported; the somatic association evidence is credible but limited, making Existing the best fit.

phenotype: Eosinophils/100 leukocytes in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: Only one article in this list reports its own human genetic-variant results linking IL5 to blood eosinophil levels: PMID 42497191, where IL5 rs2069812 showed a gene-dose association with blood eosinophilia and reduced lung function in 125 adults with asthma. A second genetic study (PMID 32009195) examined IL-5 pathway variants in EGPA patients treated with mepolizumab but found no significant associations, so it does not provide replication. The remaining literature is overwhelmingly biological/therapeutic: IL-5 drives eosinophil differentiation, survival and trafficking, and anti-IL-5/IL-5R biologics (mepolizumab, benralizumab, depemokimab) deplete blood eosinophils, which strongly supports at least a Hypothesized mechanistic link (PMIDs 38938056, 35243803, 39115364, 40766318). Because independent replication of variant-level association in separate human cohorts is not demonstrated here, "Established" cannot be supported, and "Existing" is the most probable category, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the single association is considered insufficient.

None of the provided articles report any association between CBX2 variants and height or stature in humans; the human genetic literature here concerns 46,XY/46,XX disorders of sex development (PMIDs 19361780, 23219007, 31719618, 29998616) and an incidental schizophrenia family variant (PMID 37763159), so no evidence supports Established or Existing. The only biologically suggestive link is indirect: CBX2/Polycomb regulates Hox genes and axial skeletal patterning, with mouse homeotic transformations after mutation of the nucleosome compaction region (PMID 28280206), and M33/Cbx2-deficient mice show proliferative/cell-cycle defects (PMID 15377996), which could plausibly relate to skeletal growth. These are animal/in vitro data only, supporting at most a Hypothesized relationship. Given the weakness and indirectness of even this mechanistic link, the majority of probability falls on Novel with a substantial share on Hypothesized.

The only provided article concerns AHDC1 deletions in Xia-Gibbs syndrome, where FAM76A is merely one of eight neighboring genes within a large contiguous 1p36.11 deletion; it reports no height phenotype and cannot attribute any trait to FAM76A specifically. No study in the list reports FAM76A variants associated with stature or growth in humans, families, or cohorts, so Established is untenable. There is likewise no expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking FAM76A biology to skeletal growth, leaving only a weak, speculative possibility for Hypothesized based on the deletion's association with a developmental syndrome that may include growth features. The co-mention is essentially incidental, so Novel receives the bulk of the probability mass.

The strongest human genetic evidence is the multi-ancestry lipid GWAS integration study (PMID 35931049), which prioritizes RRBP1 as a functionally supported candidate gene at a blood-lipid locus in 1.6 million individuals, with eQTL colocalization and chromatin/TF evidence. A second paper (PMID 36803854) restates that GWASs link RRBP1 variants to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and serum lipoprotein levels, but its own results concern renin trafficking and blood pressure in animal models, so it is a citation rather than independent replication. Supporting mechanistic plausibility comes from mouse liver wrappER–mitochondria contact studies showing RRBP1-dependent contacts regulate VLDL secretion and systemic lipid homeostasis (PMID 33730569, 37534187), which is animal/in vitro and thus hypothesized-level. Other listed articles concern COPD, Alzheimer's microglia, cancer, and ER polysome biology and are not relevant to cholesterol genetics. Because only one PMID provides primary human variant-level evidence, Established cannot be met and Existing is the most probable category.

Biallelic ANAPC1 variants cause Rothmund-Thomson syndrome type 1, in which short stature (a height phenotype) is a core clinical feature. Primary human genetic evidence comes from PMID 31303264, which identified a deep intronic splicing mutation plus second alleles in ten affected individuals from seven independent families with functional validation (NMD, reduced ANAPC1 protein), and PMID 35664819, an independent report of RTS type 1 with biallelic ANAPC1 mutations; PMID 42210937 adds a further clinically diagnosed proband with an ANAPC1 variant. These are point/intronic single-gene variants, not multigene CNVs, and are in humans, supporting Established. Some uncertainty remains because "height" here is a syndromic short-stature component rather than a directly measured quantitative trait association (no GWAS of height implicates ANAPC1; the GWAS locus in PMID 37629076 concerns bone mineral density), so substantial weight is retained for Existing.

None of the provided articles report a human genetic association between YLPM1 variants and height or stature. The human rare-variant studies implicate YLPM1 in BMI/severe obesity (PMIDs 41168175, 39484254) and psychiatric disease (PMID 39210047), and BMI is not a measure of height; other papers concern clonal hematopoiesis (PMIDs 34568833, 38744975, 40950448, 42262879) or brain cell-type eQTLs (PMID 42372879), all irrelevant to skeletal growth. The only "growth" context is a pig multi-omics study where YLPM1 was a TWAS candidate for teat number, not height, and it is non-human (PMID 41463911). Thus evidence for a YLPM1–height link is essentially absent, with only weak indirect biological plausibility via body-size/anthropometric traits, warranting mostly Novel with a modest allocation to Hypothesized.

Human germline hemizygous DOCK11 variants have been reported in multiple independent probands and families (Boussard et al., PMID 36952639; Block et al., PMID 37342957; PMID 40274249), with platelet-related phenotypes including autoimmune cytopenias/thrombocytopenia and, importantly, abnormal platelet ultrastructural morphology and spreading, consistent with a CDC42/actin-cytoskeleton mechanism directly relevant to platelet size determination. However, none of these abstracts explicitly report mean platelet volume as a measured quantitative outcome or a GWAS association, so the evidence supports a strongly linked precursor/mechanistic phenotype (platelet morphology abnormalities) rather than a direct, replicated MPV association. This best fits "Existing," with some probability for "Established" given multiple independent human cohorts with platelet abnormalities, and residual probability for "Hypothesized" since much of the supporting mechanistic work (CDC42 activation, actin remodeling, knockdown, mouse DOCK-D models) is in vitro or in animals.

No article in this list reports a direct association between BSN variants and hip circumference as a measured trait. However, multiple independent human studies report rare protein-truncating/predicted loss-of-function variants in BSN associated with markedly increased BMI and severe adult-onset obesity, replicated across UK Biobank, All of Us, and clinical early-onset obesity cohorts (PMIDs 38575728, 37865656, 36865254, 39228706), and rare BSN variants were also linked to BMI in the HYPOMAP population analysis (39910307); obesity phenotypes in BSN PTV carriers are also described clinically (40393460). Because BMI/adiposity is a well-recognized, tightly correlated determinant of hip circumference but not the exact trait, the evidence best supports "Existing" rather than "Established". Some weight remains for Established given the strength and replication of human adiposity findings, and a small share for Hypothesized based on hypothalamic/synaptic feeding-circuit biology and mouse/iPSC functional work.

ENTREP1/FAM189A2 is directly implicated in atrial fibrillation by two large human sequencing studies: a meta-analysis of 52,416 AF cases identifying a novel rare coding variant burden association for FAM189A2 with broad replication in MyCode, deCODE and UK Biobank (PMID 40050430), and a subsequent massive-scale rare variant association study of ~130,000 AF cases that again lists FAM189A2 among exome-wide significant genes not captured by GWAS loci (PMID 42147184). These are human, variant-level, replicated burden analyses, which strongly supports at least "Existing" and edges toward "Established"; however, the two studies come from largely overlapping consortium data and report gene-level burden associations rather than independent probands or segregating families, so full "Established" status is not unambiguous. The remaining papers (PMIDs 34927784, 38275610, 40243508, 41632327) concern ITCH/CXCR4 biology, CIRCI genotyping, and Crohn's disease TWAS, or merely restate the AF gene list as background, and thus add little independent causal evidence.

None of the provided articles measure alkaline phosphatase or report human variants in MYO1B associated with alkaline phosphatase levels or ALP-related disorders. The genetic studies cited concern esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (PMID 37673066), type 1 diabetes networks (PMID 22344559), and multigene 2q deletions (PMIDs 23840981, 17352388), none of which single out MYO1B for an ALP phenotype. The only tenuous biological rationale comes from MYO1B's role at the apical brush border of intestinal and renal proximal tubule epithelia (PMIDs 39636728, 26361046) — compartments where intestinal/tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase resides — and from hepatic stellate cell fibrosis work (PMID 40025044), where cholestatic ALP elevation is conceivable but never assessed. These are indirect, speculative connections rather than demonstrated links, so the evidence base is best described as absent, with only a minor allowance for a hypothesized brush-border/hepatobiliary mechanism.

None of the provided articles report height, stature, or growth measurements as an outcome of SCAF4 variation; no GWAS or quantitative-trait study of height implicating SCAF4 is present. The clinical series (PMIDs 32730804, 39668183, 36333968, 40290495) describe an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder with skeletal/structural anomalies (clubfoot, scoliosis, hip dysplasia), which is only indirectly and weakly suggestive of an effect on skeletal growth/height, and short stature is not explicitly reported in the abstracts. Other listed papers concern ALS structural variants, RNAPII elongation biology, Down syndrome mouse models, or carp QTL (non-human, feed efficiency), none of which address human height. Therefore, the strongest defensible position lies between a biologically plausible (skeletal involvement) hypothesis and no evidence at all, with limited support for a documented human height association.

None of the provided articles report any association between MICA gene variants and human stature/height. The only "height" mentions come from homonym acronyms: "MICA" as Minimally Invasive Chevron Akin foot surgery (PMID 35193413) and "MICA" as microphthalmia/anophthalmia, where orbital height (OH) is an ocular measurement, not body height (PMID 38538530). All genuine MICA gene articles concern NKG2D-mediated immunity, cancer risk, autoimmunity, transplantation, and viral hepatitis outcomes, with no plausible mechanistic link to skeletal growth or height. Therefore the co-mentions are incidental and provide no logical basis for a gene–phenotype relationship.

No article reports variants in NF1 being associated with mean corpuscular volume in human probands, families, or cohorts. The Tibetan sheep genome scan (PMID 27230812) lists NF1 among selection candidates but attributes the MCV/MCHC association to EPAS1 variants, and it is a non-human study, so it can only support a hypothesized biological link. The selumetinib trial (PMID 42527881) documents a statistically significant rise in MCV in children with NF1-associated plexiform neurofibromas, but this is a MEK-inhibitor drug effect in NF1 patients rather than a genotype–phenotype association, offering at best indirect human support for RAS/MAPK involvement in erythrocyte indices. All remaining papers concern NF1 mutation spectra, diagnostic criteria, and tumour surveillance with no hematologic index measurements. Therefore the weight falls on Hypothesized, with limited residual probability for Existing based on the drug-induced human MCV change and none for Established.

None of the listed articles report a genetic association between APOC3 variants and HbA1c levels; HbA1c appears mostly as a covariate or a correlate of circulating apoC-III protein in diabetic cohorts (PMIDs 35024053, 15375785, 29576550). The strongest human genetic data concern APOC3 variants (C482T, C455T, SstI) and triglyceride/metabolic syndrome phenotypes (PMIDs 21749608, 33389539, 37186438), which include hyperglycemia as a component, providing indirect, precursor-level support that could justify "Existing." Explicit APOC3 genotype studies in diabetes (PMIDs 15375785, 15642486) found no association of APOC3 polymorphisms with lipid/metabolic parameters, weakening a direct claim. Biologically, apoC-III inhibits lipoprotein lipase, influences insulin sensitivity and triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism (PMIDs 38039351, 34981790), giving a plausible mechanistic link to glycemic traits, so "Hypothesized" carries the largest weight, with "Established" essentially unsupported by replicated variant-level HbA1c evidence.

Human evidence linking PKD1 variants to cardiac dysfunction exists but is limited to isolated case reports: a 70-year-old with a PKD1 frameshift and progressive dilated/contractile dysfunction (PMID 30464138) and an infant with fatal DCM carrying a PKD1 nonsense variant, although compound heterozygous JPH2 variants confound causality (PMID 32879264). The Mayo/zebrafish study (PMID 23376035) shows heart failure phenotypes in pkd2-mutant fish and an ADPKD–idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy association in patients, but that association was strongest for PKD2, not PKD1. Reviews (PMIDs 38096797, 37023534) mention cardiovascular involvement and heart failure as ADPKD extrarenal manifestations, but this is background rather than primary evidence, and most remaining papers are renal genotype–phenotype/mutation-screening studies with no cardiac endpoints. With only one or two confounded probands and much of the mechanistic support coming from animal models, the evidence supports "Existing" rather than "Established."

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in GOLIM4 associated with height or any stature-related trait. The most relevant is a bovine genome-wide association study where GOLIM4 fell within a window associated with average daily gain and feed efficiency in Nellore cattle (PMID 27760167) — a growth-related trait, but in a non-human species and based on multi-gene genomic windows, which supports at most a hypothesized link. Other papers describe GOLIM4/GPP130 biology in Golgi trafficking, manganese sensing, podocyte cytoskeleton, and as an incidentally detected protein or somatic variant in cancer studies (PMIDs 29381698, 32820145, 28709640, 25982296, 37760635, 37760246), none of which connect it to skeletal growth or stature. Therefore the evidence base is largely incidental co-mention, favoring Novel with some weight to Hypothesized given the animal growth-trait signal.

phenotype: Eosinophils/100 leukocytes in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: No article in this list reports a germline genetic association study (e.g., GWAS) of DNMT3A variants with eosinophil percentage of leukocytes, so the strict criterion for "Established" (two or more independent human cohorts/probands demonstrating the association in their own results) is not met. The closest direct human evidence is the targeted NGS series of idiopathic hypereosinophilia (PMID 39042228), where somatic DNMT3A mutations were detected in patients with hypereosinophilia, though only in 2/28 cases and with explicit caution about interpretation; MDS with eosinophilia (PMID 42570659) is similarly suggestive but indirect. Clonal hematopoiesis studies (PMIDs 41309676, 41206888, 41746260, 40755316) show DNMT3A somatic variants in humans drive myeloid clonal expansion and inflammatory phenotypes, a plausible mechanistic route to altered leukocyte differentials, supporting an "Existing"/precursor-phenotype rationale. Mechanistic and murine/in vitro work on DNMT3A in hematopoietic stem cell fate and myeloid inflammation (PMIDs 35931086, 33087320, 25693834) supports "Hypothesized." Overall the evidence is suggestive but not definitive for this specific automated-count trait.

None of the provided articles report a primary human GWAS or variant-level finding for height at PPP6R3; the corpus is dominated by bone mineral density, hip geometry, and osteoporosis studies. The hip geometry meta-analysis (PMID 30888730) identifies rs7102273 near LRP5/PPP6R3 for femoral neck traits and mentions looking up these SNPs for association with height, but height was used as a covariate and no height result is reported, so it cannot support Established. Other papers (PMIDs 36416764, 28743860, 42260878, 41957283) implicate PPP6R3 in BMD and lean mass, skeletal traits that are biologically adjacent to but not equivalent to stature, and functional support comes from mouse Ppp6r3 deletion (animal, hence Hypothesized). The phosphatase-6/SAPS biochemistry paper (PMID 19835610) provides only mechanistic context. Overall, the evidence best supports a biologically plausible skeletal-growth link with limited, indirect human variant evidence for height.

No article reports that TET2 variants determine LDL cholesterol concentrations in humans; the human literature concerns somatic TET2 mutations (CHIP) and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, aortic valve stenosis and vasculitis, with LDL treated as a covariate or effect modifier rather than an outcome (PMID 28636844, 38349357, 40900105, 41252200). The strongest lipid-related human data are indirect: an LDL-stratified analysis of CHIP-associated ASCVD risk (PMID 38349357) and a statin/HMGCR Mendelian randomization study linking lipid-lowering pathways to clonal hematopoiesis risk (PMID 42528572), which addresses LDL pathway → CH rather than TET2 → LDL. Mechanistic support (Tet2-deficient bone marrow accelerating atherosclerosis in Ldlr-/- mice, NLRP3/IL-1β inflammasome activation, colchicine and canakinumab responses) is largely murine or in vitro and therefore supports a hypothesized, biology-based link (PMIDs 28104796, 37781816, 29471939, 39196062, 39212933). Consequently, most weight belongs to Hypothesized, with a substantial share to Existing because TET2 CHIP is robustly associated in humans with LDL-driven atherosclerotic disease, and only minimal weight to Established.

None of the three provided articles addresses height or stature in any way. ENDOD1 appears only incidentally: as an amniotic fluid protein associated with congenital kidney anomalies (PMID 33987838), as a transcript altered in murine cortical injury with IL-6 overexpression (PMID 18000830), and as a differentially expressed gene in red deer lymph nodes after mycobacterial challenge (PMID 26620077). No human genetic variant, GWAS signal, or growth-related biology is reported. The zebrafish PLS3 growth-reduction finding concerns a different gene, not ENDOD1, so it provides no hypothesized mechanism for ENDOD1 and height.

None of the provided articles report any genetic association or variant-level evidence linking ITGB8 to asthma; the human genetic studies concern inflammatory bowel disease (PMID 28067908), cognitive decline (PMID 41720779), and brain arteriovenous malformations (PMID 20019187). The only asthma-adjacent biology is indirect: ITGB8 is an activator of latent TGF-β in the airway, is altered in COPD, and is upregulated on lung fibroblasts by IL-1β via chromatin remodeling (PMIDs 21878622, 20519498), which provides a plausible mechanistic link to airway remodeling and inflammation. Additional ITGB8 lung data are cancer-related (PMID 22753015) rather than asthma-related. Thus the evidence supports at most a hypothesized, pathway-based relationship, with a substantial chance that the co-mention is essentially incidental (novel).

Only one article in the provided set reports platelet measurements in relation to SPTB variants: the whole-exome sequencing cohort of 41 hereditary spherocytosis patients (PMID 39378964), which found significantly lower platelet levels in SPTB-mutated patients compared with ANK1-mutated patients. That is a single human cohort with genotype–phenotype data, which supports "Existing" but is not replicated, so "Established" cannot be supported (no second independent proband/family/cohort study with platelet outcomes). All remaining papers concern erythrocyte membrane disorders (spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, pyropoikilocytosis) and mention SPTB only in the context of red cell phenotypes, with no platelet data. The biological plausibility (β-spectrin as a cytoskeletal component also relevant to megakaryocyte/platelet membranes, and hypersplenism/splenectomy effects on platelet counts) supports a residual "Hypothesized" weight, while "Novel" is unlikely given the direct platelet observation.

The strongest primary human genetic evidence is Ruark et al. (PMID 23242139), which found mosaic protein-truncating PPM1D variants enriched in breast and ovarian cancer cases versus controls, and Akbari et al. (PMID 24262437), which replicated an excess of truncating PPM1D mutations in blood of ovarian cancer patients with an elevated rate of prior breast cancer. However, these are mosaic/clonal hematopoiesis variants rather than classical germline predisposition alleles, and a large replication study (PMID 30850729) found no overall association with breast cancer risk, while PMID 31242196 and the clonal hematopoiesis studies (PMIDs 40950448, 42262879) indicate such PPM1D mutations often arise as a consequence of chemotherapy selection. Additional human tumor data show somatic 17q23 amplification and overexpression of PPM1D in breast tumors with functional oncogenic properties (PMIDs 12021784, 16254685, 20543821, 16897432), supporting a biological role but as a somatic driver within an amplicon rather than a replicated germline risk gene. Panel-testing reports (PMIDs 28423363, 32295079) mention PPM1D mosaic variants but do not independently establish causality. Therefore "Existing" is the most defensible category, with limited weight on "Established."

COL4A4 variants are firmly established as a cause of Alport syndrome/thin basement membrane nephropathy, and multiple human case reports and cohorts describe hypertension as a clinical feature in COL4A4-variant carriers (PMID 39398663 with a rare COL4A4 mutation; PMID 41069567 with the c.1321_1369+3del autosomal dominant family; PMID 38547857 trigenic case; PMID 40004525 cohort correlating genotype with hypertension among other features). However, in all of these, hypertension is a secondary, nonspecific consequence of progressive glomerular disease and CKD rather than a directly caused primary phenotype, and no study isolates COL4A4 as a causal determinant of blood pressure. The report of familial COL4A3/4/5 kidney disease phenocopying hypertensive nephropathy (PMID 40492141) strengthens a link to a hypertension-associated renal phenotype but again through CKD. This best fits "Existing" — credible human evidence linking COL4A4 variation to a well-recognized precursor/mechanism of hypertension — rather than replicated, definitive causal proof required for "Established."

Multiple human case-control studies directly test TNFRSF10A (DR4) germline variants against colorectal cancer risk: the German DACHS study of 659 cases/607 controls found Thr209Arg heterozygotes at reduced risk and a risk-associated 626C-683C haplotype (PMID 17035413); a Chinese study of 1,078 cases/1,175 controls reported rs13278062 GT/TT associated with lower risk and better survival, with CRISPR-based functional follow-up (PMID 29446085); and a small Pakistani study reported an association for DR4 626C>G (PMID 26518902). These are independent human cohorts, supporting more than a purely biological hypothesis, but the findings involve different variants, modest effect sizes, and inconsistent replication (e.g., Glu228Ala null in one study, significant in others), so they represent risk association rather than demonstrated causation. Additional literature is expression/functional (TRAIL receptor expression in adenomas and carcinomas, drug sensitization in cell lines: PMIDs 12845629, 15911244, 37451215), which supports mechanistic plausibility but not causality. Several listed papers concern unrelated phenotypes (AMD, MS, psoriatic arthritis, proteomic aging) and do not bear on colorectal cancer.

The strongest human evidence is the large sequencing meta-analysis of 52,416 AF cases, which found a rare coding-variant burden association for PKP2 with broad replication in MyCode, deCODE and UK Biobank (PMID 40050430), supported by other rare-variant cohort analyses (PMIDs 38922602, 36669898) and by GWAS implicating PKP2 as a prioritized AF locus (PMID 30061737). Clinical ARVC cohorts show that PKP2/desmosomal genotype influences atrial structural abnormalities and prevalence of atrial fibrillation/flutter in patients (PMIDs 27572111, 23994726), and a familial PKP2 deletion segregated with lone AF, although a multigene deletion cannot isolate PKP2 (PMID 30364518). Mechanistic support comes from a murine PKP2 cardiac-knockout model showing atrial cardiomyopathy and pro-arrhythmic calcium handling (PMID 39446303), which is corroborative but non-human. Because much of the human evidence is burden-association or AF arising as a secondary manifestation of PKP2-related cardiomyopathy rather than multiple independent probands/families with monogenic AF, points are split roughly evenly between Established and Existing, with Existing slightly favored.

No human study in this set examines BMI, obesity, or adiposity in relation to PHF3; the human genetics literature here concerns alcohol dependence (PMIDs 23324950, 22096494, 24961364) and autism/neurodevelopmental disorders via multigenic CNVs (PMIDs 38519481, 37961520), none of which are recognized precursors or mechanisms for BMI. The only body-size link is non-human: PHF3 appears among genes in runs-of-homozygosity islands annotated to body size/weight in American mink (PMID 38389405) and in selection signatures for environmental adaptation in Wuzhishan pigs (PMID 40921116), which at best supports a weak hypothesized biological relevance. Because these are livestock population-genomic annotations rather than functional or human data, they only modestly support "Hypothesized." No article demonstrates human variants in PHF3 associated with BMI, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported.

The listed articles document numerous human probands and families carrying HBB variants (β-thalassemia, sickle cell disease, unstable hemoglobins such as Hb Santa Ana, the Corfu δ0β+ allele) that produce hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis and compensatory erythroid response — mechanisms directly and unavoidably linked to reticulocyte percentage. However, none of the provided abstracts report reticulocyte percentage as a measured outcome or as a quantitative trait associated with HBB variants; the hematological phenotyping is described generically (anemia, microcytosis, HbA2/HbF levels). Thus the evidence supports HBB variation acting on a well-recognized precursor/mechanism of altered reticulocyte counts (Existing) rather than replicated direct trait association reported in these papers' own results. Points remain in Hypothesized only for the possibility that all evidence here is mechanistic/background rather than variant-level phenotype data, and Novel is essentially excluded given the clear erythrocyte biology of HBB.

Only one human genetic study directly tests ANGPTL3 variants against vitamin D levels: PMID 37955843, reporting associations of rs10789117, rs17458195 and rs11207997 with vitamin D status in 1002 cardiovascular disease/non-CVD participants. This is a single cohort with no independent replication in the provided list, so the Established threshold (two independent human variant-based studies) is not met. Supporting mechanistic plausibility comes from PMID 32510837, which shows human hepatic ANGPTL3 expression relates to vitamin D receptor/VD-related gene expression in obesity and NAFLD, but this is expression rather than variant data. All remaining articles concern ANGPTL3 in lipoprotein metabolism, therapeutics (evinacumab, zodasiran, ASO/siRNA) and cardiovascular risk, mentioning vitamin D only incidentally (e.g., PMID 41062796 in the context of cholesterol-derived hormone synthesis). Hence "Existing" best describes the evidence, with residual probability on "Hypothesized" if the single association study is judged too weak.

phenotype: Erythrocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: Multiple independent human reports describe germline PARN variants causing dyskeratosis congenita/Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome and telomere biology disorders with bone marrow failure, anemia and pancytopenia (PMIDs 26342108, 26810774, 41741124, 39649862, 40896794, 40859110, 31448843), and PARN variants are also found in young MDS cohorts (39015540). These are human studies in independent probands/families and establish that PARN disruption impairs hematopoiesis, a well-recognized mechanism reducing red cell counts. However, none of these papers directly measures or reports an association with the quantitative trait "erythrocytes [#/volume] by automated count" (e.g., no GWAS or quantitative blood-count association is presented), so the link is via a strongly related precursor phenotype (bone marrow failure/anemia) rather than direct evidence for the measured trait. Accordingly, "Existing" is the best fit, with some weight for "Established" given the replicated marrow-failure/cytopenia findings, and residual weight for "Hypothesized."

The strongest human evidence is PMID 31085352, which reported two multigenerational American families carrying heterozygous LRP6 β-propeller missense mutations (p.A201V, p.N185H) in whom all affected individuals were significantly taller than average Americans (P < 0.005), with height Z-scores measured directly as part of the phenotype. This is a single publication, however, so the requirement of at least two independent PMIDs reporting height data with LRP6 variants in their own results is not met, capping the assessment at "Existing." Other human LRP6 studies (osteoporosis/BMD/fracture, tooth agenesis) do not report height associations for LRP6 — in PMID 20390408 the height association belonged to LCT, and in PMID 16355283 the frame-size association was attributed to LRP5. Supporting biology comes from mice with nestin-Cre–driven Lrp6 deletion showing reduced body length and impaired skeletal growth (PMID 26273519), which would only support "Hypothesized," so some probability remains there.

None of the provided articles report any genetic or phenotypic association between ARMC8 and height or stature/skeletal growth traits. The human genetic studies present concern hypertension rare variants (PMID: 25519312) and HDL cholesterol SNP×SNP interactions (PMID: 25329471), neither of which relates to height. The remaining literature is molecular/functional, describing ARMC8 as a CTLH E3 ubiquitin ligase component interacting with α-catenin, HRS, and tau (PMIDs: 17467196, 18215130, 20224683, 40317322), or oncology studies in ovarian cancer and osteosarcoma cell lines (PMIDs: 26232863, 27712595). Only the osteosarcoma work touches bone-derived cells and Wnt/β-catenin signalling, offering a very tenuous biological rationale for skeletal growth, which supports a small allocation to Hypothesized. Overall the evidence base is essentially incidental co-mention, so Novel is the most likely category.

None of the provided articles report genetic variants in HOXC9 associated with waist-to-hip ratio or body fat distribution in humans; the only human GWAS/TWAS paper here links HOXC9 expression to upper gastrointestinal disease, not WHR (PMID 37198407). However, there is directly relevant biology: a review explicitly attributes to HOXC9 a central role in adipose distribution and metabolic health (PMID 39351453), and HOXC9 is used as a white/beige-versus-brown adipocyte depot marker in human adipose tissue studies across subcutaneous, visceral and perirenal depots (PMID 25706927). Additional papers concern Hox9 axial patterning in mouse limb, vertebrae and spinal circuits (PMIDs 21383175, 7547473, 29069594, 18430026), which supports a positional/regional identity mechanism plausibly underlying depot-specific fat distribution but is animal-based and not variant-based. This pattern best fits "Hypothesized," with residual probability for "Novel" since no study here measures WHR, and only small weight for "Existing/Established" given the absence of cited human variant associations.

No article in this set reports a human genetic association between UBE2Z variants and height or stature.
