Human studies of UBE2Z (chiefly rs46522) concern coronary artery disease, hypertriglyceridemia, type 2 diabetes, and insomnia/CVD pleiotropy, none of which are precursors or subtypes of height (PMIDs 26238946, 26602883, 32685059, 32127821, 28840129, 24573017, 28710368). The only growth-related evidence is a porcine GWAS/eQTL colocalization implicating UBE2Z in age to 120 kg, backfat, and loin muscle depth (PMID 42510762), which is animal data and relates to growth/body size rather than human height, supporting at most a "hypothesized" biological link. Remaining papers describe ubiquitin/FAT10 conjugation biology with no height relevance. Therefore the evidence favors Novel, with a substantial share to Hypothesized due to the pig growth-trait finding and general ubiquitin-pathway roles in growth regulation.

Three large human sequencing studies report rare protein-truncating variant burden in UBR3 associated with adiposity/cardiometabolic phenotypes: PMID 39210047 (pan-ancestry rare coding burden across three biobanks, UBR3 for cardiometabolic disease), PMID 41073786 (WGS in UK Biobank + All of Us, UBR3 PTVs independently increase BMI and T2D risk), and PMID 41651857 (WGS anthropometric traits, UBR3 PTVs associated with a 2.7 kg/m2 increase in BMI, plus WHRadjBMI analyses). These are human, gene-level (not CNV) associations in very large cohorts, which is strong evidence for an adiposity role. However, the specific endpoint here—mean waist circumference—is not itself the reported outcome; BMI, WHRadjBMI and cardiometabolic disease are closely related adiposity measures rather than the exact trait, and the studies substantially overlap in datasets (UK Biobank, All of Us), limiting true independent replication. Therefore Existing is the most defensible category, with meaningful probability for Established given the replicated multi-biobank adiposity signal.

The GIANT meta-analysis of 32 GWAS with follow-up in 29 additional studies (PMID 20935629) reports a genome-wide significant WHRadjBMI signal at the NISCH-STAB1 locus, which is direct human genetic evidence, but the association is assigned to a two-gene interval and cannot unambiguously single out STAB1. No second independent human genetic study in this list replicates a STAB1-specific WHRadjBMI association, so the "at least two PMIDs" bar for Established is not met. Supporting but non-genetic human data include circulating STAB1 levels correlating positively with BMI and inversely with lipid measures alongside atherosclerotic plaque burden (PMID 41259134), and STAB1 rare variants in hypoalphalipoproteinemia (PMID 35460704), which relate to adiposity/metabolic phenotypes rather than fat distribution per se. Other listed papers concern proteomics, ferritin metabolism, Parkinson's, macrophage biology, or cancer and are not relevant to WHRadjBMI. Overall the evidence best fits Existing, with meaningful probability for Established given the size and replication design of the GWAS.

No article in this set reports human genetic variants in IGF2BP3 associated with stature; the human GWAS provided concern dental maturation (PMID 36437532) and tau PET burden (PMID 33426524), neither of which is height. The strongest growth-related evidence is biological/animal: a pigeon GWAS identifying IGF2BP3 alongside NCAPG/LCORL and MSTN for body weight and body size (PMID 38069460), HMGA2-dependent regulation of IMP family genes in pygmy-phenotype mice (PMID 15225648), and IGF2BP3 dysregulation in stunted dwarf chickens (PMID 32010193). One human-relevant paper positions IMP3/IGF2BP3 as a positional/functional candidate for Silver-Russell syndrome, a growth-restriction disorder (PMID 12161597), plus IGF2BP3's role in IGF2 signaling (PMIDs 11713986, 41343669), which nudges some weight toward Existing but falls short of demonstrated variant-level association in probands or cohorts. Most remaining papers are cancer/m6A mechanistic studies with no bearing on stature, so Hypothesized best fits the overall evidence.

Multiple independent human reports describe NEUROD1 coding variants in probands and families with hyperglycemia and documented HbA1c elevation: a novel homozygous missense (p.Ile150Asn) causing permanent neonatal diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% (PMID 29521454), a novel nonsense variant segregating across four generations of atypical familial diabetes (PMID 36222545), a heterozygous frameshift in an autoantibody-negative pediatric diabetes cohort (PMID 35769090), and a c.-108G>C variant with maternal co-segregation diagnosed via glucose/HbA1c criteria (PMID 41255541). A large gene-level burden analysis in 2,571 MODY cases versus >155,000 controls found significant enrichment of rare damaging NEUROD1 variants, establishing it as a low-penetrance MODY gene (PMID 40779032), and further cohort/review data support MODY6 (PMIDs 30793219, 31216263, 41175096). Since HbA1c is the standard diagnostic and monitoring measure of the diabetes phenotype these variants cause, the gene–trait link is supported by replicated human genetic evidence, though penetrance is modest and no direct quantitative HbA1c association study is cited, leaving substantial weight on "Existing."
open_targets_trait: maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 6

literature_justification: The listed literature is uniformly about PKD1/PKD2 variants causing autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, not about a phenotype called "protein." The term "protein" appears only generically (e.g., "PKD1 protein-truncating variants," "mechanical protein polycystin-1," "ciliary structural protein") and is a non-specific word rather than a measurable trait or disease entity, so these are incidental co-mentions rather than genetic association evidence. There is strong human variant evidence for PKD1 in ADPKD cohorts (PMIDs 22508176, 32457805, 31740684), but none of these establish an association with "protein" as a phenotype. Some weight is retained for "hypothesized" because PKD1 clearly encodes and functions through a protein (polycystin-1) whose truncation and trafficking are mechanistically characterized, giving a biologically relevant but not phenotype-specific link. Overall the pairing appears to be a generic-term artifact, favoring Novel.

None of the provided articles report any association between ZBTB1 variants and height or any growth/skeletal phenotype. The strongest human genetic evidence involves eczema susceptibility (PMID 34785669) and an incidental colorectal cancer variant annotation (PMID 37686578), neither of which is a recognized precursor or mechanism for stature. The remaining work concerns lymphoid development in mice (PMIDs 22753936, 22201126) and EYA3/ZBTB1 transcriptional control during myogenesis in vitro (PMID 38026174); the myogenesis link is only tangentially related to musculoskeletal growth and does not constitute evidence for height. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for a hypothesized biological connection via muscle differentiation.

Human evidence links de novo SMARCD1 variants to a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder / Coffin-Siris syndrome 11 (PMID 30879640, 39389935, 38114583, 23556151), and these SWI/SNF-related syndromes commonly feature growth abnormalities (small hands/feet, dysmorphism, and in CSS often short stature), which provides indirect human support for a growth/height-related phenotype, though none of the abstracts report height or stature as a measured outcome. A separate human cohort study of Caucasian women examined SMARCD1 polymorphisms with bone mineral density, a skeletal trait but not height, and reported significant associations only for CALM3 (PMID 25396734). No GWAS or replicated human association with height per se is present in this list, so "Established" is not supportable — I cannot name two papers reporting height-associated variants in independent probands or cohorts. Remaining evidence is mechanistic/animal (Drosophila Bap60, mouse cardiac and ESC studies), supporting a plausible developmental-growth biology basis, hence substantial weight to Hypothesized.

LDLR variants are definitively causal for familial hypercholesterolemia and premature atherosclerotic/coronary disease (PMID 25487149, 41166440, 31491741), which is a well-recognized precursor and major etiologic pathway to (ischemic) heart failure, supporting at least "Existing." Human case-level evidence links LDLR pathogenic variants to heart failure outcomes: HoFH with severe HF and EF 20% (PMID 41694628), ischemic HF in homozygous FH (PMID 30335000), and LDLR variant carriers among heart transplant recipients (PMID 36769882), but these are isolated case reports of a downstream ischemic complication rather than replicated proband/family evidence that LDLR variation causes HF per se. Notably, a Mendelian randomization analysis found no causal relationship between LDLR and HF (PMID 40391737), while circulating LDLR protein (not variants) tracks with CHF outcomes (PMID 33590771), which is mechanistic/biomarker-level evidence. Remaining papers (PCSK9–LDLR axis reviews, SGLT2i lipid reviews) provide biological plausibility rather than genetic proof, so a substantial share stays in "Hypothesized." Established is not warranted because two independent variant-level studies demonstrating LDLR causation of heart failure itself cannot be cited.

The only article connecting LATS2 to height is a review of Hippo signaling in exercise physiology (PMID 26940657), which states that human genome-wide association studies have linked LATS2 (along with TEAD1, YAP1, VGLL2/3/4) to body height. This is a restatement of published GWAS findings rather than primary evidence generated in that paper, so it supports a credible but secondhand human genetic association rather than replicated primary demonstration. No other listed article reports height phenotypes; the remaining papers concern cancer, Hippo pathway biology, mesothelioma, fibrosis, or a multigene 13q12 microdeletion (PMID 37239394), which cannot isolate LATS2. Because I cannot cite at least two primary human studies with LATS2 variants and height measurements, Established cannot be supported, and Existing is the most probable category, with residual weight on Hypothesized given the strong Hippo-pathway/organ-growth biology.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in SMAD9 associated with height or stature; the overwhelming majority concern SMAD9 in pulmonary arterial hypertension, arteriovenous malformations, hamartomatous polyposis, or hypertension, none of which are height-related phenotypes. The only skeletal-growth-relevant paper (PMID 31201465) is a mouse study of Adamts17 showing that short stature/short long bones arise through modulation of the BMP–Smad1/5/8 pathway, of which SMAD9 (Smad8) is a member — this provides indirect biological/pathway plausibility but no SMAD9 variant data and is not human. The DSD systems-biology paper (PMID 30550360) lists SMAD9 only as a candidate by network proximity, which is co-mention rather than evidence for height. Therefore the evidence base best supports "Hypothesized" via BMP/Smad1/5/8 signaling in growth-plate chondrogenesis, with residual probability for "Novel" since the link is only inferential.

None of the provided articles examine blood pressure, hypertension, or any cardiovascular phenotype; the literature set is dominated by DGKH associations with bipolar disorder, panic disorder, lithium response, and by molecular/enzymological studies of diacylglycerol kinase eta isoforms, plus cancer-related work (pheochromocytoma, oral and lung cancer). No human genetic study reports variants in DGKH associated with diastolic blood pressure. A weak indirect biological rationale could be argued from DGKH's role in diacylglycerol/PKC signaling and catecholamine handling (increased dopamine and phosphorylated dopamine transporter in DGKη-knockout mice; pheochromocytoma expression), which touches sympathetic/adrenergic pathways relevant to blood pressure, but this is speculative and derived from animal/tumor data. Therefore the evidence best fits "Novel," with a small allowance for "Hypothesized."

Multiple independent human studies report rare protein-truncating/predicted loss-of-function variants in BSN associated with adiposity: exome-wide analysis in ~587,000 individuals (PMID 38575728), UK Biobank plus All of Us replication and a Columbia early-onset obesity cohort (PMIDs 36865254, 37865656), and an independent All of Us diverse-ancestry replication with PheWAS (PMID 39228706); HYPOMAP also links rare BSN variants to population-level BMI (PMID 39910307). However, all of these measure BMI/obesity rather than waist circumference specifically, so the direct trait "waist-circumference-mean" is not itself demonstrated in the provided results. Because obesity and BMI are strongly linked, well-recognized correlates/components of central adiposity, the evidence best supports "Existing," with substantial weight for "Established" given the robust, replicated human adiposity association. Non-human data (mouse Bassoon models, iPSC astrocytes) and the neurodevelopmental/epilepsy papers do not add trait-specific human evidence, and homonym papers on bulbospinal neuronopathy were dismissed.

Multiple independent human case-control studies report association of NOS3 variants (G894T/rs1799983, T-786C/rs2070744, intron 4 VNTR) with essential hypertension, including Indian haplotype analyses with NOx phenotypes (PMID 18325347), a large healthy population study of T-786C (PMID 11967250), Chinese Hui (PMID 23613274), Czech resistant hypertension (PMID 11394896), and Iraqi (PMID 39241147) cohorts. These are supported by several large meta-analyses encompassing tens of thousands of subjects (PMIDs 34372765, 28287883, 21963726, 24846690) and by an independent gene-centric large-scale genotyping array that identified NOS3 as a genome-wide significant blood-pressure locus with supporting regulatory/expression data (PMID 22100073). All evidence is human, replicated across ethnicities, though some negative studies exist (PMID 16765468) and effect sizes are modest, which keeps some probability on "Existing" rather than a definitive monogenic-style causal role.

phenotype: Specific developmental disorders of scholastic skills
literature_justification: No article reports ANKRD12 variants causing specific developmental disorders of scholastic skills (dyslexia/dyscalculia) in independent probands or families, so Established is untenable. However, two human genetic studies provide indirect but credible support: a large exome study found rare protein-coding variants in ANKRD12 with large effects on adult cognitive function, with partial overlap with neurodevelopmental disorder architecture (PMID 37231097), and a family-based linkage/exome study of childhood apraxia of speech listed ANKRD12 among candidate variants with possible additive effects (PMID 27120335) — speech/language impairment is a recognized correlate and risk factor for learning disorders. Other exome-wide biobank studies link ANKRD12 to sleep traits with cognitive phenotypic associations, neuroticism, depressive symptoms, and alcohol consumption (PMIDs 38177695, 39511343, 39472661, 38982111), supporting neurobehavioral relevance but not the specific phenotype. The pig alternative splicing paper and the BRaVa asthma/COPD findings are not relevant. Overall the evidence is limited and indirect, best fitting "Existing," with substantial residual probability for "Hypothesized."

None of the provided articles examine stature/body height in relation to NFATC4. The only human genetic-variant study (PMID 19653005) tested an NFATC4 Gly160Ala polymorphism against elite endurance athlete status, muscle fiber composition and VO2max — phenotypes unrelated to height. The remaining literature concerns calcineurin/NFAT signaling in cardiac and mesangial cell hypertrophy, muscle fiber type specification, adipocyte and immune biology, fibrosis, and neurodegeneration, mostly in rodents or cell culture; "hypertrophy" here means cell size, not linear growth. A small residual probability is retained for "Hypothesized" because NFATc4 acts in growth/differentiation pathways (skeletal muscle, chondro/osteoclast-adjacent NFAT biology) that could conceivably touch skeletal growth, but no article makes that link. Overall the evidence base is best described as Novel.

The strongest PDZK1–HDL evidence in this set is mechanistic and non-human: PDZK1 is the scaffold that stabilizes hepatic SR-BI, and mouse/rat and in vitro work (PMIDs 12754212, 16174736, 18403724, 28134663, 20089950) shows PDZK1 loss or modulation markedly alters plasma HDL levels — this squarely supports "Hypothesized". Only one human genetic study directly interrogates PDZK1 variants against lipid/metabolic phenotypes (PMID 19321583), reporting association of PDZK1_i33968C>T with metabolic syndrome, triglycerides, VLDL and adiponectin (not HDL itself), which provides limited, single-cohort support for "Existing" via a closely related lipid phenotype. The Mexican FH study (PMID 41287107) implicates PDZK1 through a whole-gene duplication (a CNV that cannot isolate the gene) plus non-coding variants in an LDL/FH context, so it cannot serve as replication for HDL. Remaining human PDZK1 literature concerns urate/gout, unrelated to HDL. With fewer than two independent human studies showing PDZK1 variant–HDL association, "Established" is not supportable.
open_targets_trait: total phospholipids in lipoprotein particles measurement

literature_justification: No article in this list reports a direct association between YLPM1 variants and hip circumference. However, a large human rare-variant, cross-ancestry gene-based association study of BMI in 839,110 individuals across two biobanks identified YLPM1 as conferring ~three-fold risk of severe obesity, with links to related adiposity traits such as body-fat percentage (PMID 41168175 and its preprint version 39484254, which are the same study rather than independent replications). Obesity/BMI and body-fat percentage are well-recognized, mechanistically linked determinants of hip circumference, which supports the "Existing" category. Other listed papers concern clonal hematopoiesis, psychiatric disease, cardiomyocyte miRNA biology, or pig traits and are irrelevant or non-human for this phenotype. Because the human adiposity evidence essentially derives from a single study and does not directly measure hip circumference, "Established" is not justified.

None of the listed articles report genetic variants in ABCB11 associated with C-reactive protein levels in humans; the ABCB11 literature here is overwhelmingly about progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, BSEP deficiency, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, and gallstone disease (PMIDs 18395098, 32087350, 35894240, 39262913, 36046230), none of which involve CRP as a phenotype. The single article co-mentioning CRP (PMID 22475270) simply measured CRP as an IL-6-inducible acute-phase marker alongside downregulation of transporter genes including ABCB11 in cultured human hepatocytes — a shared inflammatory regulatory context rather than any genetic or causal relationship. This provides at most a weak, incidental mechanistic co-regulation basis (IL-6/acute-phase signaling affecting both), supporting a modest allocation to Hypothesized. No credible human genetic association study is present, so Established and Existing receive minimal weight.

No article in the list reports a human genetic association between DENND4C variants and total cholesterol or any lipid trait; the human genetic findings concern hematological traits (PMID 29958078) and a passing mention of a DENND4C variant moderately associated with type 2 diabetes (PMID 21454697), which is metabolic but not a direct cholesterol association. Biologically, DENND4C is a Rab10 GEF required for insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation in adipocytes (PMID 21454697), and it emerges as a candidate gene within selection signatures for intramuscular fat in rabbits, annotated to fatty acid and lipid metabolic processes (PMID 32618550) — an animal/functional line of evidence that supports a plausible but unproven link to lipid levels. Remaining papers (circRNA-DENND4C in cardiac, renal, hepatic, and breast contexts; endosomal proteomics; tilapia body color; testis gene expression) are unrelated to cholesterol. Therefore the relationship is best described as hypothesized, with a substantial chance it is effectively novel for total cholesterol specifically.

None of the provided articles reports any platelet phenotype, megakaryocyte biology, or mean platelet volume measurement in relation to DOCK5. Human genetic studies cited involve obesity VNTRs (PMID 22595969, 28615046), bipolar disorder (PMID 32920599), and Parkinson disease CNVs that failed validation (PMID 21829596) — none relevant to platelet indices. The only indirect biological rationale is that DOCK5 is a Rac1 GEF regulating actin cytoskeleton, podosome formation, and cell spreading (PMIDs 19004829, 24992711, 25022758), processes conceptually relevant to megakaryocyte proplatelet formation and platelet size, and DOCK5/8 activity in hematopoietic (AML) cells (PMID 30668141). This provides only a weak, speculative pathway link rather than direct evidence, so the evidence sits between Novel and Hypothesized, with no support for Existing or Established.

Only one article in this list provides primary human genetic evidence: the KORA F3 GWAS (PMID 19110211), which identified rs2138852 upstream of TAOK1 associated with mean platelet volume and replicated it in an independent UK GWAS and two German population samples (combined n=10,048, p=7.19×10⁻²⁸). This is strong, internally replicated cohort-level evidence, but it comes from a single publication in this set, so per the citation requirement (≥2 independent primary reports) the evidence is scored as Existing rather than Established. All other retrieved articles concern TAOK1 in neurodevelopmental disorders, autism, craniosynostosis, cancer cachexia, IL-17 signaling, and liver fibrosis, and are irrelevant to platelet volume. No functional or animal data linking TAOK1 to megakaryocyte/platelet biology appear here, so Hypothesized and Novel receive minimal weight.

FAM234A (formerly ITFG3) lies in the alpha-globin cluster region on 16p, a locus repeatedly implicated in hemoglobin and HbA1c variation. Two independent human cohort GWAS report single-variant associations at ITFG3/FAM234A with hemoglobin and related red-cell traits: the COGENT African American analysis (lead SNP rs13335629 in ITFG3; PMID 23446634) and the Ugandan General Population Cohort multivariate blood-count GWAS (PMID 31080455) — but these measure total hemoglobin/RBC indices rather than HbA1c directly. The UK Biobank exome study (PMID 34662886) reports rare protein-altering variants in FAM234A lowering diabetes risk, a phenotype defined largely by HbA1c, providing supportive but indirect human evidence, and a recent African HbA1c PheWAS (PMID 40446072) addresses this trait class. Because the strongest single-variant human results concern hemoglobin/erythrocyte traits (a well-recognized determinant of the HbA1c/total-hemoglobin ratio) rather than HbA1c itself, and the large alpha-thalassemia deletions (PMIDs 28838269, 31223040) span multiple genes and cannot isolate FAM234A, Existing is slightly favored over Established.

Rare protein-truncating variants in APBA1 were identified in a large human exome-sequencing study of adult BMI (PMID 38575728) and independently replicated in the diverse All of Us cohort (PMID 39228706) and in cross-ancestry rare-variant analyses of 839,110 individuals across two biobanks (PMIDs 41168175, 39484254), with additional clinical cases of PTV carriers in minors with severe obesity (PMID 42018264). These are genuine human genetic results in independent cohorts, but they measure BMI/obesity and body-fat percentage rather than waist circumference itself, which is a closely related but distinct adiposity trait. Because waist circumference is a well-recognized adiposity measure strongly linked to BMI and obesity, the evidence best supports "Existing," with substantial probability for "Established" given the replication across independent human cohorts. Remaining non-human/mechanistic papers (synaptic trafficking, CASK/Mint1 structure) only support biological plausibility.

None of the provided articles report any human genetic association between PCOLCE2 variants and height or any skeletal growth phenotype; the human genetic work cited concerns HDL-cholesterol/apoA-I maturation and red blood cell fatty acid levels (PMIDs 25500335, 29652918, 21771977, 19237735), which are unrelated to stature. Therefore neither "Established" nor "Existing" can be supported, as no PMID demonstrates variants in people associated with height. However, PCOLCE2 encodes a procollagen C-proteinase enhancer homolog acting with BMP-1 in collagen processing and extracellular matrix biology (PMIDs 10873381, 39374805, 28427244), a pathway plausibly relevant to connective tissue and skeletal growth, giving a biological, though indirect, basis for a hypothesized relationship. Mouse data (PMIDs 21771977, 23845568) are non-human and only support hypothesized status. Points are therefore split mainly between Hypothesized (collagen/ECM biology) and Novel (purely incidental co-mention with height).

None of the listed articles reports MYBPC3 variants as a direct cause of paroxysmal tachycardia in independent probands or families; the literature is dominated by MYBPC3 as the leading cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (PMID 32841044, 37445689, 12707239, 35626289), a well-recognized substrate for ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, arrhythmic syncope and sudden cardiac death (PMID 31513939, 37445689). Two human reports provide indirect but credible arrhythmia-specific links: a familial HCM case with a fasciculoventricular accessory pathway carrying a pathogenic MYBPC3 variant (PMID 35199016) and an NGS study in which a pre-excitation syndrome was explained by genotyping in an HCM cohort (PMID 27600940). Because these are single case-level observations and the main evidence is via the HCM phenotype (a strongly linked precursor/mechanism), "Existing" is the best fit, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" since much supporting data is mechanistic (haploinsufficiency, splicing, iPSC models; PMIDs 19574547, 28679633, 37317833). Established cannot be supported, as I cannot cite two studies with their own results demonstrating MYBPC3 variants causing paroxysmal tachycardia in separate families.

Only one article in this list reports primary human genetic evidence linking CEBPE variation to basophil traits: the HCHS/SOL genome-wide association study (PMID 28158719), which identified novel loci involving hematopoietic transcription factors, including CEBPE-SLC7A7, associated with basophil count in Hispanics/Latinos. That is a single credible human cohort finding without an independent replication cohort within this set, so "Established" cannot be supported by the required two independent primary studies. The remaining articles concern CEBPE variants in acute lymphoblastic leukemia susceptibility, specific granule deficiency/neutrophil biology, and inflammasomopathy; these support the gene's role in myeloid/granulocyte differentiation (biologically relevant to basophil lineage) but do not directly measure basophil percentage. Accordingly, the weight falls on "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" (given CEBPE's recognized status in blood-cell trait GWAS) and "Hypothesized" (granulocyte differentiation biology from CEBPE loss-of-function and gain-of-function human/mouse studies).

No article in this set reports an association between MARK3 variants and human height; no GWAS, family, or cohort study of stature is present, so Established is untenable. The closest human genetic evidence is the bone mineral density GWAS locus at 14q32 near MARK3 (PMID 19079262) and its functional dissection showing regulatory SNPs altering MARK3 splicing/expression with effects on osteoblast mineralization and bone mass in mice (PMID 33792563); BMD is a skeletal trait but is not a recognized precursor or subtype of height, so this supports at most limited "Existing" credit. The strong skeletal biology—MARK3 regulation of osteoblast Notch/Jag1 signaling, osteoclast differentiation, and increased bone mass in Mark3-null mice (PMIDs 33792563, 36581219)—provides a plausible biological pathway to skeletal growth and therefore favors Hypothesized. Other papers concern tau phosphorylation, polarity kinase signaling, eye development, otosclerosis, and DNA damage responses, which are irrelevant to stature and leave residual probability for Novel.

phenotype: Erythrocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in CBFA2T3 associated with erythrocyte count; the overwhelming majority concern the somatic CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion in pediatric acute megakaryoblastic/myeloid leukemia (PMIDs 28112737, 30592296, 26186939, 33832921, 31648321), which is a somatic oncogenic rearrangement affecting megakaryoblastic lineage rather than a germline determinant of red cell counts. The only human germline-variant study cited (PMID 29491472) links CBFA2T3 super-enhancer SNPs to coronary artery disease, not to erythrocyte parameters. However, CBFA2T3 (ETO2/MTG16) is a hematopoietic transcriptional corepressor whose disruption clearly perturbs hematopoietic differentiation, supported by mouse models and functional studies (PMIDs 37716355, 31792123, 31681706), providing a plausible biological basis for influencing blood cell indices. This biology-based, indirect support best fits "Hypothesized," with residual probability for "Novel" since erythrocyte count itself is never assessed, and limited probability for "Existing."

The clearest human evidence is a single case report (PMID 40062121) in which a child with biallelic EMILIN1 loss-of-function variants presented with short stature alongside arterial tortuosity and fractures, and the original human series describing biallelic EMILIN1 deficiency (PMID 36351433) documents a connective-tissue/skeletal phenotype with osteopenia and bone fragility, which is mechanistically linked to growth and stature. However, no GWAS or cohort study of height per se implicates EMILIN1; the soccer-player study (PMID 34633711) uses peak height velocity only as a maturity marker for injury genetics, not as a height-association result, and other papers describe ECM/elastogenesis biology or animal/in vitro models (bone strength in Emilin1−/− mice, zebrafish skeletal abnormalities). This supports at most one credible human report plus strong supporting skeletal biology, so "Established" is not warranted (fewer than two independent human variant-based studies of height). Weight therefore falls mainly on Existing, with substantial probability on Hypothesized given that most mechanistic support is non-human.

Multiple human reports link 17p13.3 rearrangements involving CRK to growth phenotypes: deletions of YWHAE/CRK with intrauterine growth restriction, short stature and postnatal growth failure (PMID 35086092, 20833799, 32323081, 39513527), and class I microduplications including CRK with overgrowth/tall stature and elevated growth factors (PMID 27633569, 36551834). However, all of these are copy number changes spanning several contiguous genes (YWHAE, BHLHA9, etc.), so they cannot isolate CRK from its neighbours, and one large duplication cohort explicitly failed to confirm the overgrowth association with YWHAE/CRK (PMID 23813913). No single-gene point-variant study in humans demonstrates a CRK–height association, and supporting mechanistic work (Drosophila, mouse endocardium) is non-human. This places the evidence firmly in the "Existing" range—credible but not definitive human association—with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the reliance on multigenic CNVs and animal/functional data.

No articles were provided, so there is no citable evidence linking DNAAF9 (C20orf194) variants or biology to height. DNAAF9 is characterized as a dynein axonemal assembly factor associated with primary ciliary dyskinesia phenotypes, not with skeletal growth or stature. Without any human genetic association study, family, or cohort data in the provided list, neither "Established" nor "Existing" can be supported. A small residual probability is assigned to "Hypothesized"/"Existing" because ciliary genes can influence skeletal development and large height GWAS occasionally implicate many loci, but no such evidence is present here.

Human genetic evidence for a PLIN4–body weight/adiposity link exists in more than one independent cohort: PMID 21533135 reports meta-analysis of PLIN4 SNPs (notably rs8887 and rs884164) in two populations of European ancestry showing association with anthropometric (obesity-related) phenotypes, plus a functional miR-522 seed-site mechanism; PMID 29361938 examined PLIN4 polymorphism in relation to long-term weight loss in people with obesity, and PMID 30293593 genotyped rs8887 in children with interactions involving birth weight. Additional support comes from perilipin-locus association studies with BMI/body weight (PMID 15355432, 20495294, 19385027, 18812483), though these use the older "PLIN4" SNP nomenclature for variants at the perilipin-1 locus, which weakens their attribution to the PLIN4 gene itself. Human epigenetic data (PMID 38660759) link cord-blood PLIN4 methylation to infant weight outcomes with replication in an independent cohort, and mouse Plin4-/- data (PMID 41391763) provide biological plausibility but are non-human. Given the nomenclature ambiguity and modest replication of true PLIN4-gene variant associations, weight is split between Established and Existing, favoring Established slightly.

Only one human genetic study directly tests HRH4 variants in psoriasis (PMID 27725312), a case-control analysis of promoter SNPs in 206 patients and 213 controls; it found no overall association but reported subgroup associations (rs615283 with moderate-to-severe PASI and palmoplantar psoriasis). This single, partially negative, unreplicated study supports "Existing" but falls well short of "Established," which would require at least two independent studies with variants demonstrated in patients. Substantial supporting biology exists—HRH4 overexpression on plasmacytoid dendritic cells in psoriatic patients and lesions (PMID 21614010), functional H4R on Th17 cells in psoriatic plaques (PMID 22063299), murine imiquimod model data (PMID 26900758), and clinical trials of H4R antagonists such as toreforant in plaque psoriasis (PMIDs 30124726, 28233185)—which alone would justify "Hypothesized." Because the genetic evidence is human but weak/subgroup-based, probability is split mainly between Existing and Hypothesized.

Biallelic MMP2 mutations cause multicentric osteolysis, nodulosis and arthropathy (MONA/Winchester spectrum), a skeletal dysplasia in which short stature is a cardinal feature. PMID 39540058 reports a consanguineous Pakistani family with a homozygous MMP2 missense variant (c.539A>T, p.Asp180Val) and explicitly documents "severe short stature" in three affected siblings, providing direct human variant–height evidence. PMID 39463871 independently describes three MONA probands (including two siblings) with pathogenic/homozygous MMP2 variants and progressive skeletal degeneration, and PMID 27687687 describes further MMP2-mutant MONA patients with skeletal disease; these support replication of the gene–skeletal phenotype, though short stature is not always spelled out in the abstracts. Additional human reports (PMID 40730687) identify MMP2 variants in patients with skeletal/neuromuscular presentations. Remaining uncertainty reflects that only one cited paper explicitly measures stature, so points are also allocated to Existing; the remaining articles (mouse tendon, rat injury, Turner syndrome markers, blood pressure GRS) are not height-specific evidence.

The provided literature consistently links ABCC6 to inorganic pyrophosphate/phosphate (PPi/Pi) homeostasis, since loss of ABCC6 reduces hepatic ATP efflux and thus PPi, lowering the PPi/Pi ratio and permitting calcium-phosphate deposition (PMIDs 28486967, 28891970, 38392293, 30446375). However, these are largely reviews or mechanistic/background statements rather than primary human studies measuring serum/urine phosphate in genotyped individuals; the strong human genetic evidence for ABCC6 concerns PXE and GACI type 2 phenotypes, not phosphate levels per se. Hypophosphatemia (ARHR2) is attributed principally to ENPP1 rather than ABCC6 (PMIDs 39343470, 39343469), and the DMP1/SPP1 hypophosphatemic case carries only an incidental heterozygous ABCC6 variant (PMID 31843680). Human case reports of ABCC6 heterozygotes with calcium-phosphate nephrolithiasis and low PPi provide suggestive but limited direct human evidence (PMID 41908612), as does the CKD/candidate-gene calcification work invoking Pi/PPi metabolism (PMIDs 30985656, 24994603). I therefore favor Hypothesized, with substantial weight to Existing, and cannot cite two independent primary human studies tying ABCC6 variants to phosphate measurements, so Established is low.

literature_justification: The Tsimane/Moseten study (PMID 36574663) is the only human genetic work here: it identifies PSD4 within a candidate selective-sweep region and explicitly links this region to immune biomarker phenotypes, with the enriched gene set relating to lymphocyte and eosinophil abundance. That constitutes one credible human genotype–phenotype report, sufficient for "Existing" but not replicated in independent cohorts, so "Established" cannot be supported (no second human study with variant-level evidence). The remaining papers are mechanistic: Tiam1-dependent Psd4 expression in murine neutrophils (PMID 38077328) and SNAI1/FOXA1 regulation of PSD4/ARF6 in breast cancer cells (PMID 42586969) support plausible immune-cell biology but are non-human/in vitro, contributing to "Hypothesized". The plasma PSD4 methylation liver-fibrosis paper (PMID 42564411) is a biomarker study unrelated to lymphocyte counts and does not add genetic evidence.

The strongest direct human evidence is a single family report (PMID 35205406) in which a pathogenic BAG3 variant segregated in a proband and his father, both of whom presented with recurrent atrial fibrillation in the context of dilated cardiomyopathy — one family only, so replication in independent probands is lacking and Established cannot be supported. Additional support is indirect: BAG3 p.Pro209Leu myofibrillar myopathy/restrictive cardiomyopathy series report atrial arrhythmias including atrial flutter and ectopic atrial tachycardia (PMID 41378130, 40493734), and BAG3 is a validated cause of DCM and rare loss-of-function heart failure risk (PMID 40195560, 39535783, 39744939), with HF GWAS loci including BAG3 sharing genetic aetiology with atrial fibrillation (PMID 31919418). Because BAG3 variants robustly cause cardiomyopathy/heart failure — well-recognized substrates and risk factors for AF — the "Existing" category best fits, with AF appearing largely as a secondary manifestation rather than a primary BAG3-driven phenotype. Some probability remains for Hypothesized, since much of the AF link is mechanistic/secondary rather than a demonstrated direct genotype–AF association.

No articles were supplied, so there is no citable evidence of any kind linking HDHD5 (CECR5) variants to serum alkaline phosphatase levels or alkaline phosphatase–related phenotypes. Established and Existing both require at least one credible human genetic study, and none can be named here. HDHD5 encodes a haloacid dehalogenase-like hydrolase domain protein, a broad phosphatase-related superfamily, which leaves a small residual possibility of biologically plausible (hypothesized) links via phosphatase/metabolic pathways, but no supporting literature is presented. In the absence of any evidence, the relationship is best described as Novel.

phenotype: Erythrocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: None of the provided articles report an association between GIGYF1 variants and erythrocyte (red blood cell) count measured by automated count. The human exome studies link GIGYF1 loss of function to type 2 diabetes, glucose/HbA1c, BMI/obesity, cognitive function, hand grip strength, and alcohol consumption (PMIDs 34732801, 35177841, 39484254, 37231097, 37301943, 37072623), none of which are erythrocyte indices. The closest hematologic evidence is the association of GIGYF1 LOF with mosaic loss of chromosome Y in leukocytes (PMID 34234147), a clonal hematopoiesis phenotype that involves blood cell biology and cell-cycle/DNA-damage pathways, providing only an indirect, mechanistic rationale rather than direct evidence for red cell counts. Functional work on GIGYF1/IGF-1R signaling (PMIDs 12771153, 35917186) is biologically relevant to growth-factor signaling that could plausibly influence hematopoiesis, supporting some weight for "Hypothesized." Because no human study here reports erythrocyte count associations, most probability falls on Novel with a secondary weight on Hypothesized.

PMID 15355432 provides direct human genetic evidence: the PLIN4 11482G>A variant was significantly associated with lower waist-to-hip ratio (as well as BMI, glucose and triacylglycerol) in women from a general Spanish population of 1589 subjects. PMID 21533135 adds independent human support, showing rs8887 and rs884164 in PLIN4 associate with, and interact with dietary PUFA to modulate, anthropometric and lipid phenotypes in two European-ancestry cohorts, with a functional miR-522 seed-site mechanism; however, WHR itself is not explicitly named as the outcome, so this is supportive rather than a clean independent replication of the WHR association. PMID 34875679 (rare LoF variants and body fat distribution) and the review PMID 23035807 restate or contextualize such associations rather than clearly providing PLIN4-specific WHR results. Remaining papers (myopathy repeat expansions, Plin4-/- mice, cancer transcriptomics, methylation) are either different phenotypes or non-human/non-variant evidence. Overall the evidence is credible and human but only definitively replicated once for WHR, favoring "Existing" with meaningful probability for "Established."

The strongest evidence is the population-scale whole-genome sequencing study (PMID 41073786), which reports that protein-truncating variants in IRS2 in UK Biobank and All of Us are associated with chronic kidney disease independent of diabetes status — a phenotype defined largely by creatinine-based eGFR, directly supporting a human variant-level link to serum creatinine. Reviews of diabetic nephropathy genetics (PMIDs 26069720, 34609116) cite replicated GWAS/linkage signals at the MYO16/IRS2 locus, but these are secondary citations rather than primary results, and the locus cannot cleanly isolate IRS2. Supporting biology comes from mouse knockouts assessing serum creatinine/creatinine clearance and renal hemodynamics (PMID 33270683) and proximal tubule transport work (PMID 28428931), which are non-human/mechanistic and count only toward Hypothesized. Because I can cite only one primary human genetic study with its own variant-level results, Established cannot be firmly supported, making Existing the most probable category.

No article in this set reports a human genetic variant in SLC38A2 associated with stature/height; the only human variant findings concern hypertension (rs1873793, PMID 40901922), which is unrelated to height. The strongest growth-relevant evidence is mechanistic and animal-based: placenta-specific Slc38a2/SNAT2 knockdown causes fetal growth restriction in mice, with accompanying observation of reduced placental SLC38A2 expression in human late-onset FGR (PMID 34406367), and human placental transcript-usage differences including SLC38A2 in small-for-gestational-age infants (PMID 35646058) — expression/transcript data, not variant associations. Additional biology (SNAT2-mediated amino acid uptake driving mTORC1 signaling and cell growth; PMIDs 40425534, 34003553, 17237199) makes a plausible mechanistic link to body growth. Many other listed papers use "height" only as villus/albumen height (homonymous usage) and were discounted. Therefore Hypothesized is most appropriate, with modest weight to Existing because of the human FGR/birth-weight expression data.

None of the provided articles mention red cell distribution width, erythrocyte indices, or any hematologic phenotype. The GAK literature here concerns Parkinson's disease risk loci (TMEM175/GAK/DGKQ), clathrin uncoating and endocytic/lysosomal trafficking, glial autophagy, podocyte injury in mice, and a Taiwan Biobank glycemia PheWAS — none of which addresses RDW or erythropoiesis. The only human genetic association data (PD risk, age at onset, glycemic traits) are for unrelated phenotypes and are not recognized precursors or mechanisms of RDW variation. A small residual probability is assigned to Hypothesized given GAK's ubiquitous expression and general roles in membrane trafficking, which could conceivably touch erythrocyte biology, but no such link is presented. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

Multiple independent human cohort studies report kidney cysts in carriers of heterozygous pathogenic COL4A3/COL4A4 variants: a multicenter cohort showing increased cyst prevalence (PMID 38317457), a genetic/radiologic cohort of autosomal dominant Alport patients with multicystic kidney disease (PMID 38178635), and a cohort defining the cystic phenotype in Alport syndrome (PMID 38514012). These are supported by independent families/probands in which COL4A4 variants explained an ADPKD-mimicking cystic phenotype (PMIDs 42336693, 40683378) and by diagnostic sequencing of renal cyst patients identifying COL4A4 (PMID 39019822). However, the relationship is a secondary/associated phenotype rather than a classic cystogenic disease gene, cysts may partly reflect advanced CKD, and at least one study explicitly challenges the link (PMID 39694697), so points are split roughly evenly between Established and Existing.

literature_justification: None of the provided articles report a human genetic association between PTPRH variants and lymphocyte count. The closest human genetic evidence is the TOPMed whole-genome sequencing study (PMID 34553764), which identified a gene-based signal at PTPRH for platelet traits (platelet count/MPV) — a different hematologic trait, so it only weakly supports pleiotropic involvement in blood cell indices. The remaining literature concerns PTPRH/SAP-1 in cancer (EGFR dephosphorylation, NSCLC, murine mammary tumors) and intestinal epithelial biology, including immune-relevant roles such as exacerbated colitis and cytokine/chemokine upregulation in SAP-1-deficient IL-10-null mice (PMIDs 26195794, 19170756, 39181073), which are murine/in vitro and provide only indirect biological plausibility for immune-cell regulation. Thus the evidence base is best split between Novel and Hypothesized, with limited support for Existing.

phenotype: Erythrocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: No article in this set reports a germline variant association between SPRED2 and erythrocyte count (automated) in any human cohort, so Established cannot be supported. The closest human genetic evidence is the UK Biobank somatic exome analysis (PMID 38744975), which identifies SPRED2 as a novel clonal hematopoiesis driver under positive selection in blood, linking SPRED2 variation to hematopoietic clonal expansion and hematological malignancy — a plausible mechanistic/precursor link to blood cell indices, supporting some weight on Existing. Otherwise, evidence is biological: SPRED2 negatively regulates RAS-MAPK signaling (PMIDs 22305891, 37149146), and Spred1/2-deficient mice show erythrocyte-filled lymphatics and hematopoietic/vascular phenotypes (PMID 17438136), while human RASopathy phenotypes from SPRED2 loss of function (PMIDs 34626534, 38254922, 36608738) involve MAPK dysregulation but not documented red cell count changes. This pathway relevance to hematopoiesis makes Hypothesized the most likely category, with residual probability for Novel given the purely incidental co-mention of erythrocytes.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary results linking ABCA1 variants to HDL-C: PMID 11086027 identified 13 ABCA1 mutations in 11 Tangier/familial hypoalphalipoproteinemia families and showed 77 heterozygotes have reduced HDL-C correlated with cholesterol efflux; PMID 35460704 performed whole-exome sequencing in 204 low-HDL-C subjects and found genome-wide significant burden of damaging ABCA1 variants; PMID 37048678 and PMID 38538338 report novel homozygous/pathogenic ABCA1 variants causing Tangier disease with markedly low HDL-C; PMID 29773422 describes a novel homozygous variant with profound hypoalphalipoproteinemia. Population-level evidence adds replication: a systematic review/meta-analysis of ABCA1 polymorphisms and plasma lipids (PMID 34575660) and cohort association of rs9282541 with low HDL-C in Mexican adults (PMID 36678241), plus functional allele-specific enhancer work (PMID 31039173). These are independent human probands, families, and cohorts, so the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report APOB variants directly linked to LDL cholesterol levels in their own results: the Russian FH cohort of 595 index patients identified 14 APOB variants (PMID 33418990), the Dutch national program identified six causative APOB mutations among ADH index cases (PMID 16250003), the Hungarian cohort found APOB c.10580G>A p.(Arg3527Gln) in index patients (PMID 35052492), and the Portuguese study identified novel APOB variants causing hypobetalipoproteinemia with low LDL-C (PMID 37138899). Additional human evidence includes a case-control polymorphism study in Kurdish hypercholesterolemic patients (PMID 39469407) and GWAS/Mendelian randomization identifying APOB RNAm-SNPs associated with LDL-C (PMID 35880552). Both directions of the phenotype (familial defective apoB raising LDL-C; truncating variants lowering LDL-C) are replicated across independent probands, families, and cohorts. This constitutes clear, replicated human genetic evidence for an Established gene–phenotype relationship.

Multiple independent human studies report APOB variants directly affecting total cholesterol. PMID 39733208 reports an original cross-sectional cohort of Brazilian children showing the APOB XbaI T allele associated with increased total cholesterol; PMID 28874158 is a meta-analysis of human studies linking APOB rs693/rs17240441 to plasma APOB and lipid levels; PMID 22247256 screened two large cohorts of hypobetalipoproteinemic subjects (total cholesterol <5th percentile) and identified APOB mutations. Additional large human mutation-screening cohorts in familial hypercholesterolemia (PMIDs 16250003, 33418990, 35052492, 32770674) identify pathogenic APOB variants (e.g., p.Arg3527Gln) in independent probands and families with elevated cholesterol, and FHBL reviews/case reports document APOB truncations causing markedly low total cholesterol. This constitutes replicated, bidirectional human genetic evidence, supporting an Established relationship.

Multiple human genetic studies directly link APOB variants to plasma triglyceride phenotypes: resequencing of hypertriglyceridemia patients versus normolipidemic controls found a burden of rare APOB variants alongside LPL, GCKR and APOA5 (PMID 22033228), and a meta-analysis of Chinese cohorts reported associations of the APOB XbaI/EcoRI polymorphisms with serum lipids including triglycerides (PMID 26446158). A systematic review of severe hypertriglyceridemia cohorts likewise reports APOB variants associated with intermediate TG elevations (PMID 41300829). At the opposite extreme, loss-of-function/truncating APOB variants cause familial hypobetalipoproteinemia with markedly reduced VLDL/triglyceride secretion and low serum TG in heterozygous and homozygous probands and families (PMIDs 15818469, 35918255, 38710625, 41665936), providing independent, replicated human variant-level evidence in both directions. Reviews and population studies further corroborate APOB allele effects on apoB-containing, triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism (PMIDs 19200547, 32448433).

GOT1 encodes cytosolic aspartate aminotransferase, so the gene–phenotype link is direct. Two independent human genetic studies present primary evidence with variants in people: a genome-wide association study in 866 Amish participants that identified rs17109512 and a rare in-frame deletion (p.Asn389del) in GOT1 markedly lowering serum AST activity, with functional validation (PMID 21900944), and a separate report of a heterozygous GOT1 mutation segregating with familial macro-aspartate aminotransferase (PMID 28716744). Additional human sequencing work (PMID 32143588) and mapping studies (PMIDs 10360399, 12707951, 7292252) confirm the locus and gene identity but address other phenotypes. The many autophagy/liver-injury papers merely use "GOT1/AST" as an abbreviation for a serum enzyme readout and contribute no genetic evidence.

Many of the listed papers are homonym hits (bacterial gpt reporter transgene in mutagenicity assays, "Guipi Tang", "GPT-4" language model, GlcNAc-1-P-transferase) and were dismissed. However, several genuine human population-genetic studies directly type GPT (red-cell glutamic-pyruvic transaminase/alanine aminotransferase) electrophoretic alleles and report allele/phenotype frequencies in independent, unrelated cohorts: southwestern Germany including a novel GPT9 variant (PMID 511157), Galicia, Spain (PMID 3579235), Bologna with family linkage analysis (PMID 7353890), northern Japan including Ainu (PMID 478553), and Saudi Arabia (PMID 109010). These independent human cohorts demonstrate that allelic variation at the GPT locus determines the alanine aminotransferase enzyme phenotype, satisfying replication in humans. Supporting biochemical/pathway context (ALT in pyruvate–alanine transamination and its association with insulin resistance, PMID 24029012) reinforces relevance, though it is background rather than variant-level evidence.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own results linking APOC3 variants to triglyceride levels: exome sequencing identified loss-of-function APOC3 mutations associated with lower plasma triglycerides and coronary disease (PMID 24941081), a meta-analysis of rs5128 showed association with plasma APOC3 and lipid/TG levels (PMID 25928461), the SstI polymorphism/haplotype was associated with endogenous hypertriglyceridaemia (PMID 9792993), and the insulin-response-element genotype associated with plasma triglycerides in aboriginal Canadians (PMID 9194755). Kinetic studies in Amish R19X heterozygotes demonstrated 35% lower plasma TG and altered VLDL-TG clearance (PMID 30580564), and rs2070667 associated with serum triglyceride species in NAFLD patients (PMID 33294458). Additional GWAS-type work links APOC3 variation to atherogenic index (TG/HDL) (PMID 37372394), and drug-target MR analyses use APOC3 as a canonical triglyceride-lowering target (PMID 35213538). These are human cohorts and independent populations, satisfying replication for an Established call.

Multiple independent human studies report PKD1 pathogenic variants identified in ADPKD probands/families with progressive loss of kidney function and end-stage kidney disease. PMID 24611717 screened 180 Japanese patients from 161 unrelated families, identifying 89 PKD1 mutations and demonstrating faster eGFR decline in PKD1 carriers; PMID 37509056 independently genotyped Japanese ADPKD patients and linked PKD1 mutations to renal function outcomes; PMID 26139440 identified PKD1 mutations (including de novo) in 42 early-onset patients from 41 families; PMID 40762980 (HALT PKD) related PKD1 variant type and molecular domain to disease progression in a separate cohort. Additional cohort screening (PMID 34890546) confirms PKD1 as the major locus (~78% of families) in large multi-cohort ADPKD populations. These are human genetic studies with variant-level, patient-level evidence, replicated across independent populations, supporting an Established causal relationship with chronic renal failure/kidney failure.

Multiple human studies provide primary evidence: the original linkage analysis mapped BRCA2 in 15 high-risk breast cancer families (PMID 8091231), and large-scale case-control sequencing of 96,691 breast cancer cases versus 302,116 controls demonstrated pathogenic BRCA2 variant enrichment and enabled variant classification (PMID 40413188). Independent family-based evidence includes a recurrent BRCA2 exon 3 deletion segregating in five Assyrian families with classic BRCA2-associated cancers (PMID 37657917), founder BRCA2 variants in Portuguese HBOC families (PMID 36230639), and the BRCA2 c.5576_5579del founder variant in Japanese breast cancer patients (PMID 38707742). Additional cohort and risk-estimation studies in carriers (PMIDs 39475295, 33597508, 40664060, 27616075) reinforce replication across independent probands and populations. The evidence is unambiguous, replicated, and entirely human, supporting an Established gene–disease relationship.

Multiple human studies report LCAT variants in probands and families with low HDL-C: PMID 34256778 describes clinical/genetic characterization of Mexican kindreds with LCAT deficiency plus a systematic review of reported cases; PMID 37138899 reports an independent index case with compound heterozygous LCAT variants causing Fish Eye Disease and low HDL-C; PMID 9162740 catalogs 36 natural LCAT mutations underlying FLD/FED with severe HDL deficiency. Common-variant evidence also exists in human cohorts (PMID 29570220, rs2292318 associated with HDL-C and HDL subclasses; PMID 24789697, LCAT sequencing in extreme HDL-C groups; PMID 31039173, allele-specific enhancers at LCAT linked to GWAS lipid signals). These are independent human probands/cohorts, not merely background citations, so the association is strong and replicated. A minority of the listed papers are reviews, mouse, or in vitro/structural work, which alone would support only Hypothesized, leaving little residual uncertainty.

Multiple primary human studies report their own results linking PCSK9 variants to LDL cholesterol: Abifadel et al. identified gain-of-function PCSK9 mutations in French families with autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia (PMID 12730697); Cohen et al. showed nonsense/sequence variants in PCSK9 lowering LDL-C and CHD risk in the large ARIC cohort (PMID 16554528); Shioji et al. found common PCSK9 polymorphisms associated with LDL-C in a Japanese general-population cohort of 1,793 (PMID 14727156). Independent mutation-spectrum cohorts in Japanese HeFH patients (PMID 31491741) and 595 Russian FH index patients (PMID 33418990) further replicate PCSK9 variants in hypercholesterolemic probands, as does sequencing of severe hypercholesterolemia patients (PMID 27050191). Mendelian randomization using PCSK9-locus variants and LDL-C/apoB (PMID 40347490) adds human genetic support, and pharmacologic PCSK9 inhibition confirms the mechanism. Evidence is human, replicated across independent probands, families and cohorts, so Established.

Multiple independent human studies report pathogenic germline BRCA1 variants identified in their own cohorts of breast cancer probands and families: Jordanian high-risk breast cancer patients (PMID 29409476), Mauritanian breast cancer patients (PMID 35858847), Albanian carriers of the recurrent BRCA1 c.3700_3704del founder variant (PMID 36299383), 649 Brazilian probands with 126 distinct BRCA1 pathogenic variants (PMID 29907814), and German familial breast/ovarian cancer patients screened by panel sequencing (PMID 27616075). Large-scale carrier studies further quantify penetrance and risk modification in BRCA1 mutation carriers (PMIDs 33597508, 27528622, 18710587), and Chinese meta-analysis of germline BRCA1/2 variants documents pathogenic variant frequencies in breast cancer (PMID 31825140). These are single-gene point/indel variants in humans across independent populations, satisfying replication requirements. Functional/mechanistic reviews and splicing assays add supportive biological plausibility but are not needed for the classification.

Multiple independent human cohort studies report PCSK9 variants associated with total cholesterol in their own results: PMID 17550346 found the R46L allele associated with significantly lower total cholesterol in 2444 healthy UK men; PMID 14727156 showed intron1 C(-161)T and I474V variants associated with TC and LDL-C in 1793 Japanese subjects; PMID 29321358 confirmed rs2479409 associations with lipid traits in 1900 Chinese individuals; PMID 26295473 re-analyzed PCSK9 rs2479409 effects on TC across Framingham Heart Study generations; and meta-analyses (PMIDs 31036026, 28606094) aggregate associations of rs562556, rs505151 and rs11591147 with serum lipids. Additional supportive human data include PCSK9 plasma level correlations with TC (PMIDs 18436719, 17645871) and monogenic hypo-/hypercholesterolemia caused by PCSK9 loss- and gain-of-function mutations (PMIDs 21874758, 25637042). This constitutes replicated, independent human genetic evidence, so the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report LDLR variants in probands, families and population cohorts with elevated LDL cholesterol: 595 Russian FH index patients (PMID 33418990), 750 Taiwanese index patients (PMID 33994402), exome sequencing of 9,793 genomes showing rare LDLR non-synonymous and null alleles raising LDL-C and MI risk (PMID 25487149), the Dutch national FH screening program identifying >130 causative LDLR variants and thousands of mutation-carrying relatives (PMID 16250003), and a Mexican community study of p.Asp360His carriers (PMID 32113782). Deep mutational scanning of ~17,000 LDLR coding variants correlated functional scores with hyperlipidemia phenotypes in prospective human cohorts (PMID 41166440), and a founder mutation in Gran Canaria was characterized in carriers (PMID 37511081). These are original results in humans across independent populations, satisfying replication requirements. The evidence is unambiguous and definitive for an Established gene–phenotype relationship.

Several listed articles report primary human genetic results linking CETP variants to HDL-C in independent cohorts: PMID 37250494 identified a Polynesian-specific missense variant (p.Pro177Leu) associated with higher HDL-C and reduced CETP activity; PMID 38265339 showed CETP SNPs/haplotypes (rs3764261, rs247616, rs183130) are explanatory variables for HDL-C in a pediatric sickle cell cohort; PMID 33358712 reported a loss-of-function CETP mutation affecting HDL-C in acute myocardial infarction patients; PMID 25410905 describes Japanese CETP-deficient patients with extremely high HDL-C; PMID 27590083 links CETP Taq1B to blood lipids in hyperlipidemic patients. Additional Mendelian randomization work (PMIDs 34561430, 38906890, 36701426) uses CETP genetic instruments scaled to HDL-C in humans, and 18468607 functionally characterizes Asian CETP variants expected to raise HDL-C. These are independent human probands and cohorts with replication, so the association is unambiguously established.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own primary results linking ANGPTL3 loss-of-function variants to lower plasma triglycerides: the DiscovEHR/exome-sequencing cohort analysis (PMID 28538136), the familial combined hypolipidemia/CAD study of inactivating mutation carriers (PMID 28385496), and a kinetic study of individuals with compound heterozygous ANGPTL3 LOF showing >10-fold lower TG and TRL particle concentrations (PMID 40446802). Additional human work includes candidate-variant genotyping in severe hypertriglyceridemia (PMID 18596051), Finnish population variant/serum studies (PMID 28972399), and Mendelian randomization of ANGPTL3 as a triglyceride-modifying drug target (PMID 35213538). Pharmacologic antagonism in humans (evinacumab, ASOs, siRNA, CRISPR) independently corroborates the direction and mechanism. This constitutes replicated, human, gene-specific evidence, supporting an Established classification.

Multiple independent human studies report ABCA1 variants associated with total cholesterol: a systematic review/meta-analysis of ABCA1 69C>T, 825V>I and 230R>C polymorphisms with plasma lipid concentrations (PMID 34575660), a cohort of chronic hepatitis C patients where rs2230808 (R1587K) genotypes associated with lower total cholesterol in males (PMID 36421770), a Chinese population study of V825I with serum lipid levels (PMID 21247457), and an ABCA1 polymorphism/plasma lipid variability cohort (PMID 26722555). Mendelian evidence also exists: a homozygous ABCA1 (ABC1) R527W mutation in a Tangier proband with markedly low plasma total cholesterol (PMID 11257260), and R219K carriers show 33% lower CSF total cholesterol (PMID 12600718). These are human probands and independent cohorts, not merely background citation, supporting an Established relationship. Some studies show null effects on TC (PMIDs 12700893, 30720955, 14644402), which slightly tempers certainty and supports partial weight on Existing; animal/in vitro work (PMID 35829808, 12377786) is only supportive mechanistically.

Multiple independent human studies report their own results linking LDLR variants to total cholesterol levels: PMID 2906577 shows a common LDLR PvuII RFLP associated with total serum cholesterol in a healthy population; PMID 8879444 compares plasma total cholesterol across three specific LDLR mutation groups in 266 FH children; PMID 9360938 reports mean total cholesterol of 413.7 mg/dl in 83 LDLR-mutation patients versus FDB carriers; PMID 39407785 documents untreated total cholesterol in 105 carriers of four identical-by-descent LDLR variants in France and Quebec; and PMID 36619676 tests LDLR rs6511720 association with lipids in a Thai cohort. Additional large-scale sequencing (PMID 25487149) and deep mutational scanning correlated with hyperlipidemia phenotypes in human cohorts (PMID 41166440) reinforce replication across independent probands, families, and populations. The evidence is human, replicated, and mechanistically coherent (LDLR mediates LDL/cholesterol clearance), so Established is overwhelmingly supported.

Multiple independent human studies report ADAMTS17 variants causing Weill-Marchesani-like syndrome whose cardinal feature is short stature: Al-Haggar/Morales et al. (PMID 19836009) identified three homozygous ADAMTS17 mutations in independent Arabian families with short stature; PMID 22486325 reported a novel homozygous ADAMTS17 mutation in a Saudi family with spherophakia and short stature; PMID 24940034 found a novel splice-site variant in an Indian family; PMID 37506754 identified six novel ADAMTS17 variants in four probands, all with apparent short stature; PMID 31726086 and 32616716 add further families with short stature and functional support. Additionally, population-scale human data support common/rare variant association with height itself: the All of Us WGS analysis replicated a gene-based rare loss-of-function burden association of ADAMTS17 with height (PMID 37072623), and ADAMTS17 lies at a GWAS height locus (PMID 24065112). Evidence is human, replicated across independent probands and cohorts, and single-gene resolved (not CNV-based), supporting the Established category.

Multiple independent human studies report heterozygous ACAN variants segregating with short stature in unrelated probands and families: novel pathogenic variants in non-syndromic short stature (PMID 28396070), de novo and familial nonsense/frameshift variants in two families (PMID 29264551), 16 probands with heterozygous aggrecan variants and brachydactyly (PMID 29464738), a large Chinese cohort with a high proportion of novel ACAN mutations (PMID 33606014), and a Chinese family with a novel frameshift variant (PMID 37025453) plus a splice-site variant pedigree (PMID 38782218). Additionally, a large GWAS of adult height in the general population identified ACAN as one of 20 loci influencing height (PMID 18391952), and a VNTR in ACAN correlates with population height (PMID 40517756). Mouse and mechanistic work (PMID 40685060) further supports causality but is not needed given the abundant human genetic evidence. This constitutes replicated, independent human evidence for an Established gene–phenotype relationship.

Hypertension is a core, early manifestation of ADPKD caused by PKD1 mutations, and several human studies with genotype/linkage data report it directly in their own results. PMID 1360045 compared 18 PKD1-linked families with 5 non-PKD1 families and found significantly higher hypertension odds in PKD1-linked patients; PMID 1614046 independently identified the PKD1 gene and hypertension as determinants in 580 affected subjects; PMID 40269498 shows in a multicenter cohort and UK Biobank that PKD1/PKD2 rare variant carriers develop hypertension years before kidney disease diagnosis (PPV 74% for PKD1); PMID 26150605 (Genkyst, n=1341) incorporates early hypertension with truncating/nontruncating PKD1 mutations. Mechanistic human/mouse work (endothelial polycystin-1 deficiency, PMID 36093769) supports biological plausibility but is not needed for the human-based conclusion. Some residual uncertainty remains because hypertension may be partly secondary to cystic kidney disease rather than a directly ascribed independent phenotype, which keeps meaningful weight on "Existing".

The only human genetic-variant studies of MRC1 in this set concern leprosy (PMID 22392581, 20035344), asthma (PMID 19902202), and a rodent hantavirus GWAS (PMID 37956745) — none reports variants associated with aspartate aminotransferase levels or liver enzyme phenotypes, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The remaining papers merely co-mention Mrc1/CD206 as an M2-macrophage marker alongside serum AST as a generic tissue-damage readout in mouse, bovine, or in vitro liver-injury models (PMIDs 36921490, 28822324, 33718268, 39647630, 32742385, 39486177). These provide only indirect biological plausibility — M2 macrophage polarization modulating hepatic inflammation and thereby transaminase release — which is a pathway-level, non-human argument fitting "Hypothesized." Because MRC1 is used purely as a phenotypic marker rather than shown to influence AST, a substantial probability remains that the co-mentions are entirely incidental (Novel).

Multiple human genetic studies provide primary evidence linking TTN variants to dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure. Gerull et al. (PMID 11788824) identified segregating TTN frameshift and missense mutations in two independent large DCM kindreds, and Herman et al. (PMID 22335739) reported TTN truncating variants in independent DCM probands. Replication comes from large cohorts: 1,041 sporadic DCM patients with 11.5% tTTN enrichment versus population controls (PMID 33996946), 332 probands plus affected relatives with genotype–phenotype correlation (PMID 39844436), and UK Biobank data showing hiPSI TTNtv carriers have increased incident heart failure risk (PMID 39196037). Additional cohorts link TTN-TV to progression to advanced heart failure requiring LVAD/transplant (PMID 41282741). Together these constitute strong, replicated human evidence for causality.

phenotype: Benign and in situ intestinal neoplasms
literature_justification: Benign and in situ intestinal neoplasms encompass adenomatous polyps/polyposis, and germline APC variants are the cause of familial adenomatous polyposis. Multiple listed papers report primary human genetic evidence: PMID 41801175 determined APC mosaicism prevalence in independent patients with unexplained colorectal adenomatous polyposis; PMID 31383941 identified an APC 5'UTR variant (c.-190G>A) in a 4-generation FAP family with reduced APC transcription; PMID 36828923 identified a novel deep intronic APC pathogenic variant with co-segregation in an affected family; PMID 39357517 classified >10,000 patient-derived APC variants from ClinVar/InSiGHT LOVD; PMID 32743790 quantified pathogenic germline APC variants in 7225 individuals with colorectal adenomas. These represent replicated, independent human probands and families, well beyond background citation. Mouse Apc models (PMIDs 39148929, 12584170) provide supporting mechanistic evidence but are not needed for the human causal claim.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary results linking APOA5 variants to plasma triglyceride levels: PMID 12417524 identified APOA5*2/*3 haplotypes associated with high TG across three independent Caucasian, African-American and Hispanic samples; PMID 12436249 showed the -1131T>C promoter SNP associated with serum TG in 552 Japanese schoolchildren; PMID 31903892 found rs964184, rs662799 and rs3135506 strongly associated with hypertriglyceridemia in 209 Czech patients vs 379 controls; PMID 25487149 found rare non-synonymous APOA5 alleles in ~10,000 exomes associated with higher plasma triglycerides; PMID 18596051 and 27599772 add replication in severe HTG and Saudi Arab cohorts. Rare biallelic/compound heterozygous APOA5 variants also cause familial chylomicronemia/severe hypertriglyceridemia (PMIDs 41165100, 36689289, 38117614). The evidence is human, replicated across ancestries and both common and rare variant classes, so the relationship is clearly Established.

Multiple independent human studies report APOC3 variants associated with HDL cholesterol: PMID 23701270 identified two novel and one known APOC3 mutation in families with hyperalphalipoproteinemia showing high HDL-C and low triglycerides; PMID 25363704 found the rare R19X null variant associated with cardioprotective lipid profiles in a diverse population-based survey; PMID 26516010 linked APOC3 loss-of-function mutations to plasma lipids in the multi-ethnic BioImage Study; PMID 9194755 reported the APOC3 insulin-response-element genotype associated with HDL cholesterol and apoA-I in aboriginal Canadians; and PMID 25928461 is a meta-analysis of rs5128 with lipid levels. Additional cohort evidence comes from pregnant Chinese Han women (PMID 28915626) and the APOA1/C3/A4/A5 cluster in diabetic women (PMID 16781717), plus pharmacologic APOC3 inhibition raising HDL-C in humans (PMID 41240900), supporting causality. The evidence is human, replicated across independent cohorts and families, and points to single-gene resolution, so "Established" is strongly favored. A small residual probability is left for "Existing" given some studies report HDL effects secondarily to triglyceride effects.

Multiple independent human studies report their own results linking ANGPTL3 variants to total cholesterol levels: PMID 22247256 screened 913 American and Italian hypobetalipoproteinemia subjects (TC <5th percentile) and defined ANGPTL3 mutations as determinants of low total cholesterol; PMID 22659251 clinically and biochemically characterized ANGPTL3-mutation carriers with familial combined hypolipidemia; PMID 28538136 analyzed loss-of-function variants in large human cohorts with reduced lipid levels and cardiovascular risk; PMID 28633452 examined ANGPTL3 levels and lipoprotein phenotypes in homozygous and heterozygous carriers; PMID 28972399 identified Finnish carriers of ANGPTL3 sequence variants with atypical TC; and PMID 34417926 tested rs1748195/rs11207997 against lipid profiles including TC in an Iranian cohort. These are independent probands, families, and population cohorts, all human, with replication across ancestries. Additional MR and therapeutic-inactivation studies (39763524, 41211945) reinforce the causal direction. Therefore the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report their own results linking SCARB1 variants to HDL-C: PMID 15186961 (population-based Geneva cohort of 1756 adults showing A350A/exon 8 genotype effects on HDL-C), PMID 23091409 (rs5888 and serum lipids in Guangxi Mulao and Han populations), PMID 25245032 (impact of SCARB1 variants on plasma lipid traits), PMID 35097019 (functional promoter indels associated with lipid profile and CHD in >10,000 Chinese subjects), PMID 27651445 (SCARB1 variants in subjects with high HDL-C and Lp(a)), and resequencing studies of HDL-C phenotypic extremes (PMIDs 29987113, 41486059). These represent replicated evidence across independent cohorts and ethnicities, with supporting functional mechanisms (SR-B1 expression, FOXA1 binding) and Mendelian-level descriptions of very high HDL-C due to SCARB1 mutations (PMID 31686116). Animal/in vitro work (PMID 23722970) further supports causality but is not needed for classification. Therefore the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report rare TTN loss-of-function/truncating variants in patients with atrial fibrillation, with their own primary results: Choi et al. found enrichment of TTN LOF variants in early-onset AF probands (PMID 30535219); clinical broad genetic testing identified high prevalence of TTN LOF in very-early-onset AF (PMID 31638414); UK Biobank monogenic/polygenic analysis showed independent TTNtv association with incident AF (PMID 31691645, 33373724); All of Us gene-based burden testing replicated TTN–AF association in both European and African ancestry cohorts (PMIDs 37072623, 39196186); and a clinical cohort characterized outcomes of AF patients with pathogenic TTN variants (PMID 39453294). Common variants in TTN also reach genome-wide significance for AF (PMID 29290336), and mechanistic iPSC-derived atrial cardiomyocyte models of patient TTN variants support causality via atrial myopathy and electrical remodeling (PMIDs 39851047, 41569083). This constitutes replicated, human, variant-level evidence in independent probands/cohorts, satisfying the Established criteria; the small residual probability reflects that many TTNtv carriers develop AF in the context of cardiomyopathy/atrial myopathy rather than as an isolated monogenic AF syndrome.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary results linking LCORL variants to height and height-related skeletal measures: PMID 19343178 (GW meta-analysis of adult stature with LCORL SNPs rs6817306/rs6830062 for trunk and hip axis length), PMID 22021425 (GWAS in African-American women replicating 4p15/LCORL), PMID 19266077 (longitudinal Finnish birth cohort, LCORL associated with peak height velocity), PMID 25281659 (LCORL associated with birth and infant length and adult height), and PMID 28744006 (LCORL among height loci associated with familial short stature in Han Chinese). These are independent cohorts of differing ancestries with single-variant (not CNV) associations, satisfying replication. Extensive animal work (cattle, horses, dogs, goats, donkeys, geese) further supports causality but is not required for the human classification. Therefore the LCORL–height relationship is Established.
