Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own primary evidence that ANGPTL4 coding variants alter plasma triglycerides: resequencing in the Dallas Heart Study identified rare loss-of-function ANGPTL4 alleles associated with low TG (PMID 19075393); the E40K and T266M variants were associated with lower TG across five cohorts totaling 13,527 individuals (PMID 18974381); a 1000G-imputed meta-analysis of 49,549 individuals identified an exonic damaging ANGPTL4 variant determining fasting TG (PMID 27036123); a Finnish protein-truncating variant lowered TG by ~14 mg/dL (PMID 33909604); and whole-genome sequencing in Icelanders plus large exome studies replicated ANGPTL4 lipid/CAD associations (PMIDs 27135400, 26934567). Additional cohort studies in Tunisian type 2 diabetes and obesity populations replicate E40K effects on TG (PMIDs 27004807, 30820332), and Mendelian randomization analyses use ANGPTL4 variants as TG-lowering instruments (PMIDs 33351885, 36372100). This constitutes replicated, human, variant-level evidence across independent cohorts, satisfying the Established criteria.

Multiple independent human case-control studies report their own primary data showing rare protein-truncating/pathogenic PALB2 variants significantly enriched in breast cancer cases: the East Anglia sequencing study of 13,087 cases vs 5,488 controls (PMID 28779002), the German Consortium panel study of 5,589 BRCA1/2-negative index patients (PALB2 OR 9.53; PMID 29522266), the French GENESIS familial breast cancer study (PMID 30303537), and a German panel-sequencing cohort identifying deleterious PALB2 variants with early-onset, family-history-positive disease (PMID 27616075). Additional independent replication comes from Italian male breast cancer patients (PMID 30613976), Chinese/Hong Kong hereditary cohorts (PMID 32068069), French-Canadian founder variant analyses (PMID 32300229), and a Brazilian hereditary cancer cohort (PMID 35534704). A formal meta-analysis of 12 studies estimates ~48% cumulative breast cancer risk by age 80 in PALB2 pathogenic variant carriers (PMID 38654400), and contralateral breast cancer risk is also elevated (PMID 36623243). Evidence is human, replicated across ancestries, and gene-specific (point/truncating variants, not multigene CNVs), so the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report IHH variants affecting height. GWAS of adult height identified IHH as a genome-wide significant locus (PMID 18391952), replicated in African-derived populations (PMID 20400458), and exome-array analyses found rare/low-frequency IHH coding variants with large effects on height (PMID 28146470). Monogenic evidence includes 16 families with heterozygous IHH variants causing short stature with mild skeletal anomalies (PMID 32311039), a cohort with IHH mutations causing short stature responsive to GH (PMID 29155992), and homozygous IHH missense mutations causing acrocapitofemoral dysplasia with short stature in independent consanguineous families (PMIDs 12632327, 34530144, 40045933). Functional studies of patient variants confirm defective secretion and pathogenicity (PMID 38917024). This constitutes replicated human evidence across probands, families, and population cohorts.

The only human study in this set that presents its own genetic association results for ZFAT and height is the Japanese adult-height replication study (PMID 19834501), which found ZFAT significantly associated with height (P=3.8x10-9 combining Japanese and Korean data, the locus originally reported in Koreans). A second human paper (PMID 41015547) reports ZFAT rs13267329 associated with lean mass index, a related anthropometric/body-composition trait rather than height itself. All other supportive statements come from horse, cattle, sheep and pig GWAS (PMIDs 22615965, 22808074, 29270069, 32091312, 32271776, 41925102), which either cite human height findings as background or provide non-human evidence, and mechanistic ZFAT papers concern hematopoiesis, cell cycle and cancer. Since I cannot cite two independent human PMIDs whose own results demonstrate ZFAT–height association, Established cannot be fully supported, and Existing is the most appropriate category.

Multiple independent human cohort studies report their own primary results linking CD36 variants to HDL-C. PMID 18305138 found the CD36 nonsense variant rs3211938 associated with increased HDL-C and protection from metabolic syndrome in 2,020 African Americans (HyperGen), and PMID 23236364 independently replicated rs3211938 with HDL-C at genome-wide significance (p=1.3×10⁻¹²) in African Americans using the IBC array. PMID 23726366 further validated this African-specific HDL-C locus at CD36 in Women's Health Initiative SHARe participants, and PMID 39830278 shows colocalization of CD36 rs3211938 pQTL with HDL-C GWAS signal. Additional support comes from meta-analyses of rs1761667 with HDL-C (PMIDs 35396566, 40040886) and candidate studies in Chinese, Korean, and Mexican populations. This constitutes replicated, human-based genetic evidence across independent cohorts and ancestries.

Multiple human studies report their own primary data identifying pathogenic germline MSH2 variants in independent colorectal cancer probands and families: the German multicentre cohort found 134 index patients with pathogenic MSH2 mutations among 1,721 HNPCC-suspected families (PMID 15849733), and six novel MSH2/MLH1 germline mutations were characterized in HNPCC families with MSI-H tumours and loss of protein expression (PMID 12655562). Large segregation analyses of 224 MSH2 mutation-carrying families quantify lifetime colorectal cancer risks (~37–47% by age 70) (PMID 23255516), replicated by prospective cohort risk estimates (PMID 21642682, PMID 40231433). Additional independent reports include a founder MSH2 exon 9–10 deletion segregating with early-onset CRC in Ethiopian Jewish families (PMID 33837488), a novel MSH2 c.1774_1775insT case (PMID 37685569), and early-onset CRC panel testing (PMID 40097831). The gene–disease relationship (Lynch syndrome/HNPCC) is definitively established in humans with abundant independent probands and families.

Multiple independent human studies report heterozygous NPR2 variants in short stature cohorts with segregation and functional validation: Olney et al. (PMID 16384845), Vasques et al. (PMID 24001744), Amano et al. (PMID 24471569), Wang et al. (PMID 25703509, 192 patients vs 192 controls, 7 heterozygous variants), a Czech ISS cohort (PMID 35741827, 6.7% frequency), and a Korean ISS cohort (PMID 31960617). Independent families with gain-of-function NPR2 mutations causing tall stature/overgrowth further establish bidirectional effects on height (PMIDs 22870295, 24057292, 24259409). Biallelic loss-of-function causes acromesomelic dysplasia Maroteaux type with severe short stature, and a large-scale functional/PheWAS study links NPR2 activity scores near-linearly to standing height in humans (PMID 41512838). This is replicated human genetic evidence in independent probands, families, and cohorts, so the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary evidence linking LIPC variants to HDL-C: Guerra et al. (PMID 9114024) showed linkage in 218 nuclear families plus association of a novel promoter allele with higher HDL-C, replicated in a second independent sample; Zambon et al. (PMID 9812910) tied the -250G>A promoter variant to lower hepatic lipase activity and higher HDL2-C in normolipidemic and CAD men; a meta-analysis of 25 studies (>24,000 individuals, PMID 15292318) confirmed a dose-dependent -514C>T effect on HDL. Additional independent cohorts (Korean GWAS PMID 31910446, Taiwan Biobank GWAS with functional promoter haplotype assays PMID 33499410, Mexican cohort PMID 32617858, Dutch Doetinchem cohort PMID 18660489) replicate the association across ancestries. All key evidence is human and variant-based, so the relationship is firmly Established.

Multiple independent human studies in this list report germline MLH1 variants segregating with colorectal cancer in families and probands: linkage of HNPCC kindreds to the 3p MLH1 locus with heritable MLH1 mutations (PMID 7942843), loss of the wild-type MLH1 allele in HNPCC tumors supporting a two-hit tumor-suppressor mechanism (PMID 7894494), a segregating pathogenic missense variant c.2054C>T in a Chinese Lynch pedigree (PMID 32076465) and independently in four CRC patients with functional MMR defect (PMID 42269807), novel frameshift variants in unrelated probands (PMIDs 37001204, 38317368), and constitutional MLH1 epimutation/synonymous variant families (PMIDs 19564652, 40715574). Large cohort risk estimates from 166 MLH1 mutation-carrying families quantify lifetime CRC risk (~34-36% by age 70; PMID 23255516). These are human clinical genetic studies with independent probands and families, satisfying the criteria for a replicated causal relationship.

Multiple independent human cohort studies report pathogenic PKD2 variants in unrelated ADPKD probands/families with direct renal outcome data: PMID 12707387 identified 50 distinct PKD2 mutations in 71 families and analyzed onset of chronic renal failure and ESRD; PMID 22508176 screened 700 unrelated patients and expanded the PKD2 mutation spectrum by ~24%; PMID 24611717 found 23 PKD2 mutations in Japanese families with measured eGFR decline; PMID 35778421 documented a PKD2 p.Arg803* founder variant in 164 Taiwanese families. ADPKD due to PKD2 is a well-recognized major genetic cause of progressive CKD/kidney failure (PMID 38097330), and additional human studies (PMID 22383692, 40269498) replicate variant identification with renal phenotype. These are human, variant-level, replicated data from independent probands, satisfying the criteria for Established. Only minimal probability is left for the weaker categories.

Bi-allelic SCUBE3 loss-of-function causes SSFSC syndrome, whose cardinal feature is reduced growth/short stature, and this is supported by multiple independent human reports with identified variants: PMID 33308444 (18 affected individuals from 9 unrelated families with reduced growth and skeletal/craniofacial features, plus functional validation), PMID 40331102 (a novel homozygous missense variant in a patient with short stature), PMID 34142127 (an independent patient with recessive SCUBE3 mutations and skeletal disease alongside a mouse model), and PMID 39706863 (Indian skeletal dysplasia cohort noting SCUBE3-related disease). These are independent probands/cohorts with point variants, not multigene CNVs, satisfying replication. Supporting mouse and mechanistic work (PMIDs 33308444, 27815347, 37237303) shows SCUBE3 modulates BMP signaling and endochondral bone growth, reinforcing biological plausibility. Livestock GWAS for body height (PMID 25090094) adds cross-species support but is not human evidence.

Multiple independent human studies report APOA1 coding variants directly causing HDL cholesterol deficiency: PMID 35778257 describes a novel homozygous frameshift (c.614_615delTC) in a Japanese proband and affected relatives with markedly low HDL-C; PMID 17991756 reports a kindred with a nonsense mutation (Q[-2]X) with homozygotes showing undetectable apoA-I and very low HDL-C and heterozygotes losing alpha-1 HDL particles; PMID 17991432 reports another new APOA1 mutation with severe HDL-C deficiency; and PMID 30333156 identified APOA1 mutations in 5% of 201 sequenced subjects with severe HDL deficiency in a large cohort. Additional human genetic/association support comes from candidate variant and GWAS-type studies at the APOA1 locus (PMIDs 27599772, 21729881) and reviews of monogenic HDL disorders (PMIDs 31686116, 32022753, 37138899). These are independent probands, families, and cohorts with single-gene resolution, satisfying the criteria for Established.

Only one article in this list provides primary human genetic evidence linking CRISPLD2 to height: the GIANT exome-array study of rare and low-frequency coding variants (PMID 28146470), which explicitly names CRISPLD2 among genes harboring low-frequency coding variants with effects up to ~2 cm per allele. Although that study is a very large multi-cohort meta-analysis with internal discovery/replication, it is a single publication in the provided set, so the two-independent-report threshold for "Established" is not met here. All other articles concern CRISPLD2 in asthma/glucocorticoid response, sepsis, orofacial clefting, MSC immunomodulation, or hepatic fibrosis, none of which are height-relevant phenotypes or precursors. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" given the strength and scale of the single cited human study.

Multiple independent human studies report NR1H3 variants associated with HDL cholesterol in their own results: the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 GWAS identified a new HDL association at NR1H3 (LXRA) (PMID 19060910); the Icelandic whole-genome sequencing study of 119,146 individuals discovered a large-effect HDL variant in NR1H3 (PMID 27135400); and the HELENA adolescent study tested NR1H3 polymorphisms against serum HDL-C concentrations (PMID 21316679). Additional functional-genomic human work colocalizes an HDL GWAS signal with an NR1H3 splice QTL in adipose tissue and shows the alternative isoform lacks a DNA-binding domain, providing a mechanism (PMID 34995504). Other papers (multiple sclerosis, IOP, hypertension, dyslipidemia in hemodialysis) support that NR1H3 variation is functional in humans but are not the primary evidence. The presence of at least two independent cohorts with directly reported HDL associations supports the Established category.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary results linking LIPG variants to HDL-C: PMID 14984737 (resequencing of LIPG in extreme HDL-C subjects, intronic SNPs associated with HDL-C), PMID 12884003 (two common EL SNPs associated with serum HDL-C in Japanese schoolchildren), PMID 12601178 (584C/T association with HDL-C in 372 humans), PMID 16023652 (LIPG haplotypes with HDL3-C and apoAI in 541 Japanese Americans), PMID 22174694 (rare and common regulatory variants affecting EL levels and HDL-C), and PMID 21303902 (dense candidate-gene genotyping identifying HDL-C variants). Rare-variant/clinical evidence also exists in hyperalphalipoproteinemia carriers of LIPG mutations (PMID 33414088, 40703622). These are independent cohorts and ethnicities, satisfying replication, with supportive functional and mouse data (PMID 12601178, 37693454, 23536757). A few null studies (PMID 20466371) address CAD/DVT risk rather than negating the HDL-C association.

None of the provided articles examine height or any anthropometric/skeletal growth phenotype. The papers describe CRISPLD1 within the CAP superfamily (reproduction, immunity, cancer), a role in cardiac remodeling and Ca2+ handling in heart failure, and reduced expression in an orofacial clefting case with a ZFHX4 variant and 16q24.1 deletion. No human genetic variants in CRISPLD1 are associated with stature, and no animal or expression data connect the gene to growth or skeletal development. Only a very weak indirect plausibility exists via craniofacial/extracellular matrix and branching morphogenesis roles, justifying a small allocation to Hypothesized.

Multiple independent human cohorts report short stature/reduced height as a core feature of NF1 with molecularly confirmed intragenic NF1 variants: PMID 41225058 (148 pediatric patients, NGS/MLPA-confirmed NF1 variants, short stature in 29.3%), PMID 34619926 (27 genetically confirmed pediatric NF1 patients, short stature linked to missense variants), and PMID 22752476 (170 children; height z-scores significantly lower than population, mid-parental targets, and unaffected siblings, directly attributing the effect to germline NF1 mutation). These are supported by large clinical/epidemiological cohorts (PMID 7853369, 10353939, 35586386) and by NFNS case reports with specific NF1 nonsense/frameshift variants and short stature/GH deficiency (PMIDs 35633639, 31088041). Microdeletion studies (26111455, 28213670) showing overgrowth/tall stature also implicate this locus but were not counted, since multigene deletions cannot isolate NF1. Given at least two–three independent human studies with intragenic NF1 variants and quantified height outcomes, the relationship is best classified as Established, with some residual probability for Existing because some cohorts relied on clinical rather than molecular diagnosis.

Several independent human studies report ABCB4 variants in probands/cohorts together with measured alanine aminotransferase elevations: PMID 38623015 describes 11 children with PFIC3 carrying 17 ABCB4 variants (including 9 novel) all with raised ALT (113±40 U/L); PMID 36046230 reports novel ABCB4 (Ile377Asn) and related transporter mutations in an ICP cohort with higher mean ALT than controls; PMID 39865141 shows ICP patients carrying combined ABCB4 exonic variants including c.1954A>G had higher ALT/AST/γ-GT; PMID 22675952 documents an obstetric cholestasis patient with heterozygous ABCB4 p.R590Q and >40-fold ALT rise; and PMID 38864694 identified morbid ABCB4 variants in a child with recurrent hypertransaminasemia. PMID 37511794 further links ABCB4 polymorphisms to ALT changes under UDCA therapy in NASH patients. All evidence is human, with multiple independent cohorts/probands, supporting an Established-to-Existing relationship; some residual uncertainty remains because ALT elevation is a nonspecific marker of the cholestatic liver disease rather than a directly studied quantitative trait.

The strongest direct T2D evidence comes from the large rare-variant meta-analysis of 51,256 T2D cases and 370,487 controls (PMID 39379762), which found a rare GCK ClinVar variant conferring ~eightfold increased T2D risk in its own results, and from the UK Biobank exome analysis (PMID 35177841), where GCK was among Mendelian genes with striking rare-variant risk for diabetes/glucose traits. Additional human population-association work reported GCK microsatellite/variant associations with late-onset NIDDM and glucose intolerance (PMIDs 8200207, 8359581, 7555485), though other Caucasian cohorts were negative (PMIDs 8261750, 8314445), indicating heterogeneous replication for common T2D. Much of the remaining literature concerns GCK-MODY (monogenic diabetes), a well-recognized diabetes subtype with high penetrance (PMIDs 36257325, 8168652), which supports at minimum the "Existing" tier and arguably an established causal role for hyperglycemia phenotypes. Because the definitive large-effect human evidence for common T2D rests mainly on one recent study with older, inconsistent association data, probability is split roughly evenly between Established and Existing, with little support for a purely hypothesized or novel relationship.

The only direct human evidence linking PIEZO1 variants to stature is a single case report of compound heterozygous PIEZO1 variants (intragenic deletion plus p.Arg953His) in a patient with lymphatic dysplasia who also had short stature, scoliosis and fractures (PMID 34371190), together with review statements that PIEZO1 participates in bone formation (PMID 40628291, 29331020). This is one proband, not independent replication, so Established cannot be supported. Other "height" mentions are homonymous or unrelated: disc height index in disc degeneration studies (PMIDs 42153663, 36250343) and jumping height performance rather than body stature (PMID 34031557); the varicose-vein GWAS only reports genetic correlation of the trait with height, not a PIEZO1–stature variant association (PMID 30998689). Given the strong skeletal/mechanotransduction biology but limited human genetic evidence, Existing is most likely, with substantial residual probability for Hypothesized.

Multiple large human genetic studies implicate PDE3B variation in blood lipid and cardiometabolic traits: the Million Veteran Program lipid GWAS highlights PDE3B loss-of-function variants for triglycerides and coronary disease (PMID 30275531), UK Biobank pLOF analysis links PDE3B to improved body fat distribution and CAD protection (PMID 29691411), WES-imputation replicates PDE3B for triglycerides (PMID 36490288), exome burden testing links rare PDE3B variants to metabolic syndrome (of which low HDL-C is a defining component; PMID 42472903), and metabolomic/NMR-based analyses identify PDE3B among lipoprotein-related loci alongside APOC3/APOA5 (PMID 39442521). However, none of the provided abstracts explicitly reports an HDL-C–specific association for PDE3B variants in their own results (the HDL findings in PMID 36490288 are attributed to PLIN1/ANGPTL3), so the criterion of two independent HDL-specific human replications is not clearly met. Supporting biology—PDE3B as the insulin-regulated phosphodiesterase controlling adipocyte lipolysis (PMIDs 40680056, 31492854)—provides a strong mechanistic rationale for effects on HDL-C. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with meaningful probability that full HDL-specific replication exists within these lipid GWAS.

Multiple independent human studies present primary results linking LPL variants to HDL cholesterol: LPL resequencing in US non-Hispanic Whites found gene-based and single-site association with HDL-C (rs295) (PMID 24212298); an independent resequencing study in African Blacks found LPL variants associated with HDL-C/ApoA1 (PMID 25626708); a large candidate-pathway study in the Doetinchem cohort identified LPL SNPs (rs3208305, rs328, rs268) associated with HDL-C (PMID 18660489); and a HuGE meta-analysis of ~72,000 individuals showed HindIII and S447X carriers have favorable HDL-C/triglyceride profiles (PMID 18922999). Additional supporting human data include LPL genotype–lipid associations in meta-analysis of T2DM cohorts (PMID 32886944), Kurdish hypertriglyceridemia patients (PMID 37954769), gene–physical activity interaction on HDL-C (PMID 22330029), and human LPL deficiency HDL subpopulation profiles (PMID 27573733). These are independent cohorts with primary genotype–phenotype results, satisfying replication in humans, so Established is strongly favored.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report ANGPTL8 coding variants associated with triglyceride levels: the Exome Array study of 56,538 individuals found ANGPTL8 rs145464906 (p.Gln121*) with large effects on HDL-C/triglycerides (PMID 24507774); a Finnish population study identified rs760351239 PTV lowering serum triglycerides by ~24 mg/dL with reduced CAD risk (PMID 33909604); and a consanguineous Pakistani cohort confirmed lower TG and higher HDL-C in heterozygous carriers of multiple ANGPTL8 loss-of-function variants including a novel splice donor variant (PMID 42056369). Further human genetic support comes from R59W (rs2278426) lipid-trait associations and genetic mimicry/Mendelian-randomization-style analyses in UK Biobank (PMIDs 37755252, 36372100, 33619548), plus MetS GWAS mapping C19orf80/ANGPTL8 (PMID 38201907). These are independent cohorts with variant-level human evidence, supporting the Established category; the remaining probability reflects minor uncertainty from a few negative/null reports (PMID 40192643).

Multiple independent human studies report LPL variants with triglyceride phenotypes in their own results: PMID 36476373 characterizes TG levels in a cohort of heterozygous carriers of LPL pathogenic variants; PMID 31599081 identifies a novel D151N LPL variant cosegregating with familial combined hyperlipidemia in a large pedigree; PMID 38025240 reports a homozygous loss-of-function LPL variant causing type I hyperlipoproteinemia; PMID 40132937 reports a novel homozygous p.Cys291Tyr LPL variant in an infant with extreme hypertriglyceridemia; PMID 40747209 reports a heterozygous p.N318S variant with severe HTG; and cohort studies (PMID 36689289, 39278772) find rare LPL variants among severe hypertriglyceridemia patients across populations. A curated catalog of 300 disease-causing LPL variants (PMID 39858602) further confirms replication across many probands and families. This is a canonical, replicated human gene–phenotype relationship, so Established is nearly certain.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report ANGPTL8 variants associated with HDL-C in their own results: Romeo/Hobbs-type discovery of rs2278426 (R59W) with lower LDL-C and HDL-C in three populations (PMID 23150577), replication in Pima Indians and San Antonio Mexican Americans (PMID 27117576), exome-array analysis of ~56,000 whites and blacks identifying the low-frequency PTV rs145464906 with large HDL-C/TG effects (PMID 24507774), trans-ancestry fine mapping of the ANGPTL8 HDL-C GWAS locus with functional regulatory variants (PMID 28754724), and PTV carriers in the Pakistan Genomic Resource with increased HDL-C (PMID 42056369). Additional GWAS in Taiwan Biobank list ANGPTL8 among HDL-C loci (PMID 35238325), and Finnish PTV work confirms lipid effects (PMID 33909604). This constitutes replicated, independent, human cohort-level evidence, supporting the Established category, with only residual uncertainty because some HDL-C effects are secondary to the ANGPTL3/8–endothelial lipase axis.

The strongest human-genetic evidence is the prospective insulin/IGF-1 signalling study (PMID 15771611), where an IRS1 SNP was among the variants contributing to composite IIS scores associated with lower body height and old-age survival in women; this is a single cohort with modest, composite-score-based effects, so it supports "Existing" rather than "Established". Other human genotype–phenotype work on the IGF/IRS pathway (PMID 16030120) linked IRS1 G972R to waist-to-hip ratio, not stature, and the IRS1 frameshift case report (PMID 38572380) concerns insulin resistance rather than a demonstrated stature phenotype. The GWAS of lean body mass (PMID 28724990) implicates IRS1 in body composition but explicitly adjusts for height. Remaining support is mechanistic/animal or review-level: IRS-1 as a growth-signalling node in SGA/fetal growth restriction, 3-M syndrome (CUL7–IRS-1), SHORT syndrome (PIK3R1–IRS-1), and LEOPARD syndrome mouse models with short stature and Shp2–Irs1 binding — these justify substantial weight for "Hypothesized" but do not provide replicated human IRS1 variant–height associations.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own primary evidence linking CREB3L3 variants to triglyceride levels: Lee et al. identified multiple nonsynonymous hypomorphic/nonfunctional CREB3L3 mutations in patients with extreme hypertriglyceridemia (PMID 21666694); an independent family with autosomal dominant hypertriglyceridemia carried a novel nonsense mutation (PMID 26427795); a case-control targeted sequencing study found ~20-fold enrichment of rare loss-of-function CREB3L3 variants in 265 severe HTG patients versus 477 controls (PMID 32580631); a rare-variant accumulation study in polygenic HTG also implicated CREB3L3 (PMID 22135386); and exome-wide gene-collapsing analysis in 412,393 UK Biobank participants found significant associations of rare CREB3L3 variants with lipid metabolite measurements (PMID 36809768). Additional case reports (PMIDs 29954705, 39562229) and mechanistic human/mouse work (PMIDs 34491909, 36649378) corroborate. These are independent probands, families, and cohorts in humans, satisfying the criteria for Established.

Multiple independent human cohorts report their own results linking APOA5 variants to HDL-C: the Vancouver SCA cohort found -1131T>C and the APOA5*1 haplotype independently predicted HDL-C (PMID 15306190); a lipid clinic cohort of 915 patients found the -1131C allele associated with decreased HDL-C (PMID 12937897); a Chinese case-control study plus large meta-analysis (>51,000 subjects) showed significantly lower HDL-C in C allele carriers (PMID 23468858); a Korean GWAS identified APOA5 SNPs associated with low HDL-C (PMID 31910446); and sequencing/mediation analysis of p.S19W in premature CAD showed correlation with HDL-C (PMID 30024021). Additional supporting human evidence includes gene-environment interaction analyses (PMID 22425169, 27827461), Framingham haplotype analyses (PMID 15342688), and fine-mapping at 11q23.3 (PMID 33753020). Evidence is replicated across ethnicities and study designs in humans, meeting the Established criteria; the small remainder reflects the possibility that some HDL effects are secondary to triglyceride metabolism.

Multiple independent human studies report intragenic loss-of-function ANKRD11 variants (not just multigene deletions) in probands and families with KBG syndrome, in which short stature/postnatal growth restriction is a core feature: the original exome study identified truncating and splice variants segregating in a family and de novo in simplex cases (PMID 21782149), and large independent cohorts confirmed this with sequence-level variants (PMID 27667800, 32124548, 31191201, 35861666, 36446582). A dedicated literature/ClinVar analysis quantified short stature in ~50% of 245 KBG patients with height data and reviewed rhGH response (PMID 39135054), and a Chinese patient with idiopathic short stature carried a heterozygous ANKRD11 point mutation (PMID 31566922). These are human, replicated, and gene-specific, satisfying the criteria for Established. A small residual probability is left for "Existing" in case one considers height an incidental syndromic feature rather than a directly measured association trait.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own primary results linking ANGPTL4 variation to HDL cholesterol: the ARIC prospective cohort found carriers of the E40K variant had ~4 mg/dL higher HDL-C (PMID 18940399), and a separate ARIC analysis directly examined ANGPTL4[E40K] genotype–HDL-C associations with dietary carbohydrate modification (PMID 18599063). A large GWAS of ~40,000 individuals identified genome-wide significant HDL cholesterol association at the ANGPTL4 locus (PMID 19060906), and whole-genome sequencing in >119,000 Icelanders identified ANGPTL4 variants affecting lipid fractions and CAD (PMID 27135400). Additional human data (E40K effects on lipids, loss-of-function phenome studies) corroborate this, and mechanistic reviews note loss-of-function ANGPTL4 mutations associate with higher HDL-C. This constitutes replicated evidence across independent human cohorts, supporting an Established relationship.

Multiple independent human studies report germline MSH6 pathogenic variants in probands and families with colorectal cancer/Lynch syndrome, including the original identification of a germline MSH6 mutation causing HNPCC (PMID 9354786), mutation prevalence in HNPCC and endometrial cancer cohorts (PMID 18269114), quantitative CRC risk estimates in MSH6 carriers from family-based cohorts (PMID 21642682), a large multigene panel cohort of MMR carriers with CRC phenotypes (PMID 28514183), and population-based Icelandic MSH6 carrier series with metachronous CRC (PMID 36801211). Additional cohorts of early-onset CRC and Turkish CRC patients detect MSH6 pathogenic variants in patients (PMIDs 40097831, 32658311), and prospective surgical outcome data stratify by path_MSH6 carriers (PMID 40231433). The evidence is replicated, human, single-gene resolved, and clinically actionable, supporting an Established gene–disease relationship.

Several papers report their own human genetic results linking ANGPTL3 variants to HDL-C: PMID 22247256 identified ANGPTL3 mutations in two large independent American and Italian hypobetalipoproteinemia cohorts with combined hypolipidemia characterized by low HDL-C; PMID 28538136 analyzed ANGPTL3 loss-of-function carriers in large human cohorts showing reduced HDL-C and CVD risk; PMIDs 34417926 and 38634215 report ANGPTL3 variant (rs1748195, rs11207997) associations with serum HDL-C in the Iranian MASHAD cohort; PMID 23150577 reports variant associations with HDL-C in three populations for the paralog while confirming ANGPTL3 inactivation lowers HDL-C in humans. Additional human genetic/clinical support comes from GWAS at the ANGPTL3 locus (PMID 18193044) and Finnish sequencing/hypolipidemia work (PMID 28972399), plus rare dyslipidemia panels including ANGPTL3 (PMID 37138899). Animal/mechanistic studies (PMID 34371033) and biological data (PMID 38462608) reinforce plausibility but are not needed given replicated human evidence. Hence the relationship is Established, with a small residual for the possibility that some HDL findings are secondary or inconsistent.

APC–colorectal cancer is the canonical gatekeeper gene relationship, and the provided literature includes primary human evidence, not just background citation. PMID 36828923 reports a novel deep intronic germline APC pathogenic variant discovered by genome sequencing in an FAP proband with co-segregation and functional RNA confirmation; PMID 39021676 analyzes adenoma-to-carcinoma evolution in FAP families carrying germline APC mutations; PMID 33352971 identifies APC mutations in 72% of an early-onset CRC patient cohort; PMID 10638959 documents somatic APC mutations across human adenomas and carcinomas; PMID 40928069 reports truncating APC mutations in rectal cancer patients with prognostic impact. Additionally, PMID 37800450 reflects an expert-panel consensus that germline APC variants underlie FAP, a definitive CRC-predisposing condition, and PMID 41091816 quantifies biallelic APC genotypes in >2,500 human colorectal cancers. Evidence is human, replicated across independent probands, families, and tumor cohorts, so Established is overwhelmingly supported.

None of the provided articles report any association between CNPY2 variants and height. The only human genetic association study (PMID: 26785701) identified a CNPY2 locus for waist circumference adjusted for BMI in East Asians — an abdominal adiposity trait, not stature — and PMID: 41671953 links a CNPY2 SNP to noise-induced hearing loss. Remaining papers concern ER stress, angiogenesis, cancer, neurodegeneration, and tendon stem cell senescence, which are biologically unrelated to skeletal growth, although the anthropometric/musculoskeletal (tendon, connective tissue) involvement provides a very weak speculative basis. Therefore the relationship is best characterized as Novel, with modest probability for Hypothesized given tangential body-size and connective tissue biology.

Multiple independent human studies report PROS1 variants identified in their own results in VTE patients and families: a Han Chinese case-control study found 24 heterozygous PROS1 mutations with an 8.1-fold odds ratio for VTE with protein S deficiency (PMID 35815065); a Danish cohort identified 13 coding PROS1 variants with higher VTE frequency in carriers (PMID 34729451); and independent probands/families with novel pathogenic variants are described (PMIDs 32653888, 32971918, 38034377, 39465133, 33076619 with co-segregation, 41869914). PROS1-related protein S deficiency is a classic autosomal dominant thrombophilia, and the evidence is replicated across ethnicities (Japanese/Chinese, European) in humans. This clearly meets the bar for Established, with only a small residual probability that a stricter reading would consider case reports insufficient.

The only direct human genetic evidence linking DTL to height is the large exome-based rare variant study (PMID 42396316), which explicitly names DTL among genes whose rare/singleton pLoF variants confer large effects on adult height, with discovery in 826,066 exomes and replication in a further 624,567 individuals. Although this includes internal replication, it is a single publication, so per the criteria the evidence cannot be scored as "Established" (no second independent article reporting variants in people). All other DTL articles concern cell-cycle/CRL4(Cdt2) biology, cancer expression, embryonic lethality in mice/Drosophila, or a rice "DTL" dwarfing gene (a plant homonym, not the human gene), and thus do not support a human height association. Some indirect biological plausibility exists (DTL essential for cell division/proliferation; rice DTL mutants alter internode elongation), supporting a small "Hypothesized" weight.

Multiple independent human reports document pathogenic G6PC1 variants in probands with marked hypertriglyceridemia as a core biochemical feature of GSD Ia: PMID 32436859 (homozygous c.248G>A, p.R83H infant with extreme hypertriglyceridemia), PMID 23312056 (homozygous R83C with triglycerides >5000 mg/dL and long-term lipid follow-up), and PMID 27511118 (c.518T>C p.L173P with elevated triglycerides). Larger human cohorts additionally relate G6PC1 genotype and serum triglyceride concentrations to outcomes (PMID 40586975, n=164 with genotype and TG data; PMID 35811762 examining HCA risk in relation to sex, G6PC1 genotype, and TG). These are independent probands and cohorts with variant-level data and measured triglycerides, satisfying the replication requirement. Animal/mechanistic work (PMIDs 31816064, 25561689, 29428299) supports the biology but is not needed to reach the Established threshold; a small residual probability is left for Existing in case reviewers consider hypertriglyceridemia only a secondary manifestation of the metabolic disease rather than a direct gene–trait association.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own results linking ANGPTL3 variants to LDL cholesterol: PMID 28538136 (loss-of-function carriers in DiscovEHR/large cohorts with lower LDL-C and reduced coronary disease risk), PMID 28385496 (sequencing-based identification of ANGPTL3 deficiency carriers with reduced lipid fractions and protection from CAD), PMID 28972399 (Finnish FINRISK/Health 2000 sequencing and variant–lipid analyses), and PMID 30827231 (ANGPTL3 variants identified in unrelated Chinese Han FH patients). GWAS data at the ANGPTL3 locus (PMID 18193044) further support common-variant association with lipid traits in independent cohorts. Human kinetic studies of complete ANGPTL3 deficiency (PMID 40446802) and therapeutic inhibition trials (PMID 28538111, 41211945) corroborate the causal mechanism lowering LDL-C. The evidence is replicated across probands, families, and population cohorts in humans, so Established is strongly favored.

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic COL27A1 variants in patients with Steel syndrome, in which short stature is a consistent core feature: the original Puerto Rican founder study (PMID 24986830), a Korean proband with novel compound heterozygous variants (PMID 33963180), a European homozygous missense case (PMID 32360765), non-Puerto Rican families with novel missense variants (PMID 35568358), and a second unrelated family (PMID 28276056). Beyond Mendelian cases, a population-scale health-system study using identity-by-descent mapping in BioMe linked COL27A1 directly to extreme short stature and showed height effects in heterozygous carriers (PMID 28895531), and a large cohort analysis explored carrier contributions to common traits (PMID 32376988). These are independent human probands, families, and cohorts, satisfying replication for a causal/associative role with height (short stature). Animal modelling (Col27a1 mouse showing reduced body length) provides supporting mechanism but is not needed for the human-based conclusion.

Several independent human studies report their own results linking LIPG variants to total cholesterol: PMID 23536757 found the T111I (rs2000813) variant associated with elevated total cholesterol and LDL-C in Hispanic subjects from a biethnic population sample; PMID 21816559 reported that serum TC levels differed by LIPG 584C>T genotype/allele in Chinese nondrinkers; PMID 20923576 and PMID 30621702 similarly examined LIPG SNPs/haplotypes against serum lipid panels including TC in independent Chinese population subgroups. A large multi-cohort GWAS of blood lipids including total cholesterol in ~30,000 European-ancestry individuals also implicated LIPG (PMID 31566214), and METSIM exome/GWAS analyses identified LIPG signals for lipid/lipoprotein traits (PMID 29084231). These constitute replicated human genetic evidence across ancestries, supporting Established, though the strongest and most consistent LIPG effect is on HDL-C with TC being a secondary/less consistent readout, leaving some probability for Existing. Animal/in vitro work (PMID 12909635) only supports the biological plausibility layer.

Most articles in this set concern APOB variants and LDL-C/apoB (familial hypercholesterolemia, hypobetalipoproteinemia) or use apoB merely as a clinical biomarker alongside non-HDL-C, which does not constitute genetic evidence for HDL-C. Two human genetic studies do touch HDL-C directly: a meta-analysis of the APOB rs693 and rs17240441 polymorphisms with plasma apoB and lipid levels including HDL-C (PMID 28874158), and screening of APOB (with ANGPTL3) in cohorts with combined hypolipidemia defined by low total and low HDL cholesterol (PMID 22247256), though in that study the HDL-lowering signal was chiefly attributed to ANGPTL3. Additional supportive but indirect human data come from rare dyslipidaemia cohorts where APOB variants were sought among patients with low LDL-C and low HDL-C (PMID 37138899) and pathway/missense analyses of lipid GWAS including APOB (PMID 36098472). Because replication specifically for HDL-C is limited and the strongest, best-replicated APOB genetic associations are with LDL-C/apoB rather than HDL-C, "Existing" is the most probable classification, with some chance of "Established" given large lipid GWAS/meta-analytic support.

Multiple independent human genetic studies present primary evidence linking HNF1A variation to type 2 diabetes, not merely to MODY. PMID 39379762 (rare-variant GWAS in 51,256 T2D cases/370,487 controls) identifies a rare HNF1A variant conferring ~fivefold increased T2D risk; PMID 38278947 reports an exome-wide significant gene-level HNF1A rare-variant association in 3,005 youth-onset T2D cases versus matched controls; PMID 12726923 describes the private G319S HNF1A variant associated with T2D across an Oji-Cree population with high positive predictive value; and PMID 36323883 reports functional HNF1A variants linked to T2DM risk in European-ancestry populations. Additional supporting work (PMID 40774250) shows loss-/gain-of-function HNF1A coding variants respectively predisposing to or protecting against polygenic T2D with mechanistic β-cell data, and penetrance studies (PMID 36257325) show HNF1A pathogenic variants are common in unselected populations with diabetes risk modified by background genetics. A minority of probability remains for "Existing" because several of the listed papers concern MODY rather than common T2D, but the replicated large-scale human T2D case-control associations satisfy the Established threshold.

Several human studies report direct associations between PPARG variants (mainly Pro12Ala/rs1801282) and HDL cholesterol: the European Project on Genes in Hypertension family study found higher HDL in Ala12 carriers with an alcohol-intake interaction (PMID 15716591), and the METSIM-derived crossover trial found higher baseline HDL in Ala12Ala versus Pro12Pro men (PMID 26446033). Additional human data include gene–diet and gene–PUFA interactions affecting HDL (PMIDs 31675538, 32713352, 31050749), PPARG–HDL interaction in hypertension (PMID 26877853), and lipid/dyslipidemia associations in Chinese elderly and Japanese cohorts (PMIDs 22001700, 32755657). However, the largest syntheses—a meta-analysis of 74 studies (PMID 25265984) and a Pro12Ala lipid meta-analysis (PMID 21185561)—did not demonstrate a robust HDL effect, and several candidate-gene studies were null (PMID 17653445), so replication is inconsistent and often interaction-dependent. Biological plausibility is strong (PPARγ agonists raise HDL; PMID 31929323), but that supports Hypothesized only. Overall the weight of evidence supports "Existing," with a substantial minority probability for "Established."

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic ADAMTS10 variants in patients with Weill-Marchesani syndrome, whose cardinal feature is proportionate short stature. Primary evidence with variants in people includes PMID 15368195 (nonsense and splice mutations in two consanguineous families plus a sporadic case), PMID 19836009 (two additional unrelated families with homozygous missense mutations), PMID 25469541 (novel homozygous missense in a patient with short stature, with functional characterization), PMID 37240210 (novel homozygous pro-domain missense in an extended consanguineous family), and PMID 41639873 (novel homozygous frameshift in a Chinese family). These are independent probands/families with single-gene point mutations, not multigene CNVs. Additional human population-level support comes from the UK Biobank GWAS implicating ADAMTS10 in carpal tunnel syndrome with Mendelian randomization linking short stature (PMID 30833571).

The Million Veteran Program lipid GWAS (PMID 30275531) reports, in its own results, loss-of-function variants in PDE3B associated with triglycerides (and coronary disease) across ~300,000 multi-ethnic participants meta-analyzed with the Global Lipids Genetics Consortium. Independently, the UK Biobank exome-imputation study (PMID 36490288) identifies PDE3B loss-of-function variants associated with triglycerides as a novel finding in a distinct cohort. Supporting human genetic evidence comes from UK Biobank pLOF analyses of body fat distribution and cardiometabolic risk (PMID 29691411), rare-variant burden for metabolic syndrome including lipid pathways (PMID 42472903), metabolite-level rare variant signals at PDE3B (PMID 39442521), and adiposity-depot rare-variant work (PMID 35773277). Mechanistic adipocyte data (PDE3B mediating insulin suppression of lipolysis and triglyceride hydrolysis; PMIDs 9500857, 31105056) provide a coherent biological basis. Together this constitutes replicated human variant-level evidence, supporting an Established classification.

Multiple independent human studies report intragenic SHOX point mutations and gene-specific deletions in probands and families with short stature phenotypes: Rao et al. identified a functionally significant SHOX point mutation by screening 91 individuals with idiopathic short stature plus PAR1 deletions in 36 short-statured individuals (PMID 9140395); SHOX point mutations and deletions were found in Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis (PMID 12070265); SHOX mutations were identified in a family and fetus with Langer mesomelic dysplasia (PMID 15214013); SHOX variants were detected by FISH and direct sequencing in short-stature patients (PMID 12566529); and targeted SHOX variant screening cohorts confirm the association (PMID 33240610). These are human genetic studies in independent probands/families, not restatements of background, and are complemented by regulatory-region CNV and duplication series (PMIDs 31228230, 36927524, 38914686) and dosage effects on sex differences in height (PMID 38987196). SHOX haploinsufficiency is one of the most common monogenic causes of growth failure, and gene dosage correlates with stature (tall stature with extra copies, short stature with haploinsufficiency). The evidence is replicated, human, and mechanistically supported, so the relationship is Established.

No human genetic association study in this set links THBS3 variants to height; the only GWAS present (PMID 31396565) concerns lobar brain volumes and merely notes THBS3 in a histone-modification-enriched region, not stature. The strongest relevant evidence is the mouse combinatorial knockout study (PMID 18467703), where Thbs3/Thbs5/Col9 triple-null mice showed disorganized growth plates and a ~20% reduction in limb length, explicitly likened to human short stature—this is animal, not human, evidence and therefore supports "Hypothesized." Additional biology (thrombospondin family roles in cartilage/musculoskeletal extracellular matrix, TSP5 mutations causing pseudoachondroplasia) makes a growth-plate mechanism plausible for THBS3, though indirect. Other papers (metaxin locus, CML gene expression, cardiomyopathy, miRNA regulation, biomarker panels) are incidental co-mentions with no height relevance. Thus the evidence is biologically suggestive but lacks any human variant-level data.

Multiple independent human reports describe LCAT coding mutations in probands/families with markedly altered plasma cholesterol: a novel homozygous p.Gly119Asp mutation in a Romanian proband with extraordinarily high total cholesterol and affected siblings (PMID 28942093), compound heterozygous LCAT mutations (Tyr83Stop/Arg99Cys) with reduced total cholesterol (PMID 11718688), and a familial fish-eye disease kindred with low total cholesterol and demonstrated recessive transmission (PMID 1778223). Population-level human genetic studies add support: candidate-gene analysis of LCAT variants with lipid traits including TC in Ghanaian adults (PMID 33193594), LCAT haplotypes contributing to lipid trait variance in German families (PMID 12023990), LCAT tagging SNPs and plasma lipid profiles (PMID 22229114), and LCAT SNPs associated with dyslipidaemia including elevated TC in HIV patients (PMID 33173066). Some LCAT-deficiency reports note normal total cholesterol (PMID 8445342), and much of the strongest genetic signal concerns HDL-C rather than TC, which tempers certainty; animal/hamster and baboon data (PMIDs 41195480, 1350465) are only supportive mechanistically. Overall the human evidence across independent probands and cohorts favors Established, with residual weight on Existing.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in ANGPTL2 associated with height or stature; the literature focuses on chronic inflammation, obesity/metabolic disease, senescence, fibrosis, and tumorigenesis. The only mention of "stature" comes from an Arabidopsis CAP1 study (PMID 17635992), an unrelated plant gene and a homonym-type irrelevance that should be dismissed. A weak biological thread exists in the review noting angiopoietin-related proteins have pleiotropic effects on chondrocytes (PMID 15293564) and in the sheep transcriptome study identifying ANGPTL2 polymorphisms related to muscle/meat traits (PMID 36830461), but these are non-human and only tangentially related to skeletal growth. Therefore the co-mentions are essentially incidental, supporting a Novel classification with a modest allowance for Hypothesized based on chondrocyte/growth-related biology.

The phenotype here is the CRP protein level itself, and multiple human studies with their own primary results show CRP gene variants determine circulating CRP concentrations. PMID 16266402 resequenced CRP and replicated SNP associations with baseline CRP levels across three independent cohorts (WHS, PRINCE, PHS), and PMID 34915091 independently reported CRP SNP genotypes (rs3093059, rs3091244) associating with serum CRP concentration in an eastern Indian patient cohort. Additional supporting human genetic work includes CRP-region variants driving CRP levels in Mendelian randomization/polygenic analyses (PMID 38511149) and genetic-architecture/colocalization analyses of CRP GWAS loci (PMID 38785970), while reviews (PMIDs 17868801, 21468143) summarize the well-replicated genotype–CRP-level relationship. Evidence is human, replicated, and gene-specific, so the relationship is Established.

A large human GWAS/replication effort in African-American women reported genome-wide significant association at 11q13/SERPINH1 with adult height, replicating a locus previously reported in European-ancestry populations (PMID 22021425). In addition, multiple independent human families/probands with biallelic SERPINH1 variants (OI type X) show short stature and growth retardation as a core feature: the homozygous p.Leu78Pro family (PMID 20188343), compound heterozygous siblings with a frameshift plus upstream regulatory deletion and moderate short stature (PMID 31179625), two Turkish siblings with a novel homozygous p.G84R variant and short stature (PMID 41424307), and a Chinese boy with compound heterozygous mutations and growth retardation (PMID 29520608). These are single-gene, non-CNV variants in independent probands from separate reports, satisfying replication. Remaining uncertainty concerns whether the GWAS signal is truly attributable to SERPINH1 (nearest-gene labeling) and whether OI-related short stature counts as the height phenotype, which supports some weight on "Existing"; animal/in vitro work (PMID 26004778) only supports mechanism.

Multiple independent human reports describe point mutations (not just multigene deletions) in IGF1R segregating with pre- and postnatal growth restriction/short stature: PMID 17264177 (familial Arg481Gln in a family with intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation), PMID 28649085 (novel heterozygous splice/missense variant across three generations with functional validation in patient fibroblasts), PMID 32037650 (two novel heterozygous IGF1R mutations with growth failure), and PMID 40269620 (two novel heterozygous variants in short-stature patients). Larger cohort studies replicate this in independent probands (PMID 31680140 comparing IGF1R mutation carriers with SGA children; PMID 32356191; PMID 35431446 with 11 patients; PMID 38710621 with 13 Japanese patients). In addition, common IGF1R polymorphisms have been associated with adult height in population studies (PMID 18349294) and antenatal/postnatal growth measures (PMID 25054682). All key evidence is human, with variant-level resolution, satisfying the criteria for an Established gene–phenotype relationship.

Nearly all of the listed articles concern the GHRH receptor gene (GHRHR), not GHRH itself; homozygous GHRHR mutations (Itabaianinha, Sindh, Israeli Arab, Indian, Japanese cohorts) robustly cause severe short stature, but these are a different locus and one review explicitly notes that GHRH gene mutations have never been reported (PMID 15196883). The only direct human GHRH evidence is the 752 kb 20q11.23 microdeletion producing a TTI1–GHRH chimeric transcript with GHRH overexpression and pituitary gigantism (PMID 37070740); although mechanistically compelling and supported by a genome-edited mouse recapitulating the growth phenotype, it is a multigene copy-number change and therefore cannot alone establish the gene by the stated criteria. This supports "Existing" (one credible human report plus strong pathway/mechanistic linkage of GHRH signaling to stature) rather than "Established," since no second independent human proband/family with an intragenic GHRH variant affecting height is presented. Substantial probability remains for "Hypothesized," as one could argue the human evidence is a CNV plus animal-model data with the ligand-level genetics otherwise inferred from receptor biology.

Multiple independent human studies present primary evidence of CHEK2 germline variants causing increased breast cancer risk: the original CHEK2*1100delC family study (PMID 11967536) in 718 non-BRCA1/2 breast cancer families, large case-control sequencing of protein-truncating variants in 13,087 cases vs 5,488 controls (PMID 28779002), the German Consortium panel study with OR 2.93 in 5,589 index patients (PMID 29522266), and the GENESIS familial breast cancer study (PMID 30303537). Additional functional-plus-association studies of missense variants (PMIDs 37449874, 34903604) quantify risk in carriers, and contralateral breast cancer risk studies (PMIDs 36623243, 37401034) confirm clinical impact in carriers. These are independent cohorts, populations, and probands, with variant-level (not multigene deletion) resolution. The evidence is replicated, human, and clinically actionable (screening recommendations, PMID 38985133), fully supporting the Established category.

Multiple independent human studies demonstrate FLNB variants influencing stature. A GWAS in 1,000 unrelated Caucasians identified FLNB SNPs (e.g., rs9834312) associated with stature with replication in independent Caucasian family, unrelated Caucasian, and Chinese cohorts (PMID 19039035). Independently, numerous Mendelian reports document biallelic or heterozygous FLNB variants in distinct families with disproportionate short stature: seven Argentinian SCT families (PMID 39086440), ten patients from seven families with novel truncating variants (PMID 29566257), a consanguineous Pakistani family with a stop-gain variant (PMID 37781000), intragenic deletions in two unrelated individuals (PMID 33916386), a dimerization-domain frameshift family (PMID 28145000), and FLNB haploinsufficiency-related short stature (PMID 39080191), plus enrichment in an SGA short-stature cohort (PMID 37019085). These constitute replicated, human, variant-level evidence in independent probands and families, satisfying the Established criteria.

Multiple independent human studies report pathogenic PROC variants in probands and families with venous thromboembolism, including a novel nonsense mutation (Trp29Term) segregating in a family with recurrent venous thrombosis (PMID 8462980), four unrelated families with hereditary protein C deficiency and thromboembolism (PMID 38433129), two probands with heterozygous missense mutations p.Leu278Pro and p.Trp444Arg confirmed by in vitro expression (PMID 40355354), compound heterozygous variants in a patient with recurrent thrombosis (PMID 40008275), and Met343Val in two unrelated patients with recurrent thrombosis (PMID 38788977). Population-level case-control genetic evidence also supports PROC c.574_576del as a common VT risk factor in Chinese subjects (PMID 22817391) and p.R147W in Thai children (PMID 28511552). GWAS/PWAS-based work lists PROC among robustly associated VTE loci (PMIDs 26354877, 37537391). The evidence is human, replicated, and mechanistically supported, satisfying the Established criteria.

Multiple independent human case-control and family-based studies provide primary evidence that rare protein-truncating and deleterious missense variants in ATM increase breast cancer risk: PMID 28779002 (13,087 cases vs 5,488 controls from East Anglia), PMID 29522266 (German Consortium, 5,589 index patients, OR 3.63), PMID 19781682 (pooled mutation screening showing rare evolutionarily unlikely missense substitutions confer risk), PMID 30303537 (GENESIS familial BC cohort confirming ATM LoF association), and PMID 36161273 (Finnish founder allele c.7570G>C co-segregating with breast cancer in seven families plus population cohort association). Additional replication comes from UK Biobank exome data (PMID 39209703) and contralateral breast cancer risk studies (PMID 36623243). These are independent human cohorts and families, satisfying the replication requirement, with functional data (PMID 11805335, 40580951) supporting mechanism.

Multiple independent human cohorts report PTPN11 missense variants in probands and families with Noonan syndrome, in which proportionate short stature is a defining, systematically assessed feature. Direct primary evidence with variants found in people includes Tartaglia et al. (PMID 11992261, 119 unrelated NS patients with genotype–phenotype analysis including short stature), Zenker et al. (PMID 12634870, 96 patients, 15 different mutations), the Japanese cohort of 116 individuals analyzing frequency of short stature by genotype (PMID 38572385), a 16-patient novel mutation cluster with documented short stature prevalence (PMID 28074573), and the Mexican cohort of 91 probands with 82% short stature (PMID 39596579). Additional human studies link PTPN11 mutation status to growth factors and growth hormone treatment response (PMIDs 16263833, 35245205). Evidence is replicated across independent human cohorts and single-gene resolution (missense variants, not CNVs), supporting Established for the height/short stature phenotype.

Several independent human studies report their own primary results linking APOB variants to elevated alanine aminotransferase and hepatic steatosis/injury. PMID 12872264 identified four novel APOB truncating mutations in five FHBL families and found mildly increased plasma ALT in ~50% of affected subjects; PMID 15514099 documented an apoB-80.5 heterozygote presenting with raised ALT and biopsy-proven steatosis. Independently, PMID 33207932 compared 111 hypobetalipoproteinemia patients and found monogenic (APOB/PCSK9) carriers had markedly higher rates of liver injury (raised ALT, 47% vs 0%) than polygenic cases, and PMID 41665936 showed rare APOB variants in multiple cohorts (case-control, family, MVP, UK Biobank) associate with greater MASLD activity, fibrosis and HCC. Additional cohorts (PMID 40155282, 39100627, 42100254, 41549954) and pleiotropy analyses (PMID 36400032) reinforce this in humans. Evidence is replicated across independent probands, families and biobank cohorts, supporting Established.

APOB loss-of-function variants cause familial hypobetalipoproteinemia, whose hallmark complication is hepatic steatosis/steatohepatitis with transaminase (AST/ALT) elevation, and several human studies with genotyped probands and cohorts report these liver enzyme abnormalities. PMID 40155282 is a retrospective cohort of heterozygous and homozygous APOB-FHBL patients detailing hepatic complications; PMID 22855658 reports a genotyped compound heterozygote (R463W/V703I) with abnormal liver enzymes and steatosis plus family sequencing; PMID 39100627 describes adolescents with h-FHBL and incidentally detected liver dysfunction; PMID 41549954 and PMID 39365223 assess APOB variant carriers for chronic liver disease risk in human cohorts. These are human, variant-level, and independent, supporting Established, though AST is often reported as part of a broader liver-injury phenotype rather than as the primary quantitative trait, leaving substantial weight on Existing. Papers on FH/R3500Q or dietary trials (e.g., PMID 36331011, 37654445) are not evidence for this gene–trait link.

The only human genetic evidence in this set is the whole-exome rare-variant burden analysis of birth weight (PMID 39809772), which reports a fetal-acting NRK association with birth weight, a growth/anthropometric trait genetically correlated with and considered a precursor of stature, though not height itself and not independently replicated for height. No article reports NRK variants directly associated with adult or childhood height in independent cohorts, so Established cannot be supported (no two qualifying human-variant studies). Other NRK papers concern nicotinamide riboside kinase enzymology, structure and engineering (PMIDs 17698003, 39481026, 40859812, 39055245), which are unrelated to skeletal growth, and several hits are homonyms (NRK-52E rat cell line, Drosophila Nrk, Chlamydomonas Nrk/CNK4) that should be dismissed. Thus the evidence best fits Existing, with residual probability for Novel given the phenotype mismatch.

Multiple independent human studies report ABCG5 variants directly associated with elevated total cholesterol. Monogenic evidence comes from independent sitosterolemia cohorts with biallelic ABCG5 variants and markedly elevated TC/LDL-C: 18 Chinese children (PMID 32143815), 14 Vietnamese children (PMID 39860331), and additional probands with novel ABCG5 variants (PMIDs 29886606, 36444439, 37020702, 41340881). Common-variant evidence in populations also exists: the ABCG5 C1950G (Q604E) genotype was associated with higher baseline serum cholesterol in 486 subjects (PMID 12220438), an ABCG5 polymorphism modified plasma cholesterol response to dietary cholesterol (PMID 16614398), and ABCG5/8 variants were associated with lipid levels in Thai subjects (PMID 36619676), with GWAS reviews listing ABCG5 among total-cholesterol loci (PMID 21860704). Some studies are null for specific ABCG5 SNPs (PMIDs 15311998, 20581104), which tempers common-variant strength but does not offset the replicated monogenic human evidence.

Multiple independent human reports present their own primary results linking ABCG5 variants to elevated LDL cholesterol: a case series of unrelated infants and a child with pathogenic ABCG5 mutations and extremely elevated LDL-C (PMID 35705271), an infant plus mother with a heterozygous ABCG5 p.Arg389His variant and LDL-C of 449 mg/dL (PMID 37020702), a homozygous ABCG5 exon 3 insertion/deletion proband with elevated LDL-C responsive to ezetimibe (PMID 15375183), compound heterozygous ABCG5 variants in a child with LDL-C 10.2 mmol/L (PMID 41539482), three siblings with homozygous ABCG5 mutations (PMID 41102112), and larger cohorts of sitosterolemia patients with genotype–phenotype data (PMIDs 34969652, 41130816, 38509578). In addition, common ABCG5/ABCG8 variants have been examined for association with LDL-C and sterol markers in population cohorts (PMIDs 32088153, 34680591, 36619676). These are human probands, families and cohorts across independent populations, satisfying replication. Only a small residual probability remains for "Existing," since some of the common-variant signals are at the shared ABCG5/ABCG8 locus and cannot always be resolved to ABCG5 alone.

Biallelic ADAMTSL2 variants cause geleophysic dysplasia type 1, in which severe short stature is a cardinal, defining feature, so height is directly determined by variants in this gene. Primary human genetic evidence with variants identified in independent probands and families includes the original mapping and mutation discovery in six families (PMID 18677313), molecular screening of 33 patients (PMID 21415077), a natural-history and genotype–phenotype cohort of 38 cases (PMID 33082559), an international cohort of nine patients with Al-Gazali skeletal dysplasia (PMID 36896612), and additional single-proband reports (PMID 28917829, 36246610, 42017525). These constitute replicated, independent human evidence rather than background citation. Mouse and cell models (PMIDs 38300707, 32913123) provide supporting mechanistic data but are not needed for the classification.

FBN1 pathogenic variants cause Marfan syndrome, in which mitral valve prolapse/regurgitation and aortic valve incompetence (non-rheumatic valvular disease) are cardinal cardiovascular manifestations. The international genotype–phenotype study of 1,013 probands with pathogenic FBN1 mutations (PMID 17701892) reports in its own results a higher probability of mitral valve abnormalities and aortic dilatation/surgery for specific mutation classes, and the mutation-detection series of 193 novel/known FBN1 mutations in 508 consecutively ascertained Marfan/Marfan-related patients and 331 relatives (PMID 17657824) independently documents causal variants in probands with these cardiovascular features. A further large independent pediatric cohort of 373 MFS patients with severe cardiovascular phenotypes and pathogenic FBN1 variants (PMID 35058154), plus additional mutation reports (PMIDs 19059503, 8136837, 38958168), provides replication across independent human probands and families. Several remaining articles (diabetes, sphingomyelins, miR-222) concern degenerative valvular disease without FBN1 and are not informative. Because valvular involvement is characterized within these primary human genetic studies rather than only cited as background, Established is favored, with residual weight on Existing since valvular disease is a component of a syndromic phenotype rather than the primary endpoint in most studies.

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic loss-of-function DDR2 variants causing spondylo-meta-epiphyseal dysplasia short limb–abnormal calcification type, whose cardinal feature is severe disproportionate short stature. Primary evidence with variants identified in distinct probands/families includes PMID 19110212 (missense and splice-site mutations in several consanguineous families), PMID 20223752 (novel p.E113K in two siblings plus a second family with p.R752C), PMID 26463668 (Moroccan patient, p.Arg124Trp), PMID 29884795 (novel homozygous nonsense), PMID 31406622 (Indian patient, p.Gln808Ter), PMID 33953858 (Iranian family), and PMID 36720430 (three new patients from three unrelated families, two novel variants). These are replicated, independent human genetic findings directly tied to stature, supported functionally by Ddr2-null mouse dwarfism (PMID 24036888) and DDR2 trafficking/ligand-binding defects. The evidence therefore strongly supports the Established category.

Multiple independent human studies report LMNA variants in probands/families with atrial fibrillation as a primary phenotype: a novel nonsense variant (p.Trp498Ter) segregating in a four-generation AF family (PMID 27373676), a novel frameshift indel (c.825_826insCAGG) in a family with AV block and AF (PMID 34106654), a novel mutation causing isolated early-onset AF with progressive AV block (PMID 19328042), and a multigenerational heart-hand pedigree with atrial myopathy due to p.R335W (PMID 34808346). These family-based findings are corroborated at population scale by a meta-analysis of genome/exome sequencing in 52,416 AF cases identifying a rare coding variant burden association for LMNA, replicated in independent cohorts (MyCode, deCODE, UK Biobank; PMID 40050430). Large cohort studies of LMNA mutation carriers additionally document high incidence rates of atrial arrhythmias/AF as part of the cardiolaminopathy phenotype (PMIDs 27884249, 29237675, 40738567). All key evidence is human genetic, supporting an Established causal relationship, with residual uncertainty only about whether AF is primarily secondary to the broader cardiomyopathy/conduction disease phenotype.

Two independent human genetic studies report their own results linking LTBP1 to stature: the East Asian whole-genome reference panel study (PMID 37556544) discovered rare protein-altering LTBP1 variants associated with height in a large imputed GWAS of >72,000 subjects, and the Korean KoGES analysis (PMID 37049604) identified LTBP1 rs4630744 among the height-associated variants contributing to an adult-height polygenic score in a discovery cohort with confirmation in a second cohort. Additional supportive human evidence comes from bi-allelic truncating LTBP1 variants causing a cutis laxa syndrome with skeletal/growth abnormalities (PMID 34861177), and from CNV work nominating LTBP1 copy number as a body-height-related marker (PMID 28457514), though the latter is methodological. Mechanistic plausibility is strong given LTBP1's role in TGFβ sequestration and fibrillin microfibril biology underlying acromelic dysplasias and Marfan-spectrum stature phenotypes (PMIDs 19396027, 22242013), and animal work links LTBP1 InDels to growth traits in sheep and bone growth in horses (PMIDs 31625451, 37184429). Because the two human height-association reports come from partly overlapping East Asian populations and one is a PRS-component report rather than a dedicated locus discovery, some probability remains on "Existing".

The strongest evidence is PMID 42396316, a rare protein-coding variant study of height in >1.4 million people that directly implicates IGF2BP2 among 207 height-associated genes with a large per-allele effect, using an 826,066-exome discovery set and a 624,567-individual replication set. However, this is a single publication, and the rules require at least two independent articles demonstrating the link in their own human results for "Established." The whole-genome sequencing anthropometric study (PMID 41651857) reports rare IGF2BP2 variants for waist-hip ratio adjusted for BMI, an adiposity trait rather than height, so it supports body-size relevance but not height directly. Canine studies (PMID 39871672) show an IGF2BP2 exon 1 variant reducing height across dog breeds, and pigeon SNP work (PMID 39879902) links IGF2BP2 to body weight/skeletal traits—these are non-human and count toward Hypothesized. Remaining papers concern type 2 diabetes, cancer, fibrosis, or adipogenesis and are not height-specific.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report NPC1L1 sequence variation directly associated with LDL-C: the large exome-sequencing study of inactivating NPC1L1 mutations (PMID 25714175, with commentary PMID 25445133) showing lower LDL-C and CHD risk, the Copenhagen general population cohorts examining NPC1L1 variation, LDL-C and ischaemic vascular disease/gallstones (PMID 25841872), resequencing/genotyping of NPC1L1 in clinical trial cohorts linked to LDL-C response to ezetimibe (PMID 16297596), and GWAS-derived RNA-modification SNPs in NPC1L1 associated with LDL-C levels (PMID 35880552). Meta-analytic work using NPC1L1 LDL-C-lowering alleles as instruments in human cohorts (PMID 27701660) and drug-target MR studies (PMIDs 34675202, 35213538) further presuppose and replicate robust NPC1L1 variant–LDL-C associations. These are independent human probands and population cohorts, satisfying the replication criterion. Remaining probability is allocated to Existing in case one considers some studies as citation-based rather than primary evidence.

Several listed articles present primary human genetic results linking LDLR variants to coronary/myocardial disease: PMID 25487149 sequenced ~9,793 genomes and found rare LDLR coding mutations conferring 4.2-fold (null alleles 13-fold) increased early-onset myocardial infarction risk; PMID 27050191 sequenced FH genes in severe hypercholesterolemia patients and showed mutation carriers have CAD risk beyond LDL-C levels; PMID 9360938 compared 83 LDLR-defect patients with FDB patients and reported significantly higher rates of MI, bypass grafting, positive angiography and CAD in LDLR mutation carriers. Additional cohort studies (PMIDs 33418990, 16250003, 31491741, 40618456) report independent probands/families carrying LDLR pathogenic variants with premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and functional maps (PMID 41166440) correlate variant scores with human hyperlipidemia phenotypes and improved risk inference. LDLR-driven familial hypercholesterolemia is a definitively established monogenic cause of premature coronary artery disease, supported by replication across independent populations, so Established dominates.

Multiple independent human studies with their own primary results link MC4R variation to BMI: a GWAS meta-analysis in ~83,000 East Asians identified MC4R as a genome-wide significant BMI locus (PMID 22344219); a cross-ancestry rare-variant gene-based association study of BMI in 839,110 individuals across six ancestries found consistent MC4R effects (PMID 41168175); rare deleterious MC4R variants associated with BMI at the population level in the HYPOMAP study (PMID 39910307); and the Ile269Asn loss-of-function mutation was associated with obesity in 1,683 Mexican adults (PMID 36553534). Additional coding-variant reports in independent probands and families (PMIDs 11443223, 10078568) and functional evidence of MC4R-agonist-induced weight loss in MC4R-deficient humans (PMID 29031731) reinforce causality. Evidence is human, replicated across ancestries and study designs, so "Established" is clearly warranted; only minimal probability remains for weaker categories.

Multiple independent human studies report causal, functionally validated ABCG2 variants in gout patients. PMID 19506252 identified rs2231142 (Q141K) as a causal urate-transport-impairing variant associated with gout in a large population cohort; PMID 20368174 sequenced ABCG2 in Japanese hyperuricemia/gout patients and found nonfunctional variants (Q126X, Q141K) with large odds ratios; PMID 20421215 replicated rs2231142 association with gout in an independent Japanese population; PMID 29225919 and PMID 28968913 extended this to rare and additional non-synonymous variants in gout cohorts. These are independent probands/cohorts with variant-level, gene-specific evidence plus functional transport assays, and are reinforced by GWAS (PMIDs 18834626, 19503597, 31578528). This constitutes replicated causal evidence in humans.

None of the provided articles report a direct human genetic association between B4GALNT3 variants and height as an outcome in their own results. The strongest human genetic evidence concerns circulating sclerostin, bone mineral density and fracture risk (PMID 31170332) and α-Klotho levels (PMID 34542150), with functional confirmation that B4GALNT3 glycosylates sclerostin and regulates bone mass (PMID 37023531) — skeletal biology that is mechanistically plausible for, but not equivalent to, stature. The polyneuropathy GWAS (PMID 34975738) mentions genetic correlation of the trait with height, but this is a trait-level correlation, not a B4GALNT3-height variant association. A multigene 12p13.33 deletion report (PMID 24613754) cannot isolate B4GALNT3. Therefore the evidence best supports a hypothesized/biologically plausible link, with a modest chance of qualifying as "Existing" via the bone-related human genetic findings.

Multiple independent human studies report their own results linking NPC1L1 variants to cholesterol levels: the large GLGC GWAS of >100,000 European-ancestry individuals with replication in East Asian, South Asian and African American samples identified NPC1L1 as a genome-wide significant lipid locus (PMID 20686565); a Chinese cohort found the g.-762T>C promoter variant associated with higher serum total cholesterol and LDL-C with supporting promoter-activity data (PMID 19265861); a Korean cross-sectional study of 1404 subjects found rs217434 A>G carriers had higher total cholesterol and LDL-C (PMID 38280151); resequencing showed rare NS variants in NPC1L1 associated with reduced sterol absorption and lower LDL-C in African Americans (PMID 16449388); and large-scale exome sequencing showed inactivating mutations lower LDL-C and CHD risk (PMID 25390462, 25841872). These are independent cohorts with directly measured lipid phenotypes, satisfying replication criteria. Additional smaller studies (24648913, 22646906, 34680591) provide supportive but weaker evidence.

Multiple independent human studies report NPR3 variants causing or associating with stature. Boudin et al. (PMID 30032985) identified bi-allelic loss-of-function NPR3 variants in four individuals from three unrelated families with tall stature and extra epiphyses; a separate report (PMID 40171685) describes three siblings with a novel homozygous p.Pro128Ser variant causing tall stature with functional validation; PMID 35233476 further broadens the LOF variant spectrum in NPR-C-related extreme tall stature. Independently, human GWAS in large cohorts identified common NPR3 variants (rs10472828) associated with adult height (PMIDs 19343178, 19570815), implicating the CNP/NPR3 signaling pathway in height variation. These are replicated human genetic findings across families and population cohorts, meeting criteria for Established.

Multiple independent human studies directly demonstrate FBN1 variant effects on stature: PMID 32499652 identifies a common missense variant (E1297G) reducing height by 2.2 cm per allele in Peruvian cohorts; PMID 17024364 reports an exonic SNP (rs8033037) associated with tall stature in a case-control cohort; PMID 7738200 describes an FBN1 missense mutation segregating with tall stature in a family without cardiac/ocular Marfan features; PMID 24833718 shows rare FBN1 variants associated with tall stature in scoliosis cohorts; and PMID 36380655 shows FBN1 haploinsufficiency variants associate with greater height in Marfan patients. Additionally, domain-specific FBN1 mutations cause short-stature acromelic dysplasias (geleophysic, acromicric, Weill-Marchesani), demonstrating bidirectional, replicated, human genetic evidence.
