This constitutes strong, replicated evidence across independent probands, families, and populations.

Multiple human studies report their own primary results linking GHR variants to stature. PMID 26366551 is a sequencing-based whole-genome association in 6,307 Sardinians identifying a GHR stop-codon variant that reduces height by 4.2 cm in heterozygotes and causes Laron syndrome in homozygotes. PMID 37780997 reports a consanguineous Pakistani family with three siblings homozygous for GHR c.508G>C causing Laron-type dwarfism, and PMID 24150201 describes a heterozygous GHR V144I variant with functional signaling studies in a child with severe idiopathic short stature. Additional independent cohorts examine the exon 3 GHRd3 polymorphism and growth/height response (PMIDs 38356830, 34453799, 23696513), and reviews catalog >90 human GHR mutations associated with short stature (PMID 29748515). This constitutes replicated, independent human evidence across probands, families, and cohorts.

Two independent human genetic studies report variants in TET1 associated with height in their own results: the Icelandic whole-genome sequencing study (PMID 27848971) identified a novel TET1 variant associated with both adult height and birth length in 88,835 imputed individuals, and the large exome-based rare variant study (PMID 42396316) directly implicated TET1 among 207 height-associated genes with large effect sizes in a discovery set of 826,066 exomes with replication in 624,567 additional individuals. These are single-gene, variant-level associations in humans from independent cohorts, satisfying replication requirements. The remaining articles (animal nutrition/growth studies, cancer, epigenome editing, neurodegeneration) concern TET1 biology generally or use "height" as a homonym context (villus height) and do not add human genetic evidence. A modest weight remains on "Existing" in case one considers the two reports insufficiently independent or the rare-variant gene-based signal preliminary.

Multiple human genetic studies report their own results linking PLIN1 variation to HDL cholesterol: the UK Biobank exome-imputation study identified PLIN1 loss-of-function variants as a novel association with HDL-C (PMID 36490288); a multi-ancestry rare coding variant analysis of >170,000 exomes prioritized PLIN1 among genes associated with blood lipid levels including HDL (PMID 34932938); rare non-synonymous PLIN1 variants associated with lipid metabolite measurements in UKB exomes (PMID 36809768); and PLIN1 haploinsufficiency carriers showed a favorable metabolic/lipid profile (PMID 35235652). Older candidate-gene work in Han Chinese also reported PLIN genotype differences in HDL-C (PMID 15601966), and pediatric PLIN locus studies report lipid/Apo A-I associations (PMID 35893926, though the HDL signal there was for PLIN2). Because at least two independent cohorts (UKB European and multi-ancestry TOPMed-type exome cohorts, plus Chinese candidate-gene samples) report PLIN1 variant–HDL associations from their own data, Established is favored; some weight remains on Existing given partial cohort overlap (UKB) and the fact that several signals are for composite lipid traits rather than HDL specifically.

Direct human genetic evidence with primary results: PMID 26902202 reported two unrelated families with distinct homozygous PAPPA2 mutations (p.D643fs25*, p.Ala1033Val) causing progressive growth failure with low free IGF-I, plus functional proof of lost proteolytic activity; PMID 34272725 independently identified a third, unrelated Saudi family with a novel homozygous nonsense variant (p.Glu886*) and the same short-stature phenotype; PMID 36646053 describes additional affected siblings with PAPP-A2 deficiency. Treatment studies in these patients (PMIDs 27648969, 29029190, 34358737) show rhIGF-1 restores growth velocity and adult height, reinforcing causality. Population-level human data (PMID 33142306 on PAPPA2 genotypes, height and pubertal timing; PMID 39809772 rare-variant burden of PAPPA2 with birth weight) add supportive association evidence beyond single families. Mouse (PMID 30445407, 38589872) and in vitro work provide mechanism but are not needed for the human classification.

Human genetic evidence is direct and replicated: the UK Biobank exome study (PMID 33087929) reported novel loss-of-function variants in PIEZO1 with large effects on varicose veins, and an independent large clinical cohort exome study (PMID 34358671) replicated the association of rare protein-truncating PIEZO1 variants with varicose vein risk; a further exome study (PMID 38980841) and the first large GWAS of varicose veins (PMID 30998689) also prioritize PIEZO1 as a causal gene. These are single-gene rare-variant associations, not multigene CNVs, and derive from independent populations, supporting Established. Supporting mechanistic human and mouse work (PMIDs 41055734, 39249600) shows altered PIEZO1 expression in human varicose veins and modulation of experimental disease, consistent with causality. Some uncertainty remains because the evidence is population-level association rather than familial segregation in probands, so a substantial share is retained for Existing.

None of the provided articles report any association between LOXL2 variants and human height or stature; the human genetic reports involving LOXL2 concern intracranial aneurysm (PMID 29107163), occipital encephalocele (PMID 37345575), and mid-dermal elastolysis (PMID 29845638), none of which are height phenotypes or recognized precursors of stature variation. Therefore neither Established nor Existing can be supported. However, LOXL2 biology is directly relevant to skeletal/connective tissue growth: it cross-links collagen and elastin, is required for chondrogenic differentiation and cartilage anabolism (PMID 33214607), participates in ligament ossification and vascularization (PMID 38594260), and is implicated in axial skeleton tumor biology (PMID 40481032), providing a plausible mechanistic, though indirect and largely non-human, link to growth-plate/skeletal size. This favors Hypothesized, with substantial residual probability for Novel given the entirely incidental nature of the co-mentions with height.

Multiple independent human studies report their own results linking PPARG variants to triglyceride levels: PMID 16029943 (Pro12Ala carriers had significantly lower triglycerides in a Caucasian cohort), PMID 27560839 (rs1801282 associated with lower triglycerides in Mexican children), PMID 38492104 (rs1801282 CC homozygotes had higher triglycerides in a Russian cohort), PMID 21833536 (P12A/C161T genotypes associated with serum triglyceride levels in Turkish CHD patients), and PMID 26446033 (Ala12Ala carriers had lower total triglycerides in a randomized crossover trial). In addition, rare heterozygous pathogenic PPARG variants cause FPLD3 with severe hypertriglyceridemia in probands and families (PMIDs 40615268, 34515658, 42440509), providing Mendelian-level human evidence. Gene–diet interaction studies (PMID 21949049) and pharmacogenetic meta-analysis of TZD response on TG (PMID 37376225) further support replication across designs and ancestries. This constitutes strong, replicated human evidence for an established gene–phenotype relationship.

Direct human genotype–height evidence in this list is limited: PMID 33142306 genotyped PAPPA (alongside PAPPA2 and STC2) and related it to height, IGF-I and pubertal timing in girls, which supports at least an "Existing" level of evidence. PMID 24065112 identifies a CNV overlapping PAPPA in short stature and notes PAPPA lies near a GWAS height locus, but multigene CNVs cannot single out PAPPA and the GWAS statement is cited background rather than the paper's own result. PMID 28146470 implicates the STC2–PAPP-A–IGFBP-4 axis in adult height, but the variants tested were in STC2, with PAPP-A involvement shown by in vitro proteolysis assays, so this is mechanistic/functional support rather than PAPPA variant evidence. Extensive biology (PAPP-A cleaving IGFBP-4 to liberate bioactive IGF-I, pappalysin studies in PWS, mouse models, sheep GWAS) strongly supports plausibility, keeping "Hypothesized" nontrivial. Because I cannot cite two independent human studies reporting PAPPA-specific variants associated with height in their own results, "Established" is not warranted.

Two or more independent human studies report INSR variation directly linked to triglyceride levels in their own results: the gene-centric meta-analysis of 66,240 European-ancestry individuals with replication identified INSR as a novel locus for triglycerides (PMID 23063622), and human cohorts carrying INSR receptor-level pathogenic variants uniformly showed markedly low serum triglycerides, reduced de novo lipogenesis, and TG-depleted VLDL versus post-receptor insulin-resistance groups (PMID 19164855), replicated in an independent NIH cohort with metabolic phenotyping and lipidomics (PMIDs 32191645, 26273324). An additional common INSR SNV (rs7248104) is cited as an established TG risk variant (PMID 33407432), and INSR is also a GWAS locus for hepatic steatosis, a closely linked lipid trait (PMID 37709864). Countervailing evidence exists (the Y1355H family variant was not confirmed causal in a mouse knock-in model, PMID 34271222), which tempers but does not negate the human genetic data, so a portion of probability remains on "Existing."

Multiple independent human reports present their own primary findings of biallelic LTBP2 variants co-segregating with stature abnormalities: PMID 20179738 describes homozygous truncating LTBP2 mutations in two consanguineous families with tall stature and increased arm span/height ratio; PMID 30565850 reports two unrelated Roma/Gypsy probands homozygous for p.R299X with tall stature and Marfan-like habitus; PMID 33766794 documents a homozygous LTBP2 frameshift with macrosomia/overgrowth; PMID 33958902 and PMID 38772353 report LTBP2 variants in Weill-Marchesani(-like) syndrome, which is defined by short stature. These are single-gene point/truncating variants in independent probands and families rather than multigenic copy-number changes, satisfying replication for stature as a phenotype. Several remaining papers (e.g., LTBP3 aortic studies, ADAMTS10/17 reports, donkey LTBP2 polymorphisms) only cite LTBP2 as background or are non-human, so they do not add to human evidence but do support biological plausibility via the fibrillin/TGF-β acromelic dysplasia pathway.

None of the provided articles report any association between GFPT2 variants and height or stature in humans; human genetic studies are limited to type 2 diabetes/diabetic nephropathy (PMID 14764791, 20353610) and asthenozoospermia (PMID 30849544), none of which relate to height. Some indirect biological plausibility exists: GFPT2 catalyzes deamidation of SMAD6 modulating BMP signaling, a pathway central to skeletal development and birth defects (PMID 38913236), and GFPT2 expression changes were observed in human foetal femur-derived skeletal progenitor cultures under BMP-2 (PMID 19438813). These are pathway/expression-level hints rather than evidence that GFPT2 variation influences height. The remaining literature is dominated by cancer metabolism (hexosamine biosynthesis) with no stature phenotype, so co-mentions are largely incidental, favoring Novel with meaningful weight on Hypothesized.

The strongest direct evidence is PMID 34732801, a gene-based collapsing analysis of 379,066 UK Biobank exomes reporting that GIGYF1 predicted loss-of-function variants associate with decreased cholesterol levels alongside glucose/HbA1c/T2D effects — a credible human genetic finding specific to this gene. Other human exome studies (PMIDs 35177841, 34234147, 37072623, 41168175) firmly establish GIGYF1 rare LOF variants with cardiometabolic phenotypes (T2D, fat mass, obesity, IGF-1 signaling) that are recognized risk factors/mechanisms linked to lipid levels, but they do not independently report a total cholesterol association in their own results. Therefore replication for the cholesterol phenotype specifically is lacking, precluding "Established." Remaining papers (Drosophila, zebrafish/mouse, C. elegans, AlphaFold interaction studies) provide only biological/functional context and cannot support human genetic categories.

The ExomeChip/GIANT study of rare and low-frequency coding variants (PMID 28146470) directly reports height-associated coding variants and explicitly highlights NOX4 as a new biological candidate for growth, which is genuine human genetic evidence. However, this is a single publication; no independent replication article in this list reports NOX4 height variants in separate probands, families, or cohorts, so "Established" cannot be supported under the two-study requirement. Supporting biology comes from human leprechaunism fibroblasts, where Nox4 downregulation impairs growth-factor ROS signaling in a syndrome featuring growth retardation (PMID 16249442), and from NOX4's roles in oxidative stress, bone/osteoclast biology and disc height (PMIDs 38379095, 42393347), which reinforce plausibility but are mechanistic rather than variant-based for stature. Other listed papers concern kidney, liver, lung, cancer, or Alzheimer phenotypes and only incidentally use the word "height."

The strongest evidence is the exome-wide association study of plasma lipids (PMID 29083408), which identified JAK2 as one of the loci significantly associated with total cholesterol in >300,000 human participants with replication in >280,000, and additionally validated the lipid effect experimentally in mice. A second human candidate-gene study of 10 tagging SNPs in 2,760 female twins (PMID 18239666) found nominal association of rs3780378 with total cholesterol and LDL-C, but these did not survive multiple-testing correction, so it is supportive but not confirmatory. The psoriasis genetics paper (PMID 37893484) reports JAK2 SNPs and cholesterol data, but the lipid finding there is tied to A20 expression, not JAK2 variants, so it counts only as incidental. The remaining papers concern JAK2 somatic driver mutations in myeloproliferative neoplasms or JAK/STAT pharmacology and are irrelevant to total cholesterol genetics. Because only one paper (albeit an internally replicated, very large one) demonstrates the variant–trait association in its own human results, the evidence sits at the boundary between Existing and Established.

Human genetic evidence directly supports TIMD4 variants influencing lipid levels: the large GWAS (PMID 19060906, ~19,840 discovery + ~20,623 replication individuals) identified common variants near TIMD4 associated with LDL cholesterol, a major component of total cholesterol. Independent candidate-gene cohort studies in Southern Chinese Han populations report TIMD4-HAVCR1 variant associations with serum lipid parameters including the TC/HDL-C ratio and gene–environment interactions on TC (PMID 29208769), and TIMD4 rs6882076 associations with lipids/TG plus CHD and IS risk (PMID 31337960); the latter also notes prior reported associations with total cholesterol. An additional population-genetics review cites TIMD4 variants among susceptibility loci for dyslipidemia in Amerindian-derived populations (PMID 24768220). Because these are multiple independent human cohorts with variant-level data, but the strongest genome-wide result is for LDL-C rather than TC specifically, points are concentrated on Established with substantial weight retained for Existing. The remaining TIMD4 papers concern immunology, efferocytosis, and cancer and are not relevant to cholesterol genetics.

The only human genetic evidence linking FIBIN to height is the large CNV meta-analysis (PMID 28963451), which identified an 11p14.2 rare CNV with large effects on height and stated that FIBIN harbors both common and rare variants affecting body size. However, this is a multigene CNV region (encompassing BBOX1/FIBIN), so it cannot single out FIBIN from neighboring genes and, per the rules, does not count toward "Established"; no second independent human variant-level study is provided. The other papers are non-height contexts: a human deletion of BBOX1/FIBIN affecting carnitine metabolism (PMID 24986124), in vitro Schlemm's canal endothelial stretch transcriptomics (PMID 41232793), neurotoxicant biomarker screening in LUHMES cells (PMID 32870474), and TGF-beta–regulated gene expression in chicken myofibroblasts (PMID 23127594) — the latter offering only indirect biological plausibility (secreted growth factor, TGF-beta/ECM signaling relevant to growth). Therefore "Existing" is the most probable category, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the CNV evidence is deemed insufficiently gene-specific.

phenotype: Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary sarcoidosis
literature_justification: Multiple independent human studies report RTEL1 variants in patients with interstitial lung disease/pulmonary fibrosis. PMID 30523160 describes 35 affected individuals from 17 independent families with RTEL1 mutations and heterogeneous ILD phenotypes, and PMID 27540018 reports 14 additional RTEL1 mutation carriers with progressive fibrotic ILD. Large-scale whole-genome sequencing in 2,180 IPF cases (PMID 36602845) found rare RTEL1 variants significantly associated with IPF risk, providing statistical replication. Additional independent probands/families with novel likely pathogenic RTEL1 variants are reported (PMIDs 41204139, 40199602, 36090019, 40985209, 39279436), and RTEL1 is a recognized telomere biology disorder gene causing pulmonary fibrosis. The sarcoidosis component of the phenotype term is not specifically supported, but the ILD link is robustly established in humans.
open_targets_trait: pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure, Telomere-related, 3

literature_justification: Multiple independent human genetic studies report CFI variants in AMD patients with their own results: the large IAMDGC GWAS found very rare coding CFI variants implicating CFI causally (PMID 26691988), a multicenter study identified the p.Gly119Arg mutation in 20/3567 cases vs 1/3937 controls (PMID 25352734), an earlier case-control study localized association to the CFI region (PMID 18685559), rare-variant familial segregation analyses were reported (PMID 26767664), and UK Biobank rare CFI variants predicted reduced macular thickness and higher AMD risk (PMID 35285476). Additional cohorts show rare dysfunctional CFI variants predict progression to advanced AMD (PMID 36909148) and prevalence/functional characterization studies (PMIDs 35531992, 38852887, 36067162) confirm mechanism (low FI level/activity) linking genotype to disease. This constitutes replicated, human, variant-level evidence in independent probands and families, supporting an Established relationship, with residual weight on Existing given the risk-factor (rather than fully Mendelian) nature of the association.

None of the provided articles examine human stature or any height-related anthropometric trait; the literature concerns PTPRJ/DEP-1/CD148 in leukemia (FLT3-ITD), colorectal cancer predisposition, renal fibrosis and clear cell RCC, immune cell markers, platelet Src kinase regulation, chicken heterophil/lymphocyte ratio, and glaucoma/intraocular pressure genetics. No human genetic study reports PTPRJ variants associated with height, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. A small allowance for Hypothesized is warranted because PTPRJ negatively regulates growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase signaling (EGFR, PDGFR/FLT3) and cell proliferation, a biology loosely relevant to growth, and animal models exist (mouse, chicken), but these do not address skeletal growth or stature. The IOP-related GRS paper mentions a PTPRJ/AGBL2 locus but concerns eye pressure, not height, and thus does not qualify.

No article in this list reports a genome-wide or candidate-gene association between ADAMTS6 variants and stature/height as a measured trait; the hernia GWAS (PMID 35680855) implicates ADAMTS6 in connective-tissue/hernia risk, not height. The strongest human genetic evidence is the recent report of rare loss-of-function ADAMTS6 variants in four unrelated individuals with a syndromic connective-tissue disorder (CHANS) including skeletal and craniofacial involvement (PMID 40657314), which is suggestive of a skeletal/growth phenotype but does not explicitly document height as the associated trait, and it is a single cohort. Supporting biology is largely non-human or in vitro: Adamts6-null mouse embryos show limb and musculoskeletal defects (PMID 41399538), ADAMTS6 processes fibrillin-1/2 and LTBPs regulating TGFβ (PMID 36368447, 27779234), and its sister proteases ADAMTS10/ADAMTS17 cause Weill–Marchesani syndrome with short stature (PMID 32290605, 41915433, 32183147), making a height link biologically plausible. Therefore the weight sits between Hypothesized (strong mechanistic/animal-model rationale) and Existing (one human variant series with skeletal features), with Established unsupported since two independent human height-variant studies cannot be cited.

Multiple independent human studies report GHSR variants in probands/families with short stature: Pantel et al. identified a missense mutation (p.A204E) segregating with short stature in two unrelated families (PMID 16511605) and further recessive GHSR mutations in isolated GH deficiency (PMID 19789204); Inoue et al. found and functionally characterized novel GHSR mutations in Japanese short-stature subjects (PMID 21084395); Pugliese-Pires et al. reported novel inactivating GHSR mutations in idiopathic short stature/CDGP (PMID 21646290); and a recent large study linked loss-of-function GHSR variants to short stature and low IGF-I (PMID 39785833). Common GHSR polymorphisms have also been associated with stature across childhood (PMID 22457237) and in SGA/short stature cohorts (PMID 37019085), although some studies were negative (PMIDs 18945286, 22876551), indicating variable effect sizes for common variants. The evidence is human, replicated across independent families and cohorts, and supported by functional data, meeting criteria for Established.

phenotype: Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary sarcoidosis
literature_justification: Multiple independent human studies report rare deleterious PARN variants segregating in families and cohorts with pulmonary fibrosis/interstitial lung disease: exome sequencing in familial kindreds identified five novel heterozygous damaging PARN mutations with linkage evidence (PMID 25848748), an independent family-based study confirmed rare PARN variants (PMID 28414520), a multicentre retrospective series characterized ILD phenotypes in heterozygous PARN carriers (PMID 34981600), and a telomere-gene cohort included 19 PARN mutation carriers with progressive fibrotic ILD (PMID 27540018). Additional independent probands include a homozygous PARN missense in familial pulmonary fibrosis (PMID 30525901), a nonsense variant in IPF (PMID 38614962), and PARN carriers with high ILD penetrance in a registry-based telomere biology disorder screen (PMID 33035329). These are human genetic studies with variants identified in patients across multiple independent cohorts and families, satisfying replication requirements. The relationship is therefore Established for the ILD component of the phenotype, though the sarcoidosis component is not directly supported, leaving minor probability on Existing.

Multiple independent human studies report ALB variants influencing LDL cholesterol: a population-based cohort study showing heterozygous ALB loss-of-function variants raise LDL-C to familial hypercholesterolemia-like levels (PMID 42126373), a clinical case with homozygous ALB variants (congenital analbuminemia) presenting with severe LDL-C elevation after negative FH testing (PMID 36411186), and a Finnish whole-genome sequencing study identifying an ALB promoter deletion associated with low albumin and markedly increased total/cholesterol-related traits (PMID 33798444). Reviews of congenital analbuminemia consistently describe hyperlipidemia as a near-universal feature of ALB loss-of-function (PMIDs 31057599, 23612153), and a Finnish haplotype-based GWAS found LDL association at the 4q13.3-q21.1 region containing ALB (PMID 24896150), though that locus also includes PF4. Together these constitute replicated human genetic evidence in independent probands and cohorts, supporting "Established," with some residual probability for "Existing" since one key line of evidence is a single case report and the GWAS signal is not gene-resolved. Other listed papers (depression biomarkers, statin trials, testosterone, thyroid FDH) are incidental co-mentions or concern ALB variants affecting thyroid hormone binding, not lipids.

Multiple large-scale human exome-sequencing studies report rare protein-coding/loss-of-function variants in SLTM associated with BMI in their own primary results: the sex-stratified UK Biobank analysis (PMID 37601970) identified SLTM LoF as increasing adult BMI in men, and the cross-ancestry rare-variant meta-analysis of 839,110 individuals from six ancestries across two population-scale biobanks (PMIDs 39484254, 41168175) found consistent SLTM effects on BMI/severe obesity. An additional independent rare-variant analysis of adiposity and fat-distribution traits in 402,375 UK Biobank participants also implicated SLTM, and CRISPR knockdown in human adipocytes reduced lipid accumulation, providing functional corroboration (PMID 40912257). These are single-gene, variant-level human associations replicated across ancestries and cohorts, meeting criteria for Established; residual probability on Existing reflects partial UK Biobank sample overlap between studies. Remaining papers (GLI regulation, RNA localization, male infertility MR) are mechanistically unrelated to BMI.

No article reports human genetic variants in TET2 associated with HDL cholesterol levels; the human genetic literature here concerns somatic TET2 mutations in myeloid malignancies (PMIDs 19483684, 19420352, 19372255, 19262601) and clonal hematopoiesis with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (PMID 28636844, 35385050), which is a lipid-related but not an HDL-level phenotype. The strongest mechanistic link is the ABCA1/CMML study (PMID 32160545), where Tet2 loss interacts with defective cholesterol efflux and where raising HDL/apoA-I bypasses the defect—but this is mouse and in vitro work, supporting a hypothesized rather than an established/existing human association. Additional CHIP-atherosclerosis mechanistic papers (PMIDs 39196062, 40244103, 39111028) invoke macrophage cholesterol handling and inflammation, again biologically relevant but not HDL-level genetic evidence. Therefore most weight goes to Hypothesized, with residual probability on Novel since the HDL connection is largely indirect and incidental.

Several human studies report ABCB11 (BSEP) variants in probands and cohorts together with elevated alanine aminotransferase as part of the phenotype: a 62-child normal-GGT PFIC cohort where ABCB11 mutations were distinguished by high serum ALT (PMID 20232290), a 22-patient PFIC2 series where ALT levels (>165 IU/L) predicted treatment response (PMID 25847299), siblings with compound heterozygous ABCB11 mutations and ALT of 168 and 233 U/L (PMID 29886607), and a WES study of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy in which carriers of damaging ABCB11/ABC-transporter variants had higher mean ALT than controls (PMID 36046230). Additional independent human reports include ABCB11 variants in NSAID-induced cholestatic liver injury (PMID 40776909) and an obstetric cholestasis case with >40-fold ALT elevation carrying the ABCB11 p.V444A variant (PMID 22675952), plus UDCA response by ABCB11 polymorphism in NASH (PMID 37511794). These constitute replicated human evidence linking ABCB11 variation to ALT elevation, though ALT is generally a secondary measure of hepatocellular injury within cholestatic disease rather than the primary trait studied, which leaves some probability for "Existing".

Two human-based reports provide direct evidence: a case report of a heterozygous HTRA1 missense variant (p.V297M) in a patient with short stature and short limbs (PMID 41062325), and a large-scale human genetic study showing that HTRA1 loss-of-protease-function variants associate with skeletal traits in the UK Biobank and MyCode cohorts (PMID 39196222). The latter is a well-powered, replicated human association, but "skeletal traits" is not unambiguously height, and the former is a single anecdotal case, so replication specifically for height is not firmly demonstrated. Additional literature (CARASIL with spondylosis/disc degeneration, HTRA1's role in bone metabolism and TGF-β signaling) supports biological plausibility for skeletal growth effects but is mechanistic rather than height-specific. Therefore Existing is the most likely category, with meaningful probability for Established.

Multiple independent human reports describe biallelic SLC34A3 variants in probands and families with hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria presenting with nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis: PMID 21344632 (compound heterozygous novel splice mutation with nephrolithiasis, plus heterozygous relatives with stones), PMID 18523928 (homozygous p.G196R sisters with nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis), PMID 18996815 (novel mutation with recurrent kidney stones), and PMID 31352694 (homozygous p.G495R with recurrent nephrolithiasis). Large pooled and cohort analyses replicate this in independent kindreds (PMID 38364990, 304 individuals/145 kindreds; PMID 39461557, 113 patients) and population-based data show heterozygous carriers (Ser192Leu) have increased nephrolithiasis risk (PMID 37639356). Functional work (PMID 18480181) supports loss of NaPi-IIc transport as the mechanism. Evidence is human, replicated across independent probands and families, so the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report LTBP3 variants segregating with short stature in distinct families: PMID 19344874 (consanguineous Pakistani family with homozygous Y774X, oligodontia plus short stature), PMID 25669657 (four families with recessive hypomorphic LTBP3 mutations causing brachyolmia/short stature with amelogenesis imperfecta), PMID 25899461 (two sisters with homozygous truncating variants, short stature), PMID 30887145 (East Asian probands with novel missense and splice variants, acromicric dysplasia and DASS), PMID 38192829 (Egyptian and Pakistani families with novel and known LTBP3 variants and brachyolmia/short stature), and PMID 27068007 (LTBP3 mutations in acromicric and geleophysic dysplasia, both short-stature syndromes). These are single-gene point/frameshift/splice variants, not multigene copy-number events, and include replication across ethnicities and both recessive and dominant mechanisms, with genotype–phenotype correlation. Short stature is the phenotype itself, not merely a proxy. Therefore the evidence is clearly Established.

The strongest direct human evidence is the multi-ancestry blood lipid GWAS integrating functional genomics in 1.6 million individuals (PMID 35931049), which explicitly prioritizes RRBP1 as a causal lipid gene with convergent eQTL, chromatin-interaction and variant-level support. A second paper (PMID 36803854) states that GWASs have linked RRBP1 variants to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and serum lipoprotein levels, but its own results concern renin trafficking and blood pressure in animal/cellular models, so it counts as background citation rather than independent replication. Other RRBP1 papers concern cancer, COPD, Alzheimer's microglia, ER ribosome binding and collagen/secretory biology, providing at most mechanistic plausibility (secretory/ER protein handling, apolipoprotein E secretion in PMID 19037105) rather than lipid-variant evidence. Because I can cite only one article whose own results demonstrate variant-level human association with lipids, the evidence best fits "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Established" given the size and multi-ancestry replication within that single GWAS.

phenotype: Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary sarcoidosis
literature_justification: Multiple human studies report causative heterozygous TERT variants in independent probands and families with interstitial lung disease/pulmonary fibrosis: PMID 27540018 describes 75 patients with TERT mutations across families with heterogeneous but uniformly progressive ILD; PMID 32315675 reports a TERT founder mutation segregating in pulmonary fibrosis families across generations; PMID 33035329 identified causative TERT variants in 6 probands from a registry of familial hematologic/ILD presentations; PMID 40926757 and PMID 30451599 add further single-family/case evidence with functional telomere shortening. Common-variant association data (TERT rs2736100 with sporadic ILD, PMID 24434656; with AAV-ILD, PMID 33076992) further support the gene–phenotype link at the population level. Mechanistic and animal/in vitro work (PMID 35508454, 40770487) is supportive but not needed given the human genetic evidence. Sarcoidosis-specific evidence is absent, which slightly tempers certainty for the combined phenotype label, hence some residual weight on "Existing".
open_targets_trait: pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure, Telomere-related, 1

literature_justification: The only direct human evidence linking GIGYF1 to circulating lipids comes from the UK Biobank exome collapsing study (PMID 34732801), which reported that GIGYF1 predicted loss-of-function variants associate with decreased cholesterol levels alongside glucose, HbA1c and T2D effects — but this is total cholesterol rather than an explicitly replicated LDL-C signal. A second large exome study of cardiometabolic traits (PMID 35177841) notes 18 genes associated with blood lipid or glucose levels and highlights GIGYF1, though its named GIGYF1 result is type 2 diabetes, so it functions more as supportive/background than independent LDL replication. Other GIGYF1 papers concern T2D, obesity, LOY, cognition, grip strength, alcohol intake and autism (PMIDs 34234147, 34216101, 36530175, 39484254, 41168175, 37301943), which are metabolically adjacent (insulin/IGF-1R signaling, adiposity) and provide mechanistic plausibility for dyslipidemia but not direct LDL variant evidence. The All of Us study (PMID 37072623) replicated LDL burden signals only for APOB, LDLR and PCSK9, with GIGYF1 tied to T2D. I therefore cannot cite two independent human studies whose own results demonstrate GIGYF1 variants associating with LDL cholesterol, so Existing is the most probable category.

The strongest direct human evidence is PMID 31648372, in which ABCC2 rs3740065 was an independent risk factor for antituberculosis drug-induced hepatotoxicity (an ALT-defined phenotype) in a 746-patient Han Chinese cohort. PMID 36046230 reports ABCC2 missense variants (Ile681Lys, Met688Thr) in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy with higher mean ALT in the damaging-mutation group, but the ALT comparison pools variants across many genes and so does not isolate ABCC2. Other papers either test ABCC2 and find no ALT association (bosentan DILI, PMID 23863877, where CYP2C9*2 was the signal), report ABCC2-related Dubin–Johnson syndrome in which ALT is characteristically normal (PMIDs 34858902, 32758197), or mention ALT elevation only as a co-occurring toxicity (PMID 31870219). Thus there is at least one credible human genetic association plus mechanistically strong hepatobiliary transporter biology, but replication specifically attributing ALT variation to ABCC2 variants is lacking, favoring "Existing" over "Established".

Two human genetic studies present their own primary results linking TIMD4 variants to triglyceride levels: PMID 31337960 (rs6882076, 1,765 subjects, Southern Chinese Han; T allele carriers had lower serum TG) and PMID 29208769 (TIMD4-HAVCR1 rs1501908 and haplotypes associated with triglycerides and other lipids in 622 controls plus CHD/IS patients). The large GWAS (PMID 19060906) independently identified the TIMD4 locus for lipoprotein concentrations (LDL-C primarily), and a review of Amerindian/Mexican populations (PMID 24768220) reports TIMD4 variants among loci influencing triglyceride levels, supporting cross-population generalization. Additional mouse work (PMID 26821944) notes Tim-4 is genetically associated with low LDL and triglyceride levels, reinforcing biological plausibility. Some caution remains because the two Chinese studies come from the same research group/population and the flagship GWAS signal at TIMD4 was strongest for LDL-C, so a portion of probability is retained for "Existing."

Multiple independent human genetic studies provide direct evidence: the population-based CARRIERS-type case-control study estimated breast cancer risk for germline BARD1 pathogenic variants (PMID 33471974), a large exome-wide meta-analysis of 26,368 cases and 217,673 controls found protein-truncating variants in BARD1 associated with breast cancer (PMID 37592023), and saturation genome editing showed LoF missense variants in the ankyrin and BRCT domains are enriched in breast cancer cohorts, resolving VUS (PMID 41282735). Family-based/clinical evidence includes a hereditary breast/ovarian cancer family with cis BARD1 mutations causing DNA damage-response defects (PMID 33623049), patient-derived lymphoblastoid characterization of germline variants in breast cancer patients (PMID 31371347), and recurrent variant spectra in Finnish patient panels (PMID 36551643). Somatic and germline BARD1 alterations were also identified in primary breast/ovarian/uterine tumors with loss of the wild-type allele (PMID 9425226). These are independent human cohorts with replication, so the relationship is Established; only a small residual probability is left for "Existing" given some studies report modest/moderate penetrance.

None of the provided articles reports a human genetic association between SCMH1 variants and height. The strongest human evidence is a GWAS/MTAG analysis identifying SCMH1 as a novel bone mineral density locus (PMID 30690781), a skeletal trait that is related to but distinct from stature; that study also showed SCMH1 upregulates osteoblast differentiation markers in mouse MC3T3-E1 cells, which is functional/animal rather than human height evidence. The other papers describe SCMH1 as a mammalian Polycomb (Scm homolog) component involved in Prc1 function, homeotic gene regulation with axial/posterior transformations in mice, and spermatocyte biology (PMIDs 10653359, 17215307) — biologically plausible links to skeletal patterning and growth but not to height variants in people. Therefore the evidence best supports Hypothesized, with some weight to Existing given the human BMD locus as a skeletal-trait proxy, and no basis for Established.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in WDR6 associated with stature or any height-related anthropometric trait. The literature is dominated by WDR6's role as a partner of FTSJ1/Trm7 in tRNA anticodon-loop 2'-O-methylation (PMIDs 32558197, 22912484, 31586407, 26310293, 40483304), vaccinia virus host restriction (30209174), diabetic kidney lipid metabolism (42252270), and an ACL rupture exome study where the WDR6 variant was explicitly predicted non-damaging (27692106). The only tangential "growth" link is in vitro cell proliferation/G1 arrest via LKB1 and p27(Kip1) (17216128), which concerns cellular growth arrest rather than organismal height, providing at most a very weak biological rationale. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a modest allowance for Hypothesized based on the cell-growth-regulation and translation-related biology.

Multiple independent human studies report point mutations in PAX2 in probands and families with renal hypodysplasia/renal coloboma syndrome progressing to chronic kidney disease and ESRD. Direct primary evidence includes the Japanese cohort of 38 patients from 30 families with 19 pathogenic PAX2 variants presenting with CKD/renal hypodysplasia (PMID 32203253), the ESCAPE study identifying four PAX2 mutations in six families with RHD and chronic renal insufficiency (PMID 16971658), the CAKUT cohort with PAX2 mutations in five families (PMID 24429398), a 14-patient pediatric cohort with 11 PAX2 variants including five novel ones and progression to ESRD (PMID 40572647), and additional pedigree/case reports (PMIDs 35087773, 37532497, 27293569). These are single-gene sequence variants in humans, not multigene deletions, and they replicate across ethnicities and independent centers. Animal data (PMID 38482556) provide supporting mechanism but are not needed for the classification.
open_targets_trait: congenital anomaly of kidney and urinary tract

literature_justification: Multiple independent human studies report LIPC variants associated with total cholesterol. PMID 26282880 reports a case-control study in 2,969 Chinese children plus meta-analysis showing the LIPC C-514T T allele associated with higher total cholesterol; PMID 37460425 identifies a novel LIPC c.1330C>T (Arg444Cys) variant segregating with elevated TC in a familial hypercholesterolemia-like pedigree; PMID 27135400 identifies LIPC among loci harboring large-effect sequence variants for blood lipid fractions (non-HDL/HDL cholesterol) in >100,000 Icelanders; and PMID 25961943 highlights LIPC as a locus with established function explaining lipid associations including total cholesterol. Additional cohort and GWAS studies (26780889, 15292318, 16324926, 29614023) report LIPC genotype effects on TC or closely related lipid fractions across diverse populations. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence in independent cohorts and a family, supporting an Established relationship, with residual probability given that many signals are strongest for HDL rather than TC specifically.

None of the provided articles examine stature or height as a phenotype; the literature concerns age-related macular degeneration (PMIDs 14570714, 17216616, 16020313), epidermolysis bullosa simplex (39976600), podocyte/glomerular disease (29488390), splenic epidermoid cyst (25338956), various cancers, and animal/zebrafish developmental studies (22771579). No human genetic study here reports HMCN1 variants associated with height, so "Established" and "Existing" cannot be supported. A modest allowance for "Hypothesized" reflects HMCN1's role as a fibulin-family extracellular matrix protein involved in basement membrane adhesion and tissue morphogenesis, which is biologically adjacent to connective-tissue/skeletal growth, though no article links this to body size. Overall the gene–phenotype co-mention is incidental within this evidence set, favoring "Novel."

Only one paper in this set reports its own human genetic result linking PDE3B directly to height: the UK Biobank predicted loss-of-function analysis (PMID 29691411), where PDE3B pLOF variants associated with elevated height alongside improved fat distribution and coronary protection. Other human genetic studies of PDE3B (PMIDs 31492854, 35773277, 38267387, 30275531, 36490288) implicate the gene in adiposity, fat distribution, lipids and sarcopenic obesity, which are body-size but not height phenotypes, and thus provide only indirect support. Mechanistic plausibility for stature exists through PDE3 inhibition amplifying CNP/cGMP signalling in growth-plate chondrocytes to promote long-bone outgrowth (PMID 40456620), but that work is non-human/ex vivo and concerns the PDE3 family broadly. Because a second independent human cohort demonstrating a PDE3B–height association is not present here, the evidence falls short of Established and is best classified as Existing, with residual weight on Hypothesized given the chondrocyte biology.

Multiple independent human studies report SCARB1 variants associated with lipid traits including total cholesterol. The large-scale GWAS of >100,000 individuals of European ancestry identified SCARB1 as a genome-wide significant lipid locus with replication in non-European cohorts (PMID 20686565); an FH cohort found the exon 8 polymorphism associated with elevated total cholesterol, VLDL-C, and LDL-C (PMID 12519372); rs5888 was associated with serum lipid levels in Chinese Bai Ku Yao and Han populations (PMID 22583964) and in a Lithuanian cohort (PMID 23510561); further human candidate-gene and pharmacogenetic studies (PMIDs 22229114, 20064494, 33154658, 36185686) support the association. These are human cohort studies with variant-level data in independent populations, satisfying replication criteria. Rare-variant sequencing studies in extreme HDL-C subjects add functional human support (PMIDs 41486059, 31251897).

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in CCDC3 associated with height or stature. The strongest biological data are non-human/functional: Favine/CCDC3 knockout mice show a lean phenotype with reduced adipose and liver mass and impaired adipogenesis (PMID 25605713), and livestock/poultry GWAS implicate CCDC3 in body weight change and reproductive/developmental traits (PMIDs 30669351, 39765701) — these are animal studies and therefore support at most a "Hypothesized" growth/body-size link, not human evidence. Human reports involve kidney interstitium expression, ovarian cancer, Th1/17 cells, an Alu-mediated multigene deletion with an ocular phenotype, and a myopia-progression GWAS locus (PMIDs 33568476, 37601453, 31750818, 26740941, 42094695) — none address height, and the deletion spans multiple genes so it cannot isolate CCDC3. Consequently the relationship is largely unsupported, with a modest possibility of a hypothesized body-size/growth-related mechanism.

Direct human genetic evidence for height comes from the Japanese GWAS of 191,787 individuals, where gene-based analysis identified CYP26B1 as harboring multiple height-increasing rare/low-frequency nonsynonymous variants (PMID 31562340). Supporting human evidence comes from multiple independent families/probands with biallelic CYP26B1 missense or splice-altering variants causing a skeletal dysplasia with gracile long bones, angulated femurs, synostoses and disturbed longitudinal bone growth (PMIDs 27410456, 34160123, 37755482, 40999913, 30003121), plus a monoallelic truncating variant family (PMID 37100236) — these are single-gene, non-CNV findings in people affecting skeletal growth. Mechanistically, CYP26B1 degrades retinoic acid, and excess retinoic acid causes premature epiphyseal fusion and impaired longitudinal growth (PMIDs 35149382, 27589347), consistent with a causal effect on stature. The main uncertainty is that the skeletal dysplasia reports emphasize craniosynostosis/synostoses rather than explicitly quantifying height, leaving the definitive height replication resting largely on one large cohort study, hence substantial weight also on "Existing".

Multiple independent human studies report pathogenic SERPINC1 variants in distinct probands and families with antithrombin deficiency and venous thromboembolism: PMID 40097149 (family with p.Trp221Arg), PMID 22234719 (promoter mutation g.2143C>G segregating with type I deficiency), PMID 22535529 (three Chinese families with novel missense, nonsense, and frameshift mutations), PMID 16705712 (22 novel mutations in 22 French/German families with young-onset thrombosis), PMID 39534306 (novel p.Arg14Gly in two related VTE/CTEPH patients), and PMID 35486842 (two variants in four unrelated thrombophilic patients with recurrent thrombosis). A case-control study of 1,304 Chinese VTE patients identified a SERPINC1 hotspot significantly increasing VTE risk (PMID 29137435), and pediatric registry data link SERPINC1 genotype to thrombotic phenotype (PMID 36764659). Evidence is human, replicated across ancestries and independent families, with functional corroboration. This clearly satisfies the Established category.

All retrieved articles concern COL8A2 in corneal endothelial dystrophies (early-onset FECD, PPCD) and central corneal thickness, not body height. The only paper mentioning height (PMID 39928313) examines anthropometric measures (height, weight, BMI) as epidemiological risk factors for Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy, with no genotyping of COL8A2 variants, so it provides no gene–height association. Other work reports COL8A2 missense mutations (e.g., p.Gln455Lys, p.Leu450Trp) in corneal disease and modest effects on corneal thickness — a corneal measurement unrelated to stature. No human genetic study links COL8A2 variation to body height, and there is no compelling biological pathway argument presented here, though collagen biology could conceptually touch on skeletal growth, warranting a small hypothesized allocation.

Multiple independent human studies report COL1A1 (and COL1A2) pathogenic variants causing osteogenesis imperfecta with short stature/reduced height as a measured outcome. PMID 25944380 (164 Swedish OI families) directly related height to COL1A1 mutation type, showing qualitative-mutation OI type I individuals were significantly shorter; PMID 30270360 constructed longitudinal growth curves for OI types III/IV caused by structural type I collagen variants; PMID 35657380 analyzed pubertal growth specifically in COL1A1/COL1A2-mutated OI patients. Single-family/proband reports (PMID 9007315 in-frame COL1A1 deletion with reduced height; PMID 2220807 Gly904Cys with short stature in the mosaic mother) provide additional independent human genotype–height evidence. Some listed papers are only incidental co-mentions or multigene deletions and do not add evidence, but the direct cohort and family data are sufficient for an Established call.

Multiple independent human reports describe biallelic point/splice variants in HERC1 (MDFPMR syndrome) with somatic overgrowth and tall stature as a core feature: the Colombian sibship with biallelic HERC1 variants and overgrowth (PMID 26138117), a homozygous missense variant in two sisters with somatic overgrowth and macrocephaly (PMID 32921582), and an additional patient with a novel homozygous variant showing tall stature (PMID 28323226). These are single-gene sequence variants, not multigene CNVs, and come from independent families, supporting an established gene–growth/height relationship. Additional reports (PMIDs 26153217, 27108999) describe overgrowth-related features (megalencephaly, macrocephaly), and mechanistic work linking HERC1 to TSC2/mTORC1 and bone remodeling provides biological plausibility for stature effects (PMIDs 16464865, 36635269). Residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because the phenotype documented is syndromic overgrowth/tall stature rather than height as a quantitative trait in population cohorts.

Multiple independent human studies report LMNA variants segregating in probands and families with dilated cardiomyopathy, conduction disease, and progressive heart failure: PMID 11561226 (two families with novel lamin A/C mutations and DCM/conduction disease), PMID 12015247 (two families with novel missense mutations and heart failure from ventricular dilatation), PMID 15720451 (familial DCM with novel LMNA mutation), PMID 16314145 (family with severe DCM and quadriceps myopathy), and PMID 25988045 (Arg190Pro carrier with progressive heart failure). Larger cohort and population-based human data reinforce this: a meta-analysis of 299 mutation carriers reporting heart failure in 64% after age 50 (PMID 15551023), population-level LMNA variant risk for adult-onset cardiac disease (PMID 35772917), LMNA mutations and right heart failure in LVAD recipients (PMID 36871612), and a large adult-onset laminopathy cohort deriving a severe heart-failure prediction model (PMID 41790128). Romanian DCM cohort sequencing also identified LMNA among the top three genes explaining disease (PMID 38473809). The evidence is replicated across independent human probands and families, so Established is strongly favored; a small residual probability is left for Existing given that heart failure is often framed as a consequence of LMNA cardiomyopathy rather than the primary phenotype.

No human study in this set reports SMOX variants associated with height or stature. The strongest relevant finding is a porcine GWAS in Diannan small-ear pigs where a suggestive SNP mapped to SMOX for back height and related body-size traits (PMID 37174608) — an animal genetic result, which supports at most a "Hypothesized" relationship. Additional supportive biology comes from mouse muscle work showing Smox/polyamine metabolism modulates muscle growth and fibrosis in LAMA2-CMD (PMID 29566247), and from growth/development-relevant Drosophila Smox (a distinct gene/homonym, Smad2) papers that should be discounted (PMIDs 17651718, 23293296, 25255438). The osteoarthritis meta-analysis discusses height but concerns SMO, not SMOX (PMID 30374069), and other SMOX papers are cancer, kidney, or neurodegeneration focused with no height phenotype. Hence probability mass concentrates on Hypothesized, with substantial residual weight on Novel.

Multiple independent human studies report FLNC variants segregating in probands and families with cardiomyopathies that cause heart failure: Ortiz-Genga et al. identified truncating FLNC variants in 23 families with high-risk dilated/arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (PMID 27908349); Begay et al. reported FLNC truncations in independent arrhythmogenic DCM families (PMID 30067491); a 222-patient DCM cohort found 10 unrelated FLNC truncating carriers (PMID 28436997); a large French-Canadian family with FLNC-Ile1937Asn showed full penetrance with 43% progressing to end-stage heart failure/transplant (PMID 36864778); and pediatric RCM families with segregating FLNC variants progressed to transplantation (PMIDs 30260051, 39764157). These are human clinical genetic studies with replication across independent probands/families and single-nucleotide/indel variants, not multigene CNVs. The main residual uncertainty is that the endpoint is cardiomyopathy (a direct, well-recognized cause of heart failure) rather than "heart failure" as a primary trait, which supports some weight on Existing.

Multiple independent human studies report LIPC variants influencing triglyceride-related phenotypes in their own results: PMID 9486964 (395 Finnish men, LIPC -514C>T associated with hepatic lipase activity and with triglyceride content of LDL, IDL and HDL), PMID 18641720 (440 Canadian adults, LIPC -514C>T/-250G>A interacting with APOE on plasma triglyceride levels), PMID 11427182 (EARS-II, 714 young men, LIPC/APOC3 promoter variants and triglyceride-rich lipoprotein levels), PMID 35204909 (novel LIPC exon 1 deletion in a child with hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis), and PMID 40773003 (pediatric hypertriglyceridemia NGS panel identifying clinically significant novel LIPC variants including in a familial case). Additional human genomic work supports the locus's role in lipid/TG biology (PMID 33499410 showing TG-mediated suppression at the LIPC haplotype; PMID 25961943 and PMID 42365607 identifying LIPC among lipid/fatty-acid loci). These are independent probands and cohorts across ancestries, satisfying replication requirements, with mechanistic plausibility since hepatic lipase hydrolyzes lipoprotein triglycerides. Some residual uncertainty exists because LIPC's strongest GWAS signal is with HDL-C rather than TG per se, so a modest weight remains on "Existing."

None of the provided articles examine human stature or growth phenotypes; the literature concerns DLC1 as a RhoGAP tumor suppressor in liver, prostate, breast, gastric cancers and leukemia, plus focal-adhesion/mechanotransduction biology in cardiomyocytes. The only human genetic-variant studies involve hepatocellular carcinoma susceptibility, nephrotic syndrome/Fabry nephropathy, type 2 diabetes gene–gene interactions, and sleep-related oxyhemoglobin saturation—none of which is a recognized precursor or mechanism of height variation. A small residual probability is assigned to Hypothesized because DLC1's roles in Rho signaling, cytoskeletal remodeling and cell proliferation/migration are broadly relevant to growth processes, but no article links this to skeletal growth or body height. There are no human cohort or family studies tying DLC1 variants to height, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded.

The provided literature contains human genetic evidence linking SH2B3 to lipid traits, but not specifically and replicably to HDL cholesterol. PMID 19913121 reports a novel SH2B3 association in >12,500 individuals, yet with LDL cholesterol, not HDL. PMID 31624844 (phosphorylation-related SNPs, which include the SH2B3 rs3184504 missense variant, influencing lipid levels) and PMID 36455308 (shared genetic architecture of rheumatoid arthritis and blood lipids) plausibly implicate SH2B3 in lipid traits, but the abstracts do not confirm an HDL-specific signal. PMID 33619380 prioritizes SH2B3 among loci uncoupling adiposity from cardiometabolic risk (insulin signalling, inflammation), which is mechanistically relevant to HDL but not direct HDL variant evidence. Because I cannot name two independent human studies whose own results demonstrate SH2B3 variants associated with HDL cholesterol, "Established" is not supportable, and the weight falls on "Existing" with a substantial residual for "Hypothesized".

No article in this list reports a direct human genetic association between ANO5 variants and serum aspartate aminotransferase levels. The strongest relevant evidence is the deCODE population sequencing/imputation study (PMID 26838040), which identifies ANO5 sequence variants associating with serum creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase — muscle-derived enzymes closely mechanistically linked to AST elevation, since AST is also released from damaged skeletal muscle. Additionally, many human cohorts describe ANO5-related muscular dystrophy with marked hyperCKaemia and rhabdomyolysis (PMIDs 21186264, 36913258, 30919934, 22402862), a state that routinely produces elevated transaminases including AST, supporting an indirect but biologically strong link. Because AST itself was not the measured phenotype in any cited human study, "Established" is not supportable; the evidence best fits "Existing" (association with a strongly linked precursor/mechanism) with substantial residual probability for "Hypothesized".

Multiple independent human studies provide primary evidence linking PLIN1 variants to triglyceride levels: frameshift mutations in unrelated families with familial partial lipodystrophy present with extreme hypertriglyceridemia (PMID 25114292, 23392103), and a mechanistic clinical study showed impaired catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins in PLIN1-related lipodystrophy patients (PMID 38899472). Large-scale multi-ancestry rare coding variant analyses of >170,000 exomes (PMID 34932938) and UK Biobank exome analyses of blood metabolite/lipid measurements (PMID 36809768) independently implicate PLIN1 in circulating lipid traits, while PLIN1 haploinsufficiency yields a favorable metabolic/lipid profile (PMID 35235652). Additionally, common PLIN locus polymorphisms were associated with triacylglycerol concentrations and postprandial triacylglycerol metabolism in white populations (PMID 15355432, 18326614). These represent replicated evidence in independent probands, families, and cohorts, all in humans, supporting an Established relationship.

Multiple independent human reports document GNAS point mutations in probands/families with short stature as part of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy/PHP1A and related phenotypes: a novel nonsense variant (c.637C>T) in a boy with short stature (PMID 25045367), a novel familial GNAS mutation in three sisters with PHP1A short stature (PMID 38664677), a de novo missense W281R in a girl of small stature with POH (PMID 14723729), four germline GNAS variants causing craniosynostosis with short stature (PMID 41307550), and an Italian POH/AHO mutation series including short stature (PMID 23796510). A cohort study of patients with maternal inactivating GNAS mutations showed impaired growth and adult height improvement with rhGH (PMID 37440712), and activating GNAS mutations underlie GH-secreting tumours causing gigantism/increased final height (PMID 33805450). These are human, mutation-level, independent findings, satisfying replication criteria. Animal data (Gnas knockout mice, PMID 9671744) merely support the mechanism.

No article in this set reports a direct, variant-level association between COL24A1 and human height in probands, families, or cohorts, so Established cannot be supported. The strongest human-relevant item (PMID 34940850) reports a shared adaptive signal at COL24A1 related to bone formation in tropical indigenous Asian populations, groups characterized in part by stature differences, which offers indirect and suggestive but non-definitive support for an "Existing" classification. The equine studies (PMID 27917442, 40302410) associate COL24A1 polymorphisms with conformational/size and osteochondrosis traits, but these are non-human and therefore contribute to "Hypothesized," as does the collagen biology and skeletal/cartilage expression evidence (PMID 30941059). Remaining articles (cancer expression, preterm birth G×E) are unrelated phenotypes and provide no height-specific evidence. Overall, biology is plausibly relevant (fibrillar collagen, endochondral ossification, bone/cartilage) but direct human height genetic evidence is absent here.

Only one article in the list directly connects DNAJC13 to aminotransferase levels: the Cameron County Hispanic Cohort study (PMID 36386790), which tested 339 variants previously reported to associate with AST/ALT in UK and Japanese cohorts and lists rs62292950 (DNAJC13) among the variants of interest in this human cohort. This constitutes credible but single-study, human evidence, with the original UK/Japanese GWAS only cited as background rather than presented here as independent results, so replication cannot be verified from the provided list. All other DNAJC13 papers concern Parkinson's disease, essential tremor, Tourette syndrome, or iron biomarkers (PMID 35710628, transferrin recycling), which are not liver injury phenotypes and do not support an AST link. The iron/transferrin finding provides at most tangential biological plausibility. Therefore "Existing" is the most probable classification, with limited weight for Established.

Multiple independent human studies report GH1 point mutations and polymorphisms in probands, families, and cohorts with short stature/growth hormone deficiency. Primary evidence includes Mullis et al.'s screening of 151 subjects from 83 IGHD families identifying frameshift, stop and splice GH1 mutations (PMID 9432120), the heterozygous R77C bioinactive GH causing short stature (PMID 9076339), the homozygous G705C/C53S mutation in a Serbian patient with short stature (PMID 15713716), three siblings homozygous for a rare GH1 haplotype (PMID 41561060), and a germline GH1 splice variant (c.291+1G>T) causing severe short stature (PMID 35029852). In addition, population-based studies associate GH1 SNPs with adult height in normal-statured cohorts (PMID 17223997) and with body height and longevity in women (PMID 15771611), plus SNP association in Polish short-stature children (PMID 41543788). This constitutes replicated, human, gene-specific (non-CNV) evidence, so Established is strongly favored.

Multiple human clinical cohort studies report MYH7 variants in independent probands/families with cardiomyopathies whose dominant clinical outcome is heart failure: the natural history of MYH7-related DCM (PMID 36007715), pediatric MYH7-related DCM with outcomes including transplant/HF (PMID 39494569), MYH7 variants in restrictive cardiomyopathy with heart transplantation endpoints (PMID 40286359), and eight-family segregation of the novel p.Arg652Lys MYH7 variant with HCM including HF admissions (PMID 35205365). Additional human evidence comes from pediatric HF/CMR-genetics cohorts (PMID 40399739), Japanese pediatric DCM cohorts showing MYH7 as the most frequent gene with limited reverse remodeling (PMID 39681577), and noncompaction genotype–phenotype reviews linking MYH7 to systolic dysfunction and MACE (PMIDs 31771441, 19467449). ClinGen curation of MYH7 as a definitive inherited cardiomyopathy gene (PMID 29300372) further supports causality in humans. Because heart failure is the clinical manifestation rather than the primary Mendelian phenotype (cardiomyopathy), some probability remains on "Existing" (well-recognized precursor/subtype); animal and base-editing work (PMID 36797478) is supportive but not required.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report FGFR3 variants segregating with, or identified in, patients with disproportionate/proportionate short stature: PMID 8589686 identified the N540K mutation by linkage and sequencing in several unrelated hypochondroplasia families; PMID 8880574 detected N540K in 21 of 29 independent HCH probands; PMID 25614871 reported FGFR3 mutation frequencies in 324 cases from the International Skeletal Dysplasia Registry; PMID 36442838 described 20 Korean patients with the N540K variant and their growth outcomes; PMID 25777271 reported a novel FGFR3 variant causing proportionate short stature; and PMID 10207844 replicated Gly380Arg/Asn540Lys findings in Spanish patients. These are single-gene point mutations in human probands and families, not multigene copy-number events, and constitute replicated causal evidence for height phenotypes. Supporting therapeutic trials (vosoritide, infigratinib) further demonstrate that modulating FGFR3 signaling changes growth velocity in humans. Animal and in vitro work (e.g., PMID 33737326, 17320202) provides mechanistic backing but is not needed for the classification.

Multiple independent human studies report ABCG8 variants in probands with markedly elevated total cholesterol: PMID 15375183 describes Canadian families homozygous for ABCG8 S107X with sitosterolemia and elevated sterols/LDL-C; PMID 29886606 identifies two novel ABCG8 variants (p.R263Q, c.1528_1530delATC) in a child with TC of 14.45 mmol/L; PMID 33204594 reports two novel ABCG8 variants in a child with TC 9.4 mmol/L; PMID 39860331 reports four Vietnamese children with ABCG8 variants and elevated TC/LDL-C; PMID 36444439 documents compound heterozygous ABCG8 variants with TC 11.8–20.9 mmol/L. Additional population-level human evidence comes from candidate-SNP/cohort studies (PMID 19012522 ABCG8 251A>G in polygenic hypercholesterolemia, PMID 32088153 ABCG5/G8 variants modulating LDL-C in FH, PMID 34680591 ABCG8 rs4245791 with sterol absorption markers), and PMID 15210841 shows a founder ABCG8 mutation altering sterol metabolism in a population cohort. These are independent probands, families, and cohorts in humans with single-gene resolution, satisfying replication for an Established call.

Multiple primary human studies report germline PTEN/MMAC1 point mutations in independent families/probands with breast cancer in the context of Cowden syndrome: PMID 9399897 detected germline PTEN mutations in all five families with breast cancer plus Cowden disease and in a breast/thyroid tumor family; PMID 9345101 reported three novel MMAC1 mutations in Cowden syndrome families with breast cancer; PMID 9288766 identified a germline 4-bp deletion in a breast cancer patient with Cowden disease plus a somatic mutation in a sporadic breast cancer. Additional sequence-level somatic mutations in breast carcinoma cell lines/tumors are reported (PMID 9090379), and PTEN is a recognized breast cancer predisposition gene in hereditary breast cancer reviews and clinical panels (PMIDs 36468211, 23586058, 17920899). Some studies show PTEN mutations are rare in non-Cowden familial/early-onset breast cancer (PMIDs 9490290, 14518258), which limits penetrance in unselected cohorts but does not negate the syndromic causal link. Evidence is human, replicated across independent families, and involves point mutations rather than multigene deletions, supporting "Established."

Multiple independent human genetic studies directly report that the TM6SF2 rs58542926 (E167K) variant lowers circulating triglycerides. Kozlitina et al. (24531328) found the variant associated with lower triglycerides in three independent populations (n > 80,000). Dongiovanni et al. (25251399) reported lower serum lipids in E167K carriers in a liver biopsy cohort and in the independent Swedish Obese Subjects cohort. O'Hare et al. (28027591) replicated improved fasting lipid profiles and reduced postprandial triglycerides in two separate cohorts (bariatric and Amish), and Roberts et al. (28539357) confirmed reduced VLDL/LDL triglyceride content in METSIM with replication in FINRISK. A meta-analysis (36353245) and nutrigenetic interaction study on serum TG (36904112) further consolidate replication across adults and children.

Multiple independent human reports demonstrate that biallelic TBX15 variants cause Cousin syndrome, in which short stature is a core feature: PMID 19068278 (two unrelated homozygous probands with truncating mutations), PMID 24039145 (a novel homozygous nonsense variant p.Arg281* in an unrelated adult with short stature), PMID 42324217 (three novel individuals from two unrelated families with novel homozygous variants), and PMID 40693652 (a further proband with a biallelic missense variant, milder phenotype). These are single-gene point/truncating variants, not multigene copy-number changes, and come from independent probands and families, satisfying replication. Supporting biology includes Tbx15-null mice showing shorter body and limb length (PMID 34938962) and placental methylation correlating with newborn stature (PMID 20962579). Other listed papers (waist–hip ratio GWAS, ear morphology, congenital heart malformation) concern different phenotypes and do not detract from the stature evidence.

Biallelic ABCA1 mutations cause Tangier disease, whose lipid phenotype in humans includes markedly reduced LDL-C in addition to near-absent HDL-C, documented across independent probands and case series (PMID 33994407, 14645354, 37138899, 36876364). Common ABCA1 variants have also been tested against LDL-C in human cohorts: rs4149313/I883M carriers showed higher LDL-C in a hyperlipidemic cohort (PMID 28891316), a meta-analysis assessed ABCA1 polymorphisms against plasma lipid levels including LDL-C (PMID 30558007), rs2230806 was examined for baseline lipids and LDL-C lowering in the elderly (PMID 24854628), and large-effect ABCA1 sequence variants were discovered in a whole-genome sequencing study of LDL/non-HDL/HDL fractions in >119,000 Icelanders (PMID 27135400). These are human genetic studies in independent probands and cohorts, supporting an Established rating, although several report effects primarily on HDL-C with LDL-C effects secondary or subgroup-restricted, which leaves some probability on Existing. Animal/in vitro mechanistic work (hepatocyte-specific Abca1 knockout mice with altered LDL metabolism, PMID 22001232) supports biological plausibility but does not itself substitute for human variant evidence.

Multiple independent human reports describe biallelic point variants in PRKG2 (not multigene CNVs) causing acromesomelic dysplasia with disproportionate short stature: the original description of biallelic PRKG2 variants (PMID 33106379), two brothers with a novel splice variant (PMID 36504352), two additional patients including the first missense variant with functional validation (PMID 37789084), further families with variable skeletal phenotypes (PMID 34782440), an exome-identified novel truncating mutation (PMID 38072398), and a case with compound heterozygous frameshift/missense variants (PMID 41574272). These constitute replicated evidence in independent human probands/families for PRKG2 variants determining stature. In addition, a human GWAS meta-analysis of adult stature reported a PRKG2 signal for femur length (PMID 19343178), and CNV studies in short stature note PRKG2 near a height locus, adding supportive population-level evidence. Animal data (cattle, dog, chicken dwarfism) reinforce the mechanism but are not needed for the human-based classification.

None of the provided articles reports a human genetic association between CLEC3A variants and height; the only GWAS-type study (PMID 24376456) concerns blood pressure traits and gene–alcohol interaction, not stature. However, CLEC3A is a cartilage-specific C-type lectin shown to be present in resting, proliferating, and hypertrophic growth-plate cartilage and to modulate tPA-mediated plasminogen activation in the cartilage extracellular matrix (PMID 29146595), which is biologically relevant to endochondral ossification and thus to longitudinal bone growth and adult height. This supports a "Hypothesized" relationship based on expression and functional data rather than variant-level evidence. Remaining papers (cancer prognostic signatures, chicken vaccine response QTLs, salmon immunomodulation, antimicrobial peptides) are incidental co-mentions or non-human, contributing nothing to a height link, so substantial probability remains on "Novel".

The strongest direct human genetic evidence is the whole-exome sequencing study of hypoalphalipoproteinemia (PMID 35460704), where STAB1 was among the HDL candidate genes with the highest burden of probably damaging variants (n = 9), though it did not reach genome-wide significance and STAB1 was pre-selected from a candidate list. A second human study (PMID 41259134) reports that circulating STAB1 protein levels inversely correlate with HDL cholesterol, supporting an association but at the protein/biomarker rather than variant level. The NISCH-STAB1 locus for waist-hip ratio (PMID 20935629) and the congenic rat metabolic syndrome region containing Stab1 (PMID 27031336) provide indirect, non-gene-specific or non-human support for a role in lipid/metabolic phenotypes. Because there are not two independent human studies demonstrating variant-level association with HDL-C in their own results, "Established" cannot be supported; "Existing" is the best fit, with residual probability on "Hypothesized" given STAB1's scavenger-receptor biology (oxLDL clearance, macrophage/LSEC function).

No human study in this set reports MRC2 variants associated with height or stature; human reports concern cancer prognosis, Wolff-Parkinson-White/SVT, atrial fibrillation, and thyroid cancer expression profiling. The strongest height-relevant evidence is non-human: loss-of-function MRC2 mutations cause Crooked Tail Syndrome in Belgian Blue cattle, with skeletal anomalies attributed to impaired extracellular matrix remodeling during ossification, plus a second allele affecting muscularity (PMIDs 19779552, 22497452). Supporting biology includes Endo180/MRC2's role as a collagen endocytic receptor governing collagen turnover and ECM dynamics in mice and fibroblasts (PMIDs 12835757, 32315288), which is mechanistically plausible for skeletal growth. This constitutes functional/animal-model plausibility rather than human genetic association, so Hypothesized dominates, with a small residual for Novel (co-mention only) and minimal weight for Existing/Established given the absence of any human height-associated variant.

Two independent human genetic studies report their own primary results linking PCSK5 variation to height: PMID 24253421 found a novel secondary common-variant association signal at PCSK5 for extreme tall stature in a Dutch population sample (P = 7.8 × 10⁻¹¹), and PMID 38160284 reported a transcript-aware rare predicted loss-of-function burden association for PCSK5 (ENST00000376752) with standing height in 406,921 UK Biobank participants (P = 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁶, 0.7 SD decrease). These are independent cohorts, different variant classes (common GWAS SNPs vs. rare pLOF), and consistent gene-level implication, meeting the bar for replication. Supporting biology (PCSK5 activating GDF11, Hox patterning, skeletal/caudal development, bone mineralization defects in Pcsk5-null mice; PMIDs 18519639, 29126984, 33313955) is highly consistent with a role in skeletal growth. A small residual probability is retained for "Existing" because the GWAS signal is a secondary signal at a known GIANT locus and could be interpreted as less definitive gene-level attribution.

Two distinct human genetic publications report RIF1 as their own primary finding: PMID 41073786, a whole-genome sequencing gene-based analysis of 708,956 UK Biobank and All of Us participants showing protein-truncating variants in RIF1 with a large BMI effect (2.66 kg/m², P = 3.7 × 10⁻¹⁰), and PMID 41168175 (with its preprint version PMID 39484254), a cross-ancestry rare-variant gene burden study of 839,110 individuals across six ancestries identifying RIF1 among genes conferring ~three-fold risk of severe obesity. These are gene-level rare coding variant associations in humans, not multi-gene copy number events, and they replicate across ancestries and cohort ascertainments, supporting Established. Some caution is warranted because the two reports draw on partly overlapping biobank resources (UK Biobank and All of Us) and 39484254/41168175 represent the same underlying study, which slightly limits full independence. All other listed articles concern RIF1's DNA double-strand break repair, telomere, and replication-timing biology and provide only mechanistic context, not BMI evidence.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: Two independent human genetic studies report PDE3B associations with WHRadjBMI or body fat distribution in their own results: the African Ancestry Anthropometry Genetics Consortium meta-analysis identified PDE3B as a novel WHRadjBMI locus in women (PMID 28430825), and the UK Biobank predicted loss-of-function analysis found PDE3B pLOF variants associated with improved body fat distribution (WHRadjBMI) and lower coronary disease risk (PMID 29691411). These are reinforced by a UK Biobank MRI-based fat depot study showing rare PDE3B variants modulate depot-specific, BMI-adjusted adiposity (PMID 35773277), and by phenome-wide decomposition implicating a PDE3B pLOF variant in obesity/adipocyte-related traits with functional adipocyte validation (PMID 31492854). Additional human exome/lipid studies (PMIDs 30275531, 36490288, 38267387, 42472903) support PDE3B's role in lipid and adiposity phenotypes. Non-human/mechanistic papers (e.g., PMIDs 39435735, 27108947) and homonym-irrelevant abbreviation lists do not add evidence but do not detract from the replicated human findings.

The strongest evidence here is functional and non-human: deletion of Zfp521 in mice rescues the short-limb/growth-plate phenotype of Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, placing Zfp521 downstream of PTHR1/PTHrP signaling in chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation and directly affecting long bone length (PMID 21642473). The hominin bipedalism study implicates a SOX9–ZNF521–PTH1R regulatory pathway in human ilium growth-plate and ossification biology, which is mechanistically relevant to skeletal growth but is comparative/functional genomics rather than variant–trait association in people (PMID 40866708). No article in this set reports human genetic variants in ZNF521 associated with stature; the other papers concern leukemia, medulloblastoma, PDAC, frailty/Alzheimer's, and cattle SNP annotation, and are not height-relevant human genetic evidence.
