Therefore Established cannot be supported (no two human variant-based cohorts/families), and the evidence best fits Hypothesized, with a small allowance for Existing given the strong skeletal-growth mechanism.

Multiple independent human studies report point/truncating variants in KDM3B causing Diets-Jongmans syndrome, in which short stature (a height phenotype) is a core feature. The original cohort of 14 unrelated individuals plus three affected parents (PMID 30929739) provides primary evidence, replicated by independent single-gene-resolution case reports with de novo or inherited variants: two Chinese patients (PMID 36757469), the Albanian de novo variant case (PMID 36274669), a youngest male patient with a frameshift variant (PMID 41239187), a Turkish case (PMID 41878155), a Chinese boy with a de novo missense variant and short stature (PMID 41914422), and additional case series (PMID 41898828). These are sequence-level variants in a single gene, not multigene deletions, and are reported across independent probands and populations. Supporting biological plausibility also exists (KDM3B in osteogenic differentiation, sheep growth-trait InDel associations), but the human evidence alone is replicated and definitive.

Biallelic INPPL1 variants cause opsismodysplasia, a skeletal dysplasia whose cardinal feature is severe short stature/growth impairment, and this has been demonstrated with primary variant data in multiple independent human cohorts. Original discovery papers report mutations in independent probands/families: PMID 23273567 (12 families, ~60% explained by INPPL1) and PMID 23273569 (16 cases from 10 unrelated families with 12 distinct mutations). Additional independent replication comes from PMID 23552673 (novel in-frame deletion in a Japanese family), PMID 27233067 (compound heterozygous null variants with protein absence confirmed), PMID 24953221, and PMID 34094554 (prenatal-onset cases). Functional work in patient fibroblasts (PMID 28869677) supports the mechanistic role in endochondral ossification. The evidence is replicated, human, and gene-specific (point mutations, not multigene CNVs), supporting "Established."

Two independent human case-control studies in the list report primary genetic evidence: PMID 15761121 identified the CFH Tyr402His polymorphism associated with AMD (P = 4.95 × 10⁻¹⁰) in two independent case-control populations, and PMID 15930014 independently replicated the Tyr402His association in familial cases, sporadic cases, and controls with allele, genotype and family-based tests. Further large-scale human genetic evidence comes from the diverse-ancestry IAMDGC GWAS (PMID 41159651), where CFH is a lead risk locus, and from rare-variant/haploinsufficiency findings at the CFH locus (PMIDs 40250423, 38683564). Additional human studies (meta-analyses, pharmacogenomic and risk-allele distribution studies; PMIDs 30179527, 32138827, 28260367) and mechanistic work in patient-derived iPSC-RPE (PMID 39491736) support and explain the association. The evidence base is replicated, human, and variant-level, so Established is strongly favored, with a small residual probability for Existing given that CFH acts as a common risk allele rather than a fully penetrant causal variant.

phenotype: Lymphocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: None of the provided articles report a genetic association study (GWAS or cohort analysis) linking TET2 variants to automated lymphocyte counts as a quantitative trait; the bulk of the literature concerns somatic TET2 mutations in clonal hematopoiesis and their myeloid/inflammatory and cardiovascular consequences (PMIDs 28636844, 28104796, 29471939, 35385050, 37781816). Some human data are indirectly relevant to lymphocyte biology: TET2 disruption in a CD19 CAR T cell drove massive clonal T-cell (lymphocyte) expansion in a patient's peripheral blood (PMID 29849141), TET2 mutations in MDS patients altered circulating NK-cell phenotype and function (PMID 36737440), and TET2 mutations are recurrent in AITL, a T-cell lymphoma (PMID 40510016). These support a plausible, biologically grounded influence on lymphoid cells but do not constitute replicated human evidence that TET2 variants determine measured blood lymphocyte concentration. Much of the mechanistic support (Tet2+/- mice, IL-1 signaling, macrophage studies) is murine or in vitro, which supports Hypothesized rather than Established.

No article in this set reports a human genetic association between GAS6 variants and triglyceride levels or dyslipidemia. Human genetic studies of GAS6 variants exist (rs8191974/c.834+7G>A and c.1332C>T in stroke, preeclampsia, type 2 diabetes, Behçet's disease, carotid atherosclerosis), but their phenotypes are not triglycerides; the T2DM study (PMID 26415371) touches glucose tolerance, a metabolic but distinct trait, and the carotid atherosclerosis study (PMID 20664904) explicitly found no GAS6 association. Supportive biology is present: GAS6/TAM signalling in macrophage efferocytosis, foam-cell formation, atherosclerosis and NAFLD lipid metabolism (PMIDs 41047693, 38166463, 40915106, 39255000), which places the relationship in the hypothesized range. The MR/scRNA-seq study of TG/IDL and rheumatoid arthritis (PMID 40754101) is the only paper co-mentioning triglycerides with candidate mediating genes, but it addresses RA rather than lipid levels as an outcome and does not establish GAS6 variants influencing triglycerides. Hence hypothesized is most likely, with some probability for existing given ambiguity in the MR study.

Multiple human genetic studies link FES to blood pressure: the large ICBP GWAS identified the FURIN-FES locus for systolic/diastolic blood pressure and hypertension (PMID 21909115), and rare coding variant burden analyses in 200,000 and 470,000 exome-sequenced UK Biobank participants implicated FES at exome-wide significance for hypertension risk (PMIDs 34722352, 38090255). Multi-omics/SMR work further supports methylation-mediated FES expression influencing essential hypertension risk in blood and arterial tissue (PMID 41943668), and PPI/functional genomics prioritization plus CRISPR/mouse experiments show Fes knockout raises blood pressure and alters vascular smooth muscle remodeling (PMIDs 38326862, 41644529). However, this evidence is population-level association and burden testing plus animal functional data, not causal variants segregating in independent probands or families, so "Established" cannot be claimed; no article demonstrates Mendelian causality in patients. Several other listed papers (frataxin/FXN, fat embolism syndrome "FES") are homonym or unrelated and were dismissed.

Two human genetic studies provide direct variant-level evidence in people: a large GWAS of triglyceride-to-HDL ratio in 382,129 individuals that prioritized PLA2G12A as a candidate causal gene at an insulin-resistance/lipid locus (PMID 39277575), and an exome-wide association study in 367,188 UK Biobank participants reporting a rare PLA2G12A variant associated with metabolic syndrome, of which low HDL cholesterol is a defining component (PMID 42472903). However, neither reports a replicated, primary association with HDL cholesterol itself — the GWAS explicitly notes the signal is stronger for TG/HDL than for HDL alone, and MetS is a composite phenotype — so the criteria for "Established" (two independent human cohorts implicating this gene specifically in HDL cholesterol) are not clearly met. Strong supporting biology comes from non-human work: a mouse QTL study identifying Pla2g12a as an atherosclerosis modifier (PMID 28917158), hepatic overexpression lowering serum lipids and triglyceride clearance in mice (PMID 38703030), and pig lipid/fatness eGWAS and co-expression analyses (PMIDs 29528397, 27666082, 28422154), which would only support "Hypothesized". Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability on "Hypothesized" if the human signals are judged to be for correlated composite traits rather than HDL per se.

The primary human genetic evidence comes from Nioi et al. (PMID 27192541), which identified a rare 12-bp intronic deletion within ASGR1 itself (not a multigene CNV) in Icelandic carriers, showing significantly lower non-HDL/LDL cholesterol with replication in additional cohorts. Independent human cohort evidence comes from PMID 32679274, which used ASGR1 locus variants and LDL-lowering genetic scores in the UK Biobank, and from drug-target Mendelian randomization/PheWAS analyses using ASGR1 variants as instruments for LDL-C (PMIDs 37400795, 41465952). Additional supportive human observational data link ASGR1 expression and circulating soluble ASGR1 to total/LDL cholesterol (PMIDs 32501829, 37667265), while mechanistic work in mice, pigs, and hepatocytes (PMIDs 34622799, 34762653, 34508778, 39616371) provides a coherent biological mechanism via LDLR, SREBP/INSIG1, and HMGCR. Thus, replicated human variant-level association with LDL/non-HDL cholesterol supports "Established," with a small residual probability that reviewers would count only the single discovery study as definitive.

Two independent human studies provide primary evidence linking SLC13A1 variants to height: PMID 39747595 reports an allelic series of functional SLC13A1 variants with graded effects on plasma sulfate and on human height in a population cohort, and PMID 39925707 characterizes biallelic SLC13A1 loss-of-function variants in patients presenting with short stature, scoliosis, and skeletal dysplasia. PMID 36175384 adds a further human proband with a homozygous SLC13A1 nonsense variant and spondylo-epi-metaphyseal dysplasia, a skeletal growth phenotype. Additional human rare-variant studies (PMIDs 35110524, 36943258, 37895311) tie SLC13A1 LoF to skeletal/disc phenotypes and reduced serum sulfate, and animal models (Texel sheep, Miniature Poodle, Slc13a1 knockout mice; PMIDs 22742499, 23300579) supply mechanistic support for the growth-plate/chondrodysplasia link. Given at least two independent human reports with point variants and consistent supporting evidence, Established is most likely, with residual weight to Existing since the direct height quantification comes chiefly from one large study.

Two human genetic studies provide direct variant-level evidence: PMID 39277575 reports a GWAS of triglyceride/HDL ratio in 382,129 individuals with fine-mapping and coding/eQTL annotation prioritizing PLA2G12A as a causal gene, and PMID 42472903 identifies a rare PLA2G12A variant associated with metabolic syndrome (which includes hypertriglyceridemia) in 367,188 UK Biobank exomes. These are credible human cohort findings, but they may share overlapping biobank samples, and the phenotypes are composite (TG/HDL ratio, MetS) rather than triglycerides alone, so replication for TG specifically is not fully independent. Strong supporting functional/animal data exist (PMID 38703030 shows hepatic PLA2G12A overexpression lowers serum lipids and enhances clearance of circulating triglycerides in mice; PMID 28917158 maps Pla2g12a as an atherosclerosis modifier QTL in mice), plus livestock eGWAS/lipid-metabolism links (PMIDs 29528397, 27666082, 28422154), but these are non-human and count toward Hypothesized. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing" with a substantial chance of "Established."

Human genetic evidence directly links GUCY1A1 (GUCY1A3) to blood pressure/hypertension: the large European GWAS identified the GUCY1A3-GUCY1B3 locus for systolic/diastolic blood pressure and hypertension (PMID 21909115), and this locus was replicated in a Chinese GWAS meta-analysis (PMID 25249183) and in a Han Chinese candidate-gene study of essential hypertension (PMID 31930021). Rare compound heterozygous GUCY1A3 mutations were found in two unrelated probands with moyamoya disease who both had hypertension, with functional confirmation of blunted NO signaling (PMID 26777256), supporting causality but within a syndromic context and from a single study. Additional human association data come from hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (PMID 38469120), while zebrafish/mechanistic work (PMIDs 33716783, 29754438) provides supportive biology only. Because the strongest rare-variant causal evidence comes from one report and the common-variant data are association-level for a complex trait, Existing is favored slightly over Established.

Direct human genetic evidence tying NR1H3 variation to triglycerides exists but is modest: the Leiden 85-Plus cohort reported an NR1H3 haplotype associated with higher plasma triglycerides (PMID 17452725), and the Icelandic whole-genome sequencing study identified a large-effect NR1H3 variant among loci affecting blood lipid fractions (PMID 27135400), though that signal is primarily HDL/non-HDL rather than TG. Additional human data are supportive but indirect: NR1H3 emerges as a druggable target in multivariate insulin-resistance GWAS incorporating the TG/HDL ratio (PMID 41249132), NR1H3 shows heterogeneous effects on lipid traits in a UK Biobank mGWAS (PMID 41536999), LXRA polymorphisms were studied for dyslipidaemia in haemodialysis patients (PMID 30413149), and an NR1H3 splice QTL colocalizes with an HDL GWAS signal (PMID 34995504). Strong mechanistic support comes from non-human/in vitro work showing LXRα drives SREBP-1c-dependent hepatic lipogenesis and triglyceride accumulation (PMIDs 41090776, 39875396, 40907799, 15388491), which supports Hypothesized rather than Established. Because replication specifically for the triglyceride phenotype in independent human cohorts is thin, Existing is the most probable category.

None of the provided articles report any association between GLS variants and height, stature, or growth parameters. Human genetic reports of GLS variation describe glutaminase hyperactivity or loss-of-function causing developmental delay, infantile cataract, epilepsy, and neonatal encephalopathy (PMIDs 30239721, 37151363, 31734463), and a 5'UTR repeat expansion linked to chronic kidney and liver disease (PMIDs 41501457, 39651202) — no anthropometric phenotype is measured. Remaining papers concern cancer metabolism, neuroinflammation, COPD, and viral replication, all irrelevant to height. A small share of probability is retained for "hypothesized" because severe glutamate metabolic disturbance and developmental delay syndromes can plausibly include growth impairment, but this is not stated in any abstract.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own results linking CETP variation to LDL-C levels: the Polynesian-specific missense variant rs1597000001 (p.Pro177Leu) associated with 0.133 mmol/L lower LDL-C in Māori and Pacific cohorts (PMID 37250494); protein-truncating CETP variants associated with lower LDL cholesterol and CAD risk in Japanese heterozygous FH patients (PMID 40618456); genetically predicted lower CETP associated with lower LDL-C in UK Biobank with sex/BMI effect modification (PMID 36701426); and drug-target Mendelian randomization across European and East Asian ancestries examining CETP–LDL-C effects (PMIDs 38906890, 35921096). Earlier familial CETP-deficiency probands and families showed low LDL-C/apoB (PMIDs 3937535, 25410905), and Taq1B genotype associated with LDL subclass concentrations in African-American men (PMID 31148465). These are independent human cohorts, families, and probands with variant-level data, satisfying replication requirements for an Established call.

PMID 28134622 reports its own human results: two unrelated families in the BRIDGE-BPD collection carrying a truncating TPM4 variant segregating with macrothrombocytopenia (large platelets), supported by prior GWAS in ~70,000 individuals linking TPM4 SNVs to platelet count and volume, plus dose-dependent mouse confirmation. PMID 35170221 independently describes a novel nonsense TPM4 variant causing dominant macrothrombocytopenia in a separate kindred, and PMID 34758189 reports rare missense TPM4 variants associated with platelet dysfunction and cytoskeletal defects. PMID 21153663 (CARe) provides population-level association of the TPM4 locus with platelet traits in both Caucasians and African Americans, and PMID 31249973 detects TPM4 variants in a targeted inherited platelet disorder panel. These constitute multiple independent human probands/families/cohorts with single-gene resolution, meeting the bar for Established; a small residual probability is retained for Existing since some reports emphasize platelet count rather than MPV specifically.

Multiple human genetic association studies report PKD2 variants with gout/hyperuricaemia: a Han Chinese GWAS meta-analysis identified genome-wide significant signals in/near PKD2 and eQTL-integration implicated PKD2 (PMID 30899057), an epistasis study of PKD2 × ABCG2 in gout progression (PMID 32000861), a Korean haplotype including PKD2_rs2725220 associated with hyperuricaemia and gout (PMID 32806975), and a Han/Tibetan case-control study of PKD2 polymorphisms and gout-related metabolic indices (PMID 40264938). These are common-variant association findings in humans, not demonstrations of causal, penetrant variants segregating in probands or families, and the PKD2 signal lies adjacent to ABCG2 on chromosome 4, raising linkage-disequilibrium confounding. No article shows PKD2 mutations causing gout in independent families, so Established cannot be supported. The remaining PKD2 papers concern ADPKD biology and channel function, which are irrelevant or only incidental to gout (colchicine, HNF1B tubulopathy).

No article in the list explicitly reports a human genetic variant in HGFAC associated with serum albumin concentration, so Established cannot be supported (no two independent human cohorts naming this specific association). The UK Biobank biomarker GWAS (PMID 33462484) analyzed albumin among 35 blood/urine biomarkers in 363,228 individuals and identified thousands of fine-mapped and protein-altering associations; HGFAC is a common hepatic locus in such analyses, making a single-cohort human association plausible but not verified in the abstract, which supports "Existing" at moderate weight. Strong biological plausibility exists: HGFAC is a liver-secreted (hepatokine) protease regulated by ChREBP that modulates hepatic glucose/lipid homeostasis (PMID 36413406), and hepatic HGFAC expression correlated with plasma albumin and outcome in dogs with portosystemic shunts (PMID 21641243), plus canine plasma proteomics linking HGFAC to inflammatory/hepatic protein changes (PMID 40659816) — these are non-human/expression data and thus favor "Hypothesized." Other human variant studies concern HGF levels (PMID 25998175), GI bleeding (PMID 24949630), and Crohn's disease (PMID 37878672), which are not albumin phenotypes.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own primary evidence linking PLTP variants to HDL cholesterol: the large-scale GWAS of 19,840 + 20,623 individuals identified a genome-wide significant HDL-C locus at PLTP (PMID 19060906); resequencing of PLTP in hypoalphalipoproteinemia found c.-34G>C associated with higher HDL-C (PMID 16388083) and a companion study extended rs2294213 association to hyperalphalipoproteinemia (PMID 19013296); rs4810479 was associated with HDL-C in Chinese Maonan subjects (PMID 34385888); and PLTP locus variation affected PLTP activity and HDL particle size/concentration in humans (PMID 20644014), with an additional novel low-frequency signal near PLTP in the Finnish METSIM cohort (PMID 29084231). These represent replicated, independent human cohorts of differing ancestries, satisfying the criteria for Established. Supporting mechanistic and non-genetic human/animal data (PMIDs 19948027, 27508872, 17928634) reinforce plausibility but are not needed for the classification.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report NLRP3 variants associated with circulating CRP levels: the multiethnic ITMAT-Broad-CARe candidate gene study found NLRP3 among loci reaching array-wide/meta-analysis significance for CRP (PMID 24643644), and the WHI GWAS in African American and Hispanic American women confirmed consistent NLRP3 association with CRP (PMID 22939635). Independent candidate-variant studies also report NLRP3 rs35829419 (Q705K) associated with increased CRP in men (PMID 24649046) and an NLRP3 haplotype (GTGTA) associated dose-dependently with higher plasma CRP in an Indian ischaemic stroke cohort (PMID 35862251). These are human cohort studies with genotyped single-gene variants, satisfying replication across independent populations. Additional supportive human evidence comes from CAPS/NLRP3 mutation reports where gain-of-function NLRP3 mutations produce markedly elevated CRP that normalizes with IL-1 blockade (e.g., PMIDs 18311804, 17300660, 36873639), reinforcing the causal mechanism, while a null candidate-gene study in RA (PMID 27534721) provides some counterweight.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: None of the provided articles report a genetic association between ABCA1 variants and waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI; the literature is dominated by HDL-cholesterol biology, Tangier disease, atherosclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, and cholesterol efflux mechanisms. The closest human genetic evidence is the ABCA1 rs9282541 association with metabolic syndrome (which includes a central adiposity component) and with low HDL-C in Mexican/Maya populations, plus gene–diet interaction studies on HDL-C, which relate only indirectly to body fat distribution rather than to WHRadjBMI itself. Mechanistically, ABCA1's central role in cholesterol efflux, lipoprotein metabolism, insulin secretion and adipose/metabolic homeostasis gives a plausible but indirect biological rationale, supporting a "Hypothesized" reading. No paper here demonstrates variants in people linked to WHRadjBMI, so "Established" is effectively excluded, and a substantial probability remains that the co-mention is incidental (Novel).

No article in this set reports human genetic variants in PKN2 associated with height or stature; the human genetic reports involving PKN2 concern ventricular tachyarrhythmia, PTSD re-imputation signals, synucleinopathy risk, and adaptive admixture, none of which are height phenotypes. The strongest growth-relevant link is indirect and biological: CDK10/Cyclin M phosphorylates PKN2, and bi-allelic CDK10 loss-of-function causes severe growth retardation and spine malformations in humans and growth-retarded knockout mice (PMIDs 28886341, 27104747, 28178678) — but the causal variants are in CDK10, not PKN2. Animal/in vitro data show PKN2 is essential for embryonic development, mesoderm expansion, and cell proliferation (PMIDs 28102564, 35730579), supporting a plausible role in growth without direct human variant evidence. This pattern fits "Hypothesized," with a small residual probability that an unlisted GWAS association (height loci are extremely polygenic) supports "Existing."

MEN1 germline inactivating variants cause multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, in which primary hyperparathyroidism with elevated serum calcium is the earliest and near-universal manifestation, and several listed papers report their own human genetic results with measured serum calcium. Specific evidentiary examples include a proband with a novel germline nonsense MEN1 variant (c.978C>A) plus a somatic second hit and serum calcium of 15.0 mg/dL (PMID 37410092), a pregnancy PHPT series in which 2 of 5 patients carried MEN1 mutations with albumin-corrected calcium data (PMID 31414909), an ESRD patient with a documented MEN1 splice variant and multigland hyperparathyroidism (PMID 15619041), a nonsense mutation (Arg108stop) identified in a screened neuroendocrine tumor cohort using serum calcium/PTH (PMID 9920064), and somatic MEN1 mutations in large parathyroid adenomas with significantly higher total/ionized calcium (PMID 22454399). Independent families/cohorts with hypercalcemia as the presenting MEN1 lesion (PMID 2882676) and mechanistic parathyroid secretory studies (PMID 2880443) further support replication in humans. A small residual probability is retained for "Existing" if one views calcium as an indirect consequence of the tumor phenotype rather than a directly assayed quantitative trait association.

None of the provided articles report any association between PXDN variants and height or stature. The PXDN literature centers on biallelic variants causing microphthalmia, anterior segment dysgenesis, congenital cataract and developmental glaucoma (PMIDs 21907015, 24939590, 32015378, 33985410, 37628625), plus contiguous 2p25.3 copy-number changes where obesity/intellectual disability phenotypes are attributed mainly to MYT1L/ACP1/TMEM18 (PMIDs 24129437, 25126114, 28859103) — such multigene CNVs cannot implicate PXDN specifically. Other co-mentions concern blood pressure (PMID 29455858) and erosive tooth wear (PMID 29898447), neither a recognized precursor or mechanism for height. Only weak indirect biological rationale exists (PXDN's role in collagen IV sulfilimine cross-linking and basement membrane/extracellular matrix integrity, which could theoretically touch skeletal growth), justifying a small allocation to Hypothesized; otherwise the relationship is best described as Novel.

None of the provided articles examine height or any anthropometric trait. The human genetic evidence concerns osteoarthritis risk loci (rs11583641, rs1046934) with epigenetic/expression effects on COLGALT2 in cartilage and joint tissues (PMIDs 31173883, 36538011, 37208701, 42445562), plus a rare variant in rectal prolapse (PMID 35409030); none of these are height or a recognized precursor of height. Remaining work is murine (lipodystrophy/NAFLD, hepatitis) or in vitro enzymology of collagen galactosyltransferases. A modest allowance for "Hypothesized" is warranted because COLGALT2 glycosylates collagen, a skeletal/connective-tissue matrix process broadly relevant to growth and cartilage biology, but no study here links it to stature. Therefore the evidence best supports Novel with some hypothesized biological plausibility.

None of the provided articles report a direct human genetic association between ANO5 variants and serum alanine transaminase levels, so "Established" cannot be supported (no two independent ALT-specific studies exist here). The strongest relevant human genetic evidence is the Icelandic whole-genome sequencing study reporting ANO5 sequence variants associating with serum creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase levels (PMID 26838040), which are muscle-derived serum enzyme markers closely mechanistically linked to ALT elevation of muscle origin. In addition, numerous human studies establish that biallelic ANO5 variants cause muscular dystrophy/hyperCKaemia with rhabdomyolysis (PMIDs 20096397, 21186264, 36913258, 30919934), a well-recognized cause of raised transaminases including ALT, supporting an indirect but credible "Existing"-level link. Because ALT itself was never measured or tested as an outcome in these papers, substantial probability remains for "Hypothesized" (biologically plausible via muscle enzyme leakage) and some for "Novel" (purely incidental co-mention).

No article reports human genetic variants in BCL6 associated with stature or height; the vast majority concern BCL6 as a germinal center transcription factor in B-cell lymphoma and T follicular helper biology, which is irrelevant to height. However, one study (PMID 42214481) provides direct biological relevance: in a rat/chondrocyte model of TiO2 nanoparticle toxicity affecting bone growth and short stature, HDAC9 upregulates BCL6, and BCL6–Miz-1 interaction suppresses p21 to permit growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation via IGF1/mTOR signaling. This is animal and in vitro mechanistic evidence, not human variant data, so it supports "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing" or "Established." A modest residual probability is assigned to "Novel" since this single mechanistic link is indirect and not focused on BCL6 genetic variation.

The Genome of the Netherlands imputation study (PMID 25751400) reports its own discovery of the rare missense variant rs77542162 (p.Cys1359Arg) in ABCA6 associated with LDL-C and total cholesterol across nine Dutch biobanks (~35,000 individuals), with an effect size comparable to LDLR variants. Independent human evidence comes from the UK Biobank fish-oil gene–diet interaction GWAS with ARIC replication (PMID 33760818), where ABCA6 emerged as an LDL-C locus with strong main effects, and from the RNA-modification SNP/Mendelian randomization analysis of LDL-C GWAS summary data identifying ABCA6 RNAm-SNPs (PMID 35880552). These are single-variant, human cohort findings in distinct populations, satisfying replication. The counterweight is PMID 34274505, which confirms the variant causes loss of functional protein but finds no lipoprotein phenotype in mice or hamsters, questioning causal mechanism though not the human association; other listed papers (osteoarthritis, rivaroxaban bleeding, cattle lactose, PXE, ABCA9 cloning) are not LDL-C evidence.

One human candidate-gene study directly reports an association of the ABCA1 -565 C/T polymorphism with serum CRP (and IL-6) levels (PMID 28090279), and a Korean CRP GWAS with pathway analysis implicated ABCA1 among inflammation/CVD pathway genes contributing to CRP variation (PMID 24763700), though not as a genome-wide significant single locus. Additional human data are supportive but not variant-based: ABCA1 promoter methylation correlates with inflammation in premature CAD (PMID 33557767), and ABCA1 transcript levels are inversely associated with plasma CRP in Chinese cohorts (PMID 22614118, 33263223), which are expression/epigenetic rather than genetic evidence. A selection-scan in Bolivian populations links an ABCA1 region to immune/metabolic biomarkers alongside CRP polygenic signals, but does not establish an ABCA1 variant–CRP association (PMID 36574663). Because only a single credible variant-level human study directly ties ABCA1 genotype to CRP, without independent replication, "Existing" is the best fit, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the strong mechanistic (anti-inflammatory, HDL/RCT) rationale.

Multiple human studies report primary results identifying COL4A5 variants in independent probands/families with progressive renal failure/ESRD: PMID 8940267 identified 64 COL4A5 mutations across 131 unrelated X-linked Alport patients characterized by progressive renal failure; PMID 12105244 is a meta-analysis of 267 COL4A5 mutations in males correlating genotype with age at kidney failure; PMID 40485705 reports the p.Gly624Asp cohort with defined renal natural history; PMID 26613025 describes a familial disruptive COL4A5 p.F222C with X-linked segregation and ESRD; PMID 29198386 documents a founder COL4A5 c.T665G variant in three related families with glomerulopathy. In addition, PMID 36100708 found COL4A5 to be the most frequent gene with pathogenic variants (including nine unrelated carriers of p.Gly624Asp) in the German CKD cohort. This constitutes strong, replicated human genetic evidence that COL4A5 variants cause chronic kidney disease progressing to kidney failure.

Direct human genetic evidence exists in multiple independent studies: PMID 28661490 identified two heterozygous NPPC missense mutations in the CNP ring cosegregating with autosomal dominant short stature and small hands in families, with functional confirmation of reduced cGMP synthesis. Independent GWAS evidence links the NPPC locus (rs6717918, 2q37.1) to adult height in northwestern Europeans (PMID 19570815), and this association was replicated in a separate Filipino cohort (PMID 20966902). Additionally, rare protein-altering NPPC variants contributed to increased idiopathic short stature risk in a large sequencing analysis (PMID 33850126), and translocation/overexpression cases with overgrowth (PMID 19293575) support bidirectional dosage effects. Deletion cases (23805197, 32528716) span multiple genes and are supportive but not decisive; nonetheless replication across coding variants and independent GWAS cohorts supports "Established."

Multiple independent human reports describe short stature as a recurrent feature of heterozygous loss-of-function ERF variants. PMID 38824261 profiled 26 individuals from 15 unrelated families with germline ERF variants, with stature below the 3rd centile in two-thirds of subjects; PMID 38741564 reported a family segregating a frameshift ERF variant with short stature and Noonan-like features; PMID 35852485 described six family members with a nonsense ERF variant, four of short stature; PMID 40840652 reported a Chitayat syndrome patient with a frameshift ERF variant treated with growth hormone for short stature. These are single-gene point/frameshift variants in humans across independent families, supporting an Established relationship between ERF and height (growth/stature). Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because stature is a secondary syndromic feature rather than a systematically quantified primary outcome, and the wheat TaERF8 plant-height paper (PMID 32513101) is irrelevant homonymous/non-human evidence.

Biallelic EXTL3 missense variants cause spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia / immunoskeletal dysplasia with neurodevelopmental abnormalities, whose cardinal feature is disproportionate short stature. Primary human evidence with variants identified in probands comes from multiple independent reports: PMID 28132690 (nine affected individuals from five unrelated families with c.1382C>T, c.1537C>T, c.1970A>G, c.2008T>G), PMID 28331220 (two unrelated Turkish patients with homozygous c.953C>T), and PMID 28148688 (three patients with homozygous missense mutations), plus subsequent independent case reports (PMIDs 34089299, 35114981, 38010033, 38010729, 39215781). These are single-gene point mutations, not multigene CNVs, and are replicated across ancestries, with functional support (reduced glycosyltransferase activity, abnormal heparan sulfate, zebrafish/iPSC models). Therefore the gene–height (short stature) relationship is Established; a small residual probability reflects that the phenotype is a rare Mendelian skeletal dysplasia rather than common-variant height association.

No human study in this set reports APOB variants associated with blood hemoglobin concentration; the human genetics literature here concerns lipid phenotypes (familial hypercholesterolemia, familial defective apoB-100, hypobetalipoproteinemia) with no hematologic outcome. The only direct genetic association with HGB comes from a GWAS in yak (PMID 31212963), which identified APOB among candidate genes for HCT/HGB/RBC traits — this is animal, not human evidence, so it supports at most a Hypothesized relationship. Sickle cell disease studies (PMIDs 38265339, 24113910) measure apoB protein levels and correlate lipid fractions with Hb levels, providing biological plausibility but not gene-variant evidence for hemoglobin concentration. The Great Andamanese study (PMID 11758693) merely co-reports APOB polymorphism and hemoglobin variants in the same tribal cohort without testing association. Hence the weight falls on Hypothesized, with residual probability on Novel given the largely incidental co-mentions.

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic XYLT1 point/small variants in probands with short stature phenotypes, satisfying the requirement for replicated, gene-specific evidence. PMID 23982343 identified a homozygous missense variant (p.R481W) in a consanguineous Turkish family with an autosomal recessive short stature syndrome; PMID 24581741 reported five distinct homozygous XYLT1 mutations in seven Desbuquois dysplasia type 2 individuals from six consanguineous families with short stature; PMID 27030147 described novel compound heterozygous variants in a Polish patient with severe growth retardation and GH deficiency; PMID 27881841 found novel and recurrent homozygous mutations in two additional Turkish families. PMID 30554721 further establishes GGC repeat expansion/methylation of XYLT1 in Baratela-Scott syndrome (short stature) across 10 families, and PMID 28462984 provides functional evidence (ER retention) for pathogenic mechanism. These are human, non-CNV, independent cohorts, so the gene–height relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human cohort studies report FBN1 pathogenic variants in probands with Marfan syndrome and directly analyze mitral valve outcomes as part of their own results. PMID 17701892 examined 1,013 probands with confirmed FBN1 mutations and found mutations in exons 24–32 associated with a higher probability of mitral valve abnormalities; PMID 23176764 correlated FBN1 mutation characteristics with mitral valve disease progression; PMID 41811274 performed genotype-based risk stratification for mitral valve surgery in genotyped MFS patients; and PMID 35058154 (373 pediatric FBN1-positive patients) related variant type/location to cardiovascular phenotype. Additional clinical series (PMID 21617273, 40883581) document high mitral regurgitation/prolapse prevalence in Marfan cohorts, with mechanistic support from Fbn1 mouse models (PMID 21866385). This constitutes replicated, human, variant-level evidence that FBN1 mutations cause myxomatous mitral valve disease, supporting an Established classification, with residual probability for Existing given that mitral disease is a secondary feature within the broader Marfan phenotype.

Multiple independent human studies with their own results directly link EXT1 sequence variants to stature. PMID 15446535 (172 individuals, 78 families) found EXT1 mutation carriers significantly shorter than EXT2 carriers; PMID 17589361 (48 confirmed genotypes) showed EXT1 patients were shorter with shorter limb segments; PMID 36360300 (Argentine cohort) reported a height z-score 1.03 SD lower in EXT1 versus EXT2 variant carriers; PMID 17676624 and 18373409 independently replicated shorter stature/ulna-height ratio differences in EXT1-linked families; PMID 22139142 showed genotype-dependent growth patterns. Additionally, a population GWAS in 8,842 Koreans identified EXT1 as a locus influencing normal-range height (PMID 19893584), extending the association beyond the Mendelian exostoses phenotype. These are point mutations in single genes (not multigene deletions), so the evidence is replicated and gene-specific, supporting Established.

Multiple independent human reports demonstrate POU1F1 variants in probands with severe short stature as part of combined pituitary hormone deficiency, with variants identified in their own results: a novel compound heterozygous mutation (PMID 40584810), three variants in six Vietnamese patients from five families (PMID 40141050), a homozygous frameshift causing extreme short stature of -9.3 SD (PMID 31316460), novel POU1F1 changes in an Indian CPHD cohort (PMID 27756091), a functionally characterized c.605delC mutation (PMID 31022740), homozygous mutations with severe height deficits (PMID 30460459), a de novo R271W case (PMID 9829213) and compound heterozygous Pit-1 mutations (PMID 9485179). These are independent human probands/families across different populations, satisfying replication. Additionally, a phenome-wide association analysis linked POU1F1 variants to standing height (PMID 32445923), supporting common-variant association as well. Evidence is therefore strong, replicated, and human-based.

SLC22A12 encodes URAT1, the principal renal urate reabsorption transporter, and multiple independent human studies report genetic association with gout/serum urate: GWAS of clinically defined gout (PMID 27899376), the common dysfunctional W258X variant acting as a suppressing factor for gout (PMID 16059895), large-scale analysis of common and rare dysfunctional URAT1 variants conferring substantial anti-gout effect (PMID 33821957), a meta-analysis of rs475688/rs3825016 (PMID 29352852), and case–control studies in Vietnamese and Taiwanese cohorts (PMIDs 30621105, 29215084, 41684661), plus urate GWAS in European and African American populations identifying SLC22A12 including a functional G65W allele (PMIDs 19503597, 21768215). These are human genetic data, so Hypothesized/Novel are unlikely. However, several studies are negative or non-replicating (PMIDs 22942308, 23129426, 25268603), and most positive findings concern serum urate/gout susceptibility (often protective loss-of-function) rather than Mendelian causation in probands or families, so the evidence sits between robust replicated association (Established) and strong but not definitive causal proof (Existing).

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary results linking rare protein-truncating/predicted loss-of-function variants in BSN to higher BMI and severe obesity: the exome-wide analysis of up to 587,027 adults (PMID 38575728), the UK Biobank exome-wide association with replication in All of Us and additional Columbia early-onset obesity probands (PMIDs 36865254, 37865656), and independent replication in the diverse All of Us cohort (PMID 39228706). Further support comes from HYPOMAP, where rare deleterious BSN variants associated with BMI at the population level (PMID 39910307), and from a clinical cohort of 29 BSN PTV carriers in whom obesity was present in 34% (PMIDs 39990563, 40393460). These are human cohort/proband-based genetic findings, replicated across independent datasets and ancestries, meeting the criteria for Established. Remaining probability is minimal and reflects only residual uncertainty about effect-size definitiveness.

Several human genetic studies with their own primary results implicate RGL3 variants in blood-pressure-related phenotypes: the UK Biobank exome/CNV analyses (PMID 38548989 and its preprint 37333244) report a low-frequency partial deletion of RGL3 exon 6 — a gene-specific, intragenic variant — conferring protection against hypertension (OR 0.86); the FinnGen + UK Biobank meta-analysis (PMID 36553520) identified rs167479 in RGL3 at genome-wide significance for pregnancy hypertension; and independent Russian Caucasian case-control cohorts report rs167479 RGL3 associations with arterial hypertension and preeclampsia (PMIDs 37176017, 36556383, 36219912). The multi-ancestry hypertensive disorders of pregnancy GWAS (PMID 37248299) further identifies RGL3 as a locus. These are independent human cohorts with variants localized to RGL3 itself, supporting Established, although the specific trait analyzed is hypertension/pregnancy hypertension rather than mean diastolic blood pressure per se, which leaves substantial weight on Existing. Non-relevant co-mentions (e.g., glaucoma exome study, PMID 36833422) do not contribute.

Multiple independent human studies report their own results linking ABCG8 variants to LDL-cholesterol: PMID 18581044 (Taiwanese cohort, n=1046, D19H significantly associated with total and LDL-C and threefold risk of high LDL-C), PMID 15175352 (Finnish cohort, 19H allele associated with lower total and LDL cholesterol), and PMID 15311998 (Czech cohort, Tyr54Cys and Thr400Lys associated with LDL-C changes). Independent clinical/family evidence comes from sitosterolemia probands homozygous for ABCG8 nonsense mutations (S107X; PMID 15375183), a heterozygous ABCG8 Met429Val case with markedly elevated LDL-C (PMID 38338819), pediatric compound heterozygotes (PMID 36444439), and rare/common ABCG8 variants modulating LDL-C in FH cohorts (PMID 32088153). Additional polygenic and metabolic-marker studies (PMIDs 40076958, 34680591) reinforce these associations in humans. Evidence is replicated across independent human probands and cohorts, supporting "Established."

Two independent human reports present their own primary results linking TGFB3 variants to stature phenotypes: a family with a novel heterozygous TGFB3 c.898C>G (p.Arg300Gly) mutation segregating with tall stature and marfanoid features (PMID 26184463), and a de novo latency-associated peptide domain TGFB3 mutation in a patient with overgrowth and Loeys-Dietz features (PMID 24798638); these also cite prior probands with growth retardation (Rienhoff) and overgrowth (Matyas) at the same codon, indicating bidirectional effects on stature. Additional cohort-level series (PMIDs 25835445, 39653386) describe syndromic TGFB3 aortopathy with skeletal/marfanoid features, and targeted exome sequencing of syndromic growth disorders (PMID 28425089) supports gene-panel relevance to stature. Evidence is human and involves single-gene point mutations in independent families, supporting Established, though the number of reported probands is small and stature is a secondary syndromic feature rather than a specifically studied quantitative trait, which keeps substantial weight on Existing. Cleft-related TGFB3 association studies (PMIDs 12651933, 20170386) are not relevant to height and several papers only restate the gene as background.

All retrieved articles concern GYG1 (glycogenin-1) deficiency causing polyglucosan body myopathy, glycogen storage disease type XV, limb-girdle weakness, and cardiomyopathy; none report anthropometric measures such as stature or growth. No GWAS, family, or cohort study links GYG1 variants to Height, and no biological rationale connecting glycogenin-1-mediated glycogen priming to skeletal growth or body height is presented. Mentions of GYG1 occur exclusively in muscle/cardiac metabolic disease contexts, with no incidental relevance to Height. Therefore the evidence supports a Novel classification, with a small allowance for hypothesized indirect effects via muscle metabolism.

Primary evidence in humans comes from Zhao et al. (PMID 38575728), an exome-sequencing study of up to 587,027 adults showing rare loss-of-function/protein-truncating variants in APBA1 with large effects on BMI, and an independent replication in the All of Us Research Program across diverse ancestries (PMID 39228706). Further independent support comes from cross-ancestry rare-variant gene-based BMI analyses of 839,110 individuals from two biobanks (PMIDs 41168175, 39484254), which detected APBA1 with ancestral heterogeneity, and from clinical cases of APBA1 PTVs in minors with severe early-onset obesity segregating with affected mothers (PMID 42018264). These are single-gene variant associations in independent human cohorts and probands, not multi-gene CNVs, satisfying replication requirements. Remaining papers on Mint1/X11 synaptic biology provide mechanistic plausibility (synaptic vesicle trafficking in feeding circuits) but are not needed for the classification.

Multiple independent human studies report pathogenic CYP24A1 variants in probands and families presenting with nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis: PMID 27639704 (compound heterozygous novel genotype in a proband with recurrent nephrolithiasis, plus affected heterozygous father), PMID 40765620 (five unrelated patients with biallelic CYP24A1 variants, including a man with long-standing kidney stones), PMID 41640145 (44 Russian patients, 95% with nephrocalcinosis or urolithiasis, recurrent p.Arg396Trp and p.Glu143del), PMID 32597591 (three unrelated pediatric stone-disease cases with novel CYP24A1 variants), and PMID 40917505 (adult with heterozygous pathogenic variant and nephrocalcinosis/hypercalciuria). These are supported by large human GWAS showing a CYP24A1 locus associated with kidney stone disease and serum calcium/stone episodes (PMIDs 31729369, 40372791), and by targeted sequencing cohorts of monogenic urinary stone disease (PMID 34805638, 38544324). The evidence is replicated, human, variant-level, and gene-specific, meeting the criteria for Established.

Most of the retrieved articles concern the plant receptor kinase FERONIA (FER) in Arabidopsis/tomato, a homonymous acronym unrelated to human FER, and are irrelevant (e.g., PMIDs 37012430, 40745922, 39197037, 38831656). The only mechanistically relevant item is the zebrafish study (PMID 25184253) in which Fer kinase was identified as a downstream target of mutant Shp2 in Noonan/LEOPARD syndrome models, and Fer morpholino knockdown produced craniofacial defects and short stature — this is animal-model/functional evidence connecting FER to growth and body size, supporting "Hypothesized" rather than human genetic evidence. No article reports human variants in FER associated with height; the human-relevant papers concern adiponectin levels (PMID 22449616), lung cancer survival (PMID 39707607), pneumonia severity (PMID 33532473), and obesity/lipolysis (PMID 37329887), none of which measure stature. Therefore no PMIDs can be cited as human proband/cohort evidence for FER–height, precluding Established or Existing; residual probability is assigned to Novel given the tenuous, non-human nature of the growth link.

No study in this set reports a genetic variant in GAS6 associated with total cholesterol levels in humans, so Established is untenable (no two independent cohort/family reports exist). The strongest human evidence is PMID 31226525, which shows that circulating Gla-Gas6 protein is reduced in hyperlipidemic subjects and inversely correlates with total cholesterol and triglycerides, but this is a small biomarker correlation (n=22/19) rather than variant-based, and its mechanistic work (AMPK/SREBP1/PPARα) is in mice and hepatocytes. Human variant studies of GAS6 exist (rs8191973/rs8191974 with adiposity, inflammation and insulin resistance in adolescents, PMID 24696684; c.843+7G>A with type 2 diabetes, PMID 26415371; c.834+7G>A with stroke, PMID 15108283), and these metabolic/atherogenic traits are recognized correlates or risk contexts for dyslipidemia, which gives partial support for Existing. Most other papers concern GAS6/TAM biology in cancer, efferocytosis, neurodegeneration and atherosclerosis, supporting biological plausibility (lipid handling by macrophages, foam cells) rather than genetic association. Accordingly, weight is concentrated on Hypothesized with substantial probability for Existing.

No article in this set reports SLC38A4 sequence variants associated with height or stature in humans; the human variant studies concern hyperglycaemia/neonatal glucose (PMIDs 22945694, 33939685), lung cancer (27587543), and developmental dysplasia of the hip (41912496), none of which is height. The strongest human data are expression-based: placental SLC38A4/SNAT4 levels correlate with macrosomia and are reduced in early preterm IUGR (22969887, 36613847), which supports a biological role in fetal growth/body size but not a variant–height association. Additional support is from mouse and cell models of the imprinted gene network, placental nutrient transport, and undernutrition (24297921, 19948659, 18653658, 21806804, 33444393), which are non-human and therefore only hypothesis-generating. Growth restriction is a plausible precursor phenotype for reduced stature, giving some weight to "Existing," but since the human evidence is expression rather than genetic variation, the bulk of probability belongs to "Hypothesized."

None of the provided articles examine anthropometric height or stature; the literature centers on GRK5 in heart failure, β-adrenergic receptor desensitization, stroke, venous thromboembolism, diabetes drug response, and Alzheimer-related cognition. No human genetic study reports GRK5 variants associated with height, so Established and Existing are not supportable. The only tenuous biological link is the report that Grk5/6 phosphorylate Lrp6 in Wnt/β-catenin signaling (PMID 20229235), a pathway relevant to skeletal development and growth, which provides a weak mechanistic rationale for a Hypothesized rating. Otherwise the gene–phenotype co-mention is incidental, favoring Novel.

The only direct human evidence linking DAAM2 variants to a height-related phenotype is a single case report of two Asian Indian siblings with a homozygous nonsense variant (c.196C>T) who presented with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome plus short stature and dysmorphic features (PMID 38860410); the authors themselves note this may reflect a blended phenotype from an unidentified coexisting condition. Other human DAAM2 variant reports (PMID 33232676, 42032623, 39806532, 34685534) describe nephrotic syndrome/renal and androgen-insensitivity phenotypes without documented stature effects, so they cannot serve as independent replication for height. Supporting but indirect biology comes from skeletal work: DAAM2 is a replicated bone mineral density GWAS locus with mouse knockout showing disproportionately reduced bone strength (PMID 30598549, 30980960, 33977200), which is skeletal but not stature per se and largely non-human/functional. Because only one family provides human height-relevant variant evidence, Established cannot be supported (fewer than two independent probands/families), making Existing the most likely category, with substantial weight to Hypothesized given the bone-biology rationale.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: Two independent large-scale human exome-sequencing studies provide primary evidence: PMID 35896531 identified predicted loss-of-function variants in INHBE associated with lower WHRadjBMI in 362,679 individuals with replication in AMP-T2D-GENES, and PMID 35999217 independently found protein-truncating INHBE variants associated with favorable fat distribution in a multiancestry cohort of 618,375 individuals from the UK, Sweden and Mexico. These are separate cohorts and analyses, satisfying replication with gene-level variant resolution. Additional human data (PMID 39809772) associates rare INHBE variants with adiposity-related traits, and multiple mouse/mechanistic studies (PMIDs 37523551, 38787338, 39948368) support the biology of activin E–ACVR1C signaling in adipose lipolysis and fat distribution. The evidence therefore strongly supports an Established gene–phenotype relationship.

Multiple independent human GWAS report BAK1 variants associated with platelet count in their own results: the Korean KARE GWAS with independent replication (PMID 25705162), the Hispanic/Latino Community Health Study GWAS which discovered and replicated the ZBTB9-BAK1 locus (PMID 26805783), and a Dutch cohort study that replicated the BAK1 platelet-count locus in its own data (PMID 29066854). Additional supportive human evidence comes from a BAK1 SNP associated with dengue hemorrhagic fever, characterized by low platelet count (PMID 27401010). This human genetic evidence is complemented by strong mechanistic data showing BAK sets the platelet lifespan clock in concert with BCL-XL (PMIDs 17382885, 27221652, 19387006). The combination of replicated cohort-level human association plus clear biological mechanism supports the Established category.

PMID 25751400 provides direct human genetic evidence: a rare missense ABCA6 variant (rs77542162, p.Cys1359Arg) associated with total cholesterol (βTC=0.140) and LDL-C in ~35,000 individuals across nine Dutch biobanks. PMID 33760818 reports ABCA6 as a significant LDL-C locus with strong main effects in UK Biobank with replication in ARIC, and PMID 35880552 independently identifies ABCA6 RNA-modification SNPs associated with LDL-C in GWAS summary data, supporting replication for a major component of total cholesterol. PMID 34274505 only restates the association as background; its own functional results in mice/hamsters were negative, and other papers (ABCA6 cloning, osteoarthritis, rivaroxaban bleeding, cattle lactose) are biologically suggestive or unrelated. Because the direct TC (as opposed to LDL-C) association rests principally on one study, some probability remains on Existing.

Multiple independent human studies report MYH3 variants in probands/families with syndromes that prominently include short stature/growth deficiency. PMID 35169139 describes 17 patients from 10 unrelated families with novel dominant and recessive MYH3 variants presenting with short stature and vertebral fusions; PMID 27381093 identifies MYH3 variants in two independent families with autosomal dominant spondylocarpotarsal synostosis (short stature); PMID 28205584 reports MYH3 mutations in SCT patients with mild short stature; PMID 30228365 and PMID 39704219 add further independent probands with short stature/growth delay. These are original human genetic findings, not just background citations, supporting an Established relationship for the height/short stature phenotype, though the association is via rare Mendelian skeletal syndromes rather than population height variation, which leaves some probability on "Existing."

None of the provided articles report a direct genetic association between TACR3 variants and stature or height measurements as an outcome. The strongest human genetic evidence is for pubertal timing: a large exome/X-chromosome study of 192,974 women found the TACR3 p.W275X and other missense variants associated with later age at menarche (PMID 26239645), and multiple independent human cohorts/families report loss-of-function TACR3 mutations causing normosmic congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and absent/delayed puberty (PMIDs 20194706, 20332248, 22031817, 33363893, 39256164). Pubertal timing and hypogonadism are well-recognized determinants of growth spurt timing, epiphyseal fusion and adult stature (untreated GnRH deficiency classically produces eunuchoid proportions), which supports "Existing" through a strongly linked precursor phenotype rather than direct height data. Because no cited study measures height as the trait, "Established" is not supportable; substantial probability remains for "Hypothesized" given the link is mechanistic/indirect via the HPG axis.

The strongest human genetic evidence is the large-scale whole-genome sequencing analysis showing that protein-truncating variants in IRS2 confer a substantial increase in type 2 diabetes risk (PMID 41073786), a phenotype defined by and strongly linked to elevated HbA1c, plus a candidate-gene study reporting that IRS2 Gly1057Asp associates with T2DM and higher fasting glucose in a Kurdish cohort (PMID 22994406). However, neither reports HbA1c itself as the associated trait for IRS2 variants; in the Brazilian polymorphism study, HbA1c was associated with MC3R, while IRS2 rs1865434 related to LDL and resistin (PMID 37716291). Transcriptomic work links IRS2 expression to HbA1c-defined metformin response (PMID 32780768), and other data (β-cell signaling, hepatic Irs1/Irs2 knockout mice with glycated hemoglobin changes) are mechanistic or animal-based (PMIDs 31781030, 29867232, 27514532). This pattern—credible human variant associations with an HbA1c-defining precursor phenotype but no direct, replicated HbA1c-level association—best fits "Existing," with some chance of "Established" and residual weight on purely mechanistic support.

Biallelic PLOD2 variants cause Bruck syndrome type 2, whose defining features include postnatal short stature alongside contractures and fragility fractures, and multiple independent human reports document this. Evidence from studies with their own probands includes PMID 25238597 (Chinese proband with novel compound heterozygous PLOD2 variants and short stature), PMID 31472299 (girl with compound heterozygous p.Gly266Val/p.Asn427Ser and short stature), PMID 42147077 (child with exon 18 PLOD2 variant and length Z-score −2.69), and PMID 29178448 (six patients from four families with novel PLOD2 variants and mesomelic/limb shortening phenotypes). These are independent families across different populations, satisfying replication for a monogenic short-stature (height) phenotype. Some remaining points go to "Existing" because the linkage is to a syndromic skeletal dysplasia rather than to quantitative height variation in the general population (no GWAS-type evidence here).

Multiple independent human genome-wide association studies report HECTD4 (C12orf51) variants associated with alcohol consumption: PMID 35713687 identified rs77768175, rs2074356 and rs11066280 as significantly associated with alcohol consumption in two large Korean cohorts (KoGES-HEXA, n=50,028; Ansan/Ansung, n=7,980); PMID 35205218 independently replicated rs2074356 and rs11066280 associations with alcohol consumption in ~8,840 KoGES subjects; PMID 21270382 reported GWAS loci for alcohol consumption in Korean men; and PMID 23364009 found 12q24 common variants associated with drinking behavior in Han Chinese. Additional Korean cohort work (PMID 26891264) treats these SNPs as established alcohol-drinking-behavior variants when testing diabetes risk. The main caveat is that HECTD4 lies in the strong 12q24 LD block containing ALDH2/ACAD10/BRAP, so the causal gene assignment is uncertain, which retains some probability on "Existing." Nonetheless, the literature repeatedly reports variant-level associations in independent human cohorts, supporting an Established classification.

Biallelic loss-of-function variants in ANTXR1 cause GAPO syndrome, in which growth retardation/short stature is a cardinal feature, and this has been demonstrated with primary variant data in multiple independent human families. Original evidence includes PMID 23602711 (nonsense and splice variants in four ethnically unrelated affected individuals), PMID 25045128 (three novel homozygous variants in five affected individuals from three Turkish kindreds), PMID 30575274 (five novel variants including an intragenic deletion in seven new patients), and additional independent probands (PMIDs 27587992, 28870703, 38423276, 38691016). A systematic review of 105 clinical cases (PMID 40962491) confirms replication of the growth-retardation phenotype across cohorts. Animal and cellular work (Antxr1-null mice with shortened limbs, Runx2-regulated chondrocyte proliferation, PMID 32244499) provides supporting mechanism but is not needed for the human-based classification.

Multiple independent human studies provide direct evidence. The Japanese GWAS of 19,633 subjects (PMID 20189936) replicated PLAG1 at genome-wide significance for adult height, previously reported in Korean cohorts. Monogenic evidence comes from independent probands and families with pathogenic PLAG1 sequence variants causing Silver-Russell syndrome with pre- and postnatal growth restriction/short stature: PMID 28796236 (first human PLAG1 mutations, HMGA2-PLAG1-IGF2 pathway), PMID 33291420 (familial frameshift variant), PMID 37673301 (PLAG1-related SRS), and PMID 41276848 (additional patients with pathogenic PLAG1 variants). Livestock studies (cattle, sheep) add strong supporting biology but are not counted for human evidence.

The deCODE study (PMID 27192541) reports its own human sequencing results showing heterozygous carriers of the rare ASGR1 del12 (a 12-bp intronic deletion within a single gene, not a multigene CNV) have substantially lower non-HDL cholesterol and reduced CAD risk in Icelandic and replication cohorts. Independently, PMID 32679274 examined common ASGR1 locus variants in UK Biobank with Mendelian randomization of LDL-cholesterol-lowering genetic scores, and PMID 41465952 used ASGR1 genetic instruments as a lipid-lowering drug target, supporting replication in separate human cohorts. Human observational data also link ASGR1 monocyte expression to serum total cholesterol and LDL-C (PMID 32501829), and serum soluble ASGR1 to LDL-C (PMID 37667265). Mechanistic mouse and cell studies (PMIDs 35922515, 34622799, 39387120) corroborate a causal effect on total cholesterol but are non-human. Some residual uncertainty remains because the primary genetic endpoint was non-HDL cholesterol/LDL-C rather than total cholesterol per se, which keeps weight on "Existing."

None of the supplied articles report platelet phenotypes, megakaryocyte biology, or genetic variants in CAVIN2/SDPR associated with mean platelet volume. The papers instead concern caveolae structural biology (PMIDs 25588833, 40260863, 41668064), lung injury and ischemia-reperfusion (35174175, 36335812), cardiac fibrosis (37872863), atherosclerosis/LDL transcytosis (39887709), glaucoma trabecular meshwork expression (38704467), depression (27721187), and adipose insulin resistance (33324235). No human genetic study here identifies CAVIN2 variants linked to mean platelet volume or a recognized precursor trait, so the Established criterion (two independent human variant-level reports) cannot be met. A modest allowance is given to Hypothesized because CAVIN2 encodes a caveolar coat protein regulating membrane invagination, curvature and vesicle dynamics—biology plausibly relevant to platelet membrane/size regulation—but this is indirect and derived largely from non-platelet cell and mouse systems.

The strongest link between DISP1 and stature comes from mouse work showing that Disp1 controls Indian hedgehog distribution in the growth plate and that hypomorphic Disp1 alleles produce shortened long bones (PMID 18395198), plus general Hedgehog-release biology (PMIDs 12372258, 15110707, 34707294) — this is animal/functional data, which supports "Hypothesized" rather than human genetic evidence. Human reports mentioning short stature come from 1q41q42 microdeletions spanning DISP1 and many neighbouring genes (PMIDs 20951845, 23542665, 30160831), and by the stated rules multigene CNVs cannot isolate DISP1; indeed several papers argue DISP1 haploinsufficiency alone is insufficient and shows incomplete penetrance. Human point mutations in DISP1 (PMIDs 19184110, 38529886, 26748417) are reported for holoprosencephaly/midline craniofacial phenotypes, not for height per se, though HPE microforms can include growth impairment, which leaves some residual probability for "Existing." No independent human studies with DISP1-specific variants tied to height/stature are present, so "Established" is essentially excluded.

One human genetic association study (PMID 35980984) in a Korean cohort reports SNP-level associations of FGF genes, including FGF2, with height (alongside FGFRL1, hypertension and osteoporosis), which qualifies as at least limited human genetic evidence, but this is a single population study without independent replication, so "Established" cannot be supported. Other human variant work on FGF2 concerns preeclampsia (PMID 27324104) or bisphosphonate response in osteoporosis (PMID 31437227), and miRNA-target SNPs affecting FGF2 relate to bone mass rather than stature directly (PMID 26723575) — relevant but not height per se. Strong mechanistic support comes from non-human/in vitro data: TIMP-regulated FGF-2 bioavailability controls growth plate closure and body stature in mice (PMID 31371388), FGF2/FGFR signaling in chondrocyte proliferation and dwarfism models (PMID 23571107, 31519471), and FGF2-aptamer therapeutics for achondroplasia short stature (PMID 38569854, 37704353). Together, the biology is clearly height-relevant, but human variant evidence is limited to essentially one report, making "Existing" the most likely category with substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized".

Direct human genetic evidence comes from Weedon et al. (PMID 18391952), a GWAS of ~30,000 individuals that identified PTCH1 as one of 20 loci robustly associated with adult height, and from Kim et al. (PMID 21959382), which found a nonsynonymous PTCH1 variant associated with adult height in an independent Korean cohort following exome sequencing. Independent replication is provided by the birth/infant length meta-analysis (PMID 25281659), where PTCH1 reached genome-wide significance for infant length and is listed among known adult-height loci in an independent set of cohorts. Additional supportive but weaker human data include 9q22.3 microduplication and deletion cases with short stature (PMIDs 21567912, 15347344) and whole-gene PTCH1 deletion in syndromic tall stature (PMID 40577202), though CNVs spanning neighbouring genes cannot isolate PTCH1. Cross-species support (bovine stature selection signals, PMID 25931611) and pathway reviews (PMID 23428607) reinforce the biological plausibility via Hedgehog signalling. Most remaining papers concern Gorlin syndrome/basal cell carcinoma and are not height-focused.

Multiple independent human studies report genome-wide significant and replicated associations of F11 variants (rs2036914, rs2289252) with venous thromboembolism: the GWAS meta-analysis of 65,734 individuals (PMID 25772935), an earlier GWAS (PMID 21980494), and a large exome array meta-analysis confirming F11 (PMID 30659681). Independent case–control cohorts in different populations replicate the effect, including Czech cohorts of >2,600 cases with ORs ~1.4–1.8 (PMIDs 40094632, 41582910), Portuguese samples (PMID 29995659), a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (PMID 28353616), and a prospective cohort showing F11 rs2289252 increases recurrent VTE risk (PMID 26423325). Mechanistic and Mendelian randomization work links F11 variants to elevated FXI levels and causal VTE risk (PMIDs 37537391, 28445521), strengthening causality. The evidence is common-variant/complex-trait rather than classic Mendelian proband/family segregation, so some probability remains on "Existing".

Multiple independent human reports document PDX1 variants causing hyperglycemia/diabetes phenotypes: a missense variant (p.Glu178Lys) segregating in a family with monogenic diabetes (PMID 33746035), a de novo frameshift PDX1 mutation in a Korean girl with MODY4 (PMID 35592899), a novel nonsense mutation in a young adult with MODY4 (PMID 26543388), a frameshift co-segregating in a Korean family (PMID 37652665), a prevalence/clinical-characterization cohort of PDX1 variant diabetes in Chinese early-onset type 2 diabetes (PMID 37279936), and a large gene-level burden analysis in 2,571 MODY patients showing significant enrichment of rare damaging PDX1 variants (PMID 40779032). Additional patient-derived missense variants causing permanent neonatal diabetes with pancreatic hypoplasia are reported (PMID 40485586). These are independent probands, families, and cohorts with single-gene resolution, meeting the bar for Established; supporting mechanistic work in mice and macaques (PMIDs 11781323, 39318126) reinforces but is not required.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report PAX4 coding variants associated with type 2 diabetes: the Japanese/Okinawan R121W variant (PMID 12604352; PMID 16423628, with beta-cell dysfunction phenotyping), the Thai case-control study of R192H (PMID 27334367), a Korean whole-exome/exome-array study reaching genome-wide significance for PAX4 Arg192His (OR 1.48, p=4.5×10⁻¹⁶; PMID 29941447), an exome-chip replication in Chinese individuals (PMID 27744525), Singaporean East Asians with young-onset T2D (PMID 30528630), Chinese early-onset diabetes (PMID 33216280), and GWAS locus replication in Mongolians (PMID 26290879). These are human, independent, and replicated across East and Southeast Asian populations, with supporting functional evidence that R192H impairs repression of insulin/glucagon promoters and beta-cell survival (PMID 27334367, 42210309). The main caveat is that the evidence is largely common/low-frequency variant association rather than segregation in probands/families (PAX4-MODY9 families are reported but rare, e.g., PMID 32801813), and some listed papers only mention PAX4 as part of MODY gene panels, which is background citation rather than evidence. Overall the weight favors Established, with substantial residual probability for Existing.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report IFT140 variants in patients with cystic/progressive kidney disease leading to renal failure. Monoallelic loss-of-function IFT140 variants were identified as a cause of ADPKD-spectrum disease in 12 multiplex families plus 26 singletons (PMID 34890546), replicated in a cohort of 368 individuals with LoF variants and cystic phenotypes (PMID 39136524), in 6 unrelated probands (PMID 37844724), and further confirmed in additional cohorts (PMIDs 38404363, 39732359, 40428294, 40972705). Biallelic IFT140 variants cause Mainzer-Saldino syndrome/cranioectodermal dysplasia with nephronophthisis and early end-stage renal disease in independent probands (PMIDs 38465144, 37628605, 32007091). This constitutes strong, replicated human evidence of causation for chronic renal failure/kidney disease progression.

Multiple human studies report biallelic PKHD1 pathogenic variants in independent probands and families with cystic kidney disease (ARPKD). PMID 15698423 reports PKHD1 mutations in 164 ARPKD patients with clinical correlation; PMID 19940839 genotyped 74 fetuses/neonates and correlated truncating PKHD1 mutations with renal cystic severity; PMID 31938409 identified novel PKHD1 variants segregating in two independent families with fetal cystic kidneys; PMID 32574212 detected 24 pathogenic PKHD1 variants in a pediatric cystic kidney cohort; PMID 39071699 and 34032358 provide further independent cohort/family evidence. These are human genetic studies with variants found in patients, satisfying replication across independent probands, and PKHD1 is the recognized major ARPKD locus (PMID 38097330). Functional/mouse data (PMID 38125876, 42305588) additionally support mechanism but are not required here.

phenotype: Eosinophils/100 leukocytes in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: PMID 35935937 provides direct human evidence: gene-based rare-variant analysis of 200,000 UK Biobank whole exomes found ALOX15 among the genes significantly associated with eosinophil count, independent of common GWAS signals. PMID 41332835 independently reports an ALOX15 signal for eosinophil levels in UK Biobank quantitative-trait analyses (interaction with IL33), again from primary results with genotyped human variants. PMID 30643255 (Iceland + UK Biobank) identifies the ALOX15 p.Thr560Met loss-of-function variant, tested alongside eosinophil-count-associated markers, conferring protection against nasal polyps/chronic rhinosinusitis—eosinophilic phenotypes mechanistically tied to blood eosinophilia. Supporting biology (15-LOX in eosinophilic airway and esophageal inflammation; PMIDs 34486255, 33218117, 32973910) reinforces plausibility. The main caveat to full confidence is that the two strongest quantitative eosinophil-count analyses both draw on the UK Biobank cohort, limiting true independent replication, so some weight remains on "Existing".

Direct human evidence for SLC30A8 variation and HbA1c is present in multiple independent cohorts. PMID 19096518 is a genome-wide association study of glycated hemoglobin in 14,618 non-diabetic women reporting SLC30A8 rs13266634 at P=9.8×10⁻⁸, with the authors noting this locus as confirmatory of prior work. PMID 27600066 reports rs13266634 genotype-dependent postpartum HbA1c changes in 1,071 women with prior GDM (interaction P=0.005), and PMID 26634513 found SLC30A8 polymorphisms associated with HbA1c/glycemic traits in 1,975 Han Chinese T2D patients; PMID 38885821 also reports association with HbA1c in a North Indian GDM cohort. Additional supporting context comes from SLC30A8's well-replicated role in fasting glucose, insulin secretion, and type 2 diabetes (PMIDs 35657990, 24296717), all recognized determinants of HbA1c. The evidence is human, variant-level, and replicated across ancestries, supporting an Established classification.

The Million Veteran Program multiancestry GWAS (PMID 35654975) used chronic ALT elevation itself as the phenotype in ~90,000 cases and identified and externally replicated MTTP, which is direct human genetic evidence for an MTTP–ALT association. Independent human evidence comes from the multi-ancestry NAFLD GWAS meta-analysis (PMID 37709864), which validated MTTP variants for imaging/diagnosis-defined NAFLD, and from candidate-gene cohort work on MTTP -493G/T in fatty liver disease (PMID 19262398, 37726765) and pediatric NAFLD (PMID 35560106). A four-generation family with a rare MTTP variant causing progressive fatty liver disease (PMID 37484212) and rare inactivating MTTP variants enriched in imaging-defined steatosis in UK Biobank (PMID 34957434) provide additional proband/family and cohort-level support, with steatosis/NAFLD being a well-recognized driver of ALT elevation. Some remaining probability is kept on "Existing" because most replications target NAFLD/steatosis rather than ALT as the primary quantitative trait, and abetalipoproteinemia reports (e.g., PMID 33994405) are clinical descriptions rather than ALT association studies.

Multiple independent human studies report IGF1R variant associations with weight-related traits in their own results. PMID 39809772 performed whole-exome rare-variant gene burden testing in up to 234,675 participants and identified IGF1R with both fetal and maternal effects on birth weight, with directionally concordant replication. PMID 10690945 reported significant linkage (LOD 3.56) of a CA repeat within IGF1R to fat-free body mass in the Québec Family Study, an independent cohort. PMID 25054682 found IGF1R SNPs associated with antenatal growth measures and postnatal height/weight in the Raine cohort with replication in Generation R, and PMID 15127203 tested an IGF1R polymorphism against weight change in the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study. Human IGF1R mutation cases with low birth weight/SGA (PMIDs 40269620, 23428682, 35627241) add supporting clinical evidence; a modest residual probability is retained for "Existing" since some weight endpoints are secondary to growth phenotypes.

Multiple independent human studies report COL11A2 variants directly associated with stature. PMID 16637051 describes Egyptian sibs homozygous for a COL11A2 premature stop codon with disproportionate short stature; PMID 37646720 reports eight affected individuals from five unrelated families with biallelic loss-of-function COL11A2 variants and mean height -2.29 SDS (four novel variants from their own cohort); PMID 40386356 reports two families with autosomal dominant familial short stature carrying COL11A2 variants and their rhGH response; PMID 18381781 identifies a novel splice mutation in a family with OSMED. These constitute replicated, single-gene-resolved human evidence in independent probands and families, supported by broader collagenopathy short-stature series (PMIDs 33570564, 35250876). A small residual probability is left for "Existing" in case one considers the short-stature phenotype primarily syndromic/skeletal-dysplasia rather than height per se.

None of the provided articles examine height or stature as a phenotype. The CCDC66 literature centers on ciliary/microtubule biology (Joubert syndrome module, ciliary tip proteins), retinal degeneration in dogs and mice, high myopia, and meiotic aneuploidy risk — none of which are recognized precursors, subtypes, or mechanisms of adult height variation. The Joubert syndrome/ciliopathy connection provides only a very weak indirect biological rationale (some ciliopathies involve skeletal features), but CCDC66 itself is not implicated in a skeletal or growth phenotype in these papers. No human genetic association study of height involving CCDC66 variants is present, so Established and Existing cannot be supported.

Multiple independent human studies report HMGCR variants directly associated with LDL cholesterol levels and LDL-lowering response: PMID 17870053 (ScrF I intron 2 polymorphism and serum lipids/simvastatin response in Chinese diabetic patients), PMID 39351366 (rs17671591 and rs3761740 with lipidemia and statin response in Uyghur and Han Chinese cohorts), PMID 18559695 (HMGCR exon 13 alternative splicing variants and plasma LDL-C response to simvastatin), and PMID 37355634 (HMGCR polymorphism and residual cholesterol risk).
