Large-scale human genetic studies further use HMGCR LDL-C-lowering alleles as instruments, confirming robust variant–LDL-C effects (PMIDs 27959767, 27701660, 35213538). These are independent cohorts across different ancestries, satisfying replication in humans. HMGCR is also the biochemical target of statins, giving full mechanistic coherence, so the evidence is unambiguous and Established.

Multiple independent human studies report association between somatic TET2 mutations (clonal hematopoiesis) and COPD: the COPDGene/multi-cohort CHIP analysis (PMID 34855941), UK Biobank clonal myelopoiesis analysis specifically linking TET2 mutations to COPD (PMID 32518416), a 2530-person cohort where TET2 mutations associated with COPD (PMID 28655780), and the LifeLines ≥80-year cohort (PMID 33877299). TET2 also appears as a COPD GWAS locus on chromosome 4q (PMIDs 26423011, 39418301, 39945347), providing germline genetic support. Mechanistic and animal work (Tet2-deleted mice with exacerbated emphysema, TET2-dependent ferroptosis/apoptosis in airway epithelium; PMIDs 37812881, 38439981) reinforces biological plausibility but is non-human/in vitro. Because the human evidence is largely association-based (somatic clonal hematopoiesis and GWAS signals in a multi-gene region) rather than demonstrating causal germline variants in probands or families, "Existing" is the best fit, with some probability that the replicated multi-cohort human data would be graded "Established."

RUNX2 point mutations cause cleidocranial dysplasia, in which short stature is a cardinal feature, and several independent human studies report their own mutation-positive probands with stature data. PMID 12196916 analyzed 24 Japanese CCD patients, found 16 distinct RUNX2 coding mutations, and explicitly demonstrated a genotype–phenotype correlation in which short stature was milder with an intact Runt domain; PMID 18316777 reported four unrelated Chinese patients with nonsense/missense mutations and significantly reduced body stature, linking impaired Runt domain to short stature. Additional independent human evidence includes PMID 30468148 (novel p.T155P mutation with severe short stature and GH response), PMID 31948427 (novel mutation with GHD/short stature), and PMID 16198163, an association study of common RUNX2 SNPs with femoral length and stature in a general cohort. Animal work (PMID 36599929, miR338/Runx2 mice rescuing dwarfism) supports mechanism but is not needed for the human case. Evidence is replicated across independent probands and populations, so Established is most appropriate.

Multiple independent human studies report causal BAG3 variants in patients with dilated/restrictive cardiomyopathy progressing to heart failure: PMID 25448463 identified nonsense BAG3 mutations in independent French-Canadian early-onset DCM probands; PMID 24623017 reported a novel 10-nt frameshift deletion segregating with disease in a large autosomal dominant DCM family; PMID 30442290 characterized a cohort of BAG3-mutation DCM patients with heart failure outcomes; PMID 40493734 described 18 European families with BAG3 variants including restrictive cardiomyopathy, heart failure and transplantation. Common-variant human genetic evidence also supports the association, including the protective coding variant (PMID 39195921), the BAG3/HSPB7 locus in >2000 systolic heart failure patients (PMID 25889438), and UK Biobank ECG/DCM locus analyses (PMID 32916098). Functional and iPSC/engineered-tissue work (PMID 40995491) provides mechanistic support but the human clinical genetic replication is what drives the Established assignment. A small residual probability is left for Existing given that heart failure is typically the downstream consequence of BAG3 cardiomyopathy rather than the primary phenotype tested.

None of the provided articles report an association between ADAMTSL4 variants and stature or height measurements; the entire literature set concerns isolated ectopia lentis, ectopia lentis et pupillae, craniosynostosis, and childhood glaucoma. Notably, several studies emphasize that ADAMTSL4-related ectopia lentis is distinguished from Marfan syndrome precisely by the absence of systemic/skeletal (including tall-stature) features (PMID: 22736615, 20564469). A weak biological rationale exists because ADAMTSL4 participates in fibrillin-1 microfibril biogenesis and TGF-β pathway regulation, mechanisms shared with Marfan/Loeys-Dietz syndromes where abnormal growth occurs (PMID: 35378950, 26405179), supporting some probability for "Hypothesized." However, no human genetic study here measures or associates height, and the mouse model (Adamtsl4tvrm267) shows ocular, not skeletal/growth, phenotypes, so "Novel" remains most likely.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own primary evidence linking rare protein-truncating/loss-of-function variants in BSN to elevated BMI and obesity: PMID 38575728 (exome sequencing of up to 587,027 adults, effect size exceeding MC4R, plus functional follow-up), PMID 36865254/37865656 (UK Biobank exome-wide association, replicated in All of Us, plus two probands including a de novo variant from a Columbia early-onset obesity cohort), and PMID 39228706 (independent replication in the diverse All of Us cohort). PMID 39910307 additionally shows rare deleterious BSN variants associate with BMI at population level in the HYPOMAP study. Independent clinical cohorts of BSN PTV carriers also report obesity in ~34% of individuals (PMIDs 40393460, 39990563), further supporting the phenotype. Other papers (endometriosis, PSP, schizophrenia, endometrial cancer) are unrelated to BMI but do not detract from this replicated evidence.

None of the supplied articles report a human genetic association between GYPA variants and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration; the papers that mention MCHC are ecotoxicology studies in fish, elderly trace-element correlations, or forensic marker panels that use "GYPA" only as a PCR typing locus, providing no phenotype link. The genuinely GYPA-focused literature concerns MNS blood group antigens, glycophorin A/B hybrids, En(a-) and S–s–U– phenotypes, and hemolytic transfusion reactions/HDFN (PMIDs 20406014, 17430076, 30910255, 36102166, 41076955, 32201961), which document human variants affecting red cell membrane sialoglycoproteins but not MCHC measurements. Because GYPA encodes a major erythrocyte membrane protein whose variants can cause hemolysis and altered red cell membrane properties, a biologically plausible mechanistic link to red cell indices exists, supporting "Hypothesized". Some weight goes to "Existing" since hemolytic phenotypes are recognized correlates of altered red cell indices, but no cited study measures MCHC in carriers, so "Established" cannot be supported by two independent human variant-based reports.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report biallelic PUS7 variants causing a syndrome that consistently includes short stature/growth retardation. Primary evidence with variants in probands includes Shaheen et al. (PMID 30778726, two families with missense and frameshift variants; short stature), de Brouwer et al. (PMID 30526862, six individuals from three families with truncating variants and short stature), a Saudi family with a novel frameshift (PMID 33100873), and a new cohort of 13 patients with 15 novel variants and growth retardation (PMID 42249560), plus additional case reports (PMIDs 42226002, 37067188, 35144859). These are independent probands and families with single-gene point/frameshift variants, satisfying replication requirements. Therefore the PUS7–height (short stature) association is Established, with only minor uncertainty because "Height" as a quantitative population trait differs from syndromic short stature.

Every provided article concerns DNAJC13/RME-8 in the context of endosomal trafficking, clathrin dynamics, autophagic lysosome reformation, and familial parkinsonism; none measure or mention mean corpuscular volume or any erythrocyte/hematological phenotype. There are no human genetic association studies of blood cell indices in this set, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The biology described (Hsc70 co-chaperone, retromer/SNX1 membrane tubulation, neuronal autophagy) has no articulated mechanistic link to erythrocyte size, so even Hypothesized is weakly supported. The co-mentions are incidental to MCV, making Novel the most appropriate classification.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own results linking TM6SF2 coding variation (E167K, rs58542926) to total cholesterol: the exome-array study in Norwegians identified TM6SF2 p.Glu167Lys as a candidate causal variant for total cholesterol and myocardial infarction (PMID 24633158), the 1000 Genomes-imputed GWAS of 62,166 samples highlighted TM6SF2 as a missense-driven lipid locus including TC (PMID 25961943), and the exome-wide association study of >300,000 individuals with replication confirmed TM6SF2 among loci associated with TC/LDL-C/TG (PMID 29083408). A meta-analysis of >100,000 individuals quantified lower TC in T-allele carriers (PMID 26331730), and an independent pediatric Indian cohort replicated TM6SF2 association with LDL and TC (PMID 40841581), plus additional pediatric cohorts (PMIDs 25893821, 26756786). Mouse overexpression/knockdown work (PMIDs 26774178) supports functional causality but is supplementary. Evidence is replicated across ancestries and ages, satisfying the Established criterion.

The low-frequency missense variant CD300LG p.Arg82Cys (rs72836561) was originally discovered and reported as associated with lower fasting HDL cholesterol and higher triglycerides in an exome-sequencing study of metabolic traits (PMID 23160641), providing primary human genetic evidence. This was independently supported by a large-scale imputation-based lipid genetics study in 62,166 samples, where the candidate damaging missense variant in CD300LG explained the locus association with lipid traits (PMID 25961943), and by gene-based rare/low-frequency variant analyses of plasma lipids (PMID 32510982). Additional human carrier studies of Arg82Cys report metabolic and postprandial lipid phenotypes consistent with the HDL association (PMIDs 35382499, 26336608), while proteomic and animal/endothelial work adds mechanistic plausibility (PMIDs 39190027, 24376728). Together these constitute replicated human variant-level evidence in independent cohorts, supporting an Established relationship, with a small residual probability that only the single discovery cohort truly provides primary evidence (Existing).

Two primary human studies provide variant-level evidence: the TOPMed whole-genome sequencing study of 3,855 deeply phenotyped participants implicated SVEP1 by gene-based (rare variant) association with platelet aggregation (PMID 34131117), and the SVEP1–PEAR1 ligand study used human genomic/proteomic data and Mendelian randomization to link SVEP1 variants causally and concordantly to platelet phenotypes (PMID 36792666). These are complemented by supporting mechanistic data (mice lacking SVEP1 show reduced platelet activation; exogenous SVEP1 activates platelets via PEAR1) and by reviews restating the association (PMIDs 37673700, 39847464), which count as citation rather than evidence. Some uncertainty remains because the MR study may partly overlap with the same GWAS resources, so full independent replication is not unequivocal, leaving meaningful weight on "Existing". Other listed papers (glaucoma, CAD, dementia, VTE exome screening) are peripheral or non-platelet phenotypes.

No article in this list reports a human genetic association between TM4SF4 variants and serum alanine transaminase levels. The strongest mechanistic support is the rat study showing TM4SF4 overexpression accelerates CCl4-induced liver damage (PMID 17069928), an animal model of hepatocellular injury in which ALT release is the standard readout, which supports a "Hypothesized" relationship; hepatocyte/bile canalicular expression in HCC (PMID 39999090) reinforces liver-specific biology. Human genetic data exist for TM4SF4 but for other phenotypes: gallstone disease (rs9843304, PMID 40939965, with liver-function tests only used as model covariates) and serum uric acid (PMID 30993211); gallstone disease is a hepatobiliary trait that could be argued as loosely related to liver enzyme elevation, giving partial weight to "Existing". Since no cited study measures ALT as a genetically associated trait in humans, "Established" is essentially excluded and the bulk of the probability falls on "Hypothesized".

Multiple independent human studies report point mutations in TRPS1 (not just multigene deletions) in probands and families with tricho-rhino-phalangeal syndrome, in which short stature/reduced linear growth is a core feature. PMID 10615131 identified six nonsense mutations in ten unrelated TRPS I patients; PMID 11112658 found 35 different mutations in 44 of 51 unrelated patients and explicitly evaluated height and brachydactyly, showing genotype–phenotype correlations with severe short stature in TRPS III; PMID 25792522 characterized 103 patients confirming prenatal and postnatal growth restriction; PMID 11950061 and PMID 20394624 report additional novel and recurrent intragenic mutations in unrelated families. Further single-family/case reports (PMIDs 36291383, 36467473, 37879495, 34897794) and a Korean cohort (PMID 42361898) with growth data replicate the association in independent populations. This constitutes replicated, human, variant-level evidence linking TRPS1 to stature.

Multiple independent human studies report PROP1 point mutations segregating with severe short stature/dwarfism in distinct families and cohorts: PMID 9920061 (large family homozygous for a 2-bp exon 2 deletion, heights -8.8 to -5.9 SDS), PMID 15531542 (Tunisian kindred, homozygous R73C, height -5.7 SDS with functional validation), PMID 10946881 (novel F88S in a Brazilian proband with short stature), PMID 15472232 (nine patients with PROP1 mutations, all presenting with growth failure at -3.7 SDS), PMID 32415500 (five adult siblings with 301-302delAG, -3.7 to -4.7 SD), and PMID 36984475 (Saudi family, homozygous p.R71C, short stature). Growth response to GH therapy in PROP1 mutation carriers further supports the causal link (PMID 15472175). Isolated PROP1 mutation causing hereditary dwarfism in an island population (PMID 16909451) adds population-level replication, and phenotypic variability (normal adult height, PMID 12153609) does not undermine the association. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence, so Established is strongly favored.
open_targets_trait: Combined pituitary hormone deficiencies, genetic forms

literature_justification: Two independent human studies provide direct variant-level evidence: the Korean KoGES GWAS/PRS study reports CPZ rs3756173 among height-associated variants in large cohorts (PMID 37049604), and an exome-sequencing study of 254 families with idiopathic short stature identifies CPZ as a candidate gene within growth-related network clusters (PMID 30809043). These are complementary (common-variant cohort association and rare-variant Mendelian candidate) and support a real link, but the exome study lists CPZ as a candidate rather than a definitively validated gene, so replication is suggestive rather than conclusive. Supporting non-human evidence comes from a chicken GWAS/selection-signature study implicating CPZ in bone traits including limb/metatarsal length (PMID 34311193), consistent with a skeletal growth role but not human genetic proof. The many cuprizone (CPZ acronym homonym) demyelination papers and cancer/pharmacogenomics co-mentions are irrelevant and were dismissed.

None of the provided articles report a human genetic association between E2F7 variants and Height; the literature is dominated by cancer biology (ESCC, lung adenocarcinoma, prostate, gallbladder, pancreatic), cell-cycle/E2F transcription factor function, polyploidization, and neuroinflammation. The only genetic-association study is a porcine GWAS/ROH analysis of reproductive traits (PMID 38136955), which is non-human and does not involve stature. Functional work showing E2F7 controls cell proliferation, endoreduplication, polyploidy, and differentiation (PMIDs 14633988, 15649366, 38811726, 30928253) provides only a very general, indirect biological rationale for a role in growth, which supports a modest weight for Hypothesized. Since no article links E2F7 to skeletal growth or body size in any organism, Novel is the most probable classification.

Two independent human cohort studies provide direct genetic evidence: PMID 22560525 is a GWAS of red blood cell traits identifying the CCND3 locus among loci implicated in erythroid differentiation and cell cycle regulation, and PMID 29133146 replicates the USP49-MED20-BSYL-CCND3 rs3218097 association with erythrocyte traits including mean corpuscular volume in an independent Japanese population. PMID 41708853 further provides fine-mapped, mechanistic human evidence that rs112233623-T in an erythroid CCND3 enhancer disrupts SMAD3 binding, reduces CCND3 expression in human erythroblasts, and increases erythrocyte size (MCV) while reducing erythrocyte number. Supporting functional work in mice (PMID 39056767) shows Ccnd3 loss alters globin gene expression, reinforcing biological plausibility but not required for the human genetic case. Numerous other listed papers concern CCND3 somatic mutations in lymphoma/leukemia and are irrelevant to MCV.

Three independent human genetic studies report their own results linking LMX1B variants to body weight/BMI: the childhood BMI GWAS meta-analysis (PMID 26604143) lists LMX1B among genome-wide significant loci in >35,000 discovery plus ~12,000 replication children; a Han Chinese candidate-gene study found rs10733682 genotype associated with overweight/obesity and gene–diet interactions on BMI and waist in girls (PMID 32357537); and a Mexican pediatric study replicated LMX1B/rs3829849 association with both BMI and obesity in Central Mexican children (PMID 31936053). These are single-SNP associations (not multigene CNVs) in ethnically distinct, independent cohorts, satisfying replication requirements. The remaining articles concern nail-patella syndrome and LMX1B nephropathy and are irrelevant to weight, contributing no additional support. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because two of the replications are modest candidate-gene studies with limited sample sizes.

Multiple human genetic studies provide direct, replicated evidence: large meta-analyses of the PPARG Pro12Ala (rs1801282) variant across tens of thousands of cases and controls show a reproducible protective effect on T2DM risk (PMID 32728045, 30207237), and a separate meta-analysis of rs3856806 shows the same (PMID 36214523). Population-based association was independently demonstrated in Canadian Oji-Cree (PMID 10843190), and PPARG has long been cited as one of the first two confirmed T2D genes replicated in multiple studies (PMID 17561964, 24296717). Beyond common variants, rare dominant-negative/frameshift PPARG mutations identified in patients and pedigrees cause lipodystrophy, severe insulin resistance, and diabetes (PMID 12118251, 34764936, 16511590), giving mechanistic causal support in humans. One meta-analysis in Tunisians failed to replicate (PMID 23249316), a minor caveat consistent with modest effect sizes, so a small share is left for "Existing".

Multiple independent human studies report point mutations in CHSY1 causing Temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome, whose core features include short stature and growth retardation: PMID 21129728 mapped the locus and found causative mutations in five consanguineous families, PMID 21129727 identified a truncating frameshift in an independent syndromic brachydactyly kindred, and PMID 24269551 reported a novel missense variant (D633N) in a Pakistani family. Additionally, PMID 29205154 provides human common-variant evidence, identifying rs9920291 at the CHSY1 height GWAS locus with allelic regulatory activity and CRISPR-demonstrated regulation of CHSY1 expression in chondrocytes, linking regulatory variation to stature. Animal and in vitro data (zebrafish chsy1, Chsy1-/- mice with chondrodysplasia, cattle GWAS) reinforce biological plausibility but are not needed to reach the human threshold. A small residual probability is retained for "Existing" because the height association is largely through a syndromic short-stature phenotype rather than direct quantitative-height replication.

Multiple independent human cohort studies report pathogenic DSP variants in probands and families with an arrhythmogenic/dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype whose outcomes explicitly include heart failure hospitalization, transplant, and death: PMID 34352074 (genotype-specific DSP cohort characterizing HF risk), PMID 39288222 (large multicenter DSP carrier cohort with HF hospitalizations), PMID 39523938 (pediatric DSP variant carriers), PMID 40666337 (diagnostic and disease staging criteria derived from DSP cardiomyopathy patients), and PMID 16467215 (a recessive DSP isoform I loss in a family causing early-onset cardiomyopathy and heart failure). Additional gene-panel and biobank studies (PMID 38473809, 36129056, 39387793) independently identify DSP among the genes explaining DCM, a direct cause of heart failure. Mechanistic and animal/in vitro work (PMID 39314404, 36818425) supports plausible biology but is not needed given the abundant human genetic evidence. The evidence is replicated across independent probands and families, supporting Established.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: Two independent human genetic studies report primary results linking ACVR1C coding variants to WHRadjBMI: the UK Biobank exome-wide association study identified four ACVR1C variants (Asn150His, Ile195Thr, Ile482Val, rs72927479) independently lowering WHRadjBMI with replication of downstream type 2 diabetes protection (PMID 30389748), and an exome-sequencing study of 362,679 individuals independently detected ACVR1C variant associations with lower WHRadjBMI (PMID 35896531). Additional human rare-variant analyses of body fat distribution and birth weight further implicate ACVR1C in adipose/fat distribution phenotypes (PMIDs 34875679, 39809772). Mouse knock-in models of the human missense variants confirm graded metabolic effects, supporting causality (PMID 38307384), and mechanistic work on activin E–ACVR1C signaling provides biological plausibility (PMIDs 37523551, 36626233). Homonym/irrelevant papers (e.g., CST3 colitis, goose IGF2BP2, Toxoplasma ALK inhibitor) were disregarded.

Human genome-wide association evidence directly links common variants near TIMD4 to LDL cholesterol in a large discovery plus replication study (PMID 19060906), and a candidate-gene study in a southern Chinese Han population reports associations of TIMD4-HAVCR1 variants and haplotypes with triglycerides, LDL-C, HDL-C, atorvastatin response, and CHD/stroke risk (PMID 29208769). Additional human work uses TIMD4 as an established lipid locus showing pleiotropic effects on glucose traits (PMID 24722249), and reviews note higher frequency of TIMD4 risk alleles in hypertriglyceridemia-prone Amerindian-derived populations (PMID 24768220). Mechanistic mouse/macrophage work (Tim4 regulating ABCA1+ adipose tissue macrophages and post-prandial HDL cholesterol, PMID 34290249) supports biological plausibility but is non-human. No study reports rare causal variants segregating in independent probands or families, so Established cannot be supported; the evidence is robust association-level, i.e., Existing.

Human evidence linking CPT1A to triglycerides comes mainly from epigenome-wide studies: the REGICOR discovery plus Framingham Offspring replication identified CPT1A CpGs related to lipid traits and additionally reported that genetic variants in CPT1A were associated with lipid profile (PMID 28173150), and a separate human study found CPT1A methylation contributing to severe hypertriglyceridemia in multifactorial chylomicronemia (PMID 39756670). Variant-level human data include the Arctic P479L polymorphism studied in Greenland Inuit cohorts, where plasma triglycerides were assessed but the strongest associations were with HDL/apoA-I (PMID 19181627), and a large Greenlandic metabolic-phenotype study of a CPT1A missense variant affecting fatty acid metabolism (PMID 28611031, 41232531). Mouse liver-specific Cpt1a knockout work supports the mechanism for VLDL/triglyceride handling but is animal-based (PMIDs 40501382, 39763810, 37797918). Because the clearest replicated human triglyceride evidence is methylation-based rather than unambiguous independent variant-level replication, points are split between Established and Existing, with modest weight on Hypothesized for the mechanistic/animal data.

Most of the cited human genetic work on LDLR concerns LDL-C and familial hypercholesterolemia rather than triglycerides; e.g., the exome study (PMID 25487149) explicitly attributes higher triglycerides to APOA5, not LDLR, and PMID 31480784 found LDLR SNPs associated with TC/LDL-C while TG signals came from PCSK9 and SLC12A3. Direct human variant–TG evidence is limited: the hemodialysis cohort reported higher TG in carriers of the LDLR rs688 CT+TT genotype (PMID 37563753), and older RFLP work (PMID 8099307) plus FH phenotype studies (PMID 8399083, PMID 20826022) link LDLR-deficient states to altered triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism, but these are single, small, or indirect reports rather than replicated independent cohorts. Strong supporting mechanistic/animal data exist (LDLR-KO monkeys with elevated plasma triglycerides, PMID 37730951; apoE-KO mouse/HepG2 work, PMID 25837921), which supports biology but does not satisfy human replication. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with meaningful probability retained for Established (FH homozygotes/heterozygotes do show TG abnormalities in human cohorts) and Hypothesized (much of the causal evidence is animal/in vitro).

Two independent human studies report biallelic PRIM1 point/splice variants in probands with a primordial dwarfism syndrome, i.e., extreme growth failure/short stature: PMID 33060134 identified biallelic PRIM1 mutations in five individuals with reduced protein, replication stress, and impaired proliferation explaining their growth failure; PMID 38773012 independently describes three additional patients with distinct homozygous PRIM1 variants (c.103+2T>G; c.638+36C>G) and syndromic dwarfism features. These are single-gene variants (not multigene CNVs) in independent probands, satisfying replication in humans. Supporting mechanistic data (replication fork defects, zebrafish prim1 mutant apoptosis, cell proliferation studies) reinforce biological plausibility but are secondary. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" in case one considers the second report as confirmatory case series of limited size.

Multiple independent human studies report FLNA variants causing macrothrombocytopenia and platelet functional defects with primary data: PMID 21960593 describes three patients with FLNA missense/degradation and abnormal platelet morphology plus megakaryocyte defects; PMID 23117662 reports four unrelated patients with dominant FLNA mutations and heterogeneous platelet function alterations; PMID 28428218 identifies a gain-of-function FLNA mutation in a patient potentiating αIIbβ3 activation; PMID 29449050 reports a novel truncating FLNA mutation with macrothrombocytopenia; PMID 26133172 documents a patient with an FLNA variant and abnormal collagen responses. Additional curation (PMID 32299270) and reviews (PMID 31471375, 22372530) consolidate this, and PMID 20844545 further refines variant-level specificity by excluding a benign polymorphism. These are independent human probands/families with variant-level evidence, satisfying replication for an Established call.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
literature_justification: The strongest primary human evidence is PMID 30778226, a large exome-array association study of waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI (up to 344,369 discovery and 132,177 validation individuals) that implicates PLXND1 coding variation in body-fat distribution, with functional follow-up in Drosophila showing increased triglycerides upon knockdown. However, this is a single primary human genetic report in the provided list; other supportive items (PMID 28792859, a zebrafish plxnd1 study of visceral fat and body fat distribution; PMID 27104953, adipocyte lipolysis at WHRadjBMI loci) either restate the GWAS finding as background or are non-human/mechanistic. The remaining articles concern unrelated PLXND1 biology (Möbius syndrome, truncus arteriosus, lymphedema, endothelial mechanosensing, cancer) and do not address WHRadjBMI. Because independent replication in a second primary human study is not documented here, Existing is the most defensible category, with meaningful probability for Established given the multi-cohort, multi-ancestry design and internal validation.

Multiple independent human cohorts report direct associations of PCSK1 variants with BMI/obesity: a large east Asian GWAS meta-analysis identified PCSK1 at genome-wide significance for BMI (PMID 22344219), multi-ethnic American cohorts (CARDIA/MESA) showed rs6232/rs6235 associations with BMI and obesity (PMID 23451278), the Rotterdam Study replicated rs6232 with BMI/obesity (PMID 25031086), and additional replication comes from Greek adults (PMID 21720444), southern Chinese (PMID 25189249), Han Chinese (PMID 22592666) and Mexican adults (PMID 37761915). Rare/monogenic PCSK1 variants (e.g., N221D) also underlie severe early-onset obesity phenotypes in children (PMIDs 37877373, 40246357), and rare deleterious PCSK1 variants associate with population-level BMI (PMID 39910307). All key evidence is human, from independent probands and cohorts, with both common-variant and monogenic support. This constitutes replicated, definitive evidence for an Established gene–phenotype relationship.

Direct human genetic evidence exists in at least two independent populations. PMID 23063622 is a gene-centric meta-analysis of 66,240 European-ancestry individuals with replication, reporting DGAT2 as a previously undescribed locus for HDL-C. PMID 34901200 independently reports that DGAT2 rs11236530 A-allele carriers had significantly lower HDL-C in a Chinese case-control sample, with gene–alcohol interactions also affecting HDL-C. PMID 25997070 adds a third human cohort where DGAT2 rs3060 was associated with lower baseline HDL-C and apoAI and with HDL-C changes on niacin, though attenuated after adjustment. Remaining uncertainty (weight to Existing) reflects that the Chinese and pharmacogenetic studies are modest in size and the HDL signal is partly secondary to triglyceride effects; other listed papers (niacin/DGAT2 mechanism, animal and fish studies, obesity/CMT variant screens) provide only biological or non-HDL support.

Multiple human case–control studies test the IRS2 Gly1057Asp (rs1805097) variant in T2D, with positive associations reported in Italians (PMID 11030756), Pima Indians (PMID 12765968), Asian Indians (PMID 16652127), Kurdish Iranians (PMID 22994406) and Punjabi Pakistanis (PMID 31404179), and a meta-analysis showing a protective heterozygote effect (PMID 37173295). However, several well-powered studies found no association (PMIDs 9604879, 12519871) and reviews conclude that only IRS1 Gly972Arg has a probable pathogenic role, so the evidence is associative, inconsistent, and modulated by obesity rather than demonstrating causation. No article reports a causal IRS2 variant segregating in independent probands or families, so Established cannot be supported. Human epigenomic/functional work (PMID 31197173) and biological plausibility from Irs2-null mice add mechanistic support but do not raise the level beyond association. Therefore "Existing" is by far the most appropriate category.

Multiple independent human studies report primary data with DNAJB11 variants in patients progressing to chronic kidney disease/ESKD: PMID 29706351 identified monoallelic DNAJB11 variants (missense and frameshift) in seven multigenerational pedigrees with atypical ADPKD, interstitial fibrosis and late-onset ESRD, with functional validation; PMID 32631624 expanded this with 13 loss-of-function variants in 20 new pedigrees (54 affected individuals, 32 reaching ESKD) plus nine probands from Genomics England; PMID 38275584 reported four additional families from a single center with consistent ADPKD/ADTKD-overlap phenotypes; PMID 34177435 described a biallelic variant in a consanguineous family with prenatal PKD. These are independent probands/families with single-gene resolution in humans, and DNAJB11 is now routinely listed among ADPKD/ADTKD genes causing monogenic CKD (PMIDs 34519781, 36531871, 38097330). The evidence therefore strongly supports an established causal gene–disease relationship for chronic kidney failure.
open_targets_trait: polycystic kidney disease 6 with or without polycystic liver disease

literature_justification: Multiple independent human cohort studies report pathogenic COL4A4 variants in probands/families with progressive kidney disease and chronic renal failure: the Portuguese cohort of 25 families with COL4A3/COL4A4 mutations in which all ARAS patients developed CRF (PMID 25307543), the ARAS genotype–phenotype/RAAS study (PMID 33772369), the ADAS cohort defining kidney failure risk (PMID 33838161), the heterozygous COL4A3/COL4A4 cohort characterizing clinical and pathological outcomes (PMID 35090027), and an age-of-onset/CKD risk analysis in heterozygous carriers (PMID 41059411). Additional family-based work identifies novel COL4A4 variants segregating with hematuria/proteinuria progressing to CKD (PMID 36159970), and cystic-phenotype ADAS cohorts link COL4A3/COL4A4 variants to CKD (PMID 38178635). These are human genetic studies in independent probands and families, with replication across populations, supporting an Established causal relationship. A small residual probability is given to Existing because many COL4A4 findings are reported jointly with COL4A3 and the CKD endpoint is a downstream consequence of Alport syndrome/TBMN.

Multiple independent human studies report TPM4 variants causing or associating with platelet phenotypes. PMID 28134622 identified truncating TPM4 variants segregating with macrothrombocytopenia in two unrelated BRIDGE-BPD families (supported by Tpm4 mouse models); PMID 35170221 independently reported a novel nonsense TPM4 variant causing dominant macrothrombocytopenia with bleeding; PMID 34758189 described rare missense TPM4 variants associated with platelet dysfunction and bleeding. Common-variant evidence also exists: PMID 21153663 found the TPM4 locus (rs8109288) associated with platelet count in both Caucasians and African Americans, and PMID 31249973 detected a TPM4 variant in a targeted panel of inherited platelet disorder patients. This constitutes replicated, human, variant-level evidence in independent probands, families, and cohorts, meeting the Established criteria.

Several human studies report their own primary results linking LIPG variants to LDL-related traits: the Japanese American family study found the LIPG *4 diplotype associated with lower apoB and LDL-C (p=0.015) (PMID 16023652); a biethnic sample found T111I associated with elevated LDL-C and total cholesterol in Hispanics (PMID 23536757); and a CAD case–control study reported rs3744841 associated with higher LDL-C in both patients and controls (PMID 33882321). Additional GWAS-scale human data implicate the LIPG locus in LDL particle size and lipoprotein subclass traits (PMIDs 19936222, 29084231), while other large GWAS list LIPG mainly as an HDL locus (PMID 18193043). The LDL-C findings are modest, partly discordant in direction, and secondary to the gene's dominant HDL phenotype, so evidence sits at the boundary between Established and Existing, with points split accordingly; purely mechanistic/animal or in vitro support (PMID 36372100) contributes only to Hypothesized.

Multiple independent human studies report SPTB variants in probands and families with hemolytic red cell membrane disorders (hereditary spherocytosis/elliptocytosis) accompanied by elevated serum total bilirubin. PMID 39995895 (64 Chinese pediatric patients) directly showed significantly higher total and indirect bilirubin in SPTB-HS versus SPTA1-HS; PMID 42379836 screened Thai neonates for three common SPTB mutations and demonstrated association with significant neonatal jaundice/hyperbilirubinemia; PMID 32436265 (166 children) compared unconjugated bilirubin across genotypes including SPTB. Additional multicenter and case series (PMID 41834204, 37872089, 38175446) independently document SPTB variants with hyperbilirubinemia in distinct cohorts. This constitutes replicated, human, variant-level evidence, though the phenotype is a Mendelian hemolytic disease rather than a population quantitative-trait association, leaving some probability on "Existing".

No article in this list reports BMP6 variants associated with human stature in probands, families, or cohorts, so Established cannot be supported (the human BMP6 variant papers here all concern iron overload/hemochromatosis, POI, or PCOS, not height). The strongest biological support is non-human or mechanistic: canonical BMP-2/BMP-6 signaling differentiates growth plates of large versus small dog breeds (a direct model of adult height differences, PMID 28681971), BMP6 downregulation accompanies impaired chondrocyte differentiation and reduced tibial length in goslings (PMID 39123807), and bmp6 suppression alters cartilage/skeletal development in fish (PMID 35257888). One human multi-trait GWAS/Genomic SEM study fine-maps BMP6 among causal genes for musculoskeletal phenotypes (ALM, BMD, grip strength) with enrichment in endochondral ossification and GH/IGF-1 signaling (PMID 42166073), which is a mechanism strongly linked to linear growth and provides partial human genetic support, justifying meaningful weight on Existing. Overall the evidence is predominantly pathway/animal-based, favoring Hypothesized.

PMID 23456168 is a primary human GWAS meta-analysis in Han Chinese that identified rs12612930 in/near ZNF638 at genome-wide significance (P = 2.02 × 10⁻¹⁰) with in silico replication in an additional 1,881 subjects, providing direct variant-level evidence in humans. PMID 28744006 independently tested known height SNPs in a Han Chinese familial short stature cohort and reported ZNF638 among the genes whose variants were associated with FSS risk, a height-related human phenotype, supporting replication in a distinct cohort and design. PMID 33040080 concerns USP7/ZNF638 in hepatic lipogenesis and is not relevant to height. The evidence is thus human genetic and at least partially replicated, though both studies are in the same ancestry group and the second largely re-tests previously identified loci, leaving some weight on "Existing".

Multiple independent human reports describe FBN2 variants segregating with stature phenotypes at both extremes: PMID 40199564 reports novel FBN2 variants in two families with short stature and brachydactyly (FBN2-related acromelic dysplasia), while PMID 33571691 documents biallelic FBN2 variants in a proband with severe congenital contractural arachnodactyly, a condition featuring tall/marfanoid stature. Additional independent probands/families with novel FBN2 variants and tall, slender (marfanoid) habitus are reported in PMIDs 42299845, 39310807, 38326314, and 42305963, and PMID 24833718 links rare FBN1/FBN2 variants to tall stature in an AIS cohort. The review PMID 35419902 synthesizes the "tall" vs "short" fibrillinopathy paradigm for FBN1/FBN2, and PMID 31316167 formalizes CCA diagnostic criteria including habitus. This constitutes replicated human variant-level evidence in independent families, supporting Established, with residual weight to Existing since stature is a component feature of syndromic disease rather than a quantitative height association per se.

phenotype: Benign and in situ intestinal neoplasms
literature_justification: Germline PTEN mutations cause PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (Cowden/Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba), in which gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps and adenomatous polyps are a well-recognized, criteria-defining feature. Primary human evidence comes from the large prospective cohort of 3042 probands in which 290 pathogenic PTEN mutations were identified with phenotype–genotype correlation (PMID 21194675) and the systematic review of clinically and molecularly confirmed PHTS patients used to derive revised diagnostic criteria including GI hamartomas (PMID 24136893), supported by GeneReviews summarizing multiple independent families (PMID 20301661) and additional mutation-positive cohorts (PMIDs 29684080, 28677221, 10923032). Somatic/expression studies in colorectal adenomas (PMIDs 25596996, 12632503, 24123284, 35173208) add tumor-tissue-level support but are not germline variant evidence. Because the strongest primary probands data are somewhat concentrated in cohort/review articles rather than multiple independent primary studies focused specifically on intestinal polyps, some probability remains on "Existing".

Only one article in this set provides direct human genetic evidence: the large-scale exome sequencing study in UK Biobank (PMID 37601970), which found rare heterozygous loss-of-function variants in PTPRG associated with increased adult BMI in women with large effect sizes. This is a single, credible, well-powered human cohort analysis, but it is not independently replicated in a second proband set, family, or cohort within the provided literature. All other PTPRG papers concern cancer (CML, myeloma, lung adenocarcinoma), Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, kidney injury, or endothelial signaling, and are irrelevant to BMI. Therefore "Existing" is the most appropriate category, with limited probability assigned to "Established" given the strength and scale of the single study.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report BDNF variants associated with BMI in their own results: two large East Asian GWAS/meta-analyses reached genome-wide significance at the BDNF locus (PMID 22344219; PMID 22344221), a Metabochip fine-mapping study confirmed and narrowed the BDNF signal in 29,151 African Americans (PMID 24094743), and a candidate-gene study found lower BMI in Met/Met carriers of Val66Met in healthy adults (PMID 16707914). A dedicated systematic review and meta-analysis of BDNF polymorphisms and BMI further consolidates the evidence (PMID 28818748), and BDNF variants also predict antipsychotic-related weight gain in patient cohorts (PMID 17987059; PMID 27483421). These are human, replicated, single-gene SNP associations across multiple ancestries, satisfying the Established criteria. Only a small residual probability is left for "Existing" given some negative intervention studies (PMID 33801339).

The strongest human data are PMID 18789673, which reports that circulating soluble CD36 correlates with serum AST/ALT/GGT in subjects with altered glucose tolerance (with an independent replication for ALT), but this is a protein biomarker rather than a genotype–AST association. Human genetic evidence exists for CD36 variants in liver-relevant phenotypes (rs1761667 with liver fibrosis in chronic hepatitis C, PMID 27660673; rs3211938 with insulin resistance/metabolic traits, PMIDs 39503770, 29546316, 21912245), which are recognized risk factors/precursors of transaminase elevation, supporting "Existing" rather than "Established." No two independent human cohorts directly test CD36 variants against AST levels, so Established cannot be justified. A large body of the remaining literature (baicalin, GW9662, obacunone, hirudin, astaxanthin, FGF21, O-GlcNAcylation, DIM studies) is rodent/in vitro NAFLD work in which CD36 modulation parallels AST changes, which supports the Hypothesized weighting.

None of the listed human articles report a direct, replicated association between GPAM variants and serum alkaline phosphatase; the human genetic evidence centres on ALT, liver fat, steatosis, cirrhosis and lipid traits (PMIDs 34216018, 33347879, 38632349, 34957434, 31938246, 36280732). The GPAM liver-injury and exome-wide ALT studies establish GPAM as a determinant of hepatic injury biomarkers, a phenotype domain closely related to (though not identical with) alkaline phosphatase, which supports "Existing" as the most likely category by extension to liver enzyme/liver injury panels. The only abstract explicitly pairing "alkaline phosphatase" with a glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase is a crab nutrition study (PMID 39679167), which is non-human and effectively a homonymous/animal co-mention and should be dismissed. Mechanistic and mouse/organoid work (PMIDs 42341117, 41046275) supports biological plausibility but not variant-level ALP association, leaving substantial weight on "Hypothesized." No article in this list demonstrates variant-level GPAM–ALP association in two independent human cohorts, so "Established" cannot be supported.

Multiple independent human studies report pathogenic BAG3 variants segregating with cardiomyopathy. Norton et al. (PMID 21353195) identified frameshift, nonsense, and missense rare variants in BAG3 across several unrelated DCM probands with familial segregation (beyond the exon 4 deletion). The large European multicentre cohort (PMID 40493734) reports 26 patients from 18 families with BAG3 variants, most with restrictive cardiomyopathy, and PMID 41378130 adds three further p.Pro209Leu patients with severe restrictive cardiomyopathy; additional case reports (PMID 25728519, 35205406) confirm familial and de novo occurrences. Animal and iPSC models (PMIDs 34117258, 30499714, 40995491) provide supportive mechanistic data but the human genetic evidence alone is replicated and definitive.

Multiple independent human studies report ABCB4 variants in probands/families with cholestatic disease specifically characterized by elevated serum gamma-glutamyl transferase. PMID 17726488 molecularly characterized 68 PFIC3 index cases with 29 distinct ABCB4 mutations in a disease defined by high GGT; PMID 21119540 studied a pediatric cohort selected for chronic intrahepatic cholestasis with elevated γ-GT and estimated ABCB4 mutation frequency with genotype–phenotype correlations; PMID 38623015 reported 11 PFIC3 children with 17 ABCB4 variants and measured elevated γ-GT levels (270±156 U/L). Additional independent human reports (PMID 10767346, 19261551, 33842647, 32626542) link specific ABCB4 variants to raised γ-GT in ICP and PFIC3 patients, providing replication across separate cohorts and populations. The evidence is human genetic, replicated, and directly tied to GGT as a biochemical phenotype, supporting an Established relationship.

The only article that directly links SPTB-related disease to the HbA1c measurement is the case report of hereditary elliptocytosis with an unexpectedly low HbA1c identified by whole-exome sequencing (PMID 38148910), a single human proband — credible but not replicated. The remaining literature establishes robustly that SPTB variants cause hereditary spherocytosis/elliptocytosis/pyropoikilocytosis with hemolysis, shortened red cell lifespan and altered hemoglobin levels (PMIDs 32436265, 38294355, 39378964, 37280519, 30198572), which is a well-recognized mechanism that spuriously lowers HbA1c; this mechanistic/precursor link supports "Existing" rather than "Established." No two independent studies report SPTB variants tested against HbA1c levels themselves, so the Established threshold is not met. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized," since much of the evidence is mechanistic (red cell membrane biology and hemolysis) rather than direct HbA1c measurement.

phenotype: Monocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: The HCHS/SOL genome-wide association study (PMID 28158719) reports its own discovery and internal replication of common and rare germline FLT3 variants (including rs76428106, a variant with large frequency differences by ancestry) associated with peripheral blood monocyte count in humans — direct, variant-level evidence for this exact automated-count trait. Supporting human evidence comes from the TWAS/PheWAS work (PMID 35354918), whose phenome-wide analysis of FLT3 expression-associated variation also flags immune traits including monocyte count, and from the Icelandic/UK Biobank study of the FLT3 loss-of-function splice variant rs76428106 (PMID 32581359), which demonstrates that this germline FLT3 variant alters FLT3/FLT3-ligand biology, a receptor pathway directly governing myeloid/monocyte-dendritic progenitor output. The mechanistic plausibility is very strong since FLT3 signaling regulates hematopoietic progenitor and dendritic/monocytic lineage development. The remaining AML-focused papers (e.g., PMIDs 30651634, 37892567, 35267471) are somatic-mutation/therapy reviews and do not add germline variant evidence for the quantitative trait; because independent replication of the specific monocyte-count association rests largely on one cohort study plus a supportive PheWAS, some probability is retained for "Existing."

Multiple independent human studies report causal HTRA1 variants in patients with stroke/cerebral small vessel disease. PMID 26063658 identified a heterozygous R166L variant segregating in an index family plus 10 additional unrelated probands with damaging variants and significant case–control enrichment; PMID 34270682 independently found 20 unrelated patients with heterozygous premature stop-codon variants, significantly enriched versus population databases with mRNA evidence of haploinsufficiency. PMID 25772074 reports a novel homozygous frameshift in a CARASIL pedigree with recurrent stroke, and PMID 39196222 shows rare and common HTRA1 variants predicting ischemic stroke in UK Biobank and BioBank Japan. Additional cohorts (36261288, 31719132, 36580209, 36047879) replicate HTRA1 variants in monogenic small-vessel stroke. This constitutes replicated, human, variant-level causal evidence.

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic CHST3 variants causing chondrodysplasia/spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia in which short stature is a core, consistently described feature. Primary evidence with variants identified in probands and families includes PMID 20830804 (24 patients, 23 families, 24 different mutations, short stature), PMID 37183573 (14 Egyptian patients, 10 homozygous variants, short stature), PMID 37876363 (nine Indian individuals, five homozygous variants, short trunk short stature), PMID 36042462 (three consanguineous Pakistani families with severe short stature), PMID 18513679 (eight mutations in six unrelated individuals with short stature), and PMID 18698629/19320654 (Omani-type SED families with short stature and functional confirmation). These are independent ethnic cohorts and families, satisfying replication. Additionally, a large GWAS (PMID 30747904) implicates the SPOCK2/CHST3 region with pleiotropy involving height, supporting common-variant relevance, though the monogenic short-stature evidence alone is decisive.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary evidence linking PCSK1 variants to body weight/BMI/obesity: a GWAS meta-analysis in ~83,000 East Asians identified a genome-wide significant BMI locus at PCSK1 (PMID 22344219); a HuGE systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed rs6232/rs6234-rs6235 associations with obesity across Caucasian cohorts (PMID 25355447); a nonsense loss-of-function PCSK1 mutation was found to segregate with dominantly inherited obesity in families (PMID 24890885); population cohort studies (Rotterdam, PMID 25031086; Mexican adults, PMID 37761915; Thai families, PMID 24964673) replicate associations with BMI/obesity. Congenital PCSK1 deficiency is also an established monogenic early-onset obesity syndrome with clinical cohorts described (PMIDs 40246357, 39192769). The evidence is replicated in independent human probands, families, and cohorts, so the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human clinical cohorts report breast cancer in patients with germline NF1 pathogenic variants: a large multicenter cohort characterizing NF1-associated breast cancer subtypes and molecular spectrum (PMID 41218342), a cohort documenting increased incidence and unfavourable prognostic features in NF1 women (PMID 27931045), and a genotype-first population-scale analysis showing NF1 pathogenic variants confer increased malignancy risk (PMID 40169570); a case with a germline NF1 nonsense variant plus tumor LOH provides additional patient-level causal support (PMID 41204772). These are independent probands/cohorts based on sequence-level variants, not solely whole-gene deletions (PMID 38154814 alone would not suffice). Somatic NF1 mutations are also recurrent drivers in sporadic and metastatic breast cancer with prognostic and therapeutic implications (PMIDs 31118521, 30181556, 40804585), reinforcing the human genetic link. A minority of probability remains on "Existing" since some germline evidence comes from deletion cohorts and much of the data concerns somatic rather than inherited variants.

Multiple independent human studies report primary evidence linking HMGA2 sequence variants to height: PMID 17767157 identified and replicated rs1042725 across several adult and child cohorts (n>30,000); PMID 18391952 independently confirmed HMGA2 in a large GWAS of adult height; PMID 21769890 replicated an HMGA2 SNP (rs7968902) in a Japanese population; PMID 19132395 found a 5'UTR (TC)n repeat allele associated with decreased height in family-based analyses; and PMID 26536448 reported HMGA2 variants associated with idiopathic short stature. In addition, point mutations/intragenic HMGA2 lesions cause growth restriction in Silver-Russell-like patients (PMIDs 38516887, 19298872), providing single-gene resolution beyond multigenic 12q14 deletions. These constitute replicated, human, gene-specific evidence, so the association is Established.

RBBP8 (CtIP) biallelic truncating mutations were shown to cause Seckel syndrome (a dwarfism/short-stature disorder) and Jawad syndrome in two independent families with their own genetic and functional results (PMID 21998596). An independent consanguineous Pakistani family with the homozygous c.1808_1809delTA frameshift presented with disproportionate short stature, microcephaly and brachydactyly (PMID 26333564), and a further study reported a homozygous nonsense RBBP8 variant in a family with microcephaly and growth retardation (PMID 38795246). Additional families with RBBP8 missense/recurrent variants and microcephaly syndromes support the gene–growth phenotype link (PMIDs 24440292, 36864288). These are human, single-gene (non-CNV) findings in multiple independent probands/families, supporting an Established relationship with short stature/height; residual probability is given to Existing since some reports are confounded (e.g., co-occurring NRXN1 deletion) or focus on microcephaly rather than stature per se.

The strongest evidence comes from PMID 36413406, which integrated ChREBP ChIP-Seq with human genetic/genomic data for circulating lipid traits to nominate HGFAC, and reported that HGFAC-knockout mice phenocopy putative loss-of-function variants in human HGFAC, with HGFAC enhancing lipid and glucose homeostasis (potentially via hepatic PPARγ). This provides credible but essentially single-study human genetic support, with the mechanistic work performed in mice, so "Existing" is the best fit rather than "Established" (I cannot cite two independent human studies reporting HGFAC variants associated with triglycerides). Other human genetic reports of HGFAC variants concern HGF levels (PMID 25998175), Crohn's disease (PMID 37878672), GI bleeding (PMID 24949630), and alcohol/nicotine use (PMID 35661789), which are not triglyceride phenotypes. Animal and livestock data (PMIDs 35661789, 35614300, 39593270) supporting lipid/fat-deposition relevance sustain a substantial "Hypothesized" weight, while remaining papers are oncology/coagulation co-mentions with no lipid relevance.

The GWAS by Kathiresan et al. (PMID 19060906) reports, in its own results, common variants near TIMD4 reaching genome-wide significance for LDL cholesterol in a discovery sample of 19,840 individuals with replication in up to 20,623 additional individuals — a newly defined LDL locus. Independently, a candidate-gene study in a southern Chinese Han population (PMID 29208769) genotyped TIMD4-HAVCR1 variants in >1,700 subjects and found associations with LDL-C, other lipid parameters, and CHD/IS risk, plus gene–environment and statin-response interactions. A further human report (PMID 24768220) discusses TIMD4 variant frequencies and lipid associations in Amerindian-derived/Mexican populations, and review literature (PMID 26821944) restates that Tim-4 is genetically associated with low LDL and triglyceride levels (background citation, not independent evidence). Together, two independent human cohorts with variant-level results support an Established classification; remaining probability reflects the possibility that the second study is considered insufficiently robust for replication.

ATM is a canonical recurrent driver in CLL: primary human studies report somatic ATM point mutations in large untreated cohorts (PMID 40275070, 246/3631 cases, distinct from del(11q)), loss of ATM protein/LOH defining an aggressive CLL subgroup (PMID 9788599), and a meta-analysis of the prognostic impact of ATM mutations (PMID 34735935). Germline predisposition is supported by a case-control study reporting rare germline ATM variants associated with CLL (PMID 28652578), plus germline variant reports in CLL patients (PMIDs 36111522, 35672297). Because much of the sequence-level evidence is somatic rather than transmitted in independent families, and some cohorts (PMID 40275070) argue del(11q) rather than ATM mutations drives prognosis, a substantial share of probability remains on "Existing". Several other listed items are reviews restating the association as background (PMIDs 23633543, 27742074, 30686074) and count as citation rather than independent evidence.

The ADAMTS9 variant rs4607103 was identified at genome-wide significance in the DIAGRAM meta-analysis with large-scale independent replication (PMID 18372903), and association has been replicated in independent human cohorts including Pakistanis (PMID 33705809), African/European Americans (PMID 25273842), Italians (PMID 23161442), and Chinese T2D patients (PMIDs 26599349, 28821857). Human functional work shows the risk allele increases ADAMTS9 expression and reduces skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity/signaling, with supporting mouse and reporter/TF-binding data (PMIDs 30626608, 31948755), providing a plausible causal mechanism through insulin resistance, a core T2D precursor. However, several studies failed to replicate the association (Turkish PMID 34117605, Sikh PMID 19247373, German cohorts PMID 19670153), and the evidence is common-variant association rather than demonstration of causal mutations in probands or families. This places it firmly in the strong "Existing" range with substantial weight toward "Established" given the replicated GWAS signal and mechanistic support.

None of the listed articles report red cell distribution width (RDW) as a measured outcome, and no study associates LCAT variants with RDW directly, so "Established" cannot be supported (no two PMIDs with variant-level RDW findings in independent human cohorts). However, multiple human reports document that genetic LCAT deficiency (autosomal recessive, with defined mutations across the six exons and 16q22 mapping) produces normochromic/hemolytic anemia and abnormal erythrocyte lipid composition and morphology (target-cell-like, cholesterol-enriched membranes), which is a mechanistically direct precursor of anisocytosis and elevated RDW (PMIDs 806250, 32618730, 33867422, 11957819, 3141686, 4640953). This supports at least a limited/indirect human genetic link ("Existing") through the anemia/red cell morphology phenotype, while the strictly biological/mechanistic membrane-lipid rationale supports "Hypothesized." Because RDW itself is never quantified in relation to LCAT genotype, probability is split mainly between Existing and Hypothesized, with small residual weight to Novel.

Multiple independent human studies report germline PMS2 pathogenic variants in colorectal cancer probands and families: PMID 27435373 identified 52 distinct pathogenic PMS2 variants explaining 121 Lynch syndrome and 9 CMMRD patients with isolated PMS2 loss in tumors; PMID 25856668 compiled 234 monoallelic PMS2 carriers from 170 families with CRC; PMID 38284451 reported a Swiss PMS2 founder variant c.1831dup in multiple index CRC patients; PMID 16507833 described biallelic PMS2 R802X carriers with early colorectal neoplasia across six families. Prospective cohort data (PMID 31337882, 34111421) quantify gene-specific, age-related colorectal cancer penetrance for PMS2 carriers, and tumor studies (PMID 34302852, 32826709) confirm PMS2-deficient CRC molecular phenotype. Evidence is human, replicated across independent cohorts and populations, and mechanistically coherent (mismatch repair deficiency). Therefore the relationship is Established.

Two independent large-scale human whole-genome sequencing studies report their own primary results linking UBR3 protein-truncating variants to BMI: PMID 41073786 (UK Biobank + All of Us, n≈709,000; UBR3 PTVs independently increase BMI and type 2 diabetes risk) and PMID 41651857 (447,461 UK Biobank discovery with 225,515 All of Us replication; UBR3 PTV aggregate associated with a 2.7 kg/m² BMI increase). These are gene-based rare coding variant aggregates, not multigene CNVs, so the signal is attributable to UBR3 specifically. A third human biobank study (PMID 39210047) further implicates UBR3 in cardiometabolic disease, supporting the metabolic relevance. Some deduction is warranted because the two BMI papers rely on partially overlapping UKB/All of Us cohorts, which limits full independence of replication.

Primary human genetic evidence exists in multiple independent families: Kyndt et al. identified FLNA mutations as the cause of X-linked myxomatous valvular dystrophy mapped to Xq28 (PMID 17190868), an additional family with siblings affected by FLNA-related cardiac valvular dystrophy was reported (PMID 21815255), and a further novel FLNA mutation was described in a patient with X-linked myxomatous valvular dystrophy (PMID 36640296). Additional independent probands with FLNA truncating variants show valvular involvement including mitral valve prolapse and sinus of Valsalva aneurysm (PMID 36372407), and FLNA-related phenotypes routinely include valve defects (PMIDs 31471375, 40641615). Reviews of mitral valve prolapse genetics consistently classify "FlnA-MVP" as a distinct familial, causative form (PMIDs 36873395, 35345263), though one study notes FLNA mutations are uncommon in unselected non-syndromic MVP (PMID 35813742), which tempers effect frequency but not causality. This constitutes replicated, human, family-based causal evidence, supporting Established.

The UK Biobank exome sequencing study (PMID 33087929) explicitly reports novel loss-of-function variants in GMPR with large effects on blood cell traits in a large human cohort, providing direct genetic evidence linking GMPR variation to erythrocyte/hemoglobin-related measures. This is credible human evidence, but only a single primary cohort study in the provided list, with no independent replication cohort or family study cited, so "Established" cannot be confirmed. Other GMPR papers concern enzymology (PMIDs 29547266, 32479091, 26853689), melanoma invasion (24139804), mitochondrial DNA maintenance (31600844), coding polymorphisms without blood phenotypes (1757097), or lipoprotein loci (19936222), and animal/omics studies (41758903, 42515851) that only mention GMPR in purine/porphyrin metabolism—these support biological plausibility but not the specific association. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Existing", with some residual probability for "Established" given the size and quality of the UK Biobank analysis.

Two large-scale human genetic studies report CALCR–BMI associations in their own primary results: the exome sequencing of ~645,000 individuals identified CALCR among 16 genes with exome-wide significant association with BMI (PMID 34210852), and the HYPOMAP study independently showed rare deleterious variants in CALCR associating with BMI at the population level alongside MC4R, POMC and PCSK1 (PMID 39910307). These are independent, large human cohorts with coding variants identified in people, supporting a replicated association. Biological plausibility is further supported by amylin/calcitonin receptor signalling in appetite and energy homeostasis (PMID 41344603). Most other CALCR papers concern bone mineral density, kidney stones or non-human models and are not relevant to BMI, so some residual probability remains for "Existing" if one considers the two BMI reports as partially overlapping datasets.

Multiple independent human cohorts report HMGCR variant associations with total cholesterol in their own results: PMID 30191727 (Brisighella Italian cohort with replication in Estonian Genome Center, showing HMGCR rs3846662 effects on LDL-C and total cholesterol), PMID 24386095 (Han Chinese GWAS plus replication where HMGCR reached genome-wide significance for TC), PMID 29321358 (Chinese cross-sectional study with HMGCR rs12654264 associated with lipid traits and isolated hypercholesterolemia), and PMID 40321961 (Taiwanese population HMGCR variants and lipid profiles/LDL-C). Additional supportive human data come from statin-response pharmacogenetic studies (PMIDs 26408409, 34799335, 26466344) and SNP–cholesterol metabolism studies (PMID 34680591). These are human, replicated, independent-cohort findings, so the association is Established; a small residual probability is retained for "Existing" because some studies emphasize LDL-C rather than TC specifically.

No human genetic study in this set links FRZB variants to stature; the human FRZB variant literature concerns hip osteoarthritis, hip shape, osteolysis/heterotopic ossification, and Kashin-Beck disease (PMIDs 15210948, 15818669, 16572458, 17600823, 22544526, 28651521), none of which measure height. Supportive but non-human/indirect evidence exists: FRZB is a candidate gene for growth and hip-height traits in Holstein cattle GWAS (PMID 37641329) and in horse limb bone measurements (PMID 41096909), and Wnt-antagonist sFRP biology directly governs growth-plate height, chondrocyte hypertrophy and endochondral ossification in mouse models (PMIDs 16575902, 35763224, 26406932 — the latter for the paralog SFRP4, showing body-length effects). This constitutes plausible, mechanistically relevant biology for skeletal growth without human variant-level height data, which fits "Hypothesized." A small residual probability is retained for "Existing" given the possibility of unlisted human height GWAS signals near FRZB, and for "Novel" given the purely incidental co-mentions here.

The strongest evidence is mechanistic and in vitro/human-cell based: OAT2 (SLC22A7) transports creatinine and contributes to its renal tubular secretion (PMID 24646860, 37977812, 31176593, 26825641, 38989645), which makes a biological link to serum creatinine highly plausible — supporting "Hypothesized". The only study in this set that directly tested a human SLC22A7 variant (c.1586+206A>G) against serum creatinine found no significant contribution, with SLC47A2 instead being the significant predictor (PMID 36594679), i.e., a negative human genetic result. Other human genetic papers implicate SLC22A7 in blood pressure (PMID 26390057), serum magnesium in type 2 diabetes (PMID 38279093), hearing loss, and processing speed — related to renal function only indirectly, so at best weak/indirect support for "Existing". No two independent human cohorts report variant-level association with serum creatinine, so "Established" is not supportable; a small residual is left for unlisted GWAS evidence.

The strongest primary evidence in this set is Moyer et al. (PMID 31822495), which found an excess of rare missense BRIP1 variants in early-onset breast and ovarian cancer patients, with functional loss-of-function shown and an OR of 2.30 in a large clinical panel cohort—credible human genetic evidence of association. However, two large, well-powered studies directly contradict a breast cancer role: Easton et al. (PMID 26921362) found no association of BRIP1 protein-truncating variants with breast cancer risk, and Weber-Lassalle et al. (PMID 29368626) concluded BRIP1 confers high ovarian but not familial breast cancer risk. Other listed papers (panel-testing series, reviews, case reports such as PMIDs 26976419, 36551643, 38912178, 39061189) mention BRIP1 as a background/panel gene rather than providing independent replicated causal evidence with segregating variants. Because I cannot cite at least two independent primary studies demonstrating a causal breast cancer link, and the literature is explicitly conflicting, "Existing" is the most appropriate category, with limited weight to "Established".

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in PDE5A associated with height or stature. The only body-size-related study is a bovine GWAS of scrotal circumference in Nellore cattle (PMID 24558400), which nominates PDE5A as a candidate gene based on literature mining of growth and testicular size effects in animal models; this is non-human and indirect, supporting at most a "Hypothesized" relationship. The remaining papers concern cardiovascular function, blood pressure regulatory variants, erectile dysfunction, dementia, Parkinson's progression, melanoma, muscular dystrophy and retinal biology — none address skeletal growth or stature. Consequently there is no human evidence for an "Existing" or "Established" classification, and the weight falls between a weak biological/animal-based hypothesis and no meaningful evidence at all.

phenotype: Erythrocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
literature_justification: The UK Biobank exome sequencing study (PMID 33087929) explicitly reports novel loss-of-function variants in IQGAP2 with large effects on blood cell traits in humans, and rare/low-frequency coding variants in IQGAP2 were associated with platelet traits in the Exomechip meta-analysis of 157,293 individuals (PMID 27346686), with the Bayesian rare-variant analysis of UK Biobank exomes independently highlighting IQGAP2 and mean platelet volume (PMID 34822764). However, none of these abstracts specifically state an association with erythrocyte (red blood cell) count by automated count; the demonstrated human associations are platelet-related, with only a general "blood cell traits" statement supporting erythrocyte relevance. Additional IQGAP2 biology (platelet cytoskeletal signaling, hematopoietic scaffold functions) supports plausible but indirect relevance to red cell indices. Therefore evidence is best described as Existing (a credible but not definitive/replicated human link to the specific trait), with meaningful probability that only hypothesized biological relevance applies.

Multiple independent human studies report HNF4A coding variants in distinct probands/families with non-insulin-dependent (type 2) diabetes: the original MODY1 nonsense/missense mutations (PMID 8945471), an independent Dresden-11 family with R154X (PMID 9294105), a Japanese family with R127W (PMID 9313765), a French late-onset NIDDM family with V393I showing reduced transactivation and cosegregation (PMID 9449683), and a Val/Met255 variant found only in Danish NIDDM patients (PMID 9267996). Beyond monogenic forms, a large human rare-variant GWAS of 51,256 T2D cases identified HNF4A p.Arg114Trp associated with an eightfold increased T2D risk (PMID 39379762), and common noncoding HNF4A variants have been associated with common T2D (PMIDs 15794920, 15519277). Population-based penetrance studies (PMIDs 30665703, 36257325) confirm these variants confer diabetes risk in unselected human cohorts, albeit with reduced penetrance. The main reservation is that most causal evidence concerns MODY1, a monogenic subtype rather than polygenic T2D, which keeps a substantial share on "Existing"; nevertheless MODY is classically framed as a form of type 2 diabetes and independent replication in humans is clear.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary results linking MLXIPL variants (rs17145738, rs3812316/Q241H) to triglyceride levels: the original GWAS identifying 7q11 near TBL2/MLXIPL for triglycerides (18193044), a case-control study of severe hypertriglyceridemia (18596051), a Saudi Arab common variant association study for hypertriglyceridemia (27599772), Chinese Mulao/Han population lipid association (24160749), Central/East Asian cohorts showing the H allele lowers triglycerides (21938000), the PREDIMED trial (24448738), and Mexican Mestizo subjects (36432414). These are human cohorts across diverse ancestries with consistent direction of effect, satisfying replication. A few negative or null studies (18946681, 25573592, 19680233) exist but do not overturn the replicated positive evidence. The relationship is therefore Established.

Two independent human genetic studies report IL17RA variant associations with monocyte traits in their own results: the exome-chip meta-analysis of >52,000 individuals across multiple ancestries identified IL17RA as a new locus for monocyte count (PMID 27399967), and the Bayesian rare-variant model comparison in ~185,000 UK Biobank exomes independently found an IL17RA–monocyte count association (PMID 34822764). These are distinct cohorts and methods, supporting replication, though the reported trait is monocyte count rather than monocyte percentage specifically, which introduces some ambiguity. Additional human whole-exome gene-based analysis links rare IL17RA variants to another leukocyte trait, eosinophil count (PMID 35935937), reinforcing a role in myeloid/granulocyte lineage regulation. Other listed papers concern psoriasis, candidiasis, malaria, and autoimmunity and are relevant only as background biology on IL-17 signaling in inflammation.

Multiple independent human studies report rare coding MRAP2 variants in individuals with severe obesity/high BMI with their own primary data: Asai et al. (PMID 23869016) identified four rare potentially pathogenic MRAP2 variants in humans with severe early-onset obesity; Baron et al. (PMID 31700171) sequenced MRAP2 in 9,418 individuals and found 23 rare heterozygous loss-of-function variants associated with increased obesity risk in adults and children; a new pathogenic variant was reported in a patient with BMI 64 (PMID 37888144); and a systematic review/meta-analysis of seven independent cohorts (PMID 41596694) found an OR of 2.61 for obesity in carriers. Functional studies in humans-derived variants (PMIDs 39807633, 29704154, 27474872) confirm loss of function on MC4R/MC3R signaling, and mouse knockouts (PMIDs 23869016, 27106110) provide mechanistic support. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence across independent probands and cohorts, supporting an Established relationship, with slight residual uncertainty because much of the evidence involves rare variants and single-gene case reports.

Only one article in this list provides primary human genetic evidence linking COL18A1 to HDL cholesterol: the exome-array analysis in 56,538 individuals (PMID 24507774), which identified the low-frequency coding variant COL18A1 rs114139997 (p.Gly111Arg) with a large effect on HDL-C and/or triglycerides. This is a credible, large, multi-ancestry human study, but it is a single report and no independent replication publication is present in this set. All other articles concern Knobloch syndrome (ocular/occipital and neurological phenotypes), psoriasis methotrexate pharmacogenetics, or hypermobile EDS, and are irrelevant to lipid traits. Since I cannot cite at least two independent studies demonstrating the HDL association in their own results, the evidence best fits "Existing" rather than "Established," with residual probability for Established given the study's internal multi-cohort design.

The strongest human evidence here links PDX1 variants to monogenic diabetes (MODY4) and neonatal diabetes, with multiple independent probands and families reported (PMID 37279936, 38141807, 40779032, 37652665, 33746035, 35592899, 28436541). MODY4 is a recognized monogenic subtype of diabetes frequently misdiagnosed as, and clinically overlapping with, early-onset type 2 diabetes; the Chinese cohort study explicitly screened early-onset T2D patients and identified PDX1 variant carriers, and a burden analysis confirms PDX1 as a low-penetrance diabetes gene in humans. However, direct causal evidence for common/polygenic type 2 diabetes per se is limited in this set — most articles treat T2D association as background (e.g., epigenetic PDX1 methylation in T2DM islets, PMID 33564250) or study MODY rather than T2D. Mechanistic and animal work (macaque PDX1 mutants, mouse Pdx1 variants, beta-cell transactivation studies) supports biological plausibility but is non-human/in vitro and therefore counts toward Hypothesized. Overall, the evidence best fits "Existing," with meaningful but not decisive probability of "Established."

Multiple independent human studies report CYP11B1 variants in probands/cohorts with height phenotypes: the Turkish cohort of classic 11β-hydroxylase deficiency with novel CYP11B1 mutations and long-term final height outcomes (PMID 29626607), four Chinese patients with novel CYP11B1 variants and analysis of final height (PMID 32850530), a Tunisian family with homozygous p.Gly379Val and impaired final height (PMID 33708317), and a genotype–phenotype series correlating molecular findings with clinical features (PMID 33830237, 39952853). In addition, a GWAS meta-analysis in 4557 school-aged children identified CYP11B1 (rs6471570/rs6410) as robustly associated with skeletal age with functional splicing evidence (PMID 34754074), extending the link to common variation in healthy children and to a direct determinant of growth/final height. Several other case series document tall stature with advanced bone age and consequent short adult stature in CYP11B1-mutated patients (PMID 30817301, 28126912). This constitutes replicated, human-variant-based evidence, though most is within the monogenic CAH context where height is a downstream consequence, leaving some weight on "Existing."

Multiple independent human reports describe biallelic MIA3/TANGO1 variants with short stature as a core feature: PMID 32101163 reported four homozygously affected sibs (synonymous variant causing exon 8 skipping) with severe dentinogenesis imperfecta and short stature; PMID 40119123 described two unrelated patients with distinct homozygous MIA3 luminal-domain variants (c.354+2T>G and p.Cys38Phe) with severe short limbs and short stature; PMID 33778321 reported a homozygous 4-bp deletion in a fetus with lethal skeletal dysplasia and near-total bone loss.
